Rule: Rule 404(a)(2)(C): in a homicide case, the prosecution may offer the victim’s peacefulness to rebut any evidence that the victim was the first aggressor.

## Set 3 · Q10 · Character Evidence — Rule 405(b): character as an element
A local blog calls a roofing contractor “a con man who takes deposits and never shows up.” The contractor sues for defamation. The blogger pleads truth and offers testimony from three homeowners that the contractor took their deposits and never did the work. The contractor objects that character evidence is inadmissible in a civil case and that, in any event, character may be proved only by reputation or opinion. How should the court rule?

A. Admit the testimony under Rule 404(b) to show the contractor’s plan or scheme to defraud homeowners.
B. Exclude the testimony, because specific instances may be used only on cross-examination of a character witness.
C. Admit the testimony, because his character is an essential element of the truth defense, so specific instances may prove it.
D. Admit only reputation or opinion testimony about his honesty, because Rule 405(a) governs every use of character evidence.
E. Exclude the testimony, because the exceptions in Rule 404(a)(2) apply only in criminal cases.

Answer: C
- A: No one is trying to prove that the contractor acted a certain way on one occasion, so 404(b)’s purposes are beside the point. The right route is 405(b), because character is itself in issue.
- B: Rule 405(a) allows specific instances on cross, but Rule 405(b) independently allows them whenever character is an essential element of a claim or defense, as truth is here.
- C: Correct. 404(a)(1) bars character offered to prove that a person acted in accordance with it on a particular occasion. Here character is itself what must be proved: whether he is in fact a con man. When a trait is an essential element of a charge, claim, or defense, 405(b) allows proof by relevant specific instances, in civil and criminal cases alike.
- D: 405(a) is the general method, but 405(b) adds specific instances when character is an essential element. Reputation and opinion remain available too.
- E: Those exceptions matter only when character is offered to prove conduct on a particular occasion. When character is an element, as in a truth defense to defamation, 404(a)(1) doesn’t apply at all.
Rule: Rule 405(b): when a trait is an essential element of a charge, claim, or defense (truth in defamation, entrapment, negligent entrustment, custody), it may be proved by specific instances, in civil or criminal cases.

## Set 3 · Q11 · Impeachment and the Rape Shield — Valencia: Rule 404(b) and Rule 609 are separate tests
A defendant is charged with distributing cocaine. In its case-in-chief, the government offered his three-year-old felony conviction for possessing cocaine for sale under Rule 404(b), and the judge excluded it under Rule 403. The defendant then testifies and denies the charge. On cross-examination, the government offers the same conviction under Rule 609(a)(1)(B). The defendant argues that because the conviction failed the more lenient 403 test, it must fail 609’s stricter test as well. How should the court respond?

A. Reject the argument and weigh the conviction anew, because 609 measures its bearing on truthfulness, not on guilt.
B. Exclude the conviction, because a drug conviction is never probative of truthfulness.
C. Exclude the conviction, because once the court finds evidence fails Rule 403, that ruling binds it for the rest of the trial.
D. Admit the conviction without weighing, because a testifying defendant’s felony convictions are automatically admissible.
E. Admit the conviction under ordinary Rule 403, because the defendant chose to testify.

Answer: A
- A: Correct. This is Problem 4.4 (United States v. Valencia, 8th Cir.). The 404(b)/403 ruling measured probative force on substantive guilt; the 609(a)(1)(B) ruling measures probative force on truthfulness. Losing one doesn’t dictate the other, and appellate courts defer to the trial judge on both. (Whether a drug conviction says much about honesty is fair to question.)
- B: “Never” overstates it. Under Rule 609(a)(1)(B), the court weighs probative value on truthfulness against prejudice using the Gordon factors, and a drug felony can survive that balance.
- C: An in limine or case-in-chief ruling under one rule doesn’t control a later ruling for a different purpose under another rule.
- D: Only crimen falsi convictions under 609(a)(2) come in without balancing. A testifying defendant’s other felonies go through 609(a)(1)(B)’s special balance.
- E: 403 governs non-defendant witnesses under 609(a)(1)(A). For an accused, the conviction comes in only if probative value outweighs prejudicial effect to the defendant.
Rule: Rule 609(a)(1)(B): a testifying accused’s felony comes in only if its probative value on truthfulness outweighs its prejudicial effect to him. That’s a separate question from the 404(b)/403 ruling (Valencia).

## Set 3 · Q12 · Impeachment and the Rape Shield — Rule 609 in a civil case: felonies vs. crimen falsi
In a civil contract suit, a key defense witness has three convictions: (1) a five-year-old felony assault conviction (punishable by up to three years); (2) a three-year-old misdemeanor conviction for filing a false police report (maximum 90 days); and (3) a two-year-old misdemeanor petty-theft conviction (maximum six months). The plaintiff offers all three to impeach. Which statement is correct?

A. All three must be admitted, because theft and assault both reflect on the witness’s willingness to lie under oath.
B. Item 2 must be admitted, item 1 comes in unless Rule 403 calls for exclusion, and item 3 is out.
C. Item 2 is admissible only if it survives Rule 403, because misdemeanors always require balancing.
D. Items 1 and 2 are admissible only if their probative value outweighs their prejudicial effect.
E. Items 1 and 3 come in subject to Rule 403, and item 2 is out because it was only a misdemeanor.

Answer: B
- A: Theft and robbery aren’t crimen falsi; the crime’s elements must require deceit or false statement. A misdemeanor theft therefore fits neither 609(a)(1) nor (a)(2).
- B: Correct. 609(a)(2) requires admitting any conviction whose elements required proving a dishonest act or false statement, and a false police report qualifies, with no 403 discretion. A felony offered against a witness in a civil case falls under 609(a)(1)(A), admitted subject to 403. Petty theft is a misdemeanor and isn’t crimen falsi, so neither branch applies.
- C: 609(a)(2) applies “regardless of the punishment” and says the evidence “must be admitted.” Such convictions are “peculiarly probative” and always admitted, though 609(b)’s ten-year limit still applies.
- D: That’s the 609(a)(1)(B) test for an accused. This witness isn’t a criminal defendant, and 609(a)(2) convictions aren’t balanced at all.
- E: Backwards. A false-report conviction is crimen falsi, admissible under Rule 609(a)(2) whatever the punishment. Petty theft is a misdemeanor that isn’t crimen falsi, so Rule 609 doesn’t admit it at all.
Rule: Rule 609(a)(2) crimen falsi convictions must be admitted, with no balancing, whatever the punishment. 609(a)(1)(A) felonies offered against a non-accused witness are subject to 403. Theft isn’t crimen falsi.

## Set 3 · Q13 · Impeachment and the Rape Shield — Extrinsic evidence: Rule 608(b) vs. bias
On cross-examination, the prosecutor asks the defendant’s alibi witness two questions, each with a good-faith basis: (1) “Didn’t you falsely state on a mortgage application that you had no other debts?” and (2) “Aren’t you a paid employee of the defendant’s trucking company?” The witness answers “No” to both. The prosecutor then offers the bank’s loan officer to prove the false statement and a payroll clerk to prove the employment. How should the court rule?

A. Admit the loan officer but exclude the payroll clerk.
B. Exclude the loan officer but admit the payroll clerk.
C. Admit the loan officer, but only if the prosecution first offers the mortgage application itself.
D. Exclude both, because a party must take the witness’s answer on cross-examination.
E. Admit both, because the witness denied facts the prosecution can prove.

Answer: B
- A: That reverses the rules. Bias may be proved extrinsically; specific acts offered to show untruthful character may not.
- B: Correct. The mortgage lie is a specific instance offered only to show untruthful character, so 608(b) bars extrinsic proof, and the prosecutor must take the answer. Working for the defendant shows bias, a motive to lie in this case. Bias is never collateral, so extrinsic evidence is allowed after a denial (Abel).
- C: Whether by document or witness, extrinsic proof of a specific act offered only to attack truthfulness is barred by Rule 608(b). The prosecutor must take the witness’s “No.”
- D: That is true for 608(b) acts, but not for bias, which may be proved by extrinsic evidence.
- E: A denial doesn’t open the door to extrinsic proof of a 608(b) act. As the textbook puts it, 608(b) impeachment works only when the witness is honest enough to admit the act.
Rule: Rule 608(b) bars extrinsic evidence of specific acts offered only to attack truthfulness, so the examiner takes the answer. Bias isn’t collateral and may be proved extrinsically after a denial (Abel).

## Set 3 · Q14 · Impeachment and the Rape Shield — Rule 412(b)(1)(B): behavior with the accused
A defendant charged in federal court with sexual assault claims the encounter was consensual. By timely written motion, he seeks to offer (1) testimony that he and the complainant had a consensual sexual relationship that ended two months before the incident; (2) testimony that on the night in question she wore a revealing dress to the bar; and (3) testimony that she flirted with several other men at the bar before leaving with him. After an in camera hearing, which items may the court admit?

A. None of them, because Rule 412 bars all evidence of a victim’s sexual history in criminal cases.
B. Items 1 and 2, because what she wore that night isn’t sexual behavior.
C. All of them, because once the defendant claims consent, the complainant’s character becomes a pertinent trait under Rule 404(a)(2)(B).
D. Items 1 and 3, because flirting that same night bears directly on her state of mind.
E. Item 1 only.

Answer: E
- A: 412(b)(1) has three criminal-case exceptions, and past sexual behavior with the accused, offered to prove consent, is one of them.
- B: Dress is predisposition evidence, which Rule 412(a)(2) bars as surely as sexual behavior. Only item 1, specific behavior with the accused offered to prove consent, fits Rule 412(b)(1)(B).
- C: 404(a)(2)(B) is expressly “subject to the limitations in Rule 412.” Closing off that use of the victim-character exception is why 412 exists.
- D: Flirting with other men is offered to show a disposition toward sexual activity, the inference 412 forbids. Only behavior with the accused fits (b)(1)(B).
- E: Correct. 412(b)(1)(B) admits specific instances of the victim’s sexual behavior with the accused, offered by the defendant to prove consent. Items 2 and 3 are offered to suggest she was the type to consent, which is “sexual predisposition.” The Advisory Committee’s Note says the rule bars evidence of a complainant’s mode of dress, speech, or lifestyle offered for that purpose.
Rule: Rule 412(b)(1)(B): in a criminal case, specific instances of sexual behavior with the accused may be offered by the defendant to prove consent, or by the prosecutor. Dress, speech, or lifestyle evidence is barred predisposition evidence.

## Set 3 · Q15 · Definition of Hearsay — Rule 801(a): implied assertions after Wright v. Tatham
In a will contest, the contestants claim the testator, Arden, lacked mental capacity when he signed his will in 2024. The proponent offers letters that three longtime business associates wrote to Arden during 2024, asking his advice on complicated investment decisions and discussing the answers he had given them. None of the writers testifies. The contestants object that the letters are hearsay, because they are offered to show that the writers believed Arden was competent.

Under the Federal Rules, how should the court rule?

A. Sustain the objection unless the proponent shows that the writers are unavailable and had personal knowledge.
B. Sustain the objection, because the letters' value depends on the writers' belief in Arden's competence.
C. Overrule it, because the writers didn't intend to assert that he was competent, so the letters aren't hearsay.
D. Overrule the objection, because letters Arden kept in his files are records of his regularly conducted activity.
E. Overrule the objection, because the letters show the writers' then-existing state of mind under Rule 803(3).

Answer: C
- A: Unavailability matters only for Rule 804 exceptions. Because the letters aren't offered for the truth of anything the writers intended to assert, no exception, and no showing of unavailability, is needed.
- B: That was the common-law answer: Wright v. Doe d. Tatham treated letters like these as implied assertions and excluded them. The Federal Rules rejected that approach by defining a statement as an assertion the person intended as one (Rule 801(a)).
- C: Correct. Under Rule 801(a), words or conduct are a statement only if the person intended them as an assertion. The writers asked for advice; they didn't intend to assert that Arden was competent, so the letters aren't hearsay when offered to show their belief. The Advisory Committee Note puts it plainly: nothing is an assertion unless intended to be one (compare United States v. Zenni).
- D: Keeping letters he received doesn't make them Arden's business records. The writers weren't acting under any business duty to him, and in any case no exception is needed.
- E: Rule 803(3) covers the declarant's own state of mind when that state of mind matters. The point here is Arden's competence, not the writers' feelings, and no exception is needed because the letters aren't hearsay.
Rule: Under Rule 801(a), only an assertion the declarant intended as one is a statement. Words or conduct offered to show the declarant's unstated belief are not hearsay under the Federal Rules, which rejected the implied-assertion rule of Wright v. Doe d. Tatham.

## Set 3 · Q16 · Opposing Party and Prior Statements — Rule 801(d)(2)(E) and Bourjaily
DEA Agent Pratt, posing as a buyer, records a meeting at which Quill sells her half a kilogram of cocaine. During the deal, Quill says: “You want more, I can get it. My guy is Ferris. He drives it up from Miami every other Thursday. Buy two keys and he’ll knock off ten percent.” Two weeks later, agents watch Ferris’s car arrive at Quill’s house on a Thursday night. Ferris carries a gym bag inside and leaves without it.

Quill is never charged. At Ferris’s trial for conspiracy to distribute cocaine, the prosecution offers Quill’s recorded statement. Ferris objects.

How should the court proceed?

A. Admit the statement only if evidence other than the statement itself establishes the conspiracy and Ferris’s membership in it by a preponderance of the evidence.
B. Exclude the statement, because Agent Pratt, as a government agent, was not a member of the conspiracy, so a statement to her could not further it.
C. Submit the preliminary question to the jury, instructing it to disregard the statement unless it finds beyond a reasonable doubt that Ferris and Quill were co-conspirators.
D. Exclude the statement, because Quill was never charged, and a co-conspirator’s statement is admissible only against a co-defendant charged in the same conspiracy.
E. Admit it if the judge finds by a preponderance, considering the statement and the surveillance, that it was made during and in furtherance of their conspiracy.

Answer: E
- A: This is the pre-Bourjaily independent-evidence rule. The court may consider the statement itself, though it cannot rely on it alone.
- B: The listener need not be a conspirator. Statements made to recruit, reassure, or induce a buyer, even one who turns out to be an agent, can further the conspiracy.
- C: Preliminary questions of admissibility under 801(d)(2)(E) are for the judge under Rule 104(a), decided by a preponderance, not for the jury beyond a reasonable doubt.
- D: The co-conspirator need not be charged, tried, or even identified, as long as the court finds the conspiracy and both memberships.
- E: Correct. This is the Bourjaily standard as codified: the judge decides by a preponderance, may consider the statement, and needs some corroborating evidence.
Rule: A statement by a party’s co-conspirator made during and in furtherance of the conspiracy is not hearsay when offered against that party. FRE 801(d)(2)(E). The court decides the preliminary facts under Rule 104(a) by a preponderance of the evidence and may consider the statement itself. Bourjaily v. United States. But the statement alone does not establish the existence of the conspiracy or the party’s participation in it. FRE 801(d)(2) (final sentence).

## Set 3 · Q17 · Opposing Party and Prior Statements — Rule 806: impeaching a deposition with an unsworn statement
In a negligence suit filed in March 2027, bystander Owen Hale testified at his deposition that the defendant's truck ran a red light. Hale died before trial, and the plaintiff reads the deposition into evidence as former testimony. The defendant then offers testimony from an insurance adjuster that, the day after the crash, Hale told her in an unsworn conversation that the truck “had the green.” The defendant asks the court to let the jury consider the adjuster's account as proof that the light was green.

How should the court rule?

A. Admit it as substantive evidence, because Rule 801(d)(1)(A), as amended in 2026, no longer requires an oath.
B. Exclude it, because Hale was never given an opportunity to explain or deny the earlier statement.
C. Admit it only to impeach the deposition, because Rule 801(d)(1)(A) applies only if the declarant testifies.
D. Admit it as substantive evidence under Rule 804(b)(1), because Hale is now unavailable.
E. Exclude it, because an unsworn statement can't be used to impeach testimony given under oath.

Answer: C
- A: The 2026 amendment removed the oath and proceeding requirement, but Rule 801(d)(1) still applies only when the declarant testifies and is subject to cross-examination about the prior statement. Hale is dead and isn't testifying at this trial.
- B: Rule 806 provides that the court may admit a declarant's inconsistent statement regardless of whether the declarant had an opportunity to explain or deny it. Rule 613(b)'s foundation doesn't apply.
- C: Correct. Rule 806 lets a party attack the credibility of a declarant whose hearsay has been admitted by any evidence that would be admissible if he had testified, including an inconsistent statement. Because Hale doesn't testify, Rule 801(d)(1)(A) can't make the statement substantive, so it comes in to impeach, with a limiting instruction on request.
- D: Rule 804(b)(1) covers former testimony given at a trial, hearing, or deposition. Hale's conversation with the adjuster wasn't testimony.
- E: Any inconsistent statement, sworn or not, may impeach. The oath matters only to whether a statement can be substantive evidence.
Rule: Rule 806: once a hearsay statement is admitted, the declarant's credibility may be attacked as if he had testified, including with an inconsistent statement, without the Rule 613(b) foundation. Rule 801(d)(1)(A) makes an inconsistent statement substantive only when the declarant testifies at the trial and is subject to cross-examination about it.

## Set 3 · Q18 · Opposing Party and Prior Statements — Rule 806: impeaching a co-conspirator declarant
At Veltri’s trial for securities fraud, the court admits, as a co-conspirator statement, an email from Pask to another conspirator: “Veltri signed off on the fake revenue numbers.” Pask does not testify.

Veltri then offers (1) a certified record of Pask’s wire-fraud conviction from four years ago and (2) testimony from Pask’s former assistant that, a month after the email, Pask told her, “Veltri never knew about the revenue numbers.” Pask was never asked about this later statement because he never testified. The prosecution objects to both.

How should the court rule?

A. Admit the conviction, but exclude the later statement, because Pask was never given an opportunity to explain or deny it.
B. Admit the later statement as substantive evidence that Veltri lacked knowledge, but exclude the conviction as unfairly prejudicial.
C. Admit both to attack Pask’s credibility, even though Pask had no opportunity to explain or deny the inconsistent statement.
D. Exclude the conviction, because a non-testifying declarant’s credibility may be attacked only with evidence of inconsistent statements.
E. Exclude both, because Rule 806 applies only to hearsay, and a co-conspirator statement is by definition not hearsay.

Answer: C
- A: Rule 806 dispenses with the opportunity to explain or deny, because the declarant is not on the stand.
- B: The later statement is impeachment, not substantive evidence, unless an exception applies. The wire-fraud conviction is automatically admissible under Rule 609(a)(2), with no balancing.
- C: Correct. Rule 806 allows both forms of impeachment and waives the foundation requirement.
- D: Any impeachment that would be proper against a live witness is proper against the declarant, including convictions under Rule 609.
- E: Rule 806 expressly applies to statements under 801(d)(2)(C), (D), and (E).
Rule: When a hearsay statement, or a statement described in Rule 801(d)(2)(C), (D), or (E), has been admitted, the declarant’s credibility may be attacked by any evidence that would be admissible if the declarant had testified. The court may admit evidence of the declarant’s inconsistent statement or conduct regardless of when it occurred or whether the declarant had an opportunity to explain or deny it. FRE 806.

## Set 3 · Q19 · Hearsay Exceptions — Rule 804(b)(1): similar motive at the grand jury
A federal grand jury investigating a bid-rigging cartel subpoenas Vance, a cement contractor. Under a grant of immunity, Vance testifies that Corrigan never attended any cartel meeting. The prosecutors already believed Vance was lying but did not confront him, because they did not want to reveal their wiretap evidence while the investigation was ongoing.

Corrigan is later indicted. At trial, Vance, who now faces perjury exposure, invokes the Fifth Amendment, and the court sustains the privilege. Corrigan offers the transcript of Vance’s grand jury testimony. The government objects.

What is the court’s proper approach?

A. Admit the testimony, because the government chose to call Vance before the grand jury and, as a matter of adversarial fairness, cannot now avoid testimony it elicited.
B. Admit the testimony, because statements made under oath and under a grant of immunity carry sufficient guarantees of trustworthiness.
C. Exclude the testimony, because a declarant who invokes a privilege is not “unavailable” when the government has the power to immunize him again.
D. Admit it only if the government had a similar motive to develop Vance’s testimony, a question its reasons for not confronting him bear on.
E. Exclude the testimony, because a grand jury proceeding is not a “trial, hearing, or lawful deposition.”

Answer: D
- A: The Supreme Court rejected this adversarial-fairness argument in Salerno. The text of 804(b)(1) requires similar motive with no exception.
- B: Oath and immunity bear on reliability, but 804(b)(1) turns on similar motive, not general trustworthiness. That argument belongs under Rule 807, which has its own requirements.
- C: A sustained privilege claim makes the declarant unavailable under 804(a)(1). The government’s refusal to immunize again does not change that.
- D: Correct. This is the Salerno and DiNapoli framework: no adversarial-fairness shortcut, and a fact-specific similar-motive inquiry.
- E: Courts treat grand jury testimony as testimony given at a hearing for purposes of 804(b)(1). The fight is over motive, not the type of proceeding.
Rule: Former testimony of an unavailable declarant is admissible if, in a criminal case, it is offered against a party who had an opportunity and similar motive to develop it by direct, cross, or redirect examination. FRE 804(b)(1). A witness who properly invokes a privilege is unavailable. FRE 804(a)(1).

## Set 3 · Q20 · Hearsay Exceptions — Palmer v. Hoffman and Rule 803(6)(E)
Two days after a grade-crossing collision, the locomotive engineer, at his railroad employer’s direction, gave a statement describing the crash to the railroad’s claims agent. The railroad takes such statements after every accident, files them in its claims department, and uses them in settlement negotiations and litigation. The engineer has since died.

In the injured motorist’s suit, the railroad offers the statement as a business record, supported by a qualified custodian’s testimony satisfying Rule 803(6)(A) through (C). The motorist objects.

Which statement best describes how the court should proceed?

A. The court must admit the statement, because the railroad established every foundational element of Rule 803(6), and trustworthiness is not part of the rule.
B. The court should admit the statement, but only against the railroad, because it is the railroad’s own employee’s statement.
C. The court may exclude it if the motorist shows that its source or the circumstances of its preparation indicate a lack of trustworthiness.
D. The court should admit the statement only if the railroad proves affirmatively that it is trustworthy.
E. The court must exclude the statement, because an employee’s statement about an accident can never be a business record.

Answer: C
- A: Trustworthiness is expressly part of the rule in subsection (E).
- B: The railroad is offering its own employee’s statement. Rule 801(d)(2) applies only to statements offered against a party, and “only against the railroad” makes no sense when the railroad is the proponent.
- C: Correct. This states the 2014 allocation of the burden and the concern from Palmer v. Hoffman.
- D: Since 2014, the burden is on the opponent to show untrustworthiness, not on the proponent to prove trustworthiness.
- E: There is no categorical bar. Many accident reports qualify. The problem is records prepared in anticipation of litigation, which the court evaluates case by case.
Rule: A record of a regularly conducted activity is admissible if the foundational requirements are met and “the opponent does not show that the source of information or the method or circumstances of preparation indicate a lack of trustworthiness.” FRE 803(6)(E). The 2014 amendment placed this burden on the opponent.

## Set 3 · Q21 · Confrontation, Bruton, and the Defense — Davis v. Washington and Hammon: no ongoing emergency
Police respond to a report of a domestic disturbance at the Voss home. They find Lena Voss alone on the front porch, appearing “somewhat frightened” but saying nothing is wrong. Inside, they see a shattered glass space heater. One officer keeps Curtis Voss in the kitchen while another questions Lena in the living room. Lena describes how Curtis shoved her into the heater and punched her. The officer then has her write and sign a “battery affidavit.”

Curtis is charged with domestic battery. Lena is subpoenaed but does not appear, and the prosecution cannot locate her. The prosecution calls the officer to recount Lena’s oral statements and offers the affidavit. Curtis objects under the Confrontation Clause.

How should the court rule?

A. Exclude both unless the prosecution proves Lena is unavailable, in which case both are admissible.
B. Admit both, because Lena’s statements qualify as excited utterances, and a firmly rooted hearsay exception satisfies the Confrontation Clause.
C. Admit the oral statements but exclude the affidavit, because only formalized, sworn statements are testimonial.
D. Exclude both, because the primary purpose of the questioning was to establish past events for a possible prosecution, not to meet an ongoing emergency.
E. Admit both, because Lena is the alleged victim, and the Confrontation Clause is directed at accusatory statements by accomplices and other suspects.

Answer: D
- A: Unavailability alone is not enough. Crawford requires both unavailability and a prior opportunity for cross-examination.
- B: The “firmly rooted exception” test comes from Ohio v. Roberts, which Crawford overruled for testimonial statements. Qualifying as an excited utterance does not answer the Confrontation question.
- C: Hammon held the oral statements testimonial too. Formality matters, but a structured police interview about past events is formal enough without an oath.
- D: Correct. With the emergency over and the questioning directed at past events, the statements are testimonial under Davis and Hammon.
- E: The Clause protects against all testimonial statements of absent witnesses, whatever the declarant’s role. Victims’ statements to police are the paradigm case.
Rule: The Confrontation Clause bars testimonial statements of a witness who does not appear at trial unless the witness is unavailable and the defendant had a prior opportunity to cross-examine. Crawford v. Washington. Statements to police are testimonial when the circumstances objectively indicate that there is no ongoing emergency and the primary purpose of the interrogation is to establish or prove past events potentially relevant to later prosecution. Davis v. Washington; Hammon v. Indiana.

## Set 3 · Q22 · Confrontation, Bruton, and the Defense — Bruton: the confessing codefendant testifies
Nadia Cole and Ben Alvarez are tried jointly before one jury for a carjacking. A detective testifies that after her arrest Cole confessed: “Ben and I took the car. Ben had the gun.” The court instructs the jury to consider the confession only against Cole. Cole then takes the stand in her own defense, denies ever making the confession, and testifies that she was home that night. Alvarez's counsel cross-examines her. Alvarez is convicted and argues on appeal that admitting Cole's confession violated Bruton.

What result?

A. Reversal, because Cole's denial made any cross-examination about the confession meaningless.
B. No violation, because Cole's confession is admissible against Alvarez as an opposing party's statement.
C. Reversal, unless the confession was redacted to remove every reference to Alvarez.
D. No violation, because Cole testified and was subject to cross-examination, which satisfies the Confrontation Clause.
E. Reversal, because Bruton holds that limiting instructions are never adequate for a codefendant's confession.

Answer: D
- A: Nelson v. O'Neil holds that when the codefendant takes the stand and is cross-examined, the Confrontation Clause is satisfied even if she denies making the confession. Cross can still test her account and her credibility.
- B: Cole's confession is admissible against Cole as her own statement under Rule 801(d)(2)(A), not against Alvarez. That is why Bruton is a concern in the first place. What saves the conviction is that Cole testified.
- C: Redaction is one way to avoid Bruton when the codefendant doesn't testify. It is unnecessary when she testifies and is cross-examined.
- D: Correct. Bruton applies only to a nontestifying codefendant's confession. When the confessing codefendant testifies and can be cross-examined, there is no confrontation problem, even if she denies the confession (Nelson v. O'Neil; California v. Green). That is one of the prosecution's ways around Bruton.
- E: Bruton's rule rests on the defendant's inability to cross-examine the confessing codefendant. Once Cole testified and was cross-examined, that premise is gone.
Rule: Bruton bars a nontestifying codefendant's facially incriminating confession at a joint trial, even with a limiting instruction. If the codefendant testifies and is subject to cross-examination, there is no confrontation problem, even if she denies the confession (Nelson v. O'Neil).

## Set 3 · Q23 · Confrontation, Bruton, and the Defense — Giles: forfeiture requires intent
Dwayne is charged with murdering his former girlfriend, Brenda, by shooting her during an argument in her driveway. Three weeks earlier, Brenda gave a recorded interview to a detective at the police station in which she said that Dwayne had choked her and threatened to kill her if she “ever went to the cops again.”

The prosecution offers the recorded interview, arguing that Dwayne forfeited his confrontation right by killing Brenda. Apart from the earlier threat, there is no evidence of why Dwayne shot her other than the argument itself.

What must the court find before admitting the interview over a Confrontation Clause objection?

A. That Dwayne killed Brenda, beyond a reasonable doubt, because the forfeiture finding overlaps with the ultimate issue the jury must decide.
B. That Brenda’s statement bears adequate indicia of reliability, because forfeiture is an equitable doctrine concerned with the trustworthiness of the evidence.
C. That Dwayne’s wrongdoing was designed, at least in part, to keep Brenda from testifying, which his earlier threat may help show.
D. Only that Dwayne killed Brenda, by a preponderance of the evidence, because a defendant whose wrongdoing makes a witness unavailable forfeits the right to confront her.
E. Nothing further, because statements describing threats of violence are not testimonial.

Answer: C
- A: Federal courts use a preponderance standard for the forfeiture finding, as under Rule 104(a). The Supreme Court in Davis noted that practice.
- B: Reliability-based confrontation analysis is the Ohio v. Roberts approach that Crawford rejected. Forfeiture turns on the defendant’s wrongdoing and intent, not on the statement’s reliability.
- C: Correct. Giles requires intent to prevent testimony, and the threat about going to the police is strong evidence of it.
- D: Giles rejected forfeiture based on the killing alone. The defendant must have intended to prevent testimony.
- E: A recorded station-house interview narrating past abuse is testimonial. Its subject matter does not change that.
Rule: Forfeiture by wrongdoing applies only when the defendant engaged in conduct designed to prevent the witness from testifying. Giles v. California. Rule 804(b)(6) likewise requires that the party wrongfully caused or acquiesced in causing the declarant’s unavailability “and did so intending that result.” Federal courts apply a preponderance standard.

## Set 3 · Q24 · Lay and Expert Opinion — Rule 701: an experienced user identifies a drug
At Ray Tolan's trial for distributing cocaine, the drugs were never recovered. The government calls Gina Pace, who bought from Tolan. She testifies that she used cocaine almost daily for six years, knows its look, smell, and numbing effect, and that what Tolan sold her looked, smelled, and felt like the cocaine she had always used. She has no scientific training. Tolan objects that whether a substance is cocaine can be proved only by chemical analysis or expert testimony.

How should the court rule?

A. Overrule the objection, because the drug's identity is an ultimate issue that Rule 704(a) leaves to any witness.
B. Overrule the objection, because a lay witness with enough familiarity may identify a drug from her own perception.
C. Overrule the objection, but only if Pace first qualifies as an expert by experience under Rule 702.
D. Sustain the objection, because identifying a controlled substance is always specialized knowledge under Rule 701(c).
E. Sustain the objection, because without the drugs there's no evidence that Pace has personal knowledge.

Answer: B
- A: Rule 704(a) only removes the ultimate-issue objection. A witness still needs a proper basis under Rule 701 or 702, which Pace has here.
- B: Correct. The 2000 Advisory Committee Note to Rule 701 approves cases letting a lay witness with enough experience identify a drug as cocaine. Pace's opinion rests on her own perceptions, helps the jury, and draws on everyday familiarity rather than specialized training.
- C: Experience can qualify an expert, but Pace needn't be one. Her testimony fits Rule 701 because it rests on her own perceptions and everyday familiarity.
- D: Not always. The Committee Note distinguishes reasoning “familiar in everyday life” from specialized knowledge, and it approves lay identification of drugs by experienced users.
- E: Personal knowledge under Rule 602 can be shown by the witness's own testimony. Pace bought and used the drugs herself, which is ample foundation.
Rule: Rule 701 admits lay opinion based on perception and everyday experience. A witness familiar with a drug through long use may identify it as a lay witness (Advisory Committee Note, 2000); specialized knowledge triggers Rule 702.

## Set 3 · Q25 · Lay and Expert Opinion — Rule 703: what experts in the field rely on
In a civil commitment hearing, two psychiatrists testify that Ellis Ward is dangerous to others. Their opinion rests largely on Ward's brother's report that Ward attacked him with a hammer. The brother doesn't testify. Psychiatrists routinely rely on reports from family members in assessing dangerousness. The judge excludes the opinions, saying, “I wouldn't trust a family member's story in a case like this, so I won't let experts rely on it.”

Was the ruling correct?

A. No, because once an opinion is admitted, the expert may tell the jury everything the brother said.
B. Yes, because the judge must personally find every fact underlying an expert's opinion true by a preponderance.
C. Yes, because relying on a family member's report makes the expert a mere conduit for hearsay.
D. Yes, because an expert may rely only on facts that would themselves be admissible in evidence.
E. No, because Rule 703 asks whether experts in the field reasonably rely on such reports, not whether the judge would.

Answer: E
- A: Admitting the opinion doesn't admit its basis. Under Rule 703, the proponent may disclose inadmissible basis facts only if their value in helping the jury evaluate the opinion substantially outweighs their prejudicial effect, a presumption against disclosure.
- B: The judge decides under Rule 104(a) whether the bases satisfy Rules 702(b) and 703, not whether every underlying fact is true.
- C: An expert is a conduit when she merely passes along what others said. A psychiatrist who applies clinical judgment to a family history is using the discipline's tools, which is what Rule 703 allows.
- D: Rule 703 provides the opposite: if experts in the field would reasonably rely on the kind of facts or data, they need not be admissible for the opinion to be admitted.
- E: Correct. Rule 703 asks whether “experts in the particular field would reasonably rely on those kinds of facts or data.” Courts check the bases for minimum reliability under Rule 104(a), but the standard is what the discipline reasonably relies on, not what the judge would. The Advisory Committee Note lists statements by patients and relatives among the bases physicians use.
Rule: Rule 703 lets an expert rely on inadmissible facts or data if experts in the field would reasonably rely on that kind of information; the standard is the discipline's practice, checked for minimum reliability. Disclosing inadmissible bases to the jury requires that their value in evaluating the opinion substantially outweigh their prejudicial effect.

## Set 3 · Q26 · Lay and Expert Opinion — Rule 702(a): helpfulness and common knowledge
In which case is the proposed expert testimony most likely to be excluded as unhelpful under Rule 702(a)?

A. A trademark case, in which a survey expert will report the results of a properly designed consumer-confusion survey.
B. A drunk-driving case, in which a toxicologist will explain how blood-alcohol levels change in the hours after drinking.
C. A trademark case, in which an English professor will testify that the brand names Glo and Gloh sound confusingly alike.
D. A slip-and-fall case, in which an engineer will testify to friction tests on the wet tile where the plaintiff fell.
E. A housing-discrimination case, in which a marketing expert will testify how focus groups read all-white real estate ads.

Answer: C
- A: Properly designed consumer surveys are the standard expert evidence of likely confusion in trademark cases, because they measure how real consumers react.
- B: Alcohol absorption and elimination are scientific matters jurors don't know. Toxicology testimony plainly helps.
- C: Correct. Whether two words sound alike is something any juror can judge by listening. Rule 702(a) requires that the expertise help the jury, and courts exclude experts on matters of common knowledge, as the Ninth Circuit did with an English professor's opinion that two brand names sounded alike.
- D: Friction testing is beyond jurors' knowledge. The Eleventh Circuit reversed the exclusion of such testimony in a cruise-ship slip-and-fall case.
- E: How advertising messages are received by particular audiences is a proper subject for marketing expertise. The Seventh Circuit held its exclusion an abuse of discretion.
Rule: Rule 702(a) requires that the expert's specialized knowledge help the trier of fact. Under Ladd's test, quoted in the Advisory Committee Note, expertise is unhelpful when untrained jurors can decide the issue intelligently on their own.

## Set 3 · Q27 · Authentication and Best Evidence — Rule 901(b)(6): an outgoing call and self-identification
Investigating a fraud, Detective Moreno calls the number the phone company lists for Hal Price. A man answers, “Price speaking.” When Moreno says he is calling about a car Price sold, the man says, “That Honda's odometer was fine when I sold it,” and hangs up. Moreno has never heard Price's voice. At Price's trial for odometer fraud, the prosecution offers Moreno's testimony about the call. Price objects that the speaker wasn't identified.

How should the court rule?

A. Admit the testimony only if phone-company records are introduced to prove the call was completed.
B. Exclude the testimony, because Moreno can identify the speaker only by recognizing his voice.
C. Exclude the testimony, because the speaker denied wrongdoing, so the call is irrelevant whoever he was.
D. Exclude the testimony, because a speaker's self-identification is never enough to authenticate a phone call.
E. Admit the testimony, because the call went to Price's listed number and the speaker identified himself.

Answer: E
- A: Moreno can testify from his own knowledge that he dialed the listed number. Phone records might corroborate the call but aren't required.
- B: Voice identification under Rule 901(b)(5) is one route. Rule 901(b)(6) provides another, based on the number called and the circumstances.
- C: A denial can be highly relevant: if the government shows the odometer was rolled back, a false statement that it was fine helps prove knowledge. Relevance doesn't depend on the statement being true.
- D: Self-identification alone doesn't authenticate an incoming call, since anyone can claim a name. But Rule 901(b)(6)(A) treats self-identification on an outgoing call to the number assigned to that person as enough.
- E: Correct. Rule 901(b)(6)(A) authenticates a telephone conversation by evidence that a call was made to the number assigned at the time to a particular person, if circumstances, including self-identification, show that the person answering was the one called. The speaker's knowledge of the car sale adds to it (901(b)(4)).
Rule: Rule 901(b)(6)(A): a call to the number assigned to a particular person is authenticated if circumstances, including self-identification, show that the person answering was the one called. Voice identification (901(b)(5)) and distinctive contents (901(b)(4)) are other routes.

## Set 3 · Q28 · Authentication and Best Evidence — Rule 1001(d): a printout of electronic data is an original
In a suit over a software license, the plaintiff offers a printout of an email in which the defendant's sales manager promised free upgrades for five years. A paralegal testifies that she printed it from the plaintiff's email account and that the printout accurately shows the email as stored. The defendant objects that the “original” is the electronic file on the server, so the printout violates the best evidence rule.

How should the court rule?

A. Sustain the objection unless the plaintiff shows the electronic file is lost or destroyed under Rule 1004.
B. Overrule the objection, because an accurate printout of electronically stored information is an original.
C. Overrule the objection, because the best evidence rule doesn't apply to emails, which aren't writings.
D. Overrule the objection, but only if the defendant was shown the electronic file before trial.
E. Sustain the objection, because the paralegal didn't write the email and can't testify to its contents.

Answer: B
- A: No excuse is needed, because the printout is itself an original. Rule 1004 matters only when the proponent offers other evidence of content instead of an original or a duplicate.
- B: Correct. Rule 1001(d) provides that for electronically stored information, “original” means any printout or other output readable by sight if it accurately reflects the information. The paralegal's testimony supports that, so Rule 1002 is satisfied.
- C: Rule 1001(a) defines writings to include letters, words, or numbers set down in any form, which covers emails. The rule applies, and the printout satisfies it.
- D: There's no such condition. A printout that accurately reflects the stored data is an original; a dispute about accuracy goes to authentication and to the jury under Rule 1008.
- E: The paralegal isn't testifying to the email's content from memory; she authenticates the printout under Rule 901(b)(1). The printout proves the content, and it is an original.
Rule: Rule 1001(d): an original of electronically stored information includes any printout or other readable output that accurately reflects it. Rule 1003 admits duplicates unless there is a genuine question about authenticity or admitting the duplicate would be unfair.

## Set 3 · Q29 · Privileges — Rule 502(b): the holder's burden
In a federal employment suit, the city produces 140 pages of personnel files. Page 9 is a privileged memo from the city attorney. Two weeks later the city sends a letter asking that the memo be returned. The plaintiff doesn't respond, and the city does nothing more for two years. When the plaintiff lists the memo as a trial exhibit, the city moves to exclude it. Its only evidence of its review process is its current lawyer's statement that “a paralegal reviewed the documents.”

How should the court rule?

A. Exclude the memo, because an inadvertent disclosure never waives the lawyer-client privilege.
B. Exclude the memo, because the city's prompt written request for its return was enough to preserve the privilege.
C. Admit the memo, because producing a privileged document in discovery always waives the privilege.
D. Admit the memo, because the city didn't show reasonable steps to prevent disclosure or prompt steps to fix it.
E. Exclude the memo, because the plaintiff's failure to answer the letter violated the discovery rules.

Answer: D
- A: Inadvertence is only the first of Rule 502(b)'s three elements. The holder must also show reasonable steps to prevent disclosure and prompt, reasonable steps to rectify the error.
- B: A single request followed by two years of silence isn't a prompt, reasonable effort to rectify. The privilege must be jealously guarded by its holder (Williams v. District of Columbia).
- C: Rule 502(b) exists to prevent automatic waiver. An inadvertent disclosure doesn't waive if the holder meets the rule's requirements.
- D: Correct. Under Rule 502(b), the holder bears the burden of showing that the disclosure was inadvertent, that it took reasonable steps to prevent it, and that it promptly took reasonable steps to rectify it. A bare assertion about a paralegal's review of a small production and one unpursued letter fall short, as in Williams v. District of Columbia.
- E: Whatever the plaintiff's duties under Rule 26(b)(5)(B), the question is whether the city met its own burden under Rule 502(b). Two years of inaction defeat that claim.
Rule: Rule 502(b): an inadvertent disclosure in a federal proceeding doesn't waive the privilege if the holder took reasonable steps to prevent it and promptly took reasonable steps to rectify it. The holder bears the burden on each element.

## Set 3 · Q30 · Privileges — Marital confidences: a monitored work email
State trooper Lyle Brandt is charged in federal court with extortion. While on duty, he emailed his wife from his state police computer: “I took the cash. Don't say anything to anyone.” Every time he logged on, a banner warned that users have no expectation of privacy and consent to monitoring, and he clicked “accept.” Investigators retrieve the email from the department's server. Brandt invokes the marital confidences privilege.

How should the court rule?

A. Uphold the privilege, because marital communications are presumed confidential and he meant it for his wife alone.
B. Uphold the privilege, because only his wife, as the recipient, could waive it, and she hasn't.
C. Uphold the privilege, because he never actually read the banner and so expected privacy.
D. Reject the privilege, because the marital confidences privilege covers only spoken communications.
E. Reject the privilege, because he had no reasonable expectation of privacy on a monitored work system.

Answer: E
- A: The presumption of confidentiality can be overcome. Sending the message through a system he had been warned was monitored defeats the reasonable expectation of confidentiality the privilege requires.
- B: Most courts let either spouse claim the privilege. But it never attached here, because the email wasn't confidential.
- C: Confidentiality turns on a reasonable expectation, not only his subjective belief. Clicking through the banner every day gave him notice whether or not he read it.
- D: The privilege covers communications in any form, including letters and emails. The problem is confidentiality, not the medium.
- E: Correct. The marital confidences privilege covers only communications made in confidence. Using a work computer after accepting a banner that warned of monitoring and no expectation of privacy defeats confidentiality, as a federal court held on similar facts.
Rule: Federal courts recognize the marital confidences privilege as federal common law under Rule 501. It protects communications made in confidence during the marriage. Marital communications are presumed confidential, but the presumption fails when the spouse has no reasonable expectation of privacy, as on a monitored workplace system.

## Set 4 · Q1 · Jury Secrecy and Competency — Rule 605: the presiding judge as a witness
During a federal products-liability trial over a forklift crash at a warehouse across the street from the courthouse, the presiding judge mentions to the jury that she happened to see the crash from her chambers window and that the forklift “was clearly going too fast.” Defense counsel, startled, makes no objection. After a plaintiff's verdict, the defendant appeals on this ground.

What is the appellate court most likely to hold?

A. The issue was forfeited, because counsel had to object at the time to preserve any error under Rule 103.
B. There was error only if the judge's account was false, because a truthful account can't have prejudiced the defendant.
C. There was no error, because remarks from the bench are comments on the evidence, not testimony.
D. There was no error, because a judge with personal knowledge may testify like any other witness under Rule 602.
E. There was error, and it is preserved without an objection, because Rule 605 bars the presiding judge from testifying.

Answer: E
- A: Ordinarily a party must object to preserve error, but Rule 605 makes an exception: “A party need not object to preserve the issue.” Objecting to the very judge who is testifying puts counsel in an impossible position.
- B: The rule doesn't depend on accuracy. The problem is that the judge's account can't be tested by cross-examination and carries the authority of the bench with the jury.
- C: A judge's limited power to comment on the evidence doesn't extend to supplying new facts she saw herself. That is testimony, and Rule 605 forbids it.
- D: Rule 605 is a specific bar on the presiding judge's testimony. Personal knowledge doesn't overcome it.
- E: Correct. Rule 605 provides that the presiding judge may not testify as a witness at the trial and that a party need not object to preserve the issue. Telling the jury what she saw is testimony in substance.
Rule: Rule 605: the presiding judge may not testify as a witness at the trial, and no objection is needed to preserve the issue. Rule 606(a) likewise bars a juror from testifying before the other jurors.

## Set 4 · Q2 · Relevance and Rule 403 — Rule 104(b): knowledge as a conditional fact (Cox)
A diner owner is charged with setting fire to a rival restaurant. To prove motive, the prosecution calls the rival’s owner, who testifies that two days before the fire he told a newspaper he planned to open a second restaurant directly across the street from the defendant’s diner. The prosecution shows that the article ran the next morning and that the defendant subscribed to the paper. The defendant testifies that he never reads it. The defense objects that the rival’s plan is irrelevant unless the defendant knew about it. What should the judge do?

A. Decide herself under Rule 104(a) whether the defendant more likely than not read the article, and exclude the testimony unless she is persuaded.
B. Admit the testimony if a reasonable jury could find, by a preponderance, that the defendant knew of the plan.
C. Exclude the testimony, because the defendant’s sworn denial creates a factual dispute that makes the evidence speculative.
D. Admit the testimony without any showing of knowledge, because a rival’s plans are always relevant to motive.
E. Admit the testimony only if the prosecution proves beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant read the article.

Answer: B
- A: 104(a) is for preliminary questions such as privilege and competency. When relevance depends on a fact, 104(b) applies, and the jury decides whether the fact exists.
- B: Correct. This is conditional relevance under 104(b), as in Cox. The judge doesn’t weigh credibility or make her own finding (Huddleston). She asks only whether a jury could reasonably find the conditional fact. The subscription and the article’s timing are enough, as Cox’s near-daily visits to Hammer’s mother’s house were in that case.
- C: A denial doesn’t defeat conditional relevance. If a reasonable jury could find knowledge, the evidence comes in and the jury weighs the denial.
- D: The plan supplies a motive only if the defendant knew about it. That is the missing link 104(b) exists to police, and without a sufficient showing the evidence should be excluded or struck.
- E: Conditional relevance needs only evidence from which a reasonable jury could find the fact by a preponderance. Proof beyond a reasonable doubt applies to the elements at the end of the case, not to preliminary facts.
Rule: Rule 104(b) conditional relevance: admit if a reasonable jury could find the conditional fact by a preponderance. The judge doesn’t weigh credibility (Huddleston, Cox).

## Set 4 · Q3 · Relevance and Rule 403 — Rule 104(b): when the connection never comes
In an extortion trial, the prosecution offers a threatening letter signed only “J.” Defense counsel objects that nothing ties the letter to the defendant. The prosecutor says a handwriting examiner will testify later that the defendant wrote it, and the judge admits the letter on that condition. The prosecution then rests without calling the examiner, and no other evidence links the defendant to the letter. What should the court do on the defendant’s motion?

A. Let the letter stand, because once evidence is admitted, its weight is for the jury.
B. Strike the letter and tell the jury to disregard it, because the condition for admitting it was never met.
C. Let the letter stand if the judge personally believes, by a preponderance, that the defendant wrote it.
D. Declare a mistrial automatically, because no instruction can cure conditionally admitted evidence that fails.
E. Deny the motion, because the defense waived the issue by not objecting again when the prosecution rested.

Answer: B
- A: Conditional admission is just that. If no evidence would let a reasonable jury find the conditional fact by a preponderance, the letter has no proper path to relevance and can’t stay before the jury.
- B: Correct. The letter is relevant only if the defendant wrote it. 104(b) lets the court admit evidence “on the condition that the proof be introduced later.” When that proof never comes, the evidence fails the test of conditional relevance, and the court must instruct the jury to disregard it (or declare a mistrial if an instruction can’t cure the harm).
- C: Under 104(b) the judge doesn’t decide the conditional fact. She asks only whether a reasonable jury could find it (Huddleston). With no evidence of authorship, no jury could.
- D: Under Rule 104(b) the usual remedy is to strike the evidence and instruct the jury to disregard it. A mistrial is for the rare case where an instruction can’t cure the prejudice, and it isn’t automatic.
- E: The defense objected when the letter was offered, and a motion to strike is the proper way to raise the failure to connect it up.
Rule: Rule 104(b): evidence whose relevance depends on a fact may be admitted on condition of later proof. If the proof never comes, the court strikes it and tells the jury to disregard it.

## Set 4 · Q4 · Specialized Relevance Rules — Rule 407: the narrow impeachment exception
A shopper trips over a hose stretched across a garden-center aisle and sues the store. After the accident, the store installed retractable hose reels at the end of every aisle. At trial the store manager testifies on direct, “When I walked that aisle an hour before she fell, I thought it looked reasonably safe.” The plaintiff offers the hose reels to impeach him. How should the court rule?

A. Admit the evidence, because any defense testimony that the premises were safe opens the door to impeachment with later repairs.
B. Admit the evidence to show that the store controlled the aisle, with a limiting instruction.
C. Exclude the evidence, because Rule 407 bars evidence of later repairs for every purpose.
D. Admit the evidence to prove feasibility, because the store didn’t stipulate that hose reels were feasible.
E. Exclude it, because a later improvement doesn’t contradict his belief that the aisle was reasonably safe then.

Answer: E
- A: That reading would let the exception swallow the rule. It reaches testimony the later measure actually contradicts, like the claim in the class hypothetical that a $55.26 carpet fix would have cost $40,000.
- B: Control is a permitted purpose only if disputed, and nothing suggests the store denied controlling its own aisle.
- C: 407 bars only the listed uses: negligence, culpable conduct, a defect, or a need for a warning. Impeachment and disputed ownership, control, or feasibility remain open. The evidence fails here because it doesn’t actually impeach.
- D: Feasibility is a permitted purpose only “if disputed.” The store never claimed hose reels were impractical, and it doesn’t have to stipulate to keep feasibility out of dispute.
- E: Correct. Courts read the impeachment exception narrowly, or it would swallow the rule, since nearly every defense witness denies negligence. A later improvement doesn’t contradict a belief that conditions were reasonably safe before the accident: wiser after isn’t foolish before. A sweeping claim, such as that no safer arrangement was possible, would be different.
Rule: Rule 407’s impeachment exception is narrow: the later measure must contradict the testimony, not merely a denial of negligence. Feasibility, ownership, and control are permitted purposes only if disputed.

## Set 4 · Q5 · Specialized Relevance Rules — Rule 409: medical expenses only
Moments after backing into a cyclist in a parking lot, a driver jumps out and says: (1) “I’ll cover whatever your bike repairs cost,” (2) “and I’ll pay your doctor bills if you need to see someone,” and (3) “I never checked my mirror.” No demand had been made, and nothing was in dispute. The cyclist later sues. Which statements may the cyclist offer to prove the driver’s negligence?

A. Statements 1 and 3.
B. None of them, because Rules 408 and 409 together protect everything said while trying to make an injured person whole.
C. Statements 1, 2, and 3, because Rule 409 applies only after a claim has been made.
D. Statements 2 and 3.
E. Statement 3 only.

Answer: A
- A: Correct. 409 excludes only offers to pay “medical, hospital, or similar expenses,” so statement 2 is out, but the admission that came with it isn’t. Statement 1 offers to pay for property damage, which 409 doesn’t cover. Nor does 408: it protects offers to compromise a claim disputed as to validity or amount, and at the scene there was no claim and no dispute.
- B: Neither rule is that broad. 409 covers only medical-type expenses, and not the statements made with the offer; 408 covers only the compromise of a disputed claim.
- C: Rule 409 has no claim requirement: it excludes an offer to pay medical expenses whenever it is made, so statement 2 is out. The dispute requirement belongs to Rule 408, which is why statement 1 isn’t protected.
- D: Statement 2 is the one 409 squarely excludes: an offer to pay medical expenses resulting from the injury can’t prove liability. Statement 1 is the admissible offer.
- E: That treats the repair offer as protected. 409 is limited to medical and similar expenses, and 408 requires a disputed claim. An offer made before anyone has claimed or disputed anything isn’t a compromise.
Rule: Rule 409 excludes only offers to pay medical and similar expenses, not statements made with them or offers to pay other losses. 408 requires a claim disputed as to validity or amount.

## Set 4 · Q6 · Specialized Relevance Rules — Rule 408(a)(2): the public-office exception
Which of the following statements is admissible over a Rule 408 objection?

A. A homeowner’s admission, during negotiations with his neighbor over a property-line dispute, that he knew he was building on her land, offered in a later criminal trespass prosecution.
B. The same chemical company’s offer to pay a $2 million civil penalty, offered in the criminal prosecution to show consciousness of guilt.
C. A driver’s statement in negotiations with a pedestrian’s insurer, offered by the driver to show he acted reasonably.
D. A chemical company’s admission to the EPA, made while negotiating to settle a civil enforcement action, offered in a later criminal prosecution for the same dumping.
E. A CEO’s statement at a settlement conference that “we knew the brakes were bad,” offered to impeach his trial testimony that the company had no reason to suspect a defect.

Answer: D
- A: The criminal-case exception applies only to negotiations with a public office exercising regulatory, investigative, or enforcement authority, not with a private party.
- B: The criminal-case exception covers only conduct or statements under 408(a)(2). Offers to compromise under 408(a)(1) stay excluded even in criminal cases, since an offer may reflect a desire for peace.
- C: Rule 408 bars compromise evidence offered “by any party” to prove or disprove the validity of a disputed claim, so the driver can’t use his own negotiation statement either.
- D: Correct. 408(a)(2) excludes statements made in compromise negotiations, “except when offered in a criminal case and when the negotiations related to a claim by a public office in the exercise of its regulatory, investigative, or enforcement authority.” A party talking to a regulator is on notice that its statements may be used by prosecutors.
- E: Since 2006, 408 bars compromise statements offered “to impeach by a prior inconsistent statement or a contradiction.” That’s The Verdict clip: the bishop’s “tragic accident” can’t impeach his “act of God” testimony.
Rule: Rule 408(a)(2) exception: statements (not offers) made in negotiations with a public office are admissible in a later criminal case. 408 bars compromise statements used to impeach by prior inconsistent statement or contradiction.

## Set 4 · Q7 · Character Evidence — Rule 404(a)(2): criminal cases only
A bar patron sues another patron for battery, claiming the defendant hit him with a beer bottle without provocation. The defendant, who says he never threw a punch, calls his longtime neighbor to testify that the defendant has a reputation in the neighborhood as a peaceful, gentle man. The plaintiff objects. How should the court rule?

A. Sustain the objection, because reputation testimony is hearsay.
B. Overrule the objection, because a battery claim makes the defendant’s peacefulness an essential element.
C. Sustain it, because the exceptions letting a defendant offer his pertinent trait apply only in criminal cases.
D. Overrule the objection, because a battery claim alleges a crime, so he may defend his good name as an accused could.
E. Overrule the objection, because reputation is a proper way to prove character under Rule 405(a).

Answer: C
- A: Reputation testimony about character is admissible over a hearsay objection under FRE 803(21). The problem is 404(a)(1), not hearsay.
- B: Peacefulness isn’t an element of a battery claim or defense. Rule 405(b) applies only when character itself is at issue, as with truth in defamation or negligent entrustment.
- C: Correct. 404(a)(2) applies only in criminal cases. The 2006 amendment rejected decisions like Perrin v. Anderson, which had let civil defendants facing quasi-criminal charges offer good character. In a civil battery suit the evidence is barred by 404(a)(1).
- D: That was the reasoning of Perrin v. Anderson, which the 2006 amendment rejected. The “special dispensation” belongs only to criminal defendants, whose liberty is at stake.
- E: 405(a) governs how character is proved once some rule lets it in. It doesn’t create a right to offer character. Here no exception applies, so the method never comes into play.
Rule: The 404(a)(2)(A)–(C) exceptions apply only in criminal cases (2006 amendment). In a civil case, character offered to prove conduct is barred.

## Set 4 · Q8 · Character Evidence — Rule 404(a)(2)(B): the accused’s same trait
A defendant charged with assault claims the alleged victim attacked first. He calls a witness who testifies that the victim has a reputation for violence. In rebuttal, the prosecution offers (1) a witness who testifies that the victim has a reputation as a peaceful person, (2) a witness who testifies that the defendant has a reputation for violence, and (3) a bartender who testifies that the defendant broke a man’s jaw in a bar fight last year. The defendant didn’t offer evidence of his own character. Which rebuttal evidence is admissible?

A. Items 1 and 2 only.
B. None of them, because only a homicide victim’s peacefulness may be offered by the prosecution.
C. Item 1 only, because the defendant never put his own character in issue.
D. Items 1 and 3, because specific acts may rebut, but the defendant’s reputation isn’t at issue.
E. Items 1, 2, and 3, because the defendant opened the door to violence.

Answer: A
- A: Correct. Once the defendant offers the victim’s pertinent trait under 404(a)(2)(B), the prosecution may (i) rebut it and (ii) offer evidence of the defendant’s same trait, even though he never offered his own character (the 2000 amendment). Under 405(a) both must be by reputation or opinion. Item 3 is a specific instance offered on direct, which 405(a) doesn’t allow.
- B: That describes 404(a)(2)(C), which lets the prosecution go first in a homicide case. In any criminal case, once the defendant offers the victim’s trait, 404(a)(2)(B) lets the prosecution respond.
- C: 404(a)(2)(B)(ii) was added in 2000 precisely so that an accused who attacks the victim’s trait opens the door to the same trait in himself.
- D: Backwards. Rule 404(a)(2)(B)(ii) opens the accused’s same trait, but Rule 405(a) limits proof to reputation or opinion, so the bartender’s account of a specific bar fight stays out.
- E: Opening the door doesn’t change the method of proof. Specific acts come in only on cross of a character witness, or where character is an essential element under 405(b).
Rule: Rule 404(a)(2)(B): if the accused offers the victim’s pertinent trait, the prosecution may rebut it and offer the accused’s same trait, by reputation or opinion only (405(a)).

## Set 4 · Q9 · Character Evidence — Reverse 404(b): still no propensity
Police stop a car and find a handgun under the driver’s seat. The driver, a convicted felon, is charged with unlawful possession. He offers evidence that his passenger was convicted three years earlier of possessing a different handgun, arguing that it shows the gun was the passenger’s. The prosecution objects. How should the court rule?

A. Exclude it, because it shows only that the passenger tends to carry guns, which is propensity reasoning.
B. Exclude it, because a defendant may never offer evidence of another person’s crimes or bad acts.
C. Admit it, because Stevens applies a relaxed standard to any other-act evidence a defendant offers.
D. Admit it, because the propensity ban protects only criminal defendants, not third parties like the passenger.
E. Admit it under Rule 404(a)(2), because a defendant may offer evidence of a third party’s pertinent trait.

Answer: A
- A: Correct. This is Problem 3.10 (United States v. Williams, misreading Stevens). Reverse 404(b) evidence gets a lower similarity threshold, but the defense still must show a non-propensity inference, such as enough similarity to suggest that the same person committed both crimes (Stevens). A prior possession of a different gun shows only propensity.
- B: Reverse 404(b) evidence is admissible in a proper case. In Stevens, a similar robbery nearby whose victim said Stevens wasn’t the attacker was improperly excluded.
- C: Stevens relaxed the degree of similarity needed (no “signature” required) and the 403 balance, but it didn’t drop the requirement of a non-propensity theory of relevance.
- D: 404(b)(1) bars other-act evidence about “a person,” not just the defendant. Williams rejected the idea that Stevens licenses defense propensity evidence.
- E: Rule 404(a)(2)(A)–(B) concern the defendant’s and the victim’s character. The passenger is neither, and Rule 404(b)(1) bars the propensity inference about “a person.”
Rule: Reverse 404(b) (Stevens): a lower similarity threshold and a 401 + 403 (waste, confusion) analysis, but still no propensity inference (Williams).

## Set 4 · Q10 · Character Evidence — Pertinent traits, by reputation or opinion only
A defendant is charged with filing fraudulent insurance claims. She calls four character witnesses. Witness 1 testifies that she has a reputation in her church for honesty. Witness 2 testifies that in his opinion she is a law-abiding person. Witness 3 testifies that she has a reputation as a calm, peaceful person. Witness 4 testifies that last year she found a wallet with $900 in it and returned it to its owner. The prosecution objects to each. Which testimony is admissible?

A. Witnesses 1, 2, and 4.
B. Witnesses 1, 2, and 3.
C. Witness 1 only.
D. Witnesses 2 and 4.
E. Witnesses 1 and 2.

Answer: E
- A: The returned wallet bears on honesty, but 405(a) allows specific instances only on cross-examination of a character witness, or under 405(b) when character is an element. The ACN notes that specific acts, though most convincing, carry the greatest risk of prejudice, confusion, surprise, and delay.
- B: The accused may offer only a trait pertinent to the charge. Peacefulness doesn’t bear on whether she lied to an insurer.
- C: The Federal Rules allow opinion as well as reputation (405(a) added opinion to the common law’s reputation-only rule), and being law-abiding is generally accepted as a pertinent trait.
- D: Witness 4’s wallet story is a specific instance, which Rule 405(a) doesn’t allow on direct, and Witness 1’s testimony to a reputation for honesty, a pertinent trait, is admissible.
- E: Correct. 404(a)(2)(A) lets the accused offer a pertinent trait. Honesty is pertinent to fraud, and being law-abiding is generally treated as pertinent to any crime. Peacefulness has nothing to do with a fraud charge. Witness 4 describes a specific instance, and on direct examination 405(a) limits proof to reputation or opinion.
Rule: Rule 404(a)(2)(A): the accused may offer a pertinent trait, proved on direct only by reputation or opinion (405(a)). Specific instances come in only on cross or when character is an element.

## Set 4 · Q11 · Impeachment and the Rape Shield — United States v. Whitmore: foundation and good faith
A federal agent is the only witness who saw the defendant toss a gun. The defense offers (1) a criminal defense lawyer who will testify that the agent has a bad reputation for truthfulness in the “courthouse community,” based on talks with three other defense lawyers, and that in his own opinion the agent is a liar because the agent testified against his clients; and (2) cross-examination of the agent about his failure to disclose a bankruptcy on his security-clearance form. The defense’s only support for item 2 is a credit-bureau printout that would itself be inadmissible hearsay. Which rulings fall within the court’s discretion?

A. Admitting both and allowing the defense to introduce the credit-bureau printout if the agent denies the omission.
B. Admitting the defense lawyer’s opinion but not his reputation testimony, because opinion needs no foundation.
C. Excluding both, because character for truthfulness may be proved only by reputation.
D. Barring the cross-examination, because the defense has no admissible proof that the agent omitted the bankruptcy.
E. Excluding the defense lawyer’s testimony for lack of foundation, while allowing the cross-examination.

Answer: E
- A: 608(b) forbids extrinsic evidence of specific instances offered to attack character for truthfulness. The defense may ask but can’t prove the omission with the printout.
- B: Opinion testimony also needs an adequate basis of acquaintance, and an opinion grounded in the agent’s testifying against the lawyer’s clients reflects bias, not knowledge of character. United States v. Whitmore upheld excluding such witnesses.
- C: 608(a) permits opinion as well as reputation, and 608(b) separately permits cross about specific instances probative of untruthfulness.
- D: Whitmore rejected exactly this reasoning. The questioner needs only a reasonable, good-faith basis. The bar on extrinsic evidence means the defense must take the agent’s answer, not that it can’t ask.
- E: Correct. Whitmore upheld excluding character witnesses whose knowledge of the reputation was too thin or too remote, and the lawyer here spoke with only a few colleagues and based his opinion on testimony against his own clients. But 608(b) cross needs only a good-faith basis, not admissible proof, and omitting a bankruptcy on an official form is probative of untruthfulness. Barring that cross was the reversible error in Whitmore, where the officer was the key witness.
Rule: Rule 608(a) witnesses need an adequate foundation (Whitmore). 608(b) cross requires only a good-faith basis, and no extrinsic evidence is allowed.

## Set 4 · Q12 · Impeachment and the Rape Shield — Rules 608(b) and 609: impeaching an accused
At his 2026 trial for grand theft, the defendant testifies that he was out of state when the theft occurred. In 2022 he shot a man in the arm during a bar fight and was convicted of felony assault with a dangerous weapon. In 2024 he was convicted of misdemeanor turnstile jumping and served 30 days. The prosecutor proposes four ways to impeach him. Which may the court permit?

A. Evidence of the 2022 assault conviction, if it passes Rule 609(a)(1)(B)’s balancing test.
B. Testimony from a bartender who saw him shoot the man in the arm during the 2022 fight.
C. Cross-examination asking whether he was convicted of turnstile jumping in 2024.
D. Cross-examination asking whether he shot a man in the arm during the 2022 bar fight.
E. Evidence of the 2024 turnstile conviction, because evading a fare is a crime of dishonesty.

Answer: A
- A: Correct. A felony conviction of a testifying accused is admissible under 609(a)(1)(B) if it passes that special balance. Violent crimes are weak on honesty, so admission isn’t guaranteed, but it’s the only route the rules allow among these options.
- B: This is extrinsic evidence of a specific act. 608(b) bars it as proof of character for truthfulness, and offered to show violent character it’s propensity barred by 404.
- C: A misdemeanor qualifies under 609 only if it is crimen falsi, which fare evasion isn’t, and it isn’t the kind of deceitful act 608(b) reaches either.
- D: 608(b) permits cross only about acts probative of truthfulness, and a shooting isn’t one. Asking about the underlying act would also be a back door around 609’s protections for convictions.
- E: Fare evasion is a misdemeanor whose elements don’t require proving a dishonest act or false statement, so it isn’t crimen falsi under Rule 609(a)(2).
Rule: Impeaching an accused: felony convictions go through 609(a)(1)(B). 608(b) reaches only acts probative of truthfulness, on cross, with no extrinsic proof, and it isn’t a back door around 609.

## Set 4 · Q13 · Impeachment and the Rape Shield — Rule 412(b)(1)(A): another source of injury
A defendant is charged in federal court with sexual assault and claims he wasn’t the attacker. The examining nurse found bruising and abrasions consistent with intercourse. By written motion filed a month before trial, the defense seeks to offer (1) testimony that the complainant had intercourse with her boyfriend several hours before the alleged assault, to explain the injuries, and (2) testimony that she “was sleeping around with several men” that month. Which ruling is correct?

A. Item 1 is admissible only if the prosecutor offers it, because the accused may not offer evidence under Rule 412(b)(1)(A).
B. Item 1 may be admitted under Rule 412(b)(1)(A) after an in camera hearing, but item 2 is barred.
C. Both are barred, because Rule 412 excludes all evidence of a victim’s other sexual behavior in a criminal case.
D. Item 2 may be admitted to show she had many possible partners, but item 1 is barred as predisposition.
E. Both are admissible, because a defendant claiming misidentification may offer any evidence about other possible sources of the injury.

Answer: B
- A: The source-of-physical-evidence exception is typically invoked by the defense. The “offered by the prosecutor” language belongs to 412(b)(1)(B), on sexual behavior with the accused.
- B: Correct. 412(b)(1)(A) permits specific instances of a victim’s sexual behavior offered to show that someone other than the defendant was the source of semen, injury, or other physical evidence, and the motion followed 412(c)’s procedure (written motion at least 14 days before trial, notice, in camera hearing).
