The client decides (all reserved to the client): (1) whether to settle; and, in a criminal case, (2) the plea to be entered; (3) whether to waive a jury trial; and (4) whether to testify.

Client decides (objectives) | Lawyer decides after consulting (means)
Settle or not, and material settlement terms (gag or confidentiality clauses); binding arbitration (it waives trial: Blanton v. Womancare); high-low agreements (they set the outcome); the plea; jury waiver; testifying; whether to appeal. The four listed decisions are examples: anything that is a fundamental right or the end result the client hired you for. | Claims and theories to plead; discovery; which witnesses; the defense theory at trial; nonbinding mediation (but consult); professional courtesies such as a harmless extension ("you needn't be a mad dog"). Consultation is required only for material means. In practice clients have strong input, since they can fire you.

- No end-runs: an advance blanket grant of settlement authority ("settle for any amount the lawyer considers reasonable") is void, but specific advance authority ("accept anything over $70K") is fine, subject to revocation and changed circumstances (cmt [3]).

- Fee terms that penalize the client's decision are void or unconscionable: hourly fees that kick in if the client rejects a recommended settlement, or retroactive conversion to hourly. Ordinary deposits for real next steps are fine, but coercive timing is suspect.

- Appointed criminal counsel may make means decisions over objection and needn't present a baseless theory. The client's right to discharge appointed counsel is limited (MR 1.16 cmt [5]). The client still controls the plea, jury, and testimony.

- MR 1.2(b): representation, including by appointment, is not an endorsement of the client's views. MR 1.2(d): don't counsel or assist conduct you know is criminal or fraudulent, but you may discuss the legal consequences and help the client determine what the law requires (Part XI).

Blanton v. Womancare, Inc., 38 Cal. 3d 396 (1985) — binding arbitration is the client's call NOTE CASE · WEEK 4
Facts: Without the client's consent, and against her instructions, her lawyer stipulated to binding arbitration of her medical malpractice claim.
Held: The stipulation did not bind her: agreeing to binding arbitration surrenders the right to trial, a substantial right that requires the client's authority.
Why it matters: An objectives decision (MR 1.2(a)). A lawyer's authority over procedure doesn't reach choices that waive a client's fundamental rights.

# PART V — Fees and Client Funds

## 20. Fee Arrangements and Their Formalities (MR 1.5(b), (c)) WEEK 5
Reading: MR 1.5, 1.15; Chs. 20–21; Delaware Rule 1.15. Fee agreements are contracts with special overlays, and trust money is sacred.

- Fees vs. expenses: fees pay for professional services. Expenses are out-of-pocket costs specific to this matter, never rent or general salaries. In-house charges (copying, research) must reflect actual cost or a reasonable amount agreed in advance; a markup disclosed only on the invoice doesn't count (MR 1.5 cmt [1]).

RULE MR 1.5(b) — communicating the fee The scope of the representation and the basis or rate of the fee and expenses for which the client will be responsible "shall be communicated to the client, preferably in writing, before or within a reasonable time after commencing the representation, except when the lawyer will charge a regularly represented client on the same basis or rate." Any change in the basis or rate must also be communicated (a long-time client's rate increase too). Best practice: a writing signed by the client (cmt [2]).

RULE MR 1.5(c) — contingent fees A contingent fee agreement must be in a writing signed by the client and state (all required): (1) the method of determining the fee, including the percentage or percentages that accrue to the lawyer in the event of settlement, trial, or appeal; (2) the litigation and other expenses to be deducted from the recovery; (3) whether those expenses are deducted before or after the contingent fee is calculated; and (4) any expenses for which the client will be liable whether or not the client is the prevailing party. At the end, the lawyer must give a written closing statement stating the outcome, the remittance to the client, and how it was calculated.

- A signature doesn't cure missing terms, and the lawyer's own email plus the client's "sounds good" isn't a writing signed by the client. Any contingent component of a hybrid fee (a success bonus, reverse contingency, or shares payable on sale) needs the client's signed writing.

Arrangement | What it is and what to cover
Flat | A sum certain for defined tasks. Say when, and which portions, are earned if the engagement ends early (cmt [4]). Rewards efficiency, but risks curtailed effort when the money runs out (MR 1.1, 1.3).
Hourly | Hours times each timekeeper's rate, billed in tenths. Scalable as a matter grows or shrinks, but rewards inefficiency. Losing doesn't erase a reasonable hourly fee. Billing work not done is fraud (mail or wire fraud federally).
Contingent | A percentage of the recovery, in a signed writing. Can pit lawyer against client when a trial would cost the firm more than it gains.
Hybrid | Any mix within MR 1.5's limits. Contingent parts need a signed writing.
Salary | Associates and in-house lawyers draw a salary; owners share fee revenue less overhead and reserves.

- MR 1.5 cmt [5]: no terms that might induce the lawyer to curtail services or act against the client. Don't cap services at a stated amount when more work is foreseeable unless you explain the situation (otherwise the client must bargain mid-matter). Defining services by the client's ability to pay is fine. Don't run up hourly fees with wasteful procedures.

- MR 1.5 cmt [4]: you may require advance payment but must return any unearned part (MR 1.16(d)). You may take property as a fee (e.g., an ownership interest), but not a proprietary interest in the litigation's subject (MR 1.8(i)), and it may trigger MR 1.8(a) (Part VI).

TIP Contingent-fee math: costs first vs. fee first $1M recovery, $100K costs, 30% fee. Costs first (more common, client-favorable): $900K x 30% = $270K fee, so the client nets $630K. Fee first: $300K fee, then $700K minus $100K costs, so the client nets $600K. After a loss, the client owes whatever costs the agreement says are owed regardless of outcome, plus possibly the opponent's taxable costs. "No fee unless we win" can mislead (MR 7.1) if clients still owe costs; MR 1.8(e)(1) lets lawyers make repayment of costs contingent on the outcome.

## 21. Limits on Fees, Retainers, and Fee Sharing (MR 1.5(a), (d), (e); 5.4; 7.2(b)) WEEK 5
RULE MR 1.5(a) — no unreasonable fee A lawyer shall not make an agreement for, charge, or collect an unreasonable fee or an unreasonable amount for expenses; the violation is complete on agreeing or charging, even without collecting. Factors (weighed together; none alone decides): (1) the time and labor required, the novelty and difficulty of the questions, and the skill requisite; (2) the likelihood, if apparent to the client, that the engagement will preclude other work; (3) the fee customarily charged in the locality; (4) the amount involved and the results obtained; (5) time limitations imposed by the client or the circumstances; (6) the nature and length of the professional relationship; (7) the experience, reputation, and ability of the lawyer; and (8) whether the fee is fixed or contingent. The client's ability to pay is not a factor.

- Judge fees as of the agreement, accounting for the risk assumed. A quick $150K settlement a week after a 33% agreement doesn't make the fee unreasonable. Rush premiums agreed in advance are fine (factors 2 and 5), and different rates for different work are fine.

- Statutory caps bind (workers' comp, med-mal, Social Security, probate, the FTCA's 25%). Goldfarb v. Virginia State Bar: bar minimum-fee schedules violated antitrust law, which is different from lawful statutory caps.

RULE MR 1.5(d) — prohibited contingent fees No contingent fee (any one is barred): (1) in a domestic relations matter, contingent on securing a divorce or on the amount of alimony, support, or a property settlement in lieu thereof; or (2) for representing a defendant in a criminal case. Signatures and reasonableness don't cure either.

- The book calls both anachronisms, but they're still the law. Civil plaintiff contingencies are fine. Cmt [6]: a contingent fee to collect post-judgment arrears of support, alimony, or other financial orders is allowed. Rationales: the domestic ban avoids discouraging reconciliation (McCarthy v. Santangelo: "The state does not favor divorces"); the criminal ban guards against corrupting justice (Peyton v. Margiotti).

Consequences and recovery

- Prohibited fee: voidable, a defense to collection, and disgorgement. Lying about services rendered is fraud or theft (mail fraud in federal cases).

- Formal defect (no signed writing): the agreed fee is unenforceable, leaving quantum meruit at most (usually a lodestar at a reasonable rate, often far below the contract; contingent fees usually eliminated). Some states allow nothing.

- Discharged lawyers: the client may fire you anytime but owes for services, usually quantum meruit capped at the contract price; for a contingent fee, payable only if the contingency occurs. Fee terms that unduly burden discharge are void.

Retainers
Type | What it buys | Whose money | Where it goes
"True" (classic) retainer | The lawyer's availability | The lawyer's; earned when paid | Operating account. Rare; some states ban it (ABA Op. 505)
Advance or security deposit | Future fees and costs (evergreen or wasting) | The client's until earned | Trust (MR 1.15(c)); refund the unearned balance (MR 1.16(d))

- Labels don't control. Calling an advance for future work "nonrefundable" doesn't make it earned on receipt. States that allow true retainers often require a writing signed by the client stating with particularity what is being paid for, when it's earned, and whether it's refundable. With an evergreen deposit, the client tops it back up after each draw.

Sharing fees and paying for referrals

- "Sharing" means payment measured by fees a client paid (or the profit on them). Paying rent or a loan from fee revenue isn't sharing. Within a firm, share on any terms, without telling the client (unless a lawyer is screened).

RULE MR 1.5(e) — dividing a fee between lawyers not in the same firm Allowed only if (all required): (1) the division is in proportion to the services each lawyer performs, or each lawyer assumes joint responsibility for the representation; (2) the client agrees to the arrangement, including the share each lawyer will receive, and the agreement is confirmed in writing; and (3) the total fee is reasonable.

- This authorizes co-counseling, not pure referral fees (a few states allow pure referral fees; most don't). Joint responsibility (cmt [7]) means financial and ethical responsibility as if the lawyers were partners, an unconditional guarantee usually without insurance coverage.

RULE MR 7.2(b) — no paying for recommendations Don't give anything of value to anyone for recommending your services, except (any one suffices): (1) the reasonable costs of permitted advertising; (2) the usual charges of a legal service plan or a not-for-profit or qualified lawyer referral service; (3) paying for a law practice under MR 1.17; (4) a reciprocal referral agreement with another lawyer or a nonlawyer professional, if (i) it is not exclusive and (ii) the client is informed of its existence and nature; or (5) nominal gifts as thanks, neither intended nor reasonably expected as compensation (Part XI).

RULE MR 5.4 — professional independence (a) No sharing legal fees with a nonlawyer, except (any one suffices): (1) payments over time after a lawyer's death to the lawyer's estate or designated persons; (2) the purchase price of a deceased, disabled, or disappeared lawyer's practice (MR 1.17); (3) nonlawyer employees in a compensation or retirement plan, even one based on profit-sharing; or (4) court-awarded fees shared with a nonprofit that employed, retained, or recommended the lawyer in the matter. (b) No partnership with a nonlawyer if any of its activities are the practice of law. (c) No letting whoever recommends, employs, or pays the lawyer direct or regulate the lawyer's judgment. (d) No practicing in a for-profit professional corporation or association if (any one bars it): (1) a nonlawyer owns any interest (except a lawyer's estate representative briefly); (2) a nonlawyer is a director or officer; or (3) a nonlawyer has the right to direct or control a lawyer's professional judgment.

- Client consent doesn't change MR 5.4. Why: independent judgment, though the book calls the rule hard to justify apart from guild protection; D.C. and others are experimenting with nonlawyer ownership.

TRAP Paralegal bonuses and referral fees A case-specific bonus to a paralegal (10% of the fee, or even a flat $5K) for bringing in a client violates both MR 5.4(a) and 7.2(b). A general profit-sharing retirement plan is fine. A lawyer who refers a case, does no work, and takes no joint responsibility can't be paid a share, even with the client's oral consent.

## 22. Safeguarding Client Property (MR 1.15; Delaware Rule 1.15) WEEK 5
Ch. 21. "Property" includes money (the client's, unearned fees, or a third party's), documents, and physical evidence. The fiduciary standard is being "more than ordinarily careful." Green money (operating, yours) you can spend; red money (trust, theirs) you must safeguard. A segregation failure is a disciplinary violation by itself, but civil liability usually requires a monetary loss.

- Three duties (all required): (1) safeguard; (2) segregate; and (3) account. "Substantial compliance" is hardly ever enough. The duties are nondelegable: you may use staff but keep full disciplinary and financial responsibility, even for a trusted bookkeeper's unforeseeable theft. "Delegate; don't abdicate. Trust, but verify."

- Two kinds of accounts: the operating account (the lawyer's money) and the client trust account (everyone else's).

RULE MR 1.15 — safekeeping property (a) Hold others' property separate from your own. Funds go in a separate account in the state where your office is (elsewhere only with consent). Other property must be identified and safeguarded "with the care required of a professional fiduciary" (cmt [1]); bearer bonds are cash and belong in a safe or safe-deposit box. Keep complete records for five years after the representation ends. (b) Your own funds may go in trust only to pay bank charges. (c) Advance fees and expenses go in trust, withdrawn "only as fees are earned or expenses incurred." (d) Promptly notify anyone with an interest when you receive funds, promptly deliver what they're entitled to, and on request promptly render a full accounting. (e) Keep disputed property separate until the dispute is resolved, and promptly distribute the undisputed part.

Situation | Rule
Commingling | A violation by itself, even if temporary, quickly fixed, and every dollar is there. No loss is required. An advance deposited in operating "for convenience" is commingling.
Pooled trust account | Several clients' funds together is fine, with separate ledgers. Only mixing your money with theirs is barred.
Your money in trust | Only enough for bank charges. "Top off the tank, don't overfill it." No overdraft cushions.
Fees become earned | Move them promptly to operating. Too early is misappropriation; too late is commingling. Define "earned" in the agreement. "We'll put it back" never cures an early withdrawal.
Mixed check (fee + client money) | Deposit in trust, wait until it clears, then promptly move your share and pay the client. Never deposit it in operating.
Check clearing | Provisional credit can be charged back. The retainer scam: a fake cashier's check, then an urgent "refund" wire funded with other clients' money. Disburse only against good funds (cash, a cleared check, a cashier's check confirmed with the bank).
Paying from trust | Pay a client's expenses from that client's funds only. Never pay your own bills (bar dues) from trust.
Disputed funds (MR 1.15(e)) | Hold only the disputed amount and distribute the rest. No self-help, and no holding undisputed money to coerce payment or a release (cmt [3]). Suggest arbitration. A client-vs-third-party dispute (a medical lien) may call for interpleader (cmt [4]).
Notice (MR 1.15(d)) | "Promptly notify" anyone with a colorable claim, not just the undisputed owner. An accounting on request covers the required records, but don't reveal other clients' information in it.
Interest (IOLTA) | Nominal or short-term pooled funds go to the state IOLTA program, which funds legal services for the poor or a client-protection fund. Large or long-term deposits go in a separate account earning interest for the client.
Delaware | DE Rule 1.15(a): the account is designated solely for funds held in connection with the practice of law in Delaware; the lawyer's own funds for bank charges may not exceed $2,000 and must be separately accounted for; records are kept five years after the events they record.
Records | Client ledgers, journals, and monthly reconciliation. Imperfect records are a violation even if every dollar is present (the "Al Capone problem"). Trust overdrafts are reported to the bar.

TIP Worked allocations Class example: 30% contingency, costs "off the top," $100K settlement, $10K costs. The lawyer's share is $10K costs plus 30% of $90K ($27K fee), so $37K; the client gets $63K. Deposit the whole check in trust, send the closing statement (giving a chance to object), then move the $37K to operating. Dispute on exit: $10K in trust; you bill $4K; the client disputes $1K and fires you. Take $3K, hold $1K, refund $6K now. Integrated version: 25% after costs, $100K settlement, $4K costs, so the fee base is $96K and the fee $24K. If the client disputes $6K of the fee: $18K fee plus $4K costs to operating, $6K held in trust, $72K to the client now, with a closing statement.

Formality ladder: what each consent must look like
Requirement | Where it applies
Informed consent, any form | Disclosing confidences (MR 1.6(a)); scope limits (MR 1.2(c)); third-party payment (MR 1.8(f)); evaluations that may hurt the client (MR 2.3(b)). Confirm significant ones in writing anyway.
"Preferably in writing" | Fee scope and basis or rate (MR 1.5(b)).
Confirmed in writing | Fee division between firms (MR 1.5(e)); concurrent-conflict waivers (MR 1.7(b)(4)); former-client waivers (MR 1.9(a), (b)); prospective-client consents (MR 1.18(d)(1)); government-agency consents (MR 1.11(a), (d)); former-neutral consents (MR 1.12(a)). A writing from the lawyer confirming oral consent is enough.
Written notice | To the prospective client when screening (MR 1.18(d)(2)(ii)); to the former client (MR 1.10(a)(2)(ii)); to the government agency (MR 1.11(b)(2)); to the parties and tribunal (MR 1.12(c)(2)); to clients when selling a practice (MR 1.17(c)).
Written advice + reasonable opportunity | Settling a malpractice claim with an unrepresented client (MR 1.8(h)(2)); part of MR 1.8(a)(2).
Writing signed by the client | Contingent fees, including any contingent component (MR 1.5(c)); business deals with clients (MR 1.8(a)(3)); aggregate settlements (MR 1.8(g)). Some states: true retainers.
Client independently represented | Prospective malpractice-liability limits (MR 1.8(h)(1)).
Can't be consented away | Same-litigation claims between clients (MR 1.7(b)(3)); sex with a client (MR 1.8(j)); MR 1.5(d) fees; nonlawyer ownership (MR 5.4); blanket settlement authority; a proprietary interest in the litigation beyond a lien or civil contingent fee (MR 1.8(i)); literary rights during the engagement (MR 1.8(d)); financial assistance outside MR 1.8(e)'s exceptions.

# PART VI — Conflicts of Interest

## 23. Conflicts Overview and Personal-Interest Conflicts (MR 1.8, 1.7(a)(2)) WEEK 6
Reading: MR 1.7, 1.8, 1.18; Ch. 22.A–B. Ch. 22 is "several chapters in one." The recurring hypothetical: Ron Rainmaker's firm represents Mojo, and Petrified Petroleum comes calling.
The three kinds of conflicts (CB 557)

- (1) Personal interest: the lawyer's own interests against a client's (MR 1.8; 1.7(a)(2)).

- (2) Whom you know (loyalty): ongoing relationships with clients that tempt you to favor one over another, governed by the "concurrent client rule" (MR 1.7(a)).

- (3) What you know (confidentiality): confidential information you might share with, or use for, another client to the original client's disadvantage, governed by the "successive client" or "former client rule" (MR 1.9, 1.18(c)).

- Class quiz 22.A Q1: a "client's duty to the lawyer vs. the legal system" is not one of the categories.

NOTE Two observations to keep throughout Ch. 22 A continuum (CB 559): conflicting interests run from hardly any conflict to zero-sum opposition. Many are mild enough to need nothing beyond decency and common sense. No harm required (CB 561): a serious conflict breaches the duty by its mere existence and potential to harm. The most common consequence is disqualification, an order to get out and stay out before harm occurs (class quiz 22.A Q2). Conflicts can also bring discipline (no harm needed), fee forfeiture and disgorgement of fees paid during the conflict, and damages for actual harm. Two kinds of rules (CB 560): bright-line rules that forbid arrangements or require formal steps (most of MR 1.8), and general standards with a fuzzier threshold (MR 1.7(a)(2)'s "significant risk" of "material limitation").

Financial assistance to litigation clients: MR 1.8(e)
RULE MR 1.8(e) A lawyer shall not provide financial assistance to a client in connection with pending or contemplated litigation, except that a lawyer may (any one suffices): (1) advance court costs and expenses of litigation, repayment of which may be contingent on the outcome; (2) pay court costs and expenses of litigation for an indigent client; or (3) when representing an indigent client pro bono (through the lawyer's firm, a nonprofit legal services or public interest organization, or a law school clinical or pro bono program), give modest gifts for food, rent, transportation, medicine, and other basic living expenses, if the lawyer (all required): (i) doesn't promise, assure, or imply them before retention or as an inducement to continue; (ii) doesn't seek or accept reimbursement from the client, a relative, or anyone affiliated with the client; and (iii) doesn't publicize or advertise a willingness to give them to prospective clients.

- The ban reaches almost any assistance: a loan, guarantee, or gift (CB 563).

- Implicit exceptions (CB 566; any one suffices): (1) delaying or discounting your fee, or working pro bono; (2) a contingent fee; and (3) assistance to non-litigation clients or non-clients (the Rule covers only "pending or contemplated litigation").

- Class quiz 22.A Q5: lending a litigation client money for living expenses is prohibited, whatever the collateral (a lien on the client's car doesn't help).

Gifts and bequests: MR 1.8(c)

- A lawyer shall not (either is barred): (1) solicit any substantial gift from a client, including a testamentary gift; or (2) prepare an instrument giving the lawyer or a person related to the lawyer a substantial gift, unless the lawyer or other recipient is related to the client. "Related" means a spouse, child, grandchild, parent, grandparent, or other relative or individual with whom the lawyer or client maintains a close familial relationship (CB 569).

- Another lawyer must draft it. Accepting a modest unsolicited gift (a $100 bottle of wine) is fine. Class quiz 22.A Q7: drafting a will leaving the lawyer expensive paintings is "maybe": it depends on whether lawyer and client are closely enough related.

Literary and media rights: MR 1.8(d)

- Before the representation ends, a lawyer shall not make or negotiate an agreement giving the lawyer literary or media rights to a portrayal or account based in substantial part on information relating to the representation (CB 572). Class quiz 22.A Q3: taking all media and literary rights to the litigation violates MR 1.8(d); a discounted fee, a contingent fee, or the client's own bank loan doesn't.

Proprietary interests in the litigation: MR 1.8(i)

- A lawyer shall not acquire a proprietary interest in the cause of action or subject matter of litigation the lawyer is conducting for a client, except (any one suffices): (1) a lien authorized by law to secure the lawyer's fee or expenses; or (2) a reasonable contingent fee in a civil case (CB 572). Example: no ownership stake in the disputed parcel you're litigating over.

Business transactions with clients: MR 1.8(a)
RULE MR 1.8(a) A lawyer shall not enter into a business transaction with a client or knowingly acquire an ownership, possessory, security, or other pecuniary interest adverse to a client unless (all required): (1) the transaction and terms are fair and reasonable to the client and are fully disclosed and transmitted in writing in a manner that can be reasonably understood by the client; (2) the client is advised in writing of the desirability of seeking, and is given a reasonable opportunity to seek, the advice of independent legal counsel on the transaction; and (3) the client gives informed consent, in a writing signed by the client, to the essential terms of the transaction and the lawyer's role in it, including whether the lawyer is representing the client in the transaction.

- Scope is sweeping (CB 573): any business transaction with a client, or any acquisition of an interest adverse to a client (a lien on the client's property is the classic example). Loans, investing in the client's restaurant, taking stock as a fee.

- Three recognized exclusions (any one suffices): (1) an ordinary fee agreement paid in money (MR 1.5 governs instead); (2) an attorney's lien or security interest in the litigation claim or its proceeds, which many states exempt (some exempt it only to secure a contingent fee, and require MR 1.8(a) to secure an hourly or flat fee); and (3) standard commercial transactions for products or services the client generally markets to others (cmt [1]; class quiz 22.A Q8).

- Class quiz 22.A Q6: a contractual lien on the client's home (property other than the recovery) to secure the fee is a business transaction under MR 1.8(a) (cmt [16]): allowed only if fair and reasonable, with written advice to seek counsel and informed consent in a signed writing.

- Fairness alone is never enough. Miss any formal requirement and you face discipline, and the transaction is subject to rescission and restitution, even if it was completely fair (CB 580).

- Class quiz 22.A Q4: a lawyer who takes the client's business opportunity for herself breaches her fiduciary duty and forfeits her fees (Meinhard v. Salmon, Part IV).

The rest of MR 1.8
Rule | What it says
MR 1.8(b) | No using information relating to a current client's representation to the client's disadvantage without informed consent (Part III).
MR 1.8(f) | Third-party payors: client's informed consent, no interference with judgment, confidentiality protected (Part II).
MR 1.8(g) | Aggregate settlements of claims of two or more clients (or aggregated pleas in a criminal case) require each client's informed consent, in a writing signed by the client, after disclosure of the existence and nature of all claims or pleas and of each person's participation. Majority approval doesn't count.
MR 1.8(h) | Prospective malpractice limits require independent representation; settling a malpractice claim with an unrepresented client requires written advice to seek counsel (Part II).
MR 1.8(j) | No sexual relations with a client unless a consensual relationship predated the representation (Part IV).
MR 1.8(k) | Prohibitions (a) through (i) are imputed to every lawyer in the firm; (j) is personal and not imputed.

Personal-interest conflicts under MR 1.7(a)(2)

- The test is predictive (CB 582): a "significant risk" that the representation will be "materially limited" by a personal interest of the lawyer, judged before anything bad happens and even if nothing ever does. Consent cures it if consentable (MR 1.7(b)).

- Relationships with opposing counsel or parties (ABA Op. 494; CB 582): (1) intimate and close family relationships almost always create a conflict; (2) friendships may, depending on their nature and strength; and (3) acquaintances are unlikely to. Even when no conflict arises, the connection may matter enough to disclose under MR 1.4; err on the side of disclosure and consent (CB 583).

- Lawyers related by blood or marriage on opposite sides (MR 1.7 cmt [11]): each needs the client's informed consent, and the conflict isn't imputed to their firms.

- Other personal interests: a lawyer negotiating for a job with the opponent's firm (cmt [10]); a defense lawyer angling for a prosecutor job or running for DA who calls his client a "monster"; a lawyer's own exposure for the conduct at issue.

- Class quiz 22.A Q9 and Q10: a mere acquaintance with the opposing party "generally require[s] no action," so accept without disclosing. An ex-spouse on the other side is a close personal relationship, a MR 1.7(a)(2) conflict: notify the client and proceed only with its informed consent, confirmed in writing (the ex-spouse isn't the one who consents).

- Imputation: personal-interest conflicts under MR 1.7(a)(2) generally aren't imputed unless other firm lawyers are similarly affected (CB 583; MR 1.10(a)(1)).

## 24. Concurrent Clients: The Concurrent Client Rule (MR 1.7) WEEK 6
RULE MR 1.7 — conflict of interest: current clients (a) A lawyer shall not represent a client if the representation involves a concurrent conflict of interest, which exists if (any one suffices): (1) the representation of one client will be directly adverse to another client; or (2) there is a significant risk that the representation of one or more clients will be materially limited by the lawyer's responsibilities to another client, a former client, or a third person, or by a personal interest of the lawyer. (b) Notwithstanding a concurrent conflict, a lawyer may represent a client if (all required): (1) the lawyer reasonably believes that the lawyer will be able to provide competent and diligent representation to each affected client; (2) the representation is not prohibited by law; (3) the representation does not involve the assertion of a claim by one client against another client represented by the lawyer in the same litigation or other proceeding before a tribunal; and (4) each affected client gives informed consent, confirmed in writing.

Direct adversity: MR 1.7(a)(1)

- The classic example: representing one current client in litigation or negotiation against another current client represented by other counsel. Forbidden without both clients' informed consent, confirmed in writing (CB 598).

- Unrelated matters still count (CB 600). Because the rule rests on loyalty, the adversity need not be in the same or a related matter, and no confidential information need be at risk. Suing a current closing client in a tort case is a conflict.

- "Directly adverse" means head-on, nose-to-nose adversity in the same litigation or transaction (CB 603). It also covers cross-examining a current client as an adverse witness and serving a third-party subpoena on a current client (class quiz 22.B Q4, Q6). Economic competitors aren't directly adverse (cmt [6]): representing Bullseye and Wal-Mark, each sued by its own employees, is fine (class quiz 22.B Q5).

- Prospective clients: before taking a new matter, ask whether the new client would be directly adverse to a current client; if so, decline unless both properly consent (CB 599; class quiz 22.B Q1: decline the engagement unless both Opal and Nona waive).

- Discovered midstream: if a concurrent conflict arises after both engagements are underway, withdraw as soon as possible, probably from both (CB 599).

Current or former client? The hot-potato rule

- The line matters (CB 600): you may never be adverse to a current client, but you may be adverse to a former client in any matter where you can't use its confidential information against it. When an engagement's endpoint is unclear, the client may still be current (Part II).

- The hot-potato rule (CB 601): you may not drop a current client "like a hot potato" to turn it into a former client so you can take a matter against it for a client you like better. Violating it isn't a MR 1.7 violation, so no discipline; the consequence is disqualification from the new engagement (class quiz 22.B Q1–Q2).

Material limitation: MR 1.7(a)(2)
Two rough categories, treated the same (CB 605):

- (1) Currently indirect conflicts (CB 606): adversity isn't nose-to-nose in the same matter but is serious now. Weigh how the indirectly affected client will be affected and how adverse the effects are likely to be. Positional conflicts (inconsistent positions on an issue of law or fact for two clients in different cases) usually need no consent, unless there is "a significant risk that a lawyer's action on behalf of one client will materially limit the lawyer's effectiveness in representing another client in a different case; for example, when a decision favoring one client will create a precedent likely to seriously weaken the position taken on behalf of the other client" (MR 1.7 cmt [24]). Opposite positions on the same ordinance in the same court qualify (class quiz 22.B Q3, Q8). Even a positional conflict that needs no consent can hurt client relations.

- (2) Possible future conflicts (CB 607): adversity is insignificant now, but there is a reasonable possibility it will become serious or direct later. If so, you must not proceed unless you inform all affected clients and get their informed consent, confirmed in writing, up front, or else represent only one.

Joint representation

- The most common possible-future conflict (CB 608): joint clients' interests can almost always diverge, which requires disclosure and every joint client's informed consent, confirmed in writing, at the outset. If the conflict becomes actual later, more steps are needed (below).

- Driver and passenger (class quiz 22.B Q11): the classic conflict is the passenger's possible claim against the driver; there could be a conflict if the evidence leads the passenger to want a cross-claim. Co-defendants (class quiz 22.B Q9): once the facts give one defendant reason to blame the other, the clients are actually adverse, and the lawyer should withdraw from both (MR 1.9 then bars staying on for either against the other). In criminal cases, ordinarily decline to represent more than one co-defendant (cmt [23]).

- Forming a business for several clients is permitted with each client's informed consent, confirmed in writing, about the conflicts and the lawyer's inability to advocate for any one of them (cmt [28]; class quiz 22.B Q10). Scriveners (documenting a deal the clients already struck) and aggregate settlements (MR 1.8(g); class quiz 22.B Q7) raise their own issues (CB 610–611).

- Divorcing spouses in a contested proceeding: representing both is a nonconsentable direct conflict (MR 1.7(b)(3); class quiz 22.B Q12). The clients' satisfaction is irrelevant.

Once you have a concurrent conflict (CB 614)

- (1) You must either abstain or withdraw, or obtain all affected clients' informed consent, confirmed in writing (better, signed by each), if the conflict is consentable and the clients agree.

- (2) Otherwise, discipline and disqualification can follow. The conflict exists as soon as interests conflict or a significant risk arises; no actual harm is required.

- (3) If the conflict caused actual harm, tort damages are available.

- (4) Many jurisdictions treat fees incurred under a serious unwaived conflict as unearned and forfeited.

## 25. Former and Prospective Clients: The Successive Client Rule (MR 1.9, 1.18(c)) WEEK 7
Reading: MR 1.9; Ch. 22.C.
RULE MR 1.9 — duties to former clients (a) A lawyer who has formerly represented a client in a matter shall not thereafter represent another person (all elements bar the representation): (1) in the same or a substantially related matter; (2) in which that person's interests are materially adverse to the interests of the former client; (3) unless the former client gives informed consent, confirmed in writing. (b) A lawyer shall not knowingly represent a person in the same or a substantially related matter in which a firm with which the lawyer formerly was associated had previously represented a client (1) whose interests are materially adverse to that person, and (2) about whom the lawyer had acquired information protected by MR 1.6 and 1.9(c) that is material to the matter, unless the former client gives informed consent, confirmed in writing. (c) A lawyer who has formerly represented a client, or whose present or former firm has, shall not thereafter (1) use information relating to the representation to the former client's disadvantage except as the Rules permit or when the information has become generally known; or (2) reveal information relating to the representation except as the Rules permit.

- The point (CB 637): the old engagement and the new one must not involve the same dispute or deal, or a substantively similar one, where the new client's interests are materially adverse to the former client's. Unrelated later matters are fine.

- Prospective clients (MR 1.18(c); CB 629): similar language, but the bar applies only if the information received "could be significantly harmful" to the prospective client in the matter, which makes the protection a little narrower than for former clients.

- Current clients (CB 629): the concurrent client rule already forbids adversity in any respect, so current clients' confidences get broader protection.

NOTE A practical paraphrase of the successive client rule (CB 630) When a lawyer owes a duty of confidentiality to anyone (a prospective, current, or former client, or someone else), the lawyer must not take on or continue an engagement in which the lawyer might reasonably be able to use that confidential information against the person to whom the duty is owed.

The substantial relationship test (CB 630–635)

- Where it's used: mostly in discipline and civil disqualification proceedings (CB 631).

- Two methods, often mixed (any one suffices): (1) the person seeking protection describes in general terms the confidential information actually confided, or discloses specific confidences under seal or in camera (CB 632); or (2) without revealing anything, it describes the earlier engagement from the outside, and the court infers what confidential information was likely imparted, compares it with what is likely to matter in the new engagement (also viewed from the outside), and asks whether the two are substantially related (CB 633). Don't confuse a substantial relationship between matters with how "substantial" the lawyer-client relationship was.

- Playbook information (CB 635): general information about how a client operates (its "plays") is confidential, but ordinarily isn't enough to create a substantial relationship unless it is so voluminous, detailed, or specifically applicable that it creates a substantial unfair advantage.

Consequences of violating the successive client rule (CB 637)

- (1) Discipline under MR 1.9(a) or 1.18, limited to information received from a former or prospective client.

- (2) Disqualification reaches more broadly in most states: it is also available when a lawyer holds substantially related confidential information from anyone to whom the lawyer assumed a duty of confidentiality outside an actual or prospective client relationship. Morrison Knudsen v. Hancock Rothert & Bunshoft (Cal. Ct. App. 1999): disqualified lawyers had acquired a duty to a third party because their client in the old engagement had assumed one.

- (3) Fee forfeiture for a substantial, serious conflict, with possible disgorgement of fees paid.

- (4) Damages or restitution only if the conflict actually caused compensable harm or an ill-gotten gain (e.g., insider trading on the former client's information). No use or harm is required for disqualification.

Westinghouse Elec. Corp. v. Kerr-McGee Corp., 580 F.2d 1311 (7th Cir. 1978) — confidentiality owed to non-clients NOTE CASE · WEEK 7
Facts: A law firm representing a petroleum industry trade association gathered confidential information from member oil companies, promising to keep it confidential, while another office of the firm represented Westinghouse in an antitrust suit against some of those same companies.
Held: The firm was disqualified: by promising confidentiality, it had assumed a duty to the member companies, which the court described as an implied attorney-client relationship.
Why it matters: A duty of confidentiality, and the disqualification that protects it, can arise without a full client relationship. The casebook agrees with the result but not the "implied representation" reasoning: only one duty was assumed (CB 256, 637).

## 26. Imputation and Screening (MR 1.10, 1.0(k)) WEEK 8
Reading: MR 1.10; Ch. 22.D.
RULE MR 1.10 — imputation of conflicts: general rule (a) While lawyers are associated in a firm, none of them shall knowingly represent a client when any one of them practicing alone would be prohibited by MR 1.7 or 1.9, unless (any one suffices): (1) the prohibition is based on a personal interest of the disqualified lawyer and does not present a significant risk of materially limiting the representation by the remaining lawyers; or (2) the prohibition is based on MR 1.9(a) or (b), arises out of the disqualified lawyer's association with a prior firm, and (all required): (i) the disqualified lawyer is timely screened from any participation in the matter and is apportioned no part of the fee; (ii) written notice is promptly given to any affected former client, describing the screening procedures, stating the firm's and the screened lawyer's compliance, stating that review may be available before a tribunal, and agreeing to respond promptly to written inquiries or objections; and (iii) certifications of compliance are provided by the screened lawyer and a partner, at reasonable intervals on the former client's written request and when the screening ends. (b) When a lawyer has left a firm, the firm may represent a person materially adverse to a client the departed lawyer represented and the firm no longer represents, unless (both required for the bar): (1) the matter is the same or substantially related; and (2) a lawyer remaining in the firm has material information protected by MR 1.6 and 1.9(c). (c) An imputed disqualification may be waived by the affected client under the conditions of MR 1.7. (d) Government lawyers' firms are governed by MR 1.11 (Part VII).

- The general rule (CB 647): if any lawyer in a practice organization has a conflict (or a relationship or knowledge that could create one), every lawyer and the organization itself is deemed to have it. In most situations the presumption is conclusive (CB 649). It applies across offices and states: Keisha, Chrissy, Victor in Garden, and Abigail in Keystone are all conflicted (class quiz 22.D Q1).

- Rebuttable presumptions (CB 650): in seven defined situations, the firm may rebut imputation, and other lawyers may proceed without any client consent as long as the personally disqualified lawyer stays out. Most states apply the same exceptions to disqualification.

Rebutting imputation with situational facts
Exception | When it applies
Personal interest (MR 1.10(a)(1)) | Narrower than it sounds (CB 652): most personal-interest conflicts are conclusively imputed by MR 1.8(k). The ones that aren't are sex with a client (MR 1.8(j)) and MR 1.7(a)(2) personal-interest conflicts. Class quiz 22.D Q2: Amir's religious objection to suing the church isn't imputed if he does no work on the matter and his beliefs create no significant risk of limiting Leona's representation (MR 1.10 cmt [3]).
The mobile lawyer's actual knowledge (MR 1.9(b)) | A lawyer who changes jobs brings to, and imputes within, the new firm only confidential information the lawyer personally knew (CB 654). It has no effect on concurrent conflicts. Class quiz 22.D Q3: Lulu, whose conflict was purely imputed at her old firm and who acquired no material information about the adverse party, needs no screen (MR 1.9(b), cmt [5]).
Everyone who knew has left (MR 1.10(b)) | Every lawyer exposed to the client's information must have left, and no trace of it (paper or digital) may remain (CB 658). It applies only to successive conflicts, never concurrent ones.

Rebutting imputation with an ethical screen

- What a screen is (MR 1.0(k); CB 660): prophylactic measures restricting confidential information to a lawyer or small group and keeping it from everyone else in the firm, through the timely imposition of procedures reasonably adequate to protect the information. Most conflicts can't be cured by a screen, and a screen never cures a concurrent conflict.

- Common features (MR 1.0 cmts [8]–[10]; all expected): (1) the screened lawyer's written undertaking not to communicate about the matter or touch its files; (2) written notice and instructions to all other firm personnel forbidding communication with the screened lawyer about it; (3) denial of access to files and information, paper and electronic; (4) periodic reminders to everyone; (5) no share of the fee where a Rule requires it (MR 1.10(a)(2), 1.11, 1.12, 1.18(d)); and (6) timeliness: in place as soon as practical once the firm knows or reasonably should know a screen is needed (cmt [10]).

- Only four successive-conflict situations can be cured by a screen alone (CB 663–667; any one suffices): (1) nonlawyer staff exposed to confidential information (MR 1.10 cmt [4]); (2) a lawyer exposed to the information before becoming a lawyer, e.g., as a paralegal or law clerk (MR 1.10 cmt [4]); (3) a lateral lawyer's actual knowledge from a prior firm (MR 1.10(a)(2), with notice and certifications); and (4) a prospective client's information, if the lawyer took reasonable measures to avoid more exposure than needed to decide whether to take the matter, is timely screened with no part of the fee, and written notice is promptly given to the prospective client (MR 1.18(d)(2)).

- Government lawyers (MR 1.11) and former judges and neutrals (MR 1.12) have their own screening rules (Part VII).

## 27. Addressing Conflicts: Abstention, Consent, and Conflict Checks WEEK 9
Reading: Ch. 22.E–F.
Abstain or withdraw (CB 678–679)

- Abstaining: "No conflict; no consequences." But you can abstain only from an engagement you never took on. Once the prospective client reasonably believes you're his lawyer, you are, and a conflicted engagement then requires withdrawal, likely from every engagement creating the conflict, unless all affected clients give informed consent, confirmed in writing, to which engagements continue and on what terms.

- Two ways to proceed (CB 680; any one suffices): (1) rebut imputation and staff the matter with lawyers who aren't personally disqualified (MR 1.10); or (2) if the conflict is consentable, obtain all affected clients' informed consent in the required form and substance.

When is a conflict consentable? (CB 681)
RULE The four nonconsentable conflicts A conflict can't be cured by consent when (any one suffices): (1) the representation is prohibited by law (MR 1.7(b)(2)); (2) it is one of the personal-interest conflicts MR 1.8 forbids outright; (3) it involves the assertion of a claim by one client against another client the lawyer represents in the same proceeding before a tribunal (MR 1.7(b)(3)); or (4) the lawyer doesn't reasonably believe the lawyer can provide competent and diligent representation to each affected client (MR 1.7(b)(1)). The belief must be subjectively held and objectively reasonable; if no reasonable client would consent, the conflict is nonconsentable.

- Class quiz 22.E–F Q1: co-defendants Maru and Neo blame each other and have incompatible defenses, so Oscar can't reasonably represent both (MR 1.7(b)(1), cmt [23]). Q2: a braking discrepancy and different injuries between two clients from one accident need evaluation but don't automatically bar Shiva from representing both; with informed consent, confirmed in writing, and MR 1.7(b) satisfied, she may (cmts [18], [23]).

What makes consent informed? (CB 684)

- An enforceable waiver should, and arguably must, disclose (all required): (1) "the facts and circumstances giving rise to the situation" (MR 1.0 cmt [6]); (2) "the material risks of" the proposed course (MR 1.0(e)); (3) the "reasonably available alternatives," including the client's absolute right to refuse consent (MR 1.0(e)); and (4) the client's right to seek independent advice and take the time needed (MR 1.0 cmt [6]; the casebook recommends always advising independent counsel).

- Joint representation disclosures (CB 686–687): jointly represented clients have no privilege against one another and, in most states, no confidentiality against one another. Say so up front, and say what happens if interests diverge (the lawyer may have to withdraw from both). Class quiz 22.E–F Q4: Amity can't give informed consent to a joint estate plan without learning of Buzz's child; Chuck must first get Buzz's authorization to disclose (MR 1.6(a)), and if Buzz insists on secrecy, withdraw from both rather than finish the wills while withholding material information (MR 1.7 cmts [18], [19], [31]).

- Advance waivers (MR 1.7 cmt [22]; CB 691): "The effectiveness of such waivers is generally determined by the extent to which the client reasonably understands the material risks that the waiver entails." That usually requires describing the kind of conflict that later materializes. A specific, explained waiver is more likely to work than an open-ended one, and no advance waiver can authorize a future nonconsentable conflict (class quiz 22.E–F Q7).

- When interests later diverge: the initial consent doesn't cover new antagonism. Continuing for one of two doctors requires both doctors' informed consent, confirmed in writing, plus compliance with duties to the departing client (MR 1.7 cmt [29]; MR 1.9; class quiz 22.E–F Q6). Cleo, representing her own client's litigation opponent on conflicting positions about the same trade dress, should withdraw from both (class quiz 22.E–F Q3).

- Every affected client consents. Nicole may represent Orin against current firm client Morris, even in an unrelated transaction, only if both Morris and Orin consent, confirmed in writing (MR 1.7(a)(1), cmt [7]; MR 1.10(a); class quiz 22.E–F Q5).

The form of consent (CB 692)

- Most states require informed consent confirmed in writing; a few require a writing signed by the client, which is the better practice everywhere.

- Silence is not consent: "Obtaining informed consent will usually require an affirmative response... In general, a lawyer may not assume consent from a client's or other person's silence" (MR 1.0 cmt [7]).

- Disclosure comes first. Consent given before the disclosure and explanation "is no consent at all."

Sheppard Mullin v. J-M Manufacturing Co., 6 Cal. 5th 59 (2018) — advance waivers and undisclosed conflicts NOTE CASE · WEEK 9
Facts: Sheppard, Mullin, Richter & Hampton took on J-M in a qui tam suit under an engagement letter with a broad advance waiver, without telling J-M that the firm was then also representing one of the public entities suing J-M, in unrelated matters.
Held: The advance waiver didn't cover a known, existing conflict the firm failed to disclose, so J-M's consent wasn't informed and the engagement agreement was unenforceable; the firm could at most seek quantum meruit fees, depending on the seriousness of the violation.
Why it matters: Informed consent requires disclosing conflicts you know about; boilerplate can't waive what wasn't explained (MR 1.7 cmt [22]). The casebook notes the amicus brief arguing that big firms demand such waivers on a take-it-or-leave-it basis.
Seeing conflicts coming (Ch. 22.F; CB 694)

- Practice organizations must maintain policies, procedures, and systems to recognize and respond to conflicts before agreeing to a new engagement.

- A conflicts database tracks every interaction that may have created duties to anyone: clients, prospective clients, adverse parties, co-parties, and people to whom confidentiality was promised. Check each potential engagement, and everyone involved, against it.

- Run the check before receiving more than the minimum information (MR 1.18(d)(2)), and update it when parties are added, firms merge, or lawyers join (MR 1.6(b)(7)). MR 5.1(a) makes partners responsible for having such a system (Part IX).

ROADMAP Conflicts analysis in order 1. Identify every person to whom duties are owed: current, former, and prospective clients, and non-clients promised confidentiality. 2. Classify the conflict: personal interest (MR 1.8, 1.7(a)(2)); concurrent (MR 1.7(a)(1)–(2)); successive (MR 1.9, 1.18(c)). 3. Impute it across the firm (MR 1.10(a), 1.8(k)), then ask whether imputation can be rebutted by situational facts or a screen. 4. Ask whether it is consentable (MR 1.7(b)(1)–(3); MR 1.8's outright bans). 5. Get informed consent from every affected client in the required form, or abstain or withdraw (MR 1.16(a)(1)). 6. Name the consequences: disqualification, discipline, fee forfeiture, damages.

# PART VII — Government Lawyers

## 28. The Government Lawyer's Client, Conflicts, and Extra Duties WEEK 10
Reading: MR 1.11, 1.12, 3.8; Ch. 25. Week 10 also brought the 15-question multiple-choice exam (Oct. 26).

- Same rules, with a few twists (CB 816): government lawyers follow the same Rules as everyone else, plus (1) obligations outside the Rules that apply because they are government employees; (2) recurring situations that make the general Rules hard to apply; and (3) two Rules that apply only to them: MR 1.11 (conflicts for current and former government lawyers) and MR 3.8 (prosecutors).

- Where they may practice (CB 817): state and local government lawyers need a license where they practice, like anyone else. The federal government requires a license in at least one state or D.C., and by statute (28 U.S.C. § 517) a federal lawyer may appear in any state or federal court nationwide (class quiz Ch. 25 Q5). Federal lawyers still follow the conduct rules of the jurisdiction or court where they appear (the McDade Amendment, 28 U.S.C. § 530B); with no tribunal involved, the rules of the licensing jurisdiction generally govern.

Identifying the government client (CB 818–827)

- Often clear: a specific state, county, city, or agency. Sometimes the lawyer represents an interest or function of government, nominally represents the agency head while really representing the agency, or personally represents an employee, but only to protect the employer's interests too.

- The law that creates the entity defines it (CB 818): constitutions, statutes, and regulations identify the client and the official empowered to direct counsel and speak for it. The Rules won't tell you who calls the shots.

- Prosecutors represent the sovereign: the State or "the People," not the DA personally, the victim, or the investigating officer, who are witnesses (class quiz Ch. 25 Q2, Q6). The victim's own private lawyer represents the victim (Q7).

- Defending government actors (CB 822): governments act only through people, so suits often name employees. In an official-capacity suit the true client is the agency, and the named official is its procedural representative (Q3, Q8). When a government lawyer represents an employee personally (e.g., a Bivens damages claim against a federal officer), the employee is a full client owed every duty, yet the lawyer represents her only to serve the government's interests, so the agency's interests always count too. Conflicts can develop midstream, so disclose and get informed consents from everyone at the outset (CB 827).

Conflicts within government (CB 825)

- Are two agencies one client? Sometimes substantive law says whether agencies are distinct enough to be different "clients," so one government law office can represent one against the other. Sometimes officials agree which lawyers handle each side; written informed consents resolve any lingering concern.

- Absent agreement, infer the client from reasonable expectations, considering (weighed together): (1) how the government client is legally defined and funded; (2) whether it has independent legal authority over the matter; and (3) the extent to which the matter has broader implications for the government. Resolve doubt in favor of detailed written disclosures and consents all around.

- Even when two entities aren't the same client, MR 1.7(a)(2) still bars a significant risk of material limitation.

Duties outside the Rules (CB 829)

- Leaders of government law offices and courts often expect a "higher standard" of government lawyers. Specific laws apply that don't bind private lawyers: conflict-of-interest statutes, "ethics in government" laws, codes of conduct, personnel rules, and gift rules that often bar even shared meals from people with business before the agency.

- Class quiz Ch. 25 Q1: may Patty accept Derrick's offer? "Maybe": besides the Rules, she must check the gift laws and other government ethics rules.

## 29. The Revolving Door (MR 1.11, 1.12) WEEK 10

- MR 1.11 covers service as any "public officer or employee," not only as a practicing lawyer (CB 831).

- Concurrent conflicts are not imputed in government (CB 832). An individual government lawyer may not take part in a matter adverse to her own current client, but others in her office may. MR 1.10 doesn't apply (MR 1.10(d)); MR 1.11 does.

RULE MR 1.11(a)–(c) — former government lawyers (a) A lawyer who formerly served as a public officer or employee (1) is subject to MR 1.9(c); and (2) shall not otherwise represent a client in connection with a matter in which the lawyer participated personally and substantially as a public officer or employee, unless the appropriate government agency gives its informed consent, confirmed in writing. (b) When a lawyer is disqualified under (a), no lawyer in the lawyer's firm may knowingly undertake or continue the matter unless (all required): (1) the disqualified lawyer is timely screened from any participation and is apportioned no part of the fee; and (2) written notice is promptly given to the appropriate government agency to enable it to ascertain compliance. (c) A lawyer having information the lawyer knows is confidential government information about a person, acquired as a public officer or employee, may not represent a private client whose interests are adverse to that person in a matter in which the information could be used to the person's material disadvantage. The firm may proceed only if the disqualified lawyer is timely screened and apportioned no part of the fee. (e) "Matter" includes (1) any judicial or other proceeding, application, request for a ruling or other determination, contract, claim, controversy, investigation, charge, accusation, arrest, or other particular matter involving a specific party or parties; and (2) any other matter covered by the agency's conflict rules.

Four levels of prior government involvement (CB 833–837)
Level | What it means | Response
(1) Participated personally and substantially in the same "matter" | The narrow MR 1.11(e) "matter": a particular matter involving specific parties (not rulemaking). The bar applies even if the private client's interests aren't adverse to the government: it forbids switching sides, and more. | The former government lawyer is personally out unless the agency gives informed consent, confirmed in writing (MR 1.11(a)(2)). The firm may proceed with a timely screen, no fee share, and prompt written notice to the agency (MR 1.11(b)); more measures are probably needed to make the screen effective.
(2) No personal and substantial participation, but has "confidential government information" about a third party | Information obtained under governmental authority that the government is prohibited by law from disclosing or has a privilege not to disclose, and that isn't otherwise public (e.g., that someone was secretly investigated, or a sealed indictment). It must concern a third party adverse to the new client and be usable to that party's material disadvantage. | Personally disqualified; the firm may proceed with a timely screen and no fee share (MR 1.11(c)). No notice requirement.
(3) Participated only in something that isn't a "matter" (e.g., rulemaking), or knows ordinary confidential information that isn't confidential government information | A major departure from the private-sector rules. | No one is disqualified and no screen is required (some firms screen anyway). The lawyer may not use the information to the former government client's disadvantage or disclose it (MR 1.9(c)); if she can't work on the matter without doing so, she must stay out.
(4) No involvement and no confidential information | Same as the regular rules. | No conflict; nothing required.

- No cooling-off period. The Model Rules turn on personal and substantial participation, not time (class quiz Ch. 25 Q9: the former prosecutor is disqualified only if she participated personally and substantially in the prosecution).

- Class quiz Ch. 25 Q10: Adina, personally disqualified under MR 1.11(a)(2), must be screened, with no share of the fee and written notice to the Department of Labor, before her new firm can keep the wage-and-hour case. Q11: Praveen's nonpublic Medicare data about Dr. Hildenbrant is confidential government information under MR 1.11(c); he should have been disqualified and screened, and he certainly couldn't use or share it.

RULE MR 1.11(d) — current government lawyers A lawyer currently serving as a public officer or employee (1) is subject to MR 1.7 and 1.9; and (2) shall not (either is barred): (i) participate in a matter in which the lawyer participated personally and substantially while in private practice or nongovernmental employment, unless the agency gives informed consent, confirmed in writing; or (ii) negotiate for private employment with any person who is involved as a party or as lawyer for a party in a matter in which the lawyer is participating personally and substantially, except that a law clerk to a judge, adjudicative officer, or arbitrator may negotiate as MR 1.12(b) allows.

- Why (d)(2)(i) bars even helping the former client (CB 839): MR 1.9(a) bars only adversity to a former client, but MR 1.11(d)(2)(i) bars participation altogether, to guard against using government power for the special benefit of the former client.

- Why "revolving door" (CB 841): many lawyers cycle in and out of government, some more than once.

RULE MR 1.12 — former judges, arbitrators, mediators, other neutrals, and law clerks (a) Except as stated in (d), a lawyer shall not represent anyone in connection with a matter in which the lawyer participated personally and substantially as a judge or other adjudicative officer, a law clerk to one, or an arbitrator, mediator, or other third-party neutral, unless all parties to the proceeding give informed consent, confirmed in writing. (b) A judge, adjudicative officer, arbitrator, mediator, or other neutral shall not negotiate for employment with any party or lawyer for a party in a matter in which the lawyer is participating personally and substantially. A law clerk may, but only after notifying the judge or other adjudicative officer. (c) If a lawyer is disqualified by (a), the firm may proceed only if (all required): (1) the disqualified lawyer is timely screened and apportioned no part of the fee; and (2) written notice is promptly given to the parties and any appropriate tribunal. (d) A partisan arbitrator on a multimember panel may later represent that party.

## 30. Special Duties of Prosecutors (MR 3.8) WEEK 10
Each paragraph of MR 3.8 marks a point in the criminal process where a prosecutor must favor justice over merely winning (CB 843). A prosecutor "may strike hard blows, [but] is not at liberty to strike foul ones" (Berger v. United States).
RULE MR 3.8 — the prosecutor in a criminal case shall: (a) refrain from prosecuting a charge that the prosecutor knows is not supported by probable cause; (b) make reasonable efforts to assure that the accused has been advised of the right to, and the procedure for obtaining, counsel and has been given reasonable opportunity to obtain counsel; (c) not seek to obtain from an unrepresented accused a waiver of important pretrial rights, such as the right to a preliminary hearing; (d) make timely disclosure to the defense of all evidence or information known to the prosecutor that tends to negate the guilt of the accused or mitigates the offense, and, in connection with sentencing, disclose to the defense and to the tribunal all unprivileged mitigating information known to the prosecutor, unless relieved by a protective order of the tribunal; (e) not subpoena a lawyer in a grand jury or other criminal proceeding to present evidence about a past or present client unless the prosecutor reasonably believes (all required): (1) the information sought is not protected from disclosure by any applicable privilege; (2) the evidence sought is essential to the successful completion of an ongoing investigation or prosecution; and (3) there is no other feasible alternative to obtain the information; (f) except for statements necessary to inform the public of the nature and extent of the prosecutor's action that serve a legitimate law enforcement purpose, refrain from extrajudicial comments that have a substantial likelihood of heightening public condemnation of the accused, and exercise reasonable care to prevent investigators, police, and others assisting the prosecutor from making statements the prosecutor couldn't make under MR 3.6 or this Rule; (g) when the prosecutor knows of new, credible, and material evidence creating a reasonable likelihood that a convicted defendant did not commit an offense of which the defendant was convicted: (1) promptly disclose it to an appropriate court or authority; and (2) if the conviction was obtained in the prosecutor's jurisdiction, (i) promptly disclose it to the defendant unless a court authorizes delay, and (ii) undertake further investigation, or make reasonable efforts to cause an investigation, to determine whether the defendant was convicted of an offense the defendant did not commit; and (h) when the prosecutor knows of clear and convincing evidence establishing that a defendant in the prosecutor's jurisdiction was convicted of an offense the defendant did not commit, seek to remedy the conviction.

- (a) Probable cause (CB 844): a floor, not a target; the Rule is violated only when the prosecutor knows probable cause is lacking.

- (b)–(c) Pretrial rights (CB 846): the prosecutor can't sit idly by if the court fails to advise the accused of the right to counsel. Class quiz Ch. 25 Q4: gently remind the judge that the defendant wasn't advised of the right to counsel and that her finances should be assessed for appointed counsel. MR 3.8(c) helps ensure that waivers of rights like a preliminary hearing are knowing and voluntary. It doesn't apply to an accused appearing pro se with the tribunal's approval, or forbid lawful questioning of an uncharged suspect who has knowingly waived counsel and silence (cmt [2]).

- (d) Disclosure (CB 847): broader than the constitutional rule. Brady v. Maryland and Giglio v. United States require disclosing material exculpatory and impeachment evidence as due process, but the Constitution requires less for impeachment evidence before a plea (United States v. Ruiz) and limits mandated disclosure of impeachment material (Strickler v. Greene). MR 3.8(d) has no materiality limit: everything that tends to negate guilt or mitigate, timely.

- (e) Subpoenas to lawyers (CB 849): the testimony must be (1) unprivileged, (2) essential, and (3) the only feasible source.

- (f) Publicity (CB 850): on top of MR 3.6 (Part VIII); no "perp walk" commentary that heightens condemnation.

- (g)–(h) Wrongful convictions (CB 851). "Credible" means a reasonable factfinder could believe it; "material" means it creates a reasonable likelihood the defendant didn't commit the offense, so it must bear on guilt (impeachment or mitigation evidence is covered by MR 3.8(d) instead, except impeachment so devastating that it meets the standard).

What the prosecutor knows | Conviction in the prosecutor's jurisdiction | Conviction elsewhere
New, credible, material evidence (reasonable likelihood of innocence) | MR 3.8(g)(1)–(2): disclose to an appropriate court or authority; disclose to the defendant (unless a court authorizes delay); investigate or cause an investigation | MR 3.8(g)(1): disclose to an appropriate court or authority
Clear and convincing evidence of innocence | MR 3.8(h): seek to remedy the conviction (and (g) duties) | MR 3.8(g)(1) only

- Class quiz Ch. 25 Q12–Q13: evidence that is new, credible, and material but not clear and convincing, in his own jurisdiction, triggers MR 3.8(g)(2): disclose to Norman and investigate (and (g)(1) disclosure to a court or authority too). The duty to seek to remedy the conviction requires clear and convincing evidence of wrongful conviction in the prosecutor's jurisdiction (MR 3.8(h)).

- Truthfulness binds prosecutors too: police may use some deception in interrogation (Frazier v. Cupp), but prosecutors may not lie to a suspect about the evidence (MR 4.1(a), 8.4(c); Part VIII).

Brady v. Maryland, 373 U.S. 83 (1963) — suppressing exculpatory evidence NOTE CASE · WEEK 10
Facts: The prosecution withheld a co-defendant's statement admitting that he, not Brady, did the actual killing.
Held: Suppressing evidence favorable to an accused that is material to guilt or punishment violates due process, whatever the prosecutor's good or bad faith.
Why it matters: The constitutional floor that MR 3.8(d) builds on. Giglio v. United States (1972) extends it to impeachment evidence (a promise of leniency to a key witness), and United States v. Bagley (1985) defines materiality as a reasonable probability of a different result. MR 3.8(d) has no materiality limit.
Berger v. United States, 295 U.S. 78 (1935) — the prosecutor's role NOTE CASE · WEEK 10
Facts: A federal prosecutor misstated facts, put words in witnesses' mouths, and made improper insinuations in a counterfeiting trial.
Held: The misconduct required a new trial. The prosecutor represents a sovereign "whose interest... in a criminal prosecution is not that it shall win a case, but that justice shall be done"; he "may strike hard blows, [but] is not at liberty to strike foul ones."
Why it matters: The source of the "higher standard" courts expect of government lawyers (CB 829) and the theme of MR 3.8.

# PART VIII — Ethics in Advocacy

## 31. The Lawyer as Counselor and Neutral (MR 2.1, 2.3, 2.4, 3.9) WEEK 11
Reading: MR 2.1, 2.3, 2.4, 3.1–3.7, 3.9; Ch. 24.
RULE MR 2.1 — advisor In representing a client, a lawyer shall exercise independent professional judgment and render candid advice. In rendering advice, a lawyer may refer not only to law but to other considerations such as moral, economic, social, and political factors that may be relevant to the client's situation.

- Don't soften advice because the client won't like it (cmt [1]); purely technical legal advice can be inadequate (cmt [2]). When a client proposes something unlawful, MR 2.1 is the license for extra-legal advice about whether it's wise (Part XI). The client still decides objectives (MR 1.2(a)).

RULE MR 2.3 — evaluation for use by third persons (a) A lawyer may evaluate a matter affecting a client for someone other than the client if the lawyer reasonably believes the evaluation is compatible with other aspects of the relationship. (b) When the lawyer knows or reasonably should know the evaluation is likely to affect the client's interests materially and adversely, the lawyer shall not provide it unless the client gives informed consent. (c) Except as disclosure is authorized in connection with the report, information relating to the evaluation is otherwise protected by MR 1.6.

- Examples: a title opinion for a purchaser, an opinion letter for a lender, an audit-response letter (cmts [1], [6]). Whether the lawyer owes the third person a legal duty is a question of other law (cmt [3]); the casebook treats such reliance as one way to assume a duty of care to a non-client (Part II). Distinguish an evaluation from investigating a non-client, e.g., the vendor's title for the purchaser (cmt [2]).

RULE MR 2.4 — lawyer serving as third-party neutral (a) A lawyer is a third-party neutral when helping two or more non-clients resolve a dispute or other matter (arbitrator, mediator, or similar). (b) The neutral shall inform unrepresented parties that the lawyer is not representing them, and when the lawyer knows or reasonably should know a party doesn't understand the role, shall explain the difference between a neutral and a lawyer who represents a client.

- Later representing a party in the same matter is governed by MR 1.12 (Part VII). Lawyers representing clients in ADR follow the Rules: candor under MR 3.3 in binding arbitration (a "tribunal," MR 1.0(m)); otherwise MR 4.1 (cmt [5]).

RULE MR 3.9 — advocate in nonadjudicative proceedings A lawyer representing a client before a legislative body or administrative agency in a nonadjudicative proceeding (lobbying, rulemaking, hearings) shall (all required): (1) disclose that the appearance is in a representative capacity; and (2) conform to MR 3.3(a)–(c), 3.4(a)–(c), and 3.5.

- It applies to official hearings or meetings where the lawyer presents evidence or argument, not to bilateral negotiations with the government (cmt [3]).

## 32. Gathering and Handling Evidence (MR 3.4, 4.4) WEEK 11
The officer of the court (Ch. 24.A; CB 744)
Being "an officer of the court" brings three ideas into play (all three): (1) advocacy may draw extra scrutiny beyond other lawyer conduct; (2) courts expect behavior beyond the minimum demands of the Rules and procedure; and (3) the advocate's loyalty to the client is constrained by enforceable duties owed to the court and the legal system.
Investigate lawfully (Ch. 24.B.1; CB 746)

- MR 4.4(a): in representing a client, a lawyer shall not use methods of obtaining evidence that violate the legal rights of a third person (trespass, wiretapping, intrusion into seclusion).

- Class quiz Ch. 24 A–B Q1: an investigator videotaping the "housebound" plaintiff from a public street probably doesn't violate MR 4.4(a), unless local law forbids that surveillance. The lawyer answers for an investigator's unlawful methods (MR 5.3, 8.4(a)).

- Q2: prosecutors may not lie to a suspect about the evidence ("the video shows you in the bank" when it's impossible to tell). Police may use some deception in interrogation (Frazier v. Cupp), but lawyers, including prosecutors, are bound by MR 4.1(a) and 8.4(c) (CB 746 n.4).

- Q4: a prosecutor threatening to circulate humiliating photographs of a minor to coerce cooperation uses means with no substantial purpose other than to embarrass (MR 4.4(a)).

Discovery conduct (CB 748)
RULE MR 3.4(c)–(d) A lawyer shall not (c) knowingly disobey an obligation under the rules of a tribunal, except for an open refusal based on an assertion that no valid obligation exists; or (d) in pretrial procedure, make a frivolous discovery request or fail to make reasonably diligent effort to comply with a legally proper discovery request by an opposing party.

- Discovery misconduct is a disciplinary violation as well as sanctionable (FRCP 26(g), 37; Part I). Q5: openly refusing to produce the secret soda formula on the ground that no valid obligation exists isn't a MR 3.4(c) violation (though contempt or sanctions may follow so the issue can be reviewed). Ch. 24.C Q6: citing an unpublished opinion in violation of the court's rule violates MR 3.4(c), even though the brief candidly called it unpublished.

Retaining and handling evidence (Ch. 24.B.3; CB 748–752)
RULE MR 3.4(a)–(b), (f) A lawyer shall not (a) unlawfully obstruct another party's access to evidence, or unlawfully alter, destroy, or conceal a document or other material having potential evidentiary value, or counsel or assist another to do so; (b) falsify evidence, counsel or assist a witness to testify falsely, or offer an inducement to a witness prohibited by law; or (f) request a person other than a client to refrain from voluntarily giving relevant information to another party, unless (both required) (1) the person is a relative, employee, or other agent of the client, and (2) the lawyer reasonably believes the person's interests won't be adversely affected.

- "Unlawfully" matters (CB 748): lawyers lawfully withhold all the time: proper discovery objections, instructions not to answer privileged questions, advising a client not to talk to police.

- "Potential" matters (CB 749): the material needn't be admissible or requested; it need only be relevant to or potentially useful in a pending or reasonably foreseeable proceeding. Most jurisdictions forbid spoliation, and electronically stored information has intensified the focus.

- Consequences for the client (CB 750): monetary sanctions, then evidentiary or terminating sanctions after an order compelling discovery; for lost material that should have been preserved, remedial measures even without bad faith (e.g., failing to halt automatic deletion).

- Counsel's own duty (CB 750): many courts impose personal obligations on lawyers for their clients' preservation and production. Become actively involved immediately on retention, and circulate a litigation hold (document preservation memo) to everyone who may have relevant material (Zubulake).

- Evidence handed to you (CB 752): your possession can put you in a legal and ethical bind. You may not conceal, destroy, or alter it, or counsel anyone else to (MR 3.4(a)). Class quiz Q7: driving the client's bloody knife to another town and throwing it in a dumpster is unlawful concealment and destruction, a clear MR 3.4(a) violation and likely obstruction; no proceeding need be pending. Many courts hold that a lawyer who takes possession of physical evidence of a crime may keep it a reasonable time for examination but must then turn it over to the authorities.

- MR 3.4(f) (CB 364): you may ask your own client, or the client's relatives, employees, or agents, not to talk voluntarily to the other side, but only if you reasonably believe they won't be hurt by it (Part XI).

Zubulake v. UBS Warburg LLC, 229 F.R.D. 422 (S.D.N.Y. 2004) — litigation holds and counsel's duty to preserve NOTE CASE · WEEK 11
Facts: In an employment discrimination suit, UBS employees deleted relevant emails and failed to produce others despite counsel's instructions to preserve them.
Held: Counsel must issue a litigation hold, communicate with key players, and monitor compliance, and the court gave an adverse-inference instruction for the lost emails (Scheindlin, J.).
Why it matters: Preservation is not the client's job alone. The source of the duty to send and police a litigation hold (CB 750).
Inadvertently sent material: MR 4.4(b) (CB 753–757)
