- Alvarez (Ch. 3) is not fraud: his lie about the Medal of Honor was "a pathetic attempt to gain respect," not made to secure employment or financial benefits.

### Defamation

Defamation is a traditional tort for injury to reputation. Libel is written; slander is spoken ("s" for spoken). Before 1964 the First Amendment put no limits on it: the plaintiff showed the defendant said something bad about him, truth was a defense the defendant had to prove, and damages were presumed. The First Amendment rules now vary along two axes: (a) is the plaintiff a public official/public figure or an ordinary person, and (b) is the statement on a matter of public or private concern?

Four questions to answer from the cases. (1) Why protect false statements of fact at all? (2) Why make it harder for public officials and public figures to sue? (3) Why make it harder when the statement involves a matter of public concern? (4) Are the lines convincing?

### New York Times v. Sullivan, 376 U.S. 254 (1964)

case · ch. 7New York Times v. Sullivan (1964)

9-0 on the bottom line, Brennan, J. Black, Douglas, and Goldberg would have given absolute immunity to critics of public officials.

Rule: A public official can't recover damages for a defamatory falsehood relating to his official conduct unless he proves "actual malice": the statement was made "with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not." Recklessness is enough; "malice" here does not mean ill will.

Facts: In 1960 the Times ran a full-page ad by supporters of Martin Luther King Jr. criticizing Montgomery, Alabama police's treatment of civil rights protesters. It had factual errors (how many times King had been arrested, which song protesters sang). Police commissioner L. B. Sullivan sued and won $500,000 under Alabama's easy-to-prove libel law. Held: reversed.

- Breathing space: "erroneous statement is inevitable in free debate," and it must be protected if freedom of expression is to have the "breathing space" it needs to survive.

- Truth defense isn't enough: requiring critics to guarantee the truth of every assertion, on pain of unlimited judgments, leads to self-censorship. Critics would "steer far wider of the unlawful zone," even when what they say is true, out of doubt it can be proved or fear of the expense.

- The press: the rule is especially important to the press, which roots out and reports on corrupt or inefficient officials, but the press gets no greater First Amendment rights than individuals.

- Don't confuse this New York Times case with the Pentagon Papers case (Ch. 4).

### Curtis Publishing Co. v. Butts, 388 U.S. 130 (1967)

case · ch. 7Curtis Publishing Co. v. Butts (1967)

Plurality. Described in the casebook commentary and slides; not excerpted.

Rule: The Sullivan actual-malice standard extends to public figures, not just public officials.

Facts: A magazine accused Wally Butts, former University of Georgia football coach, of conspiring with Alabama's coach to fix games. Butts couldn't recover without showing actual malice.

### Gertz v. Robert Welch, Inc., 418 U.S. 323 (1974)

case · ch. 7Gertz v. Robert Welch, Inc. (1974)

5-4, Powell, J. Burger, Douglas, Brennan, and White dissented.

Rule: When a private person sues over a statement on a matter of public concern, states may set their own standard of liability so long as they don't impose liability without fault (at least negligence). But presumed or punitive damages require actual malice.

Facts: The casebook omits the complicated facts. The key point: the plaintiff was an ordinary private person, but the false statement involved an issue of public concern.

- "No such thing as a false idea": opinions are corrected by competing ideas, not judges and juries. But false statements of fact have no constitutional value; "neither the intentional lie nor the careless error" advances debate.

- Strategic protection: because error is inevitable and strict liability causes "intolerable self-censorship," the First Amendment "requires that we protect some falsehood in order to protect speech that matters."

- Why private plaintiffs get more protection: (1) self-help: public officials and figures have greater access to the media to rebut lies, so private people are more vulnerable; (2) normative: public officials and figures voluntarily exposed themselves to scrutiny; a private person "has relinquished no part of his interest in the protection of his own good name," so he is more deserving of recovery.

- Public figures: some are public figures for all purposes (persuasive power and influence); more commonly, people become public figures by thrusting themselves to the forefront of particular public controversies. Truly involuntary public figures are "exceedingly rare."

- Damages: juries' "largely uncontrolled discretion" to award presumed or punitive damages where there is no loss compounds the chilling effect.

### Dun & Bradstreet, Inc. v. Greenmoss Builders, Inc., 472 U.S. 749 (1985)

case · ch. 7Dun & Bradstreet, Inc. v. Greenmoss Builders, Inc. (1985)

5-4; Powell, J., plurality (with O'Connor and Rehnquist). Burger and White concurred in the judgment; Brennan, Marshall, Blackmun, and Stevens dissented.

Rule: When a private plaintiff sues over a statement on a matter of purely private concern, presumed and punitive damages may be awarded without actual malice. Open question, still undecided 40 years later: may a state impose strict liability, or does the First Amendment require at least negligence?

Facts: A credit reporting company issued false credit reports about a construction contractor to the contractor's creditors. Held: presumed and punitive damages allowed.

- Balancing: the state's interest in compensating private reputational injury is the same as in Gertz, but the First Amendment interest is weaker. Speech on matters of public concern is at the heart of the First Amendment; purely private speech poses no threat to debate on self-government and no risk of press self-censorship. It is "not totally unprotected," but its protections are less stringent.

- White, J., concurring in the judgment: he had joined Sullivan but came to think it struck an "improvident balance." Under it "the lie will stand": the defeated official gets no judgment identifying the falsehood, and the public stays misinformed. He would have kept the common-law liability standard and instead capped damages, so a defamed official could at least get a judgment vindicating his reputation.

### Berisha v. Lawson, 141 S. Ct. 2424 (2021) (denying cert.)

case · ch. 7Berisha v. Lawson (2021)

Gorsuch, J., dissenting from denial of certiorari (Thomas, J., also dissented separately).

Point: Sullivan's actual-malice standard remains good law, and there is no sign a majority wants to revisit it. But Justices Thomas and Gorsuch have urged the Court to reconsider it.

- Founding view: freedom of the press meant no prior restraints, not freedom to defame without consequence. Publishers had a duty to try to get the facts right or answer in tort, the accepted view for over two centuries until 1964.

- Changed media landscape: in 1964 a handful of large, fact-checked print and broadcast outlets dominated; today virtually anyone can publish virtually anything instantly. Disinformation is cheap and profitable, while the economic model supporting reporters and fact-checkers has eroded.

- What began as tolerating occasional falsehood has become "an ironclad subsidy for the publication of falsehoods by means and on a scale previously unimaginable."

- Discussion prompt: would you keep, replace, or abolish the actual-malice standard? The casebook points to President Trump's $20 billion defamation suit against the Wall Street Journal over statements linking him to Jeffrey Epstein.

### Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress

IIED is a relatively new, more controversial tort that not all states recognize. It typically requires that the defendant intentionally or recklessly caused the plaintiff severe emotional distress through extreme and outrageous conduct. The Court has extended its defamation principles to IIED claims based on speech.

### Hustler Magazine v. Falwell, 485 U.S. 46 (1988)

case · ch. 7Hustler Magazine v. Falwell (1988)

8-0, Rehnquist, C.J. (Kennedy, J., recused).

Rule: Public figures and public officials may not recover for IIED based on a publication unless it contains a false statement of fact made with actual malice. "Outrageousness" is too subjective a standard to satisfy the First Amendment.

Facts: Hustler ran a parody ad portraying Jerry Falwell, a nationally known minister and political commentator, in a drunken incestuous encounter with his mother in an outhouse. Falwell won an IIED verdict. Held: reversed. The ad was obviously a parody and couldn't reasonably be read as stating actual facts.

- Otherwise, political cartoonists and satirists would face damages without any showing that their work falsely defamed its subject.

- The ad was "at best a distant cousin" of political cartoons, but there is no principled standard to separate them. "Outrageousness" has "an inherent subjectiveness" that lets juries impose liability based on their tastes, views, or dislike of the expression.

### Snyder v. Phelps, 562 U.S. 443 (2011)

case · ch. 7Snyder v. Phelps (2011)

8-1, Roberts, C.J. Alito, J., dissented.

Rule: Speech on a matter of public concern, in a public place, is entitled to "special protection" and can't be the basis for IIED liability just because a jury finds it outrageous. The focus is the content of the speech (public concern), not the plaintiff's identity (here, a private person).

Facts: Fred Phelps and Westboro Baptist Church members picketed near the funeral of a soldier killed in Iraq, with signs saying God kills American soldiers to punish the nation's tolerance of homosexuality. The soldier's father won millions on an IIED claim. Held: reversed.

- Public concern: judged by all the circumstances. The signs addressed the political and moral conduct of the United States, homosexuality in the military, and Catholic clergy scandals, even if they fell "short of refined social or political commentary."

- Where and how: they picketed peacefully on public land next to a public street, about 1,000 feet away and out of sight of the church, under police supervision, with no shouting, profanity, or violence, and didn't disrupt the funeral. The distress came from the content and viewpoint of the message: parishioners holding "God Bless America" signs at the same spot wouldn't have been liable.

- "If there is a bedrock principle," the government may not prohibit an idea because society finds it offensive. In public debate we must tolerate "insulting, and even outrageous, speech" to give the First Amendment "breathing space."

### Counterman Revisited: Borrowing From Defamation

Counterman v. Colorado (2023) (full case in Ch. 5) held that a true-threats prosecution requires at least recklessness as to whether the communication would be seen as threatening. Justice Kagan borrowed directly from Sullivan and Gertz: a subjective mental-state requirement is "strategic protection" against the chilling effect. It shields some proscribable speech, but by reducing an honest speaker's fear of accidental liability it gives "breathing room" to valuable speech. The First Amendment "requires that we protect some falsehood in order to protect speech that matters."

### Disclosing Information That Is True

Rule: Truthful information is protected speech. The Court is quite protective of disclosures, at least where the speaker obtained the information lawfully.

- Florida Star v. B.J.F. (1989), 6-3: a damages award against a newspaper for publishing a rape victim's name violated the First Amendment. The paper got the name lawfully from a publicly released police report. Applying strict scrutiny, the state lacked a compelling interest in preventing disclosure in those circumstances.

- Bartnicki v. Vopper (2001), 6-3: a media organization couldn't be held liable for broadcasting a tape of phone calls that a third party had illegally intercepted. Privacy is important but was outweighed by the right to publish truthful information on a matter of public concern.

- Revenge porn (state courts): the Supreme Court hasn't decided it. In Nebraska v. Zitterkopf (Neb. 2024), the defendant secretly recorded a sexual encounter and shared an image. Applying strict scrutiny, the court upheld the law: the state has a compelling interest in personal privacy, and the law is narrowly tailored even without an intent-to-harass element, because the harm from distributing intimate images is the same whatever the motive.

### Appropriation of Likeness or Intellectual Property

IP law is complicated and not covered in depth. Know only that federal and state laws can significantly protect intellectual property without violating the First Amendment, though there are limits.

### Zacchini v. Scripps-Howard Broadcasting Co., 433 U.S. 562 (1977)

case · ch. 7Zacchini v. Scripps-Howard Broadcasting Co. (1977)

5-4, White, J. Powell, Brennan, Marshall, and Stevens dissented.

Rule: The First Amendment does not immunize the media from a state right-of-publicity claim when they broadcast a performer's entire act without consent.

Facts: Hugo Zacchini performed a 15-second "human cannonball" act at an Ohio county fair. He asked a freelance reporter not to film it; the next day, on the producer's instructions, the reporter taped the entire act, which aired on the 11 o'clock news with favorable commentary. Held: Zacchini's damages suit may proceed.

- Earlier cases involved reporting on events, not broadcasting an entire act a performer is normally paid for. It is like broadcasting a copyrighted play, a prize fight, or a ball game without permission.

- Broadcasting the whole act threatens its economic value. Like patent and copyright, the right of publicity gives an incentive to invest in a performance. Zacchini didn't seek to stop the broadcast; "he simply wants to be paid for it."

- Ohio may choose to privilege the press here, but the First Amendment doesn't require it.

### Synthesis: Defamation and IIED Rules

Plaintiff / speech | Case | Liability standard | Presumed / punitive damages
Public official | NYT v. Sullivan (1964) | Actual malice | Actual malice
Public figure | Curtis Publishing v. Butts (1967) | Actual malice | Actual malice
Private person, public concern | Gertz (1974) | At least negligence (no liability without fault) | Actual malice required
Private person, private concern | Dun & Bradstreet (1985) (plurality) | Open: negligence or strict liability? | No actual malice needed
IIED, public figure/official | Hustler v. Falwell (1988) | False statement of fact + actual malice | Same
IIED, speech on public concern in public place | Snyder v. Phelps (2011) | "Outrageousness" not enough | Same

### Stretch Exercise: The AI Campaign Video

| Analysis
Issue | A mayor vetoes a living-wage ordinance. Her opponent's campaign ad uses AI to create a realistic video of her saying, "I do not care whether working families can afford rent," with a small caption: "Dramatization based on the mayor's living-wage veto." Many viewers miss the caption and think it's real. She sues for defamation.
Questions | Is the video a statement of fact, opinion, parody, or something in between? Does the disclaimer matter? Does the political context make the speech more protected or more harmful? How does actual malice apply when the defendant knowingly fabricated the image but believed it captured the "truth" of the veto?
Analysis | The mayor is a public official and the speech concerns her official conduct, so Sullivan requires actual malice. Unlike Hustler's obviously absurd parody, a realistic video can reasonably be understood as stating an actual fact (that she said those words), and an easily missed disclaimer may not change that. The defendant knew the quotation was fabricated, which points toward knowledge of falsity, though he will argue the gist (her veto) was true and the video was rhetorical characterization. The political context cuts both ways: it is core speech that needs breathing space, but fabricated quotations in a campaign are the falsehoods Gertz says have no constitutional value.

## Chapter 8: Commercial Speech

What it is: speech used to try to sell stuff (goods or services): iPhones, sneakers, a haircut, legal services. Speakers are typically for-profit businesses, but nonprofits can engage in it (a nonprofit hospital advertising its specialty services). Charitable solicitations (fundraising) are not commercial speech. Because of the money involved, commercial speech is litigated far more often than obscenity or true threats.

Big picture: the Court lets governments restrict commercial speech more easily than other speech (Central Hudson, intermediate scrutiny), and compel commercial disclosures more easily still (Zauderer). That's why drug packaging carries health warnings and food carries nutrition labels.

Commercial speech checklist. (1) Is it commercial speech? (2) Is the government restricting speech or compelling a disclosure? (3) Restriction: run Central Hudson. Is the speech misleading or about illegal activity (unprotected)? If protected: substantial interest? directly advances? not more extensive than necessary? Watch for paternalism toward adults (fails) versus kids (may work, if tailored). (4) Compelled disclosure: run Zauderer. Purely factual and uncontroversial information about the seller's own product or service? reasonably related to a substantial interest? not unjustified or unduly burdensome? If Zauderer doesn't apply (NIFLA), use heightened scrutiny.

### Restrictions on Commercial Speech

### Virginia Pharmacy Board v. Virginia Citizens Consumer Council, 425 U.S. 748 (1976)

case · ch. 8Virginia Pharmacy Board v. Virginia Citizens Consumer Council (1976)

8-1, Blackmun, J. Rehnquist, J., dissented.

Rule: For the first time, commercial speech is protected by the First Amendment. A state may not completely suppress truthful information about entirely lawful activity because it fears the information's effect on speakers and listeners. Commercial speech can still be regulated (false or misleading ads, illegal transactions, time/place/manner rules).

Facts: Virginia made it "unprofessional conduct," punishable by fines and loss of license, for a pharmacist to advertise prescription drug prices. A resident who took daily prescription drugs and two nonprofits challenged the law. Held: unconstitutional.

- Listeners have rights: where a willing speaker exists, protection extends to the communication, its source, and its recipients. "If there is a right to advertise, there is a reciprocal right to receive the advertising."

- Why protect it: the consumer's interest in commercial information "may be as keen, if not keener by far," than in the day's political debate. The ban hit hardest the poor, the sick, and the aged. Society needs intelligent, well-informed private economic decisions in a free-enterprise economy.

- Anti-paternalism: Virginia feared price competition would drive out "professional" pharmacists. The alternative is to assume "people will perceive their own best interests if only they are well enough informed" and to open channels of communication. Virginia may set professional standards but not by "keeping the public in ignorance."

- Footnote 24, why commercial speech gets less protection: it is more easily verifiable (the advertiser knows its own product) and more durable (advertising is the sine qua non of profits, so it is unlikely to be chilled). So there is less need to tolerate inaccuracy, warnings and disclaimers may be required, and the prior-restraint bar may not apply.

### Central Hudson Gas & Electric Corp. v. Public Service Commission of New York, 447 U.S. 557 (1980)

case · ch. 8Central Hudson Gas & Electric Corp. v. Public Service Commission of New York (1980)

8-1 on the bottom line, Powell, J. Brennan, Blackmun, and Stevens concurred in the judgment; Rehnquist, J., dissented.

Rule (the Central Hudson test, still good law): (1) Commercial speech is unprotected if it is misleading or concerns unlawful activity. If protected, ask: (2) Is the government's interest substantial? (3) Does the regulation directly advance that interest (not "ineffective or remote support")? (4) Is it not more extensive than necessary? Prongs 2-4 are a form of intermediate scrutiny.

Facts: New York completely banned promotional advertising by electric utilities to conserve energy. Held: the ban violates the First Amendment.

- The First Amendment's concern for commercial speech rests on the informational function of advertising, so the government may ban messages more likely to deceive than inform, or tied to illegal activity.

- Applied: the speech wasn't inaccurate or unlawful; energy conservation is plainly substantial; but the record failed to show a total ban was no more extensive than necessary.

### 44 Liquormart, Inc. v. Rhode Island, 517 U.S. 484 (1996)

case · ch. 844 Liquormart, Inc. v. Rhode Island (1996)

Unanimous on the bottom line; splintered opinions. Stevens, J., plurality (reasoning later adopted by the full Court).

Rule: Paternalism toward adults is not a valid reason to suppress truthful, non-misleading commercial speech. Blanket bans on such speech about lawful products get "special care" and rarely survive. If the government wants to reduce adult consumption, it must regulate the product directly (ban it, regulate prices, or tax it).

Facts: Rhode Island banned advertising the retail prices of alcoholic beverages to promote temperance. Held: invalid.

- Such bans rest on "the offensive assumption that the public will respond 'irrationally' to the truth." Be "especially skeptical of regulations that seek to keep people in the dark for what the government perceives to be their own good."

- Prong 4 fails: higher prices could be maintained by direct regulation or increased taxation (the state's own expert conceded this), so there was no "reasonable fit."

- No "greater includes the lesser": the power to ban alcohol doesn't include the power to ban ads for it. The Constitution presumes regulating speech is more dangerous than regulating conduct.

### Sorrell v. IMS Health Inc., 564 U.S. 552 (2011)

case · ch. 8Sorrell v. IMS Health Inc. (2011)

6-3, Kennedy, J. Breyer, Ginsburg, and Kagan dissented.

Rule: A law imposing content- and speaker-based burdens on commercial speech is subject to heightened scrutiny. The fear that people will make bad decisions if given truthful information can't justify it, even more so when the audience is sophisticated (doctors). "That the State finds expression too persuasive does not permit it to quiet the speech."

Facts: Vermont barred the sale and use of pharmacy records revealing individual doctors' prescribing practices for marketing, and barred drug makers from using them for "detailing" (sales visits to doctors). Vermont wanted to cut costs and steer doctors toward cheaper, safer generics. Held: unconstitutional.

- Content- and speaker-based: the law disfavored marketing (particular content) and drug manufacturers (particular speakers), while many other speakers could use the same information.

- The dissent argued the law regulated conduct (data mining), not speech; the casebook sets that issue aside.

### Lorillard Tobacco Co. v. Reilly, 533 U.S. 525 (2001)

case · ch. 8Lorillard Tobacco Co. v. Reilly (2001)

5-4 in relevant part, O'Connor, J. Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer dissented.

Rule: Some paternalism toward kids is allowed: the government may restrict accurate commercial speech to discourage minors' consumption, but the restriction must still satisfy Central Hudson prongs 3 and 4. If it keeps too much truthful information from adults, it fails prong 4.

Facts: Massachusetts banned outdoor tobacco ads within 1,000 feet of a school or playground, and indoor point-of-sale ads lower than 5 feet from the floor in stores within that radius. Held: both fail.

- Interest: preventing underage tobacco use is substantial, "and even compelling," and there was evidence that limiting youth exposure to ads reduces underage use.

- Outdoor ban fails prong 4: it would cover 87%-91% of Boston, Worcester, and Springfield, included in-store ads visible from outside, applied to ads of any size, and even reached oral statements. In some areas it was nearly a complete ban on truthful information to adults, who have a right to receive it (Bolger: mailbox discourse can't be limited to what suits "a sandbox").

- 5-foot rule fails prongs 3 and 4: "Not all children are less than 5 feet tall, and those who are certainly have the ability to look up."

### Florida Bar v. Went For It, Inc., 515 U.S. 618 (1995)

case · ch. 8Florida Bar v. Went For It, Inc. (1995)

5-4, O'Connor, J. Kennedy, Stevens, Souter, and Ginsburg dissented.

Rule: A 30-day ban on targeted direct-mail solicitation of accident victims and their families by personal injury lawyers survives Central Hudson. It is the rare attorney-advertising restriction the Court has upheld.

Facts: Florida Bar rules barred personal injury lawyers from sending targeted direct mail to victims and relatives for 30 days after an accident or disaster. Held: upheld.

- Background: Bates v. State Bar of Arizona (1977) struck a ban on price ads for "routine" legal services; lawyer advertising is commercial speech with a measure of protection, and most restrictions have been struck.

- Substantial interest: protecting the privacy and tranquility of victims and their loved ones against intrusive contact, and the profession's reputation.

- Directly advances: the Bar's 106-page summary of a two-year study, with statistical and anecdotal data, showed the public views post-accident mail as intrusive and reflecting poorly on lawyers.

- Tailoring: the ban is brief, and lawyers can still use TV, radio, newspapers, billboards, and untargeted letters.

- The casebook's guess: the Justices were squeamish about "ambulance chasing" tarnishing the profession.

### Compelled Commercial Speech

Compelled commercial speech means the government requires sellers to say something about their products or services, usually in ads or on packaging: "contains peanuts," drug side effects, "contains small parts," or that a "free trial" auto-renews. These are often called disclosure requirements. Zauderer gives governments much more latitude to compel disclosures than to restrict truthful commercial speech.

### Zauderer v. Office of Disciplinary Counsel, 471 U.S. 626 (1985)

case · ch. 8Zauderer v. Office of Disciplinary Counsel (1985)

Unanimous in relevant part, White, J.

Rule (the Zauderer test): The government may require purely factual and uncontroversial information about the terms under which the seller's services are available if the requirement is reasonably related to a substantial government interest (here, preventing consumer deception) and is not unjustified or unduly burdensome.

Facts: Philip Zauderer's ads said he handled cases on contingency and "if there is no recovery, no legal fees are owed by our clients." Ohio required disclosure that clients might still owe costs. Held: the Court struck Ohio's restrictions on attorney ads but upheld the disclosure requirement.

- Disclosure is not prohibition: Ohio didn't stop attorneys from conveying information; it only required "somewhat more information."

- Not Barnette or Wooley: Ohio didn't prescribe orthodoxy in politics, nationalism, religion, or opinion, only factual terms of commercial service.

- Why more lenient: commercial speech is protected mainly for its value to consumers (Virginia Pharmacy), so the advertiser's interest in not providing factual information is "minimal." Disclosure requirements "trench much more narrowly" on advertisers than flat bans.

- Applied: laypeople don't know "fees" and "costs" differ, so the ad suggested a no-lose proposition. No factual basis showed the requirement was unduly burdensome.

### Milavetz, Gallop & Milavetz v. United States, 559 U.S. 229 (2010)

case · ch. 8Milavetz, Gallop & Milavetz v. United States (2010)

9-0 on the bottom line, Sotomayor, J.

Rule: Zauderer, not Central Hudson, governs factual disclosures aimed at inherently misleading commercial ads.

Facts: Federal bankruptcy law (§ 528) required "debt relief agencies," including attorneys who help file bankruptcy petitions, to identify themselves as such in ads, with related disclosures. Milavetz preferred to be called a law firm. Held: upheld.

- Shares Zauderer's features: it combats ads promising debt relief without mentioning bankruptcy and its costs; it requires only an accurate statement of legal status and services; and it doesn't stop the advertiser from saying more.

- The "confusing label" claim fails: no evidence it confuses; it is accurate by definition; the required "helps people file for bankruptcy relief" gives context; the firm can add that it is a law firm; and it may tailor wording if substantially similar.

### National Institute of Family and Life Advocates v. Becerra (NIFLA), 585 U.S. 755 (2018)

case · ch. 8National Institute of Family and Life Advocates v. Becerra (2018)

5-4, Thomas, J. Breyer, Ginsburg, Sotomayor, and Kagan dissented.

Rule: Zauderer does not apply to a required notice that is not about the speaker's own services or that addresses a controversial topic. Even where Zauderer applies, a disclosure fails if it is unjustified (purely hypothetical harm) or unduly burdensome (drowns out the speaker's message).

Facts: California's FACT Act required (1) licensed clinics serving pregnant women to post notice that the state provides free or low-cost services, including abortion, with a phone number; and (2) unlicensed clinics to state they are not licensed medical facilities. The targets were "crisis pregnancy centers," largely faith-based pro-life organizations. Held: both requirements violate the First Amendment.

- Licensed notice: Zauderer doesn't apply. The notice in no way relates to the clinics' own services, and abortion is "anything but an 'uncontroversial' topic." It fails even intermediate scrutiny: it is wildly underinclusive (most of nearly 1,000 community clinics serving 5.6 million patients are exempt), and the state could run its own public-information campaign. It "cannot co-opt the licensed facilities to deliver its message."

- Unlicensed notice: fails even under Zauderer. Its justification was "purely hypothetical" (practicing medicine without a license is already a crime). It is unduly burdensome: a government-scripted notice on all print and digital ads, in larger or contrasting type, in as many languages as the state chooses. It "drowns out the facility's own message."

- The Court did not question "health and safety warnings long considered permissible" or purely factual disclosures about commercial products.

- Slides: the licensed notice failed because it was (1) not about services the clinics offered and (2) controversial (steering patients toward abortion). Professor Klein's guess: (1) alone would have been enough.

### CTIA - The Wireless Ass'n v. City of Berkeley, 928 F.3d 832 (9th Cir. 2019)

case · ch. 8CTIA - The Wireless Ass'n v. City of Berkeley (2019)

2-1, W. Fletcher, J. (court of appeals case). Friedland, J., dissented, finding the disclosure confusing.

Rule: Zauderer isn't limited to preventing deception. Any substantial interest, including public health and safety, can support a factual, uncontroversial disclosure.

Facts: Berkeley required cell phone retailers to give buyers a notice that federal radio-frequency (RF) exposure guidelines exist "to assure safety," that carrying an ON phone in a pocket or bra may exceed them, and to consult the user manual. It could be an 8.5 x 11 poster or a 5 x 8 handout bearing the city's logo; retailers could add their own clearly separate information. Held: upheld.

- Other circuits agree: country-of-origin labels on meat (American Meat Institute, D.C. Cir. en banc 2014); mercury labeling (NEMA v. Sorrell, 2d Cir. 2001); cigarette health warnings (Discount Tobacco, 6th Cir. 2012). NIFLA signaled agreement by preserving health and safety warnings.

- Two NIFLA limits on "factual and uncontroversial": (1) the notice can't take sides in a heated political controversy at odds with the speaker's mission; (2) it must relate to the speaker's own product or service.

- Applied: health and safety is substantial; the notice summarizes what the FCC already requires manufacturers to tell users. It is "largely reassuring," not inflammatory. Not unduly burdensome, unlike San Francisco's soda warning that had to fill 20% of each ad (American Beverage, 9th Cir. en banc 2019).

### Unpacking the Zauderer Test (Slides)

Element | What it means
Factual and uncontroversial | The Supreme Court has said little. Courts of appeals say a disclosure can qualify even if the seller dislikes it ("drinking alcohol while pregnant can cause birth defects"). NIFLA: must concern the seller's own services and not take sides in a controversy.
Substantial interest | Preventing consumer deception surely counts (Zauderer, Milavetz). Courts of appeals also accept health and safety ("contains peanuts," "nicotine is addictive") and things consumers care about, like country of origin ("Made in China"). Satisfying "idle consumer curiosity" probably isn't enough.
Reasonably related | Undefined by the Court. Less demanding than Central Hudson prong 4. Some circuits treat it as rational basis; Professor Klein's guess: more demanding than rational basis but still quite deferential.
Unjustified or unduly burdensome | "Unjustified" overlaps with reasonable relation. "Unduly burdensome" means the requirement chills commercial speech; courts say a disclosure that drowns out the seller's own message is unduly burdensome, which in practice restricts the speech.

### Synthesis: Restrictions vs. Compelled Disclosures

Case | Regulation | Result and reason
Virginia Pharmacy (1976) | Ban on drug price ads | Struck; commercial speech is protected; anti-paternalism
Central Hudson (1980) | Ban on utility promotional ads | Struck; total ban more extensive than necessary
Florida Bar (1995) | 30-day ban on targeted lawyer mail | Upheld; study evidence, brief ban, many alternatives
44 Liquormart (1996) | Ban on liquor price ads | Struck; paternalism toward adults; tax or regulate instead
Lorillard (2001) | Outdoor and 5-foot tobacco ad rules | Struck; too much burden on adults
Sorrell (2011) | Ban on using prescriber data for marketing | Struck; content- and speaker-based; "too persuasive" isn't a reason
Zauderer (1985) | Contingency-fee cost disclosure | Upheld; factual, prevents deception
Milavetz (2010) | "Debt relief agency" label | Upheld; factual, prevents deception
NIFLA (2018) | Abortion-services and unlicensed notices | Struck; not about own services, controversial; hypothetical and burdensome
CTIA (9th Cir. 2019) | Cell phone RF safety notice | Upheld; health and safety suffices

### Stretch Exercise: Graphic Cigarette Warnings

| Analysis
Issue | A 2009 federal statute requires cigarette packs and ads to carry prominent health warnings covering 50% of the front and back of packaging and 20% of ads, with FDA-developed graphic images. The Fifth Circuit rejected the manufacturers' challenge to the FDA's latest warnings (R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. v. FDA, 5th Cir. 2024); the Supreme Court denied cert. Imagine it took the case.
Questions | Does Zauderer or Central Hudson (or stricter review) apply? Are graphic images "purely factual and uncontroversial"? Is there a substantial interest? Is the size requirement unduly burdensome?
Analysis | For the government: the warnings concern the seller's own product, health and safety is a substantial interest (CTIA; NIFLA preserved health warnings), and smoking's health effects are factual and not genuinely controversial. For the manufacturers: graphic images may be designed to provoke emotion rather than inform, which arguably isn't "purely factual." And a warning covering half the package may "drown out" the seller's message, as the 20% soda warning did in American Beverage. The answer likely turns on whether each image is accurate and on the burden of the size requirement.

## Chapter 9: Content-Neutral Restrictions and Expressive Conduct

Two main topics: (1) time, place, and manner (TPM) regulations and (2) expressive conduct (aka symbolic speech). They overlap, so study them together. First, revisit the most important distinction in speech law: content-neutral vs. content-based vs. viewpoint-based.

Type | Examples | Standard
Content neutral (nothing to do with the message) | "No loudspeakers in the park between 10pm and 6am"; "No picketing on Main Street during rush hour"; "No leaflets on trees in the park" | Intermediate scrutiny; the government sometimes wins, sometimes loses
Content based (turns on subject matter) | "No speech about sports"; "No plays about politics"; "No leaflets about tutoring services" | Strict scrutiny unless an unprotected category; the government usually loses
Viewpoint based (turns on the speaker's perspective) | "No speech that criticizes baseball"; "No speech that celebrates the Phillies"; "No leaflets that support legalizing marijuana" | Strict scrutiny, even within an unprotected category (R.A.V.); the government almost always loses

- TPM regulations are the most common content-neutral rules: they regulate when, where, and how speech occurs. Wrinkle: a TPM rule that is also content based ("no loudspeakers in the park between 10pm and 8am for speech about sports") gets strict scrutiny.

- Expressive conduct is conduct intended to convey a message where, in the circumstances, the message would likely be understood (picketing, flag burning, cross burning, armbands). It is protected under rules similar to, but not identical to, those for ordinary speech.

- Outline tip: quote the specific words in the challenged law that make it content based or viewpoint based.

### Content-Based Versus Viewpoint-Based (Revisited)

### Police Department of Chicago v. Mosley, 408 U.S. 92 (1972)

case · ch. 9Police Department of Chicago v. Mosley (1972)

9-0 on the bottom line, Marshall, J.

Rule: A law that permits some picketing but not other picketing based on its subject matter is content based and violates the First Amendment. "Above all else, the First Amendment means that government has no power to restrict expression because of its message, its ideas, its subject matter, or its content."

Facts: Earl Mosley, a postal employee, peacefully picketed Jones Commercial High School alone for seven months with a sign saying it practiced "black discrimination" and had a "black quota." Chicago then banned picketing within 150 feet of a school during school hours (plus a half hour before and after), except "peaceful picketing of any school involved in a labor dispute." Held: unconstitutional.

- The operative distinction was "the message on a picket sign": labor-dispute picketing allowed, all other peaceful picketing banned.

- Casebook note: the famous sentence overstates modern doctrine. Content-based restrictions get strict scrutiny; they aren't invalid per se.

### Vidal v. Elster, 602 U.S. 286 (2024)

case · ch. 9Vidal v. Elster (2024)

Unanimous in relevant part, Thomas, J. (The Justices split on special trademark rules; that part isn't excerpted.)

Rule: A content-based rule targets a subject or topic; a viewpoint-based rule, "a particularly egregious form of content discrimination," targets particular views on a subject. The Lanham Act's "names clause" is content based but not viewpoint based.

Facts: Steve Elster sought to register "Trump too small" (with a hand-gesture illustration) for shirts and hats, drawing on a 2016 debate exchange between Trump and Marco Rubio. The PTO refused under the names clause, which bars marks identifying a living person without written consent.

- Not viewpoint based: the clause applies whether the use of the name is flattering, critical, or neutral. The PTO also refused "Welcome President Biden," "I Stump for Trump," and "Obama Pajama."

- Practical-operation argument rejected: Elster said consent is easier to get for flattering marks, but people withhold consent for many reasons (avoiding association with the goods, or preventing others from profiting from their name).

- Content based: marks containing names are treated differently from marks conveying other ideas.

- Contrast Matal v. Tam (2017, more in Ch. 10): the bar on disparaging marks was viewpoint based because it targeted one viewpoint, "giving offense."

### Chiles v. Salazar, 146 S. Ct. 1010 (2026)

case · ch. 9Chiles v. Salazar (2026)

8-1, Gorsuch, J. Jackson, J., dissented. Kagan and Sotomayor concurred.

Rule: As applied to talk therapy, Colorado's ban on "conversion therapy" for minors is a viewpoint-based regulation of speech. It permits counselors to affirm a client's identity or assist a gender transition, but forbids speech that helps a client change sexual orientation or gender identity.

Facts: Kaley Chiles, a licensed counselor, offers only talk therapy (no medication, physical treatment, or coercive practices) and helps clients pursue their own goals. Colorado's 2019 law, adopted in response to a teen mental-health crisis and evidence linking conversion therapy to depression and suicidality, banned "any practice or treatment" attempting to change a minor's sexual orientation or gender identity, while expressly allowing "acceptance, support, and understanding" and "assistance to a person undergoing gender transition." Chiles challenged it only as applied to her talk therapy.

- "The spoken word is perhaps the quintessential form of protected speech," and all Chiles does is talk.

- The law goes beyond content: it prescribes which views she may express. Any law suppressing speech by viewpoint, "however well-intentioned," is an "egregious assault" on free thought and the marketplace of ideas.

- Why tricky: Colorado argued it regulated the practice of medicine (conduct), with only incidental effects on speech. Kagan and Sotomayor joined because the law was viewpoint based. The Court left open the harder question of a viewpoint-neutral regulation of health providers' speech.

### Time, Place, and Manner Regulations

Rule (Ward two-step, still good law): (1) Is the TPM regulation content neutral? If not, strict scrutiny. (2) If so, intermediate scrutiny: it must be narrowly tailored to serve a significant government interest and leave open ample alternative channels for communication. "Narrowly tailored" is not least restrictive means; it means not burdening substantially more speech than necessary.

- Purpose is key to content neutrality: look for a reason unrelated to the message (noise, clutter, competition for shared space).

- Not every case reaches every element. Note which issues the Court skips and why; that often matters in litigation.

### Ward v. Rock Against Racism, 491 U.S. 781 (1989)

case · ch. 9Ward v. Rock Against Racism (1989)

6-3, Kennedy, J. Blackmun, J., concurred in the judgment; Marshall, Brennan, and Stevens dissented.

Rule: A content-neutral TPM rule need not be the least intrusive means. It is narrowly tailored if it promotes a substantial interest that would be achieved less effectively without it, and isn't substantially broader than necessary.

Facts: Central Park's Naumberg Bandshell sits near the Sheep Meadow (a designated quiet area) and Central Park West residences. After complaints about past concerts, New York City required bandshell performers to use city-provided sound equipment and a city sound technician. A rock concert sponsor challenged it. Held: upheld (reversing the Second Circuit).

- Music is protected expression, which was undisputed.

- Content neutral: the controlling question is whether the government adopted the rule "because of disagreement with the message it conveys." Controlling noise to protect the Sheep Meadow and residents has nothing to do with content. Incidental effects on some speakers don't matter (Renton).

- Narrowly tailored: the Second Circuit erred by demanding the "least intrusive means." The city's technician controlled volume directly and effectively, while giving sponsors autonomy over the sound mix, so it had no material impact on artistic control.

- Footnote 6: Boos v. Barry (1988) used least-restrictive-means because it involved a content-based ban on signs criticizing foreign governments. TPM rules never get strict scrutiny.

- Alternative channels easily met: performances continue; only amplification is regulated.

### City of Ladue v. Gilleo, 512 U.S. 43 (1994)

case · ch. 9City of Ladue v. Gilleo (1994)

9-0, Stevens, J.

Rule: Even a content-neutral rule fails if it forecloses an entire, unique medium of expression without adequate alternative channels. A near-total ban on residential signs violates the First Amendment.

Facts: Margaret Gilleo put a 24-by-36-inch sign on her lawn: "Say No to War in the Persian Gulf, Call Congress Now." Ladue banned residential signs except 10 exemptions (small ID signs, for-sale signs, church and school signs, commercial signs in commercial zones, and more) to prevent "ugliness, visual blight and clutter." Held: unconstitutional.

- Two ways to attack sign laws: (1) they restrict too little, because exemptions discriminate by message (underinclusiveness may favor one side of a debate); or (2) they restrict too much protected speech. The Court assumed arguendo the exemptions were content neutral and decided on ground (2).

- Entire medium foreclosed: the Court has struck total bans on pamphlets, handbills, door-to-door literature, and live entertainment. Residential signs are a "venerable" and important medium, especially in political campaigns.

- No adequate substitutes: a sign at your home identifies you as the speaker; it is unusually cheap and convenient (vital for people of modest means or limited mobility); and it reaches neighbors.

- "More temperate measures" could address Ladue's concerns.

### Thomas v. Chicago Park District, 534 U.S. 316 (2002)

case · ch. 9Thomas v. Chicago Park District (2002)

9-0, Scalia, J.

Rule: A content-neutral permit requirement is valid if it contains adequate standards to guide the official's decision and render it subject to effective judicial review. Unduly broad discretion risks content-based favoritism.

Facts: Chicago required a permit for park events with more than 50 people. Held: upheld.

- Not censorship: unlike Freedman v. Maryland (1965) (films submitted to a Board of Censors), no ground for denial concerns what a speaker might say. The rule applies to all park activity: "the picnicker and soccer player, no less than the political activist or parade marshal."

- Purpose: coordinate multiple uses of limited space, preserve facilities, prevent dangerous or unlawful uses, and ensure accountability for damage. Unregulated access "could easily reduce rather than enlarge the park's utility as a forum for speech."

- Standards: denial only for listed reasons (incomplete or false application, unpaid prior damage, earlier permit for the same time and place, unreasonable danger, violated prior permit). These are specific and objective, not "the whim of the administrator," and reviewable on appeal and in state court.

### Watchtower Bible & Tract Society v. Village of Stratton, 536 U.S. 150 (2002)

case · ch. 9Watchtower Bible & Tract Society v. Village of Stratton (2002)

8-1 on the bottom line, Stevens, J. Rehnquist, C.J., dissented.

Rule: Requiring a permit from the mayor before going door-to-door to promote any cause violates the First Amendment, even assuming intermediate scrutiny. The Court didn't decide which standard applies.

Facts: Stratton required canvassers promoting any "cause" on private residential property to first get a permit from the mayor's office. Residents could also post "no solicitation" signs. Held: unconstitutional.

- Interests: preventing fraud and crime and protecting residents' privacy are important.

- Breadth: if limited to commercial activity and fundraising, it arguably would be tailored. But it covered Camp Fire Girls, Jehovah's Witnesses, political candidates, trick-or-treaters, and neighbors seeking votes or a better garbage collector.

- It is offensive "to the very notion of a free society" that a citizen must inform the government and get a permit to speak to neighbors, even if permits are free and prompt.

- Three pernicious effects: (1) it destroys anonymity (fear of retaliation or ostracism, or privacy); (2) some people's religious scruples forbid applying for a license; (3) it bans spontaneous speech (deciding on a weekend to campaign, or crossing the street to urge a neighbor to vote against the mayor).

### Expressive Conduct

Rule (three steps): (1) Is the conduct expressive? It is if the actor intended to convey a message and, in the circumstances, viewers would likely understand it. No specific message is required, and offensive conduct still counts. If not expressive, the First Amendment isn't implicated. (2) Is the government regulating for reasons related to the message? If yes, strict scrutiny. (3) If unrelated, apply the O'Brien test (intermediate scrutiny).

- Step 1 examples: burning a flag at a protest is expressive; burning a rubbish bin that happens to hold a flag is not. People in white robes burning a cross is expressive; a construction worker burning scrap wood nailed in a cross shape is not. Trust common sense.

- Step 2: read the text. Texas's law (Johnson) covered flag desecration that "seriously offends" viewers, which is plainly about the message. The federal statute (Eichman) exempted disposing of worn or soiled flags, revealing concern with disrespect. A ban on lawn bonfires that sweeps in a book burning is (almost certainly) about fire hazards.

- Overlap with TPM: Thomas's permit rule covered picnics and soccer (non-expressive) as well as parades (expressive). In practice, TPM intermediate scrutiny and O'Brien are very similar (e.g., banning parades during rush hour).

### United States v. O'Brien, 391 U.S. 367 (1968)

case · ch. 9United States v. O'Brien (1968)

7-1, Warren, C.J. (Marshall, J., recused). Douglas, J., dissented on non-First Amendment grounds.

Rule (the O'Brien test): When "speech" and "nonspeech" elements combine in the same conduct, a regulation is justified if it (1) furthers an important or substantial government interest; (2) the interest is unrelated to the suppression of free expression; and (3) the incidental restriction on expression is no greater than essential to further that interest.

Facts: On March 31, 1966, David O'Brien and three companions burned their draft registration cards on the South Boston Courthouse steps to persuade others to oppose the Vietnam War. He was convicted under a federal law making it a crime to knowingly destroy or mutilate a registration certificate. Held: conviction upheld.

- Interest: the certificates prove registration and keep the system for raising armies running smoothly.

- Tailoring: no alternative would more precisely ensure the certificates' continued availability than banning their willful destruction.

- Casebook illustration: closing a bookstore for fire code violations advances safety, and the incidental loss of the bookstore is no greater than necessary.

### Texas v. Johnson, 491 U.S. 397 (1989)

case · ch. 9Texas v. Johnson (1989)

5-4, Brennan, J. (with Marshall, Blackmun, Scalia, and Kennedy). Rehnquist, White, and O'Connor dissented; Stevens dissented separately.

Rule: A law punishing flag desecration because it offends viewers is related to expression, so O'Brien doesn't apply. Under strict scrutiny, the conviction of a flag burner for political protest violates the First Amendment.

Facts: At the 1984 Republican National Convention in Dallas, Gregory Lee Johnson burned an American flag in front of City Hall as protesters chanted, "America, the red, white, and blue, we spit on you." No one was hurt or threatened, but witnesses were seriously offended. Texas law defined "desecrate" as physically mistreating an object in a way the actor knows will "seriously offend" observers. Held: conviction reversed.

- Expressive: the test is intent to convey a particularized message plus a great likelihood it would be understood. Examples: black armbands, sit-ins, military uniforms in antiwar theater, picketing, a peace sign on a flag, refusing to salute. A flag's very purpose is symbolic (Barnette: "a short cut from mind to mind"). Texas conceded the point.

- Related to expression: Texas's interest in preserving the flag as a symbol of nationhood and unity arises "only when a person's treatment of the flag communicates some message."

- Bedrock principle: the government may not prohibit an idea because society finds it offensive. Barnette's "fixed star": no official can prescribe orthodoxy.

- Ends vs. means: the government may encourage respect for the flag by persuasion and example, but not criminally punish flag burning as protest. Tolerating criticism is "a sign and source of our strength."

### United States v. Eichman, 496 U.S. 310 (1990)

case · ch. 9United States v. Eichman (1990)

5-4, Brennan, J. (same majority as Johnson). Stevens, Rehnquist, White, and O'Connor dissented.

Rule: A facially neutral flag-protection statute is still related to suppressing expression when its terms reveal concern with the flag's symbolic value, so it fails like the Texas law.

Facts: After Johnson, Congress passed the Flag Protection Act of 1989, punishing anyone who "knowingly mutilates, defaces, physically defiles, burns, maintains on the floor or ground, or tramples upon" a U.S. flag, with an exception for disposing of a flag that is "worn or soiled." Held: unconstitutional as applied to flag-burning protesters.

- The government argued the Act, unlike Texas's, ignores motive and effect on onlookers.

- But each verb except possibly "burns" "unmistakably connotes disrespectful treatment," and the worn-or-soiled exemption protects acts traditionally associated with patriotic respect.

- Casebook view: the authors find the four dissents in each case "astonishing," and note the split wasn't liberal versus conservative (Scalia and Kennedy were in the majority).

### Synthesis: TPM and Expressive Conduct

Case | Regulation | Result and key reason
Mosley (1972) | School picketing ban except labor disputes | Struck; content based by subject matter
O'Brien (1968) | Draft card destruction | Upheld; interest unrelated to message
Ward (1989) | City sound technician at bandshell | Upheld; neutral, not substantially broader than necessary
Johnson (1989) | Flag desecration that "seriously offends" | Struck; related to message, fails strict scrutiny
Eichman (1990) | Federal Flag Protection Act | Struck; terms reveal concern with disrespect
Ladue (1994) | Near-total residential sign ban | Struck; forecloses unique medium, no adequate alternatives
Thomas (2002) | Park permits for 50+ people | Upheld; neutral, adequate standards
Watchtower (2002) | Permit for door-to-door canvassing | Struck; too much speech, anonymity, spontaneity
Vidal (2024) | Trademark names clause | Content based, not viewpoint based
Chiles (2026) | Conversion-therapy ban as applied to talk therapy | Viewpoint based

### Stretch Exercises: Honking and Cigarette Vending Machines

| Analysis
Honking | California bans honking "except when reasonably necessary to warn of a safety hazard." A driver was cited for honking in support of a political demonstration. Arguments for her: honking at a protest is expressive conduct (intent to show support, likely understood). The ban is facially neutral, so expect O'Brien or TPM intermediate scrutiny. Argue it burns substantially more expression than needed to serve traffic safety and noise interests (a brief supportive honk creates no hazard), and that it leaves no real alternative for a driver to join a demonstration from the road.
Vending machines | A 2010 federal law bans cigarette vending machines except in adults-only areas. Arguments for manufacturers: vending machines display brands and products (commercial speech), so restricting them limits a channel for truthful information to adults (Lorillard). Counter: the law regulates a sales method (conduct) to keep cigarettes from minors, with only incidental effects on expression, so O'Brien or Central Hudson is easily met. Ads remain available elsewhere, and adults can still buy cigarettes.

## Chapter 10: Government Speech

Big picture: so far the course has addressed the government as regulator of private speech ("hate speech is unlawful," "no loudspeakers 10pm-8am," "contains peanuts"). Chapters 10-12 turn to the government acting in nonregulatory capacities, each with its own specialized First Amendment doctrine. These categories can overlap, and they aren't the only ones.

Capacity | Example involving speech | Doctrine
Administrator (running a program) | CDC ads: "Get your kids vaccinated against measles"; DMV "Don't Drink and Drive" signs | Government speech (Ch. 10)
Funder | NEA arts grants; USAID family-planning contracts; NIH grants conditioned on disavowing DEI | Funding conditions (Ch. 11)
Property owner | Limits on speech in the Capitol; banning large protests in national parks | Forum doctrine (Ch. 11)
Employer | DOJ forbids its lawyers to criticize the government's litigation positions | Employee speech (Ch. 12)
School administrator | Public school discipline for student speech | Student speech (Ch. 12)

The simple rule: The First Amendment does not restrict government speech. The government may express its own message without presenting the other side. The disputes are about whether particular speech counts as government speech or private speech.

Government-speech checklist. (1) Who is really speaking? Apply the Shurtleff holistic inquiry, looking at (weighed together)three types of evidence: (1) history of the medium, (2) public perception of who is speaking, and (3) the government's active control over the content. Control over content is often decisive. (2) If government speech, no First Amendment limit on its message, but it can't compel private people to carry its message (Wooley). (3) If private speech, apply the ordinary rules (viewpoint discrimination is forbidden). (4) Even pure government speech can't be used to coerce third parties into suppressing others' speech (Vullo).

### What Counts as Government Speech

### Walker v. Texas Division, Sons of Confederate Veterans, Inc., 576 U.S. 200 (2015)

case · ch. 10Walker v. Texas Division, Sons of Confederate Veterans, Inc. (2015)

5-4, Breyer, J. (with Thomas, Ginsburg, Sotomayor, and Kagan). Alito, J., dissented, joined by Roberts, Scalia, and Kennedy.

Rule: Texas specialty license plates are government speech, so Texas may refuse a design (a Confederate battle flag) without violating the Free Speech Clause.

Facts: Texas offers general-issue, specialty, and personalized plates. Specialty designs come from the legislature ("Keep Texas Beautiful," "Fight Terrorism"), private vendors ("Get it Sold with RE/MAX"), or nonprofit applications approved by the DMV Board, which "may refuse" a design "if the design might be offensive to any member of the public." The Sons of Confederate Veterans proposed a plate with its logo and a Confederate battle flag. After public comment, including letters from elected officials, the Board unanimously denied it because many people reasonably find the flag offensive. Held: no First Amendment violation (reversing the Fifth Circuit).

- Why government must be free to speak: a recycling program couldn't work if letters had to include the trash company's opposing plea; a vaccination campaign couldn't work if officials had to voice anti-vaccine views.

- Built on Pleasant Grove City v. Summum (2009): a city's acceptance of privately donated permanent monuments in a park is government speech, based on (1) the history of governments using monuments to speak, (2) observers reasonably reading monuments as the owner's message, and (3) the city's control over selection.

- History: plates have long carried state messages (Arizona's steer head, 1917; New Hampshire's "Old Man of the Mountain"; "America's Dairyland"; Texas's Lone Star since 1919).

- Public perception: plates are essentially government IDs, with "TEXAS" at the top, issued and owned by the state, and required by law. A driver who wanted a purely private message could use a bumper sticker; choosing a plate suggests wanting the state's endorsement.

- Control: Texas has "sole control" over design, the Board must approve every design, and it has rejected at least a dozen. Texas may offer "Fight Terrorism" without offering plates promoting al Qaeda.

- Compelled speech distinguished: drivers do convey plate messages (Wooley's "mobile billboard"), but just as Texas can't force SCV to carry its message, SCV can't force Texas to put the Confederate flag on its plates.

- Alito, J., dissenting: sit by a Texas highway and watch 350+ specialty plates go by (colleges, fraternities, a soft drink, "Rather Be Golfing," Notre Dame, a NASCAR driver). Is that really the state's message? Texas turned the plates into "little mobile billboards" for private speech and rejected one because it offends: "blatant viewpoint discrimination." Could a state do the same with highway billboards or a campus bulletin board?

### Matal v. Tam, 582 U.S. 218 (2017)

case · ch. 10Matal v. Tam (2017)

8-0 in relevant part, Alito, J. (Gorsuch, J., recused).

Rule: Registered trademarks are private speech, not government speech. The Lanham Act's bar on marks that "disparage" any persons is viewpoint discrimination and violates the First Amendment: speech may not be banned "on the ground that it expresses ideas that offend."

Facts: Asian-American band members sought to register "The Slants," a slur they hoped to "reclaim" and drain of its force. The PTO refused under the disparagement clause. Held: the clause is unconstitutional.

- Government speech is essential: requiring viewpoint neutrality would be paralyzing. WWII posters urged enlistment and war bonds without balancing posters urging the opposite.

- But dangerous: if private speech could become government speech "by simply affixing a government seal of approval," the government could silence disfavored views. So use "great caution" before extending the doctrine.

- Why trademarks are private: the government doesn't create or edit marks, and registration is mandatory if viewpoint-neutral requirements are met. Otherwise the government would be "babbling prodigiously and incoherently" ("Abolish Abortion" and "I Stand With Planned Parenthood"; "Just do it"; "Have it your way").

- Contrast Johanns v. Livestock Marketing Ass'n (2005): beef ads were government speech because the message was "from beginning to end" the federal government's, with officials setting guidelines, attending meetings, and holding the power to edit or reject.

- Slippery slope: if registration made speech the government's, copyright registration of a book might too.

### Shurtleff v. City of Boston, 596 U.S. 243 (2022)

case · ch. 10Shurtleff v. City of Boston (2022)

9-0 on the bottom line, Breyer, J. Alito, Thomas, and Gorsuch concurred in the judgment, rejecting the three-factor test.

Rule: Courts conduct a holistic inquiry into whether the government intends to speak for itself or to regulate private expression, looking at three types of evidence: (1) the history of the expression; (2) the public's likely perception of who is speaking; and (3) the extent to which the government has actively shaped or controlled the expression. Boston's flag-raising program was private speech, so refusing a "Christian flag" violated the First Amendment.

Facts: Boston flies the U.S., Massachusetts, and Boston flags on three poles outside City Hall. Since 2005 it let groups replace the city flag for a few hours during ceremonies; it approved about 50 flags at 284 ceremonies (mostly other countries' flags, plus Pride Week, EMS workers, a community bank) and never refused one. In 2017 Harold Shurtleff of Camp Constitution asked to raise a "Christian flag." The city refused, fearing an Establishment Clause violation. Held: the refusal violated the Free Speech Clause.

- History favors Boston: flags at the seat of government usually convey government messages (a foreign flag at Blair House; Boston raising the Canadiens' banner after losing a hockey bet).

- Public perception is mixed: people associate City Hall flags with the city, but Boston regularly lowered its flag for others.

- Control decides it: Boston controlled date, time, and premises (and provided a hand crank) but not the flags' content or meaning. It approved every request and had no written policy on what could be flown. That is "the most salient feature of this case."

- Boston can change its policy going forward.

- Alito, J., concurring in the judgment: neither control nor final approval authority distinguishes government speech from censorship, and focusing on public perception invites misattribution. His test: government speech occurs only if the government purposefully expresses its own message through persons authorized to speak for it, without using a means that abridges private speech.

- Slides: Shurtleff is also an example of a designated public forum (Ch. 11): flagpoles aren't traditionally open to the public, but Boston chose to open one.

### A Limit: Government Speech Can't Coerce

### National Rifle Association of America v. Vullo, 602 U.S. 175 (2024)

case · ch. 10National Rifle Association of America v. Vullo (2024)

9-0, Sotomayor, J.

Rule: Government officials may criticize views and try to persuade, but they may not use state power to coerce private parties into punishing or suppressing disfavored speech by others. An official "cannot do indirectly what she is barred from doing directly" (Bantam Books v. Sullivan, 1963).

Facts: The NRA alleged that Maria Vullo, superintendent of the New York Department of Financial Services, threatened enforcement actions against regulated insurance companies unless they cut ties with the NRA and other gun-promotion groups. Held: the allegations, if true, state a First Amendment claim.

- This isn't about whether speech is the government's; it is a separate limit on what government speech may do.

- An official may share her views forcefully, relying on "the merits and force of her ideas," but not on threats of legal sanctions. The line between persuasion and coercion can be fuzzy.

- Slides example: an official can't say, "I will revoke your company's license unless you boycott the NRA."

### Synthesis: Government or Private Speech?

Case | History | Perception | Control | Result
Summum (2009), park monuments | Favors gov't | Favors gov't | City selects | Government speech
Johanns (2005), beef ads | n/a | n/a | Message set and edited by gov't | Government speech
Walker (2015), specialty plates | Favors gov't | Plates are gov't IDs | Approves every design; rejected a dozen | Government speech (5-4)
Tam (2017), trademarks | n/a | Not gov't views | No editing; registration mandatory | Private speech
Shurtleff (2022), City Hall flagpole | Favors gov't | Mixed | None over content | Private speech
Women for America First (2d Cir. 2022), street murals | Streets carry gov't messages | City announced its values | Mayor directed, DOT funded, final approval | Government speech

### Stretch Exercises: Street Murals and AI Chatbots

| Analysis
Murals | In July 2020 New York City painted "Black Lives Matter" murals on seven streets, including Fifth Avenue in front of Trump Tower, at Mayor de Blasio's direction. Women for America First asked to paint its motto on a city street; DOT refused ("installations on City roadways that are open to traffic" aren't permitted). The Second Circuit (Women for America First v. Adams, 2022) held the murals were government speech under all three factors: streets have long carried city messages (traffic markings; anti-graffiti laws reserve them); the public would see a permanent street message as the city's, especially since the mayor said the murals "send a message that these are our values"; and the city exercised editorial control (mayor's direction, city employees painting, DOT funding, final approval).
Questions | Did the Second Circuit apply the precedent correctly? Is the precedent right? Would your answer change if the murals said "Black Lives Don't Matter," "Abortion is Murder," "Defund the Police," "Support Israel," or "Free Palestine"? Should there be any limit on the government's ability to spread its own messages?
AI chatbots | Garcia (Ch. 5) doubted chatbot output reflects the human intent needed for "speech." If the CDC deploys an AI chatbot to answer vaccine questions, are its answers government speech? Under Shurtleff, the government chooses to deploy the tool, the public likely attributes the answers to the CDC, and the agency controls training and guardrails, though not each output. Should it matter that "the government" isn't a human? Courts haven't developed a doctrine for AI-generated government communications.

## Chapter 11: Government-Funded Speech and Speech on Government Property

Big picture: two more nonregulatory capacities, which overlap heavily with government speech (Ch. 10): the government as funder of private speech and as owner of property that private speakers use (forum doctrine). "Property" includes not just streets and parks but tangible things like flagpoles and classrooms, and intangible things like a university's student activity fund. That is why the doctrines overlap.

Funding and forum checklist. Funding: (1) Is the government paying private parties to deliver its message (government speech; it may keep that message from being "garbled or distorted")? Or is the program designed to facilitate private speech (Velazquez)? (2) Does the condition define the limits of the program (OK, Rust) or leverage funding to regulate speech outside its contours (unconstitutional condition, USAID I)? Forum: (1) Is the speech private, or the government's own (Walker: no forum)? (2) What type of forum? (3) Apply that forum's standard. (4) Whatever the forum, viewpoint discrimination almost always fails.

### Government-Funded Speech

Rule: The government may fund private entities to communicate its message and may limit what the funds are used to say. Generally, funding choices get rational-basis review. "When the government disburses public funds to private entities to convey a governmental message, it may take legitimate and appropriate steps to ensure that its message is neither garbled nor distorted by the grantee." But it may not impose conditions that regulate speech "outside the contours of the spending program itself." The line is fuzzy, and the Court admits it.

- Examples: the CDC may fund nonprofits to promote measles vaccination and bar them from using the grant to say something different; a DMV may contract for "Drive Sober" signs. But the CDC couldn't bar grantees from criticizing it on unrelated matters, and the DMV couldn't bar contractors from using their own money to advocate a higher speed limit.

- Unconstitutional conditions doctrine: there are limits to the conditions the government may attach to grants. It often involves speech but isn't limited to it: the government almost certainly couldn't require grantees to give up their Sixth Amendment jury-trial right or Second Amendment rights.

- Study tip: focus on how Velazquez and USAID I distinguished Rust, and be ready to argue both cases both ways.

### Rust v. Sullivan, 500 U.S. 173 (1991)

case · ch. 11Rust v. Sullivan (1991)

5-4, Rehnquist, C.J. Blackmun, Marshall, O'Connor, and Stevens dissented.

Rule: The government may fund a program that advances its goals without funding alternatives, and may bar grantees from using program funds for speech outside the program's scope. That isn't viewpoint discrimination; the government "has merely chosen to fund one activity to the exclusion of the other." Later cases explain Rust as the government using private speakers to transmit information about its own program.

Facts: Title X funded projects where doctors counseled patients on family planning (contraception, infertility) but barred using Title X funds for abortion counseling. Grantees, staff, and patients claimed a free speech violation. Held: upheld.

- Selective funding is fine: when Congress created the National Endowment for Democracy, it didn't have to fund programs promoting communism or fascism. "When the Government appropriates public funds to establish a program it is entitled to define the limits of that program."

- Key fact, the grantee stays free outside the program: it may still perform abortions, provide abortion-related services, and engage in abortion advocacy, using separate, independent programs funded by other sources.

### Legal Services Corporation v. Velazquez, 531 U.S. 533 (2001)

case · ch. 11Legal Services Corporation v. Velazquez (2001)

5-4, Kennedy, J. Scalia, J., dissented, joined by Rehnquist, O'Connor, and Thomas.

Rule: When a funding program is designed to facilitate private speech rather than promote a government message, the government may not restrict that speech to insulate its own laws from challenge. Barring LSC-funded lawyers from challenging the validity of welfare laws violates the First Amendment.

Facts: The Legal Services Corporation funds local nonprofits whose lawyers represent indigent clients in civil matters, including welfare claims. Congress barred funded lawyers from cases involving "an effort to amend or otherwise challenge existing law": they could argue an agency got the facts wrong or misapplied a statute, but not that a welfare law was unconstitutional or conflicted with federal law, and had to withdraw if such an issue arose mid-case. (Other, unchallenged LSC limits bar political campaigns, most criminal cases, and class actions without approval.) Held: unconstitutional.

- Rust distinguished: there, the government used private speakers to convey its own program's message. Here, the LSC lawyer speaks for a private client in a claim against the government; the government's lawyer on the other side delivers the government's message. Advice and advocacy by the LSC lawyer can't be government speech "even under a generous understanding of the concept."

- Congress needn't fund LSC lawyers or every kind of representation, but it can't define the litigation it funds to exclude "certain vital theories and ideas" to insulate its own interpretation of the Constitution from judicial challenge.

- Scalia, J., dissenting: if the doctors' confidential advice in Rust was government speech, it's hard to imagine what subsidized speech isn't. Doctors also owe professional duties to patients. The subsidy prevents no one from speaking and is "indistinguishable in all relevant respects" from Rust.

### Agency for International Development v. Alliance for Open Society International (USAID I), 570 U.S. 205 (2013)

case · ch. 11Agency for International Development v. Alliance for Open Society International (2013)

6-2, Roberts, C.J. (Kagan, J., recused). Scalia, J., dissented, joined by Thomas.

Rule: The government may define the limits of what it funds, but it may not leverage funding to regulate speech outside the contours of the program. Requiring grantees to adopt as their own a government policy on an issue of public concern fails: it goes "beyond defining the limits of the federally funded program to defining the recipient." "Congress cannot recast a condition on funding as a mere definition of its program in every case, lest the First Amendment be reduced to a simple semantic exercise" (Velazquez).

Facts: The 2003 Leadership Act funded NGOs fighting HIV/AIDS abroad. Condition 1 (unchallenged): funds can't be used to promote or advocate legalizing prostitution or sex trafficking. Condition 2 (the Policy Requirement): grantees must have a policy explicitly opposing prostitution and sex trafficking. U.S. NGOs feared alienating host governments, hampering work with sex workers, and having to censor privately funded discussions. Held: the Policy Requirement violates the First Amendment.

- As a direct regulation, the requirement would "plainly violate" the First Amendment. Normally a recipient that objects to a condition can decline the funds, but some conditions unconstitutionally burden speech.

- Why outside the program: condition 1 already keeps federal money from promoting prostitution, so the Policy Requirement must do "something more." A recipient can't profess the government's belief when spending federal funds and then assert a contrary belief or neutrality "on its own time and dime."

- The government's "fungibility" argument (federal money frees private money for pro-prostitution advocacy) was unsupported.

- Scalia, J., dissenting: the requirement just selects suitable agents for the government's chosen strategy. The government needn't hire the American Gourmet Society to run a healthy-eating program. The principle wouldn't let the government exclude defense contractors who won't abjure prostitution, because there it is unrelated to the program.

### Agency for International Development v. Alliance for Open Society International (USAID II), 591 U.S. 430 (2020)

case · ch. 11Agency for International Development v. Alliance for Open Society International (2020)

5-3, Kavanaugh, J. (Kagan, J., recused). Breyer, Ginsburg, and Sotomayor dissented.

Rule: The plaintiffs' legally separate foreign affiliates operating abroad have no First Amendment rights, so the Policy Requirement may still be applied to them. Read for general con law principles.

- Two bedrock principles: (1) foreign citizens outside U.S. territory don't possess rights under the U.S. Constitution (otherwise military, intelligence, and law enforcement actions abroad would be constrained); (2) the affiliates were incorporated abroad and are legally separate (no veil-piercing argument).

### Speech on Government Property (Forum Doctrine)

Baseline (private property): when the government restricts speech on private property, content-based rules get strict scrutiny ("no political yard signs") and content-neutral TPM rules get intermediate scrutiny ("two signs per yard," probably upheld; compare Ladue). On government property, the rules depend on the type of forum. (Professor Klein: the plural is "fora," but courts say "forums," "even though it makes me wince.")

Forum | What it is | Standard
Traditional public forum | Property historically open to the public for expression: streets, sidewalks, parks, "time out of mind" used for assembly and debate | Same as private property: content- or viewpoint-based restrictions get strict scrutiny; content-neutral TPM rules get intermediate scrutiny (Thomas)
Designated public forum | Property the government chose to open to the general public for expression though not traditionally used that way (Boston's flagpole in Shurtleff; university meeting rooms, a municipal theater) | Same as traditional public forum, so long as the government keeps it open (it needn't keep it open forever)
