Limited public forum | Property opened for private speech in particular ways, for certain groups or topics (classrooms for student-group meetings; a city hall lobby for Civil War art; a bulletin board for study-abroad notices; a student activity fund) | Restrictions must be reasonable in light of the forum's limited purpose; viewpoint discrimination gets strict scrutiny; speakers get equal access consistent with the purpose
Nonpublic forum | Property used for the government's internal purposes; some private access doesn't convert it (school interoffice mail in Perry; airport terminals; military bases) | Restrictions must be reasonable and not an effort to suppress disfavored views; distinctions by subject matter and speaker identity are allowed

- Fuzzy lines: the line between a limited public forum and a nonpublic forum with some private access is fuzzy. So is defining a limited forum's purpose, which is often the heart of the dispute. Tip: the government can define the purpose narrowly up front ("Post information about opportunities to study abroad here").

Professor Klein's practice perspective (from decades at DOJ). Her old professor Richard Fallon once said the forum categories were "the result of a law clerk run amok. That was me!" In practice, ask: Is it a traditional public forum? If so, content- or viewpoint-based restrictions very likely fail. If not, there is some flexibility for content-based restrictions that are reasonable in light of the government's objectives, but viewpoint-based ones still likely fail. Anywhere, content-neutral restrictions likely survive if reasonable and alternatives remain. In litigation, argue the government wins under any characterization (nonpublic or limited; government speech or a permissible funding condition) rather than obsessing over the doctrinal box.

### Perry Education Ass'n v. Perry Local Educators' Ass'n, 460 U.S. 37 (1983)

case · ch. 11Perry Education Ass'n v. Perry Local Educators' Ass'n (1983)

5-4, White, J. Brennan, Marshall, Powell, and Stevens dissented. Most often quoted for its description of the forum categories.

Rule: A school district's interoffice mail system is a nonpublic forum. Giving the elected exclusive bargaining union access while denying a rival union is reasonable and based on status, not viewpoint. "Implicit in the concept of the nonpublic forum is the right to make distinctions in access on the basis of subject matter and speaker identity."

Facts: The Perry Township schools' internal mail system carried official messages, teachers' personal messages, and, with principals' permission, messages from groups like parochial schools, church groups, YMCAs, and Cub Scouts. PEA won an election as exclusive bargaining representative; its contract gave it access to teacher mailboxes and denied access to other unions. Rival PLEA sued. Held: no First Amendment violation (reversing the Seventh Circuit).

- Not a public forum: the system wasn't open to the general public; permission came from individual principals. Selective access doesn't create a public forum (Greer v. Spock: occasional civilian speakers at Fort Dix didn't open the base).

- Even if a limited forum was created by admitting Cub Scouts and YMCAs, access would extend only to entities "of similar character" (Girl Scouts, boys' clubs), not a group concerned with teachers' employment terms.

- Prior equal access: "it is not the forum, but PLEA itself, which has changed." PEA's official role as bargaining agent justified its special access.

- Reasonable: PLEA still had bulletin boards, meeting rooms, the PA system with approval, word of mouth, phone, and U.S. mail, and equal access during election contests.

### International Society for Krishna Consciousness, Inc. (ISKCON) v. Lee, 505 U.S. 672 (1992), and Lee v. ISKCON, 505 U.S. 830 (1992)

case · ch. 11ISKCON v. Lee (1992); Lee v. ISKCON (1992)

Airports are nonpublic forums (5-4); solicitation ban upheld (6-3, Rehnquist, C.J.); leafletting ban struck (5-4, O'Connor, J.).

Rule: Airport terminals are nonpublic forums. A ban on repetitive in-terminal solicitation of money is reasonable, but a ban on distributing literature is not. Reasonableness is judged in light of the forum's purpose and all the circumstances.

Facts: ISKCON members perform sankirtan: going into public places, distributing religious literature, and soliciting funds. The Port Authority banned continuous or repetitive sale or distribution of merchandise or literature, and solicitation of funds, inside the JFK, La Guardia, and Newark terminals, but allowed them on outside sidewalks.

- Government as proprietor: when managing its internal operations rather than acting as lawmaker, its actions don't get heightened review.

- Not a public forum: airports haven't historically been open for speech, and the Port Authority hasn't intentionally opened them; their purpose is facilitating air travel.

- Solicitation ban reasonable: solicitation disrupts the flow of hurried travelers with luggage (a missed flight costs hours), and face-to-face solicitation risks duress against the vulnerable (people with children or disabilities) who are too rushed to complain. Pedestrian congestion is a major problem, and if ISKCON gets access, so must others.

- O'Connor, J. (leafletting): the airport is also "a shopping mall," so ask whether restrictions are reasonably related to that multipurpose environment. Leaflets don't require the recipient to stop, and the Port Authority offered no justification for banning leafletting alone. It may use content-neutral TPM rules instead, like confining sankirtan to an uncongested area near the JFK chapel.

### Rosenberger v. Rector & Visitors of the University of Virginia, 515 U.S. 819 (1995)

case · ch. 11Rosenberger v. Rector & Visitors of the University of Virginia (1995)

5-4, Kennedy, J. Souter, Stevens, Ginsburg, and Breyer dissented.

Rule: A university's student activity fund is a limited public forum ("more in a metaphysical than in a spatial or geographic sense"). Once it opens a limited forum, the state may not exclude speech unreasonably in light of the forum's purpose, nor discriminate based on viewpoint. Denying printing costs to a student paper with a Christian perspective violates the Free Speech Clause.

Facts: UVA's Student Activities Fund, paid for by a mandatory $14-per-semester student fee, paid outside printers for student groups (CIOs) whose activities relate to the university's educational purpose, including student news and opinion media. It excluded "religious activities," defined as anything that "primarily promotes or manifests a particular belief in or about a deity or an ultimate reality." Wide Awake Productions published Wide Awake: A Christian Perspective at the University of Virginia and was denied $5,862 for printing. Held: the denial violated the Free Speech Clause.

- Private speech, not the university's: every CIO signs an agreement that it isn't the university's agent, isn't controlled by it, and that the university doesn't endorse its goals. In 1990-91, 118 of 135 applicant groups were funded, including 15 media groups.

- Having offered to pay printers for private speakers conveying their own messages, the university "may not silence the expression of selected viewpoints." The religious exclusion targeted a religious perspective on otherwise eligible topics.

- Rosenberger also supplied the line later cited in funding cases: when the government funds private speakers to convey its own message, it may keep that message from being garbled.

### Walker v. Texas Division, Sons of Confederate Veterans, 576 U.S. 200 (2015) (revisited)

case · ch. 11Walker v. Texas Division, Sons of Confederate Veterans (2015)

5-4, Breyer, J. Full case in Ch. 10.

Rule: When the government speaks for itself, forum analysis doesn't apply. A government creates a public forum only by intentionally opening a nontraditional forum for public discourse, not by inaction or permitting limited discourse. Texas specialty plates aren't a traditional, designated, or limited public forum.

- Why no forum: the state has final authority over each design, owns each design, and plates have traditionally carried government speech, serve as government ID, and bear the state's name. Private participation in designing a message doesn't make the government "a mere forum-provider."

### Synthesis: Funding and Forum Cases

Case | Category | Result and key reason
Rust (1991) | Funding (government message) | Upheld; defines program; grantee free outside it
Velazquez (2001) | Funding (private speech) | Struck; lawyers speak for clients; insulates laws from challenge
USAID I (2013) | Funding (condition beyond program) | Struck; compels belief that can't be confined to program
USAID II (2020) | Funding (foreign affiliates) | No First Amendment rights abroad
Perry (1983) | Nonpublic forum (school mail) | Upheld; reasonable, status-based
ISKCON (1992) | Nonpublic forum (airports) | Solicitation ban upheld; leafletting ban struck
Rosenberger (1995) | Limited public forum (student fund) | Struck; viewpoint discrimination against religious perspective
Walker (2015) | No forum; government speech | Upheld; state's own message
Shurtleff (2022) | Designated public forum (flagpole) | Struck; private speech, viewpoint-based denial

### Stretch Exercises: Grant Conditions and Bus Ads

| Analysis
#1 Opioid grants | HHS grants to nonprofits to reduce opioid addiction require recipients to refrain from advocating legalization of heroin. For HHS: like Rust, it defines the program's message, and advocating legalization would garble an anti-addiction message. Against: if it bars advocacy with the grantee's own money and on its own time, it reaches outside the program like USAID I. Likely outcome turns on whether the condition is limited to the funded program or reaches the organization as a whole.
#2 DEI education grants | Department of Education grants to teach teens about the benefits of a diverse workforce require recipients to refrain from criticizing workforce DEI initiatives. For the government: it is paying for its own message about diversity and needn't fund the other side (Rust). Against: a blanket ban on criticism reaches beyond the funded curriculum and resembles USAID I's demand that recipients adopt the government's view. It also sounds viewpoint-based. Compare the slides' example of NIH conditioning cancer grants on disavowing DEI programs: a condition unrelated to the program's subject is even harder to defend.
#3 Bus ads | A city allows commercial but not political ads on city buses. The ad space isn't a traditional public forum. The city will argue it is a limited or nonpublic forum whose purpose is revenue and a pleasant ride for a captive audience, and that excluding all political ads is a reasonable, viewpoint-neutral subject-matter line. Challengers will argue the city opened the space broadly to private messages (a designated forum, like Shurtleff), and that "political" is vague enough to invite viewpoint-based enforcement (compare Thomas's concern with official discretion).

## Chapter 12: Speech by Government Employees and Speech in Public Schools

Big picture: two more nonregulatory capacities: the government as employer and as school administrator. They overlap because public-school teachers are government employees (Pickering itself involved a teacher). Employees and public-school students have First Amendment rights, but more limited ones than the general public's. In both contexts the Court uses balancing tests that weigh the government's legitimate interests.

Why balancing here? When the government acts as regulator, the Court rejects ad hoc balancing (Stevens called a cost-benefit test for new unprotected categories "startling and dangerous") and prefers bright-line rules. But as employer or school administrator, the government often has legitimate reasons to restrict speech that are hard to catalog. The casebook suspects "there is no better alternative" to balancing.

### Speech by Government Employees

Rule (the Pickering test, as refined by Garcetti): balance "the interests of the employee, as a citizen, in commenting upon matters of public concern and the interest of the State, as an employer, in promoting the efficiency of the public services it performs through its employees." Step 1: Did the employee speak as a citizen on a matter of public concern? If not (e.g., speaking pursuant to official duties), no First Amendment claim; the speech is effectively the government's, and it controls its message. Step 2: If so, did the government have an adequate justification for treating the employee differently from any other member of the public?

- Pickering v. Board of Education (1968): a teacher fired for a letter to the editor criticizing the school board's handling of the budget won. The letter was on a matter of public concern and didn't impede classroom performance or school operations. Teachers are "most likely to have informed and definite opinions" about school funding.

- Adequate justifications (step 2): the Court hasn't given a full list. Examples: speech that is false or discloses confidential information (though the government couldn't punish a member of the public for the same speech), efficiency and integrity in official duties, and discipline in public service. A stronger showing may be needed the more the speech involves public concern.

### Garcetti v. Ceballos, 547 U.S. 410 (2006)

case · ch. 12Garcetti v. Ceballos (2006)

5-4, Kennedy, J. Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer dissented.

Rule: "When public employees make statements pursuant to their official duties, the employees are not speaking as citizens for First Amendment purposes, and the Constitution does not insulate their communications from employer discipline."

Facts: Ceballos, a deputy district attorney (calendar deputy), wrote an internal memo to supervisors concluding that a search-warrant affidavit contained serious misrepresentations and recommending how to handle the case. After heated exchanges, he suffered retaliation (the casebook says he was eventually fired) because supervisors disagreed. Held: no First Amendment violation.

- Not dispositive: that he spoke inside the office rather than publicly, and that the memo concerned the subject matter of his job. Some workplace and job-related expression is protected.

- Controlling: he wrote the memo as part of his duties, advising his supervisor on a pending case. "When he went to work and performed the tasks he was paid to perform," he acted as an employee, and supervisors may evaluate that work.

- Values on both sides: employees remain citizens, and the public benefits from their informed views. But the First Amendment doesn't "constitutionalize the employee grievance."

### Lane v. Franks, 573 U.S. 228 (2014)

case · ch. 12Lane v. Franks (2014)

9-0, Sotomayor, J.

Rule: Truthful sworn testimony, compelled by subpoena, outside the scope of an employee's ordinary job duties is speech as a citizen, even if it concerns information learned on the job. "The critical question under Garcetti is whether the speech at issue is itself ordinarily within the scope of an employee's duties, not whether it merely concerns those duties."

Facts: Lane, a state-agency employee, testified under subpoena at criminal trials about corruption and misuse of state funds in a public program he worked in. Testifying wasn't part of his ordinary job. He was fired. Held: the firing violated the First Amendment (reversing the Eleventh Circuit, which read Garcetti "far too broadly").

- Step 1, citizen speech on public concern: unlike Garcetti's internal memo, the testimony wasn't part of his paid tasks. Corruption and misuse of public funds are obviously of significant public concern.

- Why employee speech has special value: employees "are often in the best position to know what ails the agencies for which they work." Federal corruption prosecutions (1,000+ a year) depend on government employees' testimony; a contrary rule would force witnesses to choose between truthful testimony and their jobs.

- Step 2, the employer's side "entirely empty": no evidence the testimony was false, or that Lane unnecessarily disclosed sensitive, confidential, or privileged information.

### Speech in Public Schools

Principles (no single test): students do not "shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate" (Tinker), but the First Amendment applies "in light of the special characteristics of the school environment" (Hazelwood). These rules cover public schools (including public universities), not private ones.

Special characteristic of schools | What it justifies
In loco parentis | For minors (K-12), administrators stand in for parents when parents can't protect, guide, and discipline
Preventing disruption | Speech that "materially disrupts classwork or involves substantial disorder" (Tinker)
Protecting other students | Speech that invades "the rights of others" (e.g., bullying)
School imprimatur | Speech others may reasonably perceive as "bearing the imprimatur of the school" (school newspaper, assembly, play) (Hazelwood)

- Categories the Court has recognized (per Mahanoy): (1) indecent, lewd, or vulgar speech at a school assembly; (2) speech promoting illegal drug use on a class trip; (3) speech bearing the school's imprimatur; plus Tinker's substantial-disruption and rights-of-others standard.

### Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District, 393 U.S. 503 (1969)

case · ch. 12Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District (1969)

7-2, Fortas, J. Black and Harlan dissented.

Rule: Schools may restrict student expression only if they can show it would materially and substantially interfere with school work and discipline or invade the rights of others. "Undifferentiated fear or apprehension of disturbance is not enough." Officials may not suppress an opinion merely to avoid "the discomfort and unpleasantness that always accompany an unpopular viewpoint."

Facts: In December 1965, John Tinker (15), Christopher Eckhardt (16), and Mary Beth Tinker (13) wore black armbands to school to protest the Vietnam War and support a truce. Principals, learning of the plan, adopted a policy suspending any student who wouldn't remove an armband. They were suspended until after New Year's. Held: the suspensions violated the First Amendment.

- Symbolic speech "closely akin to 'pure speech'": a silent, passive expression of opinion with no disorder, not about hair, skirts, or aggressive conduct.

- No evidence of interference with schoolwork or other students' rights, and nothing that could reasonably forecast substantial disruption. The armbands caused discussion outside class, not disorder.

- Any deviating word "may start an argument or cause a disturbance," but the Constitution says we must take that risk (Terminiello). This "hazardous freedom" is the basis of national strength.

- "State-operated schools may not be enclaves of totalitarianism." Students aren't "closed-circuit recipients of only that which the State chooses to communicate."

### Hazelwood School District v. Kuhlmeier, 484 U.S. 260 (1988)

case · ch. 12Hazelwood School District v. Kuhlmeier (1988)

6-3, White, J. Brennan, Marshall, and Blackmun dissented.

Rule: Educators may exercise editorial control over the style and content of student speech in school-sponsored expressive activities "so long as their actions are reasonably related to legitimate pedagogical concerns." Tinker asks whether a school must tolerate personal expression; Hazelwood asks whether it must affirmatively promote student speech that bears its imprimatur.

Facts: Spectrum, the Hazelwood East newspaper, was written and edited by the Journalism II class for grades and credit; the teacher controlled nearly everything, and the principal reviewed each issue. More than 4,500 copies went to students, staff, and the community. The principal deleted two pages, including articles about students' pregnancies. Held: no First Amendment violation.

- Curricular activities: school-sponsored publications, plays, and other activities that students, parents, and the public might reasonably see as the school's, supervised by faculty and designed to teach. The school may make sure students learn the lesson, protect immature audiences, and avoid having individual views attributed to it.

- What the school may refuse to sponsor: speech that is ungrammatical, poorly written, inadequately researched, biased, vulgar, or unsuitable for immature audiences; speech that might seem to advocate drug or alcohol use or irresponsible sex; or anything associating the school with a non-neutral position on political controversy.

- Prior case: a student could be disciplined for a sexually explicit (not obscene) speech at a school assembly, because the school could disassociate itself from vulgarity [the casebook doesn't name it: Bethel School District v. Fraser, 1986].

- Applied: the principal reasonably feared the pregnant students could be identified, that boyfriends and parents discussed in the articles hadn't consented or been able to respond, and that frank talk about sexual histories and birth control was inappropriate for 14-year-old freshmen and their younger siblings.

- Footnote 7: the Court didn't decide whether the same deference applies at colleges and universities.

- Casebook aside: private schools aren't bound by the First Amendment, but many protect student speech. In 1989 Georgetown forced The Hoya to cancel an issue with an abortion-rights rally ad; The Hoya and The Voice (edited by Professor Klein's husband Craig) struck, and Georgetown backed down.

### Mahanoy Area School District v. B.L., 594 U.S. 180 (2021)

case · ch. 12Mahanoy Area School District v. B.L. (2021)

8-1, Breyer, J. Alito (with Gorsuch) concurred; Thomas, J., dissented.

Rule: Schools have less latitude to regulate off-campus speech, but their special interests don't always disappear off campus. No bright line between on- and off-campus speech; future cases will decide where, when, and how location matters.

Facts: After failing to make varsity cheerleading (while an incoming freshman did), B.L., a high school student, posted a Snapchat story on a weekend from the Cocoa Hut convenience store, visible to her ~250 friends for 24 hours: a photo with middle fingers raised captioned "Fuck school fuck softball fuck cheer fuck everything," and a second post complaining about JV. Screenshots spread; some cheerleaders were "visibly upset," and it came up in an Algebra class. Coaches suspended her from JV cheer for a year for profanity connected to an extracurricular activity. Held: the suspension violated the First Amendment.

- Off-campus interests that may remain significant: serious or severe bullying or harassment targeting individuals; threats aimed at teachers or students; failure to follow rules on lessons, papers, computers, or online school activities; and breaches of school security devices.

- Three features of off-campus speech that reduce school leeway: (1) the school rarely stands in loco parentis; off campus is normally parents' responsibility. (2) Regulating off-campus and on-campus speech covers a student's whole 24-hour day, so courts should be more skeptical; for political or religious speech, the school has a "heavy burden." (3) Schools themselves have an interest in protecting unpopular expression; they are "the nurseries of democracy."

- Applied: her speech was criticism of a community she belonged to, not fighting words (Chaplinsky) or obscene (Cohen). It was posted off campus, after hours, on a personal phone to private friends, without naming the school or targeting anyone.

- School's interests fail: (1) teaching good manners is weak off campus, with no evidence of any general effort to police off-campus vulgarity; (2) no "substantial disruption": 5-10 minutes of an Algebra class for a couple of days and some upset teammates; (3) team morale: only generalized "negativity," which is "undifferentiated fear."

- "Sometimes it is necessary to protect the superfluous in order to preserve the necessary."

### Synthesis: Employees and Students

Case | Speech | Result and key reason
Pickering (1968) | Teacher's letter to editor on school budget | Protected; citizen speech on public concern; no disruption
Garcetti (2006) | Prosecutor's internal memo | Unprotected; pursuant to official duties
Lane (2014) | Subpoenaed trial testimony on corruption | Protected; outside ordinary duties; employer's side empty
Tinker (1969) | Black armbands | Protected; no substantial disruption
Hazelwood (1988) | School newspaper articles | Restriction OK; school-sponsored, legitimate pedagogical concerns
Mahanoy (2021) | Off-campus vulgar Snapchat | Protected; reduced off-campus leeway; no disruption

### Stretch Exercises: Campus Protests and School Library Books

| Analysis
Campus protests | At a public university, students (1) silently hold signs saying "Stop Israel's genocide in Gaza" outside a building; (2) chant the slogan; (3) chant "Zionists deserve to die"; (4) silently hold that sign in a common space inside the building. Framework: university students are adults, so in loco parentis carries little weight, and outdoor campus spaces may resemble public forums. Silent signs (1) look like Tinker's armbands: protected absent substantial disruption. Chanting (2) adds noise, which content-neutral TPM rules may limit if they leave alternatives. "Zionists deserve to die" (3) raises true threats (Counterman), incitement (Brandenburg), and invasion of other students' rights. The indoor sign (4) removes the noise but moves the speech into a space with stronger claims to protect other students and the educational environment.
Crookshanks v. Elizabeth School District (D. Colo. 2025) | The district permanently removed 19 books (including The Kite Runner and The Bluest Eye) from school libraries. The court granted a preliminary injunction: students have a right to receive information; library curation isn't government speech (no one thinks a library endorses Mein Kampf; accord 8th Cir. 2024 and N.D. Fla. 2024); a library book doesn't bear the school's imprimatur the way a journalism-class newspaper does; and removal to promote the board's "conservative values" based on viewpoints about race, sexual orientation, and gender identity isn't "reasonably related to legitimate pedagogical concerns" (Hazelwood).
Arguing for the district | Library selection is inherently curatorial and pedagogical; a school chooses what to offer minors and is closer to Hazelwood than Tinker. Libraries are part of the educational program, and age-appropriateness is a legitimate concern. Use Mahmoud (Ch. 1): if the Montgomery County board could choose to integrate LGBTQ+-friendly books into the curriculum, a board should equally be able to choose which books to remove. (The slides ask whether you're convinced by Crookshanks.)

## Chapter 13: Speech Involving Social Media and Speech Involving Elections

Big picture: two special categories of speech, rather than more government capacities. Social media cases add a third actor: earlier cases had two (the government and the private speaker), but social media cases may involve (1) the individual user, (2) the private platform hosting the speech (Facebook, YouTube), and (3) the government. Users and platforms both have First Amendment rights against the government. Because the technology is new and evolving, the Court has been careful not to announce sweeping rules. Elections law is complicated; two cases give a feel for how First Amendment issues arise.

Social media checklist. (1) Identify the three actors and whose rights are at stake. (2) Government restricting a user's access: Packingham (the Internet is a vital forum; overbroad bans fail even intermediate scrutiny). (3) Official blocking a user: is it state action? Lindke: actual authority to speak for the state + purporting to use it, post by post. (4) Government regulating platforms' content moderation: NetChoice (curation is protected editorial judgment; "rebalancing" the speech market isn't a valid interest). (5) Government pressuring platforms: coercion violates the First Amendment (Vullo), but users must show the government, not the platform's own choice, caused the takedown (Murthy). (6) Users have no First Amendment rights against private platforms.

### Speech Involving Social Media

### Packingham v. North Carolina, 582 U.S. 98 (2017)

case · ch. 13Packingham v. North Carolina (2017)

8-0 on the bottom line, Kennedy, J. (Gorsuch, J., recused). Alito, J., with Roberts and Thomas, concurred in the judgment.

Rule: Internet access is protected by the First Amendment because it is so important for speech. Cyberspace, especially social media, is today's most important place for the exchange of views, akin to streets and parks. A law broadly barring registered sex offenders from social media fails even intermediate scrutiny. The Court declined to decide what standard applies to restrictions on Internet access.

Facts: North Carolina made it a felony for a registered sex offender to access a commercial social networking site that he knows permits minors to become members. About 20,000 people were covered and over 1,000 prosecuted. Lester Packingham, who at 21 had sex with a 13-year-old and registered as a sex offender, posted on Facebook after a traffic ticket was dismissed: "Man God is Good! ... Praise be to GOD, WOW! Thanks JESUS!" He was convicted, though he never contacted a minor or did anything illicit online. Held: the law violates the First Amendment.

- "Vast democratic forums": seven in ten American adults use social media; Facebook had 1.79 billion users. People use it to debate religion and politics, find jobs, and petition elected officials (all 50 governors and nearly every member of Congress have accounts).

- Caution: the Internet is "so new, so protean, and so far reaching" that what courts say today may be obsolete tomorrow, so the Court must be careful before suggesting it gives "scant protection" to access.

- Tailoring fails: protecting children from sexual abuse is compelling, and states may pass specific, narrowly tailored laws barring conduct that often presages a crime (contacting a minor, gathering information about a minor online). But this law "with one broad stroke" cuts off the principal sources for news, job ads, and speaking and listening in "the modern public square."

### Lindke v. Freed, 144 S. Ct. 746 (2024)

case · ch. 13Lindke v. Freed (2024)

9-0, Barrett, J. Remanded to apply the new framework.

Rule (state action): A public official's social-media activity is attributable to the state only if the official (1) possessed actual authority to speak on the state's behalf on that matter, and (2) purported to exercise that authority when speaking on social media. Appearance and function matter only at step 2 and can't make up for a lack of authority at step 1.

Facts: James Freed converted his personal Facebook profile into a public "page" (category: "public figure") before becoming city manager of Port Huron, Michigan. He then added a photo with a city lapel pin, his title, and the city's website and email. He posted mostly about family (his daughter, his dog Winston, Bible verses) but also about city work (leaf pickup, a housing survey, the fire chief's press releases, COVID-19 policies). Kevin Lindke criticized the city's pandemic response in comments; Freed deleted them and then blocked him. Lindke sued, calling the page a public forum and the deletions viewpoint discrimination. Held: vacated and remanded.

- Why it matters: the First Amendment binds only the government. If Freed acted privately, he was exercising his own First Amendment rights (editorial control over his own page), not violating Lindke's. Officials don't relinquish their rights (Garcetti; Lane).

- Step 1, actual authority: it must be real, "not a mirage," and cover the matter in question (if public health isn't in the city manager's portfolio, a post on restaurant health violations isn't state action). It can come from statutes, ordinances, regulations, or a well-settled custom and usage. Misusing real power is still state action, but one must have the power first.

- Step 2, purporting to use it: context matters. A school board president announcing a policy change at a board meeting acts officially; saying the same thing at a backyard barbecue doesn't. A "personal page" label or disclaimer earns a heavy (rebuttable) presumption that posts are personal; a "City of Port Huron" page or an account passed between officeholders is official.

- Mixed-use pages: classify post by post, focusing on content and function. A mayor suspending parking rules "pursuant to Municipal Ordinance 22.1" only on Facebook is plainly official; merely sharing a link to the city's announcement is likely private. Using government staff to post points toward official.

- Technology matters: deleting a comment implicates only that post, but blocking is page-wide, so it implicates every post Lindke wanted to comment on. Officials who mix personal and official posts expose themselves to more liability.

### Moody v. NetChoice, LLC, 603 U.S. 707 (2024)

case · ch. 13Moody v. NetChoice, LLC (2024)

9-0 on the bottom line, Kagan, J. Jackson joined in part; Thomas, Alito, and Gorsuch concurred in the judgment.

Rule: When platforms curate their feeds (deciding what third-party speech to display and how, by removing, ranking, and labeling content), they engage in expressive activity protected by the First Amendment, like newspapers and TV stations exercising editorial judgment. The government may not interfere with that curation to advance its own vision of "ideological balance." The Court remanded on the demanding facial-challenge standard and left algorithms that simply follow user preferences open (footnote 7).

Facts: 2021 Florida and Texas laws restricted large platforms' content moderation and required individualized explanations when posts were removed or altered. Texas barred platforms from "censoring" (blocking, removing, demonetizing, de-boosting, etc.) a user's expression based on its viewpoint. NetChoice, a trade association including Facebook and YouTube, brought facial challenges. The Eleventh Circuit upheld an injunction against Florida's law; the Fifth Circuit reversed one against Texas's. Held: both vacated and remanded, with guidance that the Fifth Circuit's approach was wrong.

- Precedents on editorial choice: Miami Herald v. Tornillo (1974) (no forced right of reply in a newspaper); PG&E (1986) (a utility can't be forced to include a consumer group's views in its newsletter); Turner I (1994) (cable operators' channel selection is expressive; must-carry was later upheld in Turner II to save local broadcasting); Hurley (1995) (parade organizers can't be forced to include a group's message).

- Principle: ordering a party to host others' speech implicates the First Amendment if, though only if, the party is engaged in its own expressive activity that the mandate would alter. Presenting a curated compilation of others' speech counts.

- Applied to Texas: platforms couldn't disfavor posts supporting Nazi ideology or terrorism, espousing racism or anti-Semitism, glorifying rape, encouraging teen suicide, discouraging vaccines, or advancing false claims of election fraud. That "profoundly alters" their choices about which views to convey.

- Not a defense: that platforms carry most posts (excluding select categories is an editorial choice too), or that no one would attribute a single post to the platform (protection never hinged on misattribution risk).

- Interest fails even intermediate scrutiny (O'Brien): Texas wanted to correct the mix of speech (the Governor spoke of a "dangerous movement" to "silence" conservatives). That interest is related to suppressing expression and isn't valid. Few dangers are greater than letting government change private speech "to achieve its own conception of speech nirvana."

- Discussion: given platforms' power over billions of users' speech, should government be able to regulate "private censorship," or is second-guessing private editorial choices too dangerous?

### Murthy v. Missouri, 603 U.S. 43 (2024)

case · ch. 13Murthy v. Missouri (2024)

Described in the casebook commentary; not excerpted.

Rule: Users have no First Amendment rights against platforms' own moderation. To sue the government, a user must show that government coercion, not the platform's independent editorial decision, caused the content to be taken down or obscured.

Facts: Social-media users alleged Biden Administration officials pressured platforms into deleting posts (e.g., questioning COVID-19 vaccine efficacy). Held: no standing; the platforms had been removing such posts independently, even before the alleged pressure.

### Speech Involving Elections

### Arkansas Educational Television Commission v. Forbes, 523 U.S. 666 (1998)

case · ch. 13Arkansas Educational Television Commission v. Forbes (1998)

6-3, Kennedy, J. Stevens, Souter, and Ginsburg dissented, worrying the staff had too much discretion, but not disputing the reasoning below.

Rule: Public and private broadcasters generally have broad editorial discretion not subject to forum analysis. A candidate debate is the narrow exception: it is a nonpublic forum, so a state-owned station may exclude a candidate only if the exclusion is viewpoint neutral and reasonable. Excluding a candidate for lack of public support passes.

Facts: Arkansas's state-owned public TV network excluded independent candidate Ralph Forbes from a televised debate for a congressional seat because he had little support in the polls. Held: no First Amendment violation.

- Why debates differ: (1) by design, a debate is a forum for the candidates' political speech, with views implicitly theirs, not the broadcaster's (unlike a talk show host); (2) debates are of "exceptional significance" in elections, often the only time public attention focuses in depth on the race.

- Nonpublic, not designated: a designated forum requires general access for a class of speakers. AETC made candidate-by-candidate decisions among those running for the seat (selective access).

- Opening debates to all would mean less speech: 19+ candidates were on some state ballots in recent presidential elections; after the lower court's ruling, Nebraska's public network canceled a 1996 Senate debate.

- Reasonable and viewpoint neutral: the jury found no objection to Forbes's views. "His own objective lack of support, not his platform, was the criterion." An unconventional candidate could have broad support; a conventional one might have little. AETC excluded him "because the voters lacked interest in his candidacy, not because AETC itself did."

### Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission, 558 U.S. 310 (2010)

case · ch. 13Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission (2010)

5-4 on expenditures, Kennedy, J. (with Roberts, Scalia, Alito, and Thomas). A different majority (including Stevens, Ginsburg, Breyer, and Sotomayor) upheld disclosure; the casebook calls that vote 5-4, but the reported vote was 8-1, with Thomas dissenting. Stevens, J., dissented on expenditures, joined by Ginsburg, Breyer, and Sotomayor.

Rule: The government may not ban independent expenditures by corporations (including nonprofits) from general treasury funds for political speech. Laws burdening political speech get strict scrutiny; the only sufficient interest is preventing quid pro quo corruption or its appearance, which justifies limits on direct contributions but not independent expenditures. Disclaimer and disclosure requirements survive "exacting scrutiny" (a substantial relation to a sufficiently important interest, such as informing voters).

Facts: The Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act of 2002 (BCRA) barred corporations from using general treasury funds for express advocacy or for "electioneering communications" naming a federal candidate within 30 days of a primary or 60 days of a general election. Corporations could speak only through PACs funded by shareholder and employee donations. Citizens United, a nonprofit corporation, wanted to air Hillary, a film critical of Hillary Clinton, and ads for it. Held: the expenditure ban is unconstitutional; Austin (1990) and part of McConnell (2003) are overruled.

- "Classic examples of censorship": the law would make it a felony for the Sierra Club, the NRA, or the ACLU to urge votes for or against a candidate in the pre-election window.

- PACs aren't a substitute: a PAC is a separate association, expensive, and heavily regulated; fewer than 2,000 of millions of corporations have one.

- Buckley v. Valeo (1976): upheld limits on direct contributions (risk of quid pro quo) but struck limits on independent expenditures.

- Austin's "antidistortion" rationale rejected: it would let government ban political speech just because the speaker took the corporate form, muffling "the voices that best represent the most significant segments of the economy."

- Disclosure upheld: ads must state who is responsible and that no candidate authorized them; anyone spending over $10,000 a year on electioneering communications must file with the FEC. Disclosure imposes no ceiling on speech; as-applied challenges remain if disclosure would expose contributors to threats, harassment, or reprisals.

- Stevens, J., dissenting: the dispute is about how, not whether, Citizens United could speak (through its multimillion-dollar PAC, or outside the 30-day window). Corporations can't vote or run for office, and Congress has limited corporate election spending since the Tillman Act of 1907. Corruption runs along a spectrum: "the difference between selling a vote and selling access is a matter of degree, not kind," and politicians know who spends on their behalf.

- Aftermath: SpeechNow.org v. FEC (D.C. Cir. 2010) (en banc) barred caps on contributions to independent-expenditure committees ("super PACs"). Outside spending in federal elections rose from $574 million in 2008 to nearly $4.5 billion in 2024.

### Synthesis: Social Media and Elections

Case | Actors | Holding
Packingham (2017) | Government vs. user | Internet access protected; overbroad ban fails; standard undecided
Lindke (2024) | Official vs. user | State action only with actual authority + purporting to use it
NetChoice (2024) | Government vs. platform | Content moderation is protected editorial judgment
Murthy (2024) | User vs. government (via platform) | Must show government coercion caused takedown
Vullo (2024, Ch. 10) | Government vs. third parties | Coercing others to suppress speech violates the First Amendment
AETC v. Forbes (1998) | State TV vs. candidate | Debate is nonpublic forum; reasonable, viewpoint-neutral exclusion OK
Citizens United (2010) | Government vs. corporate speakers | Independent-expenditure ban struck; disclosure upheld

### Stretch Exercise: Influencer AI-Filter Disclosures

| Analysis
Issue | A state requires social media influencers with over one million followers to disclose when they use filters or AI to alter their appearance in paid posts promoting beauty products. Influencers say it compels speech and singles out a category of speakers; the state says it requires factual disclosures to keep consumers, especially teenagers, from being misled.
Questions | What level of scrutiny applies? Does it matter that the rule covers only paid endorsements?
Analysis | For the state: paid promotions are commercial speech, and the disclosure is purely factual and uncontroversial (whether the image was altered) and about the advertised product's effect, so Zauderer applies (Ch. 8). Preventing deception is the classic substantial interest (Zauderer; Milavetz), and a short label is unlikely to "drown out" the ad (NIFLA; CTIA). Limiting it to paid endorsements helps keep it commercial. For the influencers: the million-follower threshold is speaker-based (Sorrell), so it is underinclusive if the goal is preventing deception; personal posts mixed with promotion may be noncommercial; and the state must show the harm is real, not "purely hypothetical" (NIFLA).

# First Amendment Bar Exam Questions

Subject: Con Law II | Type: Practice Questions | URL: https://supertoadman.github.io/Wilmington-University-corner/subjects/con-law-ii/first-amendment-bar-exam-questions/

## Practice Final 1 · Q1 · First Amendment Overview — Compelled affirmation; a secular objector
Lakeview High School, a public school, requires every student to stand each morning and recite a "Civic Creed" pledging loyalty to "the Constitution and the free-market system that sustains it." Nadia Orlov, 16, objects on political grounds, not religious ones, and stays silently seated. The school suspends her under a rule that treats refusal as insubordination. The district argues that the leading case protected only religious objectors and that the creed simply teaches civic values. Nadia sues.

What is the most likely result?

A. The district wins, because Nadia's objection is political rather than religious, and only religious objectors may refuse a compelled pledge.
B. Nadia wins, because the state may not compel a student to declare a belief, whatever the reason for her objection.
C. The district wins, because a school may require students to recite civic material as part of teaching history and government.
D. Nadia wins, but only because the creed's reference to the free-market system takes a side in an economic debate.
E. The district wins if it shows a rational basis for promoting loyalty to the Constitution.

Answer: B
- A: Barnette's result didn't depend on religious views or sincerity. It is a speech holding, so secular and political objectors are protected as fully as religious ones.
- B: Correct. Under West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette, no official can prescribe what is orthodox in politics, nationalism, or other matters of opinion or force citizens to confess by word or act their faith therein. The holding rests on speech and protects any objector.
- C: A school may teach civics and acquaint students with a pledge and its meaning. What it may not do is compel them to declare a belief; teaching and compelling are different.
- D: The creed's content isn't the problem. Even a pledge to the flag alone couldn't be compelled; the vice is compelled affirmation.
- E: Barnette rejected Gobitis's deference to legislatures. Speech may be restricted only to prevent grave and immediate danger, not on a rational basis.
Rule: Government may not compel anyone to affirm a belief, and the rule protects secular objectors as fully as religious ones (West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette, overruling Gobitis). A school may teach about a pledge but may not compel students to declare it.

## Practice Final 1 · Q2 · First Amendment Overview — Coercion requires more than visible prayer
Marisol Grant, a public high school softball coach, began kneeling alone at home plate for about thirty seconds after each game, once players had left the field to meet their families. She never invited anyone to join, and no player ever did. The principal disciplined her, explaining in writing that he acted because the prayer was religious and that students who saw their coach pray would feel pressure to join, which would violate the Establishment Clause. Nothing in the record shows that any student felt pressured. Grant sues under the Free Exercise Clause.

What is the most likely result?

A. Grant wins, because a public employee's religious expression at work is absolutely protected.
B. The district wins, because a coach on duty speaks for the school, so her prayer is the government's own speech.
C. The district wins, because a coach praying on the field at a school event endorses religion under the Lemon test.
D. The district wins, because avoiding an Establishment Clause problem always justifies limiting a public employee's religious exercise.
E. Grant wins, because she was disciplined because the prayer was religious, and her brief, quiet prayer did not coerce students.

Answer: E
- A: Nothing here is absolute. Grant wins because the district can't satisfy strict scrutiny on these facts; actual coercion of students could still be forbidden.
- B: The prayer came after the game, when coaches were free to attend to personal matters, so it was her private religious exercise, not speech she was paid to deliver.
- C: Kennedy v. Bremerton abandoned Lemon and the endorsement test. The Establishment Clause is read by history and tradition, and it bars coercion.
- D: The clauses are complementary; the Establishment Clause doesn't automatically trump free exercise. Government may disfavor religion only when necessary to avoid an actual violation, and there was none here.
- E: Correct. Because the district acted partly because the conduct was religious, the policy wasn't neutral and strict scrutiny applies. Under Kennedy v. Bremerton, brief, quiet, personal prayer that no student joined, with no evidence of pressure, isn't coercion.
Rule: Disciplining a public employee's private prayer because it is religious triggers strict scrutiny. The Establishment Clause is read by history and tradition and bars coercion, which requires more than visible religious exercise (Kennedy v. Bremerton).

## Practice Final 1 · Q3 · The Religion Clauses — Neutral, generally applicable law; no exemption
To reduce wildfire risk, Pine County bans all open outdoor fires from June through September, with no exceptions for any purpose: campfires, ceremonies, and agricultural burning are all covered. Members of a small faith whose central summer rite requires a sacred fire hold one on private land and are fined. They sue, arguing that the ban substantially burdens their religion and that the county could reduce fire risk in other ways.

What is the most likely result?

A. The members win, because religious conduct, like religious belief, is absolutely protected from penalty.
B. The members win, because a ban that burdens a religious rite necessarily targets religion.
C. The county wins, because the ban is neutral and generally applicable, so the Free Exercise Clause requires no religious exemption.
D. The county wins, but only because few other religions share the members' belief that the rite requires fire.
E. The members win, because any substantial burden on religious exercise triggers strict scrutiny, and the county has less restrictive means.

Answer: C
- A: Belief is absolutely protected; conduct is protected only from laws that target it because it is religious.
- B: A law targets religion when it singles out religious conduct, as the gerrymandered ordinance did in Lukumi. This ban covers every fire for every purpose, so its burden on the rite is incidental.
- C: Correct. Under Employment Division v. Smith, the Free Exercise Clause doesn't require exemptions from neutral, generally applicable laws that incidentally burden religion. With no secular exemptions and no exemption system, nothing takes the ban outside Smith.
- D: Beliefs need not be shared, logical, or comprehensible to others (Lukumi), and courts don't weigh their popularity. The county wins because the law is neutral and generally applicable.
- E: That was the pre-Smith approach, and it is now RFRA's statutory rule for the federal government. Under Employment Division v. Smith, an incidental burden from a neutral, generally applicable law triggers no heightened scrutiny.
Rule: Under Employment Division v. Smith, a neutral, generally applicable law that incidentally burdens religious conduct requires no religious exemption. Strict scrutiny applies only if the law fails neutrality or general applicability, or a recognized wrinkle applies.

## Practice Final 1 · Q4 · The Religion Clauses — Unused discretionary exemption system
A state requires every licensed adoption agency to accept applications from all qualified couples, but the director of the state's family services department may grant an exception "in his sole discretion" for good cause. No exception has ever been granted. A faith-based agency that will not certify unmarried couples, citing religious teaching, asks for one. The director refuses and ends the agency's contract. The agency sues.

What is the most likely result?

A. The agency wins, because the discretionary exception system makes the rule not generally applicable.
B. The agency wins, because faith-based agencies are categorically exempt from state licensing conditions.
C. The state wins, because its interest in treating prospective parents equally is compelling in every case.
D. The state wins, because no exception has ever been granted, so in practice the requirement applies to every agency alike.
E. The state wins, because antidiscrimination requirements are neutral and generally applicable under Smith.

Answer: A
- A: Correct. Under Fulton v. City of Philadelphia, a formal system of individualized, discretionary exemptions makes a policy not generally applicable. Strict scrutiny then asks whether the state has a compelling interest in denying this claimant an exception, which is hard to show when it keeps the power to excuse others.
- B: There is no categorical exemption. The agency wins only because the policy fails general applicability and then strict scrutiny.
- C: Equal treatment is a weighty interest, but strict scrutiny is judged as to this claimant, and in Fulton the government's own exemption system undermined it.
- D: Under Fulton, the existence of a formal discretionary exemption system is enough, even if no exemption has been granted, because it invites the government to decide which reasons are worthy.
- E: The rule would be neutral and generally applicable without the "sole discretion" clause. That clause takes it outside Smith.
Rule: A formal system of discretionary, individualized exemptions makes a policy not generally applicable even if no exemption has ever been granted; strict scrutiny then asks whether denying this claimant an exemption serves a compelling interest (Fulton v. City of Philadelphia).

## Practice Final 1 · Q5 · The Establishment Clause and Funding — Tuition benefit can't exclude religious schools
In rural districts with no public high school, State X pays tuition for students to attend an approved private high school of their parents' choosing. A statute excludes any school that "provides religious instruction." The Ortiz family chooses an accredited religious academy that teaches daily theology classes, and the state refuses to pay. The state argues that paying for religious instruction would violate the Establishment Clause and, in the alternative, that it has a compelling interest in separating church and state more strictly than the federal Constitution requires.

What is the most likely result?

A. The state wins, because its interest in separating church and state more strictly than required is compelling.
B. The state wins, because the program provides a free public education, which a state may keep secular.
C. The Ortizes win, but only if the academy agrees to make its theology classes optional for funded students.
D. The Ortizes win, because a state that funds private schooling can't exclude schools for being religious.
E. The state wins, because using public money to pay for religious instruction violates the Establishment Clause.

Answer: D
- A: Carson held that an interest in separating church and state more strictly than the federal Constitution requires isn't compelling. The "play in the joints" to decline funding religion is in retreat.
- B: Carson rejected that framing: participating private schools can be selective, charge tuition, and skip the state curriculum, so the benefit is tuition, not a public education. States may keep their own public schools secular.
- C: There is no such condition. The exclusion itself is the violation; the state may instead restructure or end the program, for example by expanding its public schools.
- D: Correct. Under Carson v. Makin, once a state subsidizes private schooling, excluding schools because they are religious, including because the money would pay for religious instruction, violates the Free Exercise Clause.
- E: Aid that reaches religious schools only through parents' genuine and independent private choice is permissible (Zelman), so there is no Establishment Clause violation to avoid.
Rule: If a state subsidizes private schooling, it can't exclude schools because they are religious, even when the money pays for religious instruction, and a stricter-separation interest isn't compelling (Carson v. Makin; Trinity Lutheran; Espinoza). The state may end or restructure the program instead.

## Practice Final 1 · Q6 · Compelled Speech — Passive display of a state motto
State Y requires every car registered as a taxi to display a rear-window decal with the state slogan "Liberty Through Order," and makes covering it a misdemeanor. Each taxi already carries a unique medallion number for identification. Dmitri Volkov, a cab driver who believes the slogan endorses authoritarian government, tapes over it and is fined. The state argues that a decal is far less than a spoken pledge and that most residents approve of the slogan.

What is the most likely result?

A. Volkov wins, but only if he shows that the slogan conflicts with a sincerely held religious belief.
B. Volkov wins, because the state can't force him to carry its ideological message on his own vehicle.
C. The state wins, because passively carrying a slogan isn't the kind of affirmation that the compelled-speech cases forbid.
D. The state wins, because the slogan is government speech, which the First Amendment doesn't restrict.
E. The state wins, because observers attribute the slogan to the state, not the driver, as with "In God We Trust" on currency.

Answer: B
- A: The Wooley plaintiffs were Jehovah's Witnesses, but the speech rationale protects any objector.
- B: Correct. Under Wooley v. Maynard, the right to speak includes the right not to speak, and the state may not require a person to display its ideological message on private property for the public to see. Majority approval is irrelevant, and identification is already served by the medallion number.
- C: Wooley v. Maynard rejected this. Carrying a motto is less than saluting a flag, but the difference is "one of degree."
- D: The state may speak for itself, but it can't compel private people to carry its message on their own property. Even Walker, which treated specialty plates as government speech, recognized that.
- E: Wooley distinguished currency because it is carried privately and not associated with the bearer. A decal displayed to the public turns the car into a "mobile billboard."
Rule: The state may not require a person to display its ideological message on private property for the public to see; majority approval is irrelevant, and a passive display differs from a pledge only in degree (Wooley v. Maynard).

## Practice Final 1 · Q7 · Content-Based Restrictions — No general exception for false statements
A state law makes it a misdemeanor to "falsely claim, orally or in writing, to have received the State Medal of Valor." At a neighborhood association meeting, Curtis Hale tells the audience he won the medal for rescuing children from a fire. He sought no money, job, or other benefit. Reporters quickly exposed the lie, and Hale was widely ridiculed. Prosecuted under the law, he challenges it.

What is the most likely result?

A. The law is valid, because the state's interest in protecting the integrity of its highest civilian honor is compelling.
B. The law is invalid, because the First Amendment protects anything said at a public meeting.
C. The law is valid, because false statements of fact have no constitutional value.
D. The law is valid, because Hale's lie was a form of fraud, which has been unprotected since 1791.
E. The law is invalid, because there is no general First Amendment exception for false statements.

Answer: E
- A: The interest in a medal's integrity is compelling, as Alvarez agreed, but the ban isn't actually necessary to serve it when there's no evidence of dilution and counterspeech is effective.
- B: There's no blanket protection for statements at public meetings. Defamation, fraud, or a true threat made at a meeting can still be punished.
- C: The statements that falsehood has no value came from cases involving legally cognizable harm, like defamation and fraud. This law targets falsity and nothing more (United States v. Alvarez).
- D: Fraud requires a knowing falsehood made to obtain money, property, or a similar benefit. Hale sought nothing; like Alvarez's lie, his was an attempt to gain respect, not fraud.
- E: Correct. Under United States v. Alvarez, there is no general First Amendment exception for false statements. A content-based ban on lies must be "actually necessary," and here counterspeech worked: Hale was exposed and ridiculed.
Rule: There is no general First Amendment exception for false statements. A content-based ban on lies that cause no legally cognizable harm must be actually necessary, and the ordinary remedy for false speech is true speech (United States v. Alvarez).

## Practice Final 1 · Q8 · Incitement — Intent, imminence, and likelihood
At a rally in a rural field attended only by about forty members of his movement and two reporters, Royce Delancey said: "This government has betrayed us. The day may come when patriots must take up arms to take it back, and we should be ready when it does." No one took any action. He is convicted under a state law that makes it a crime "to advocate the duty, necessity, or propriety of violence as a means of political reform."

On appeal, what is the most likely result?

A. Affirmed, because he advocated to his followers the necessity of taking up arms against the government.
B. Affirmed, because his speech created a clear and present danger, given how committed his audience was to the cause.
C. Reversed, because his speech wasn't directed to inciting imminent lawless action likely to occur.
D. Reversed, because political speech at a private gathering is absolutely protected.
E. Affirmed, because the reporters' presence meant that his advocacy would reach a wider audience.

Answer: C
- A: Abstract advocacy of force can't be punished. Brandenburg distinguishes teaching the moral necessity of force from preparing a group for violent action and steeling it to such action.
- B: The clear-and-present-danger and bad-tendency tests of Whitney and Abrams were replaced in practice by Brandenburg's intent, imminence, and likelihood test.
- C: Correct. Under Brandenburg v. Ohio, advocacy of force may be punished only if it is directed to inciting imminent lawless action and is likely to produce it. "The day may come" lacks imminence, and the statute, like Ohio's, punishes mere advocacy without any intent, imminence, or likelihood element.
- D: Nothing makes speech at a private gathering absolutely protected. True incitement at a private rally could be punished.
- E: A wider audience supplies neither imminence nor intent. Brandenburg's own rally was filmed for broadcast.
Rule: Advocacy of force or law violation may be punished only if it is (1) directed to inciting or producing (2) imminent (3) lawless action and (4) likely to produce it (Brandenburg v. Ohio, overruling Whitney). A law that punishes mere advocacy is facially invalid.

## Practice Final 1 · Q9 · Prior Restraints and National Security — Injunction against future publication
A local news blog publishes a series accusing the county sheriff of corruption. The sheriff sues the blog's owner under a state statute that lets courts permanently enjoin any publication that "regularly prints malicious and scandalous matter." The trial court enjoins the blog from publishing further articles about the sheriff.

On appeal, what is the most likely result?

A. The injunction is reversed, because it is a prior restraint, which is presumptively unconstitutional.
B. The injunction stands, because restraints may protect public officials from publications that damage their reputations.
C. The injunction is reversed, but only because the articles turned out to be true.
D. The injunction stands, because a court order, unlike a statute, comes with the procedural safeguards of litigation.
E. The injunction stands, because the sheriff could sue for defamation, and an injunction is a milder remedy than damages.

Answer: A
- A: Correct. Near v. Minnesota struck an injunction under a nearly identical "malicious, scandalous" newspaper statute. Prior restraints carry a heavy presumption of invalidity, and Near's only exception, wartime troop movements and sailing dates, has never been applied.
- B: Near reversed exactly this kind of injunction against a paper that criticized local law enforcement as corrupt.
- C: Truth isn't the reason. Even false articles would be addressed by after-the-fact defamation liability, not by an order barring future publication.
- D: The Pentagon Papers case applied the heavy presumption to court injunctions. An injunction against publication is the classic prior restraint.
- E: Prior restraints are treated as worse than punishment after the fact: they shut off speech before it happens and sweep more expression under official scrutiny. A damages remedy doesn't make an injunction milder.
Rule: A prior restraint (an injunction or licensing scheme that stops speech before it occurs) carries a heavy presumption of invalidity, and the government bears a heavy burden (Near v. Minnesota; New York Times Co. v. United States).

## Practice Final 1 · Q10 · True Threats — Recklessness as to the threatening character
Over eight months, Silas Brandt sent dozens of messages to a city council member he had never met, including "You'll see me when you least expect it" and "Your days in office are numbered, and maybe not just in office." She feared for her safety and stopped holding public office hours. Brandt is prosecuted under a statute punishing communications "that a reasonable person would regard as a serious threat of violence." The trial court refuses to instruct the jury on Brandt's mental state, and he is convicted.

On appeal, what is the most likely result?

A. Reversed, because the state must prove that Brandt acted for the purpose of frightening her.
B. Affirmed, because a true threat is judged solely by how a reasonable recipient would understand it.
C. Reversed, because the state must prove that Brandt actually intended to carry out the violence his messages described.
D. Reversed, because the state had to prove Brandt was at least reckless about how his messages would be taken.
E. Affirmed, because messages aimed at a public official are never protected political hyperbole.

Answer: D
- A: Purpose was the concurrence's view. The majority held that recklessness is enough, so purpose or knowledge isn't required.
- B: A purely objective test was the dissent's position (Barrett and Thomas). The majority in Counterman requires a subjective mental state as well.
- C: No true-threat case requires an intent to carry out the threat. The harm is the fear and disruption the threat causes.
- D: Correct. Counterman v. Colorado: the statement must be a serious expression of intent to commit unlawful violence, judged by a reasonable recipient, and the First Amendment also requires proof that the speaker consciously disregarded a substantial risk that it would be viewed as threatening.
- E: Messages to officials can be political hyperbole (Watts). The error here is the missing mental-state element, not the target.
Rule: A true threat is a serious expression of intent to commit unlawful violence, judged by how a reasonable recipient would understand it, and the speaker must have been at least reckless about its threatening character (Counterman v. Colorado).

## Practice Final 1 · Q11 · Speech Integral to Crime — Publisher's intent; aiding and abetting
A small press sells "Clean Exit," a step-by-step manual on poisoning a spouse without detection. A reader follows it exactly to kill his wife. In the estate's aiding-and-abetting suit against the press, the press stipulates that it marketed the book to people planning murders and intended to help them commit them. The press moves to dismiss on First Amendment grounds.

What is the most likely result?

A. Dismissed, because a publisher isn't responsible for how readers misuse a book sold to the general public.
B. Not dismissed, because speech that intentionally aids and abets a crime is unprotected.
C. Not dismissed, because instructional material that could facilitate a crime is categorically unprotected.
D. Dismissed, because publishers, like news organizations, are never liable for the content they print.
E. Dismissed, because a book is protected unless it is directed to inciting imminent lawless action.

Answer: B
- A: That describes copycat cases, in which readers misuse novels and films that publishers didn't intend to assist crime. Here the stipulation establishes intent, and the book was used precisely as intended.
- B: Correct. Rice v. Paladin held that the First Amendment didn't bar an aiding-and-abetting claim against a publisher that stipulated it intended to assist murderers, where its manual was used exactly as intended.
- C: Not every manual is unprotected. Paladin stressed that its stipulations, the detail, the exhortation to murder, and the lack of any legitimate purpose made the case unique.
- D: Publishers aren't exempt. Paladin said news reporting is never a basis for liability, but a murder manual published with intent to assist isn't news reporting.
- E: Brandenburg governs advocacy. Aiding and abetting is a different category, speech integral to crime, which Rice v. Paladin applied to a publisher.
Rule: Speech, including publishing, that aids and abets a crime is unprotected when the publisher intended to assist and the material was used as intended (Rice v. Paladin). Without extrinsic evidence of such intent, how-to material generally stays protected.

## Practice Final 1 · Q12 · Protecting Adults: Obscenity and Secondary Effects — Miller prong (c): the work taken as a whole
A state prosecutes a bookseller for selling a 400-page literary novel, widely reviewed and taught in several university courses, that contains two graphic sex scenes. The prosecutor argues that those two scenes, standing alone, appeal to the prurient interest, are patently offensive, and lack any value.

Which is the bookseller's strongest argument?

A. Obscenity must be judged by national community standards, not local ones.
B. Adults who are offended by the scenes can avert their eyes or put the book down.
C. A prohibition on obscene material must survive strict scrutiny.
D. Sexually explicit material is protected unless it depicts children.
E. Taken as a whole, the novel has serious literary value.

Answer: E
- A: Miller allowed local rather than national community standards, and those standards apply to prurient interest and offensiveness, not to value.
- B: Averting the eyes (Cohen) explains why offensive but protected speech can't be suppressed. It doesn't help if the work is obscene, because obscenity isn't protected at all.
- C: Obscenity is an unprotected category, so a ban on it gets only rational-basis review. The real fight is whether the work meets the Miller definition.
- D: Obscenity is unprotected even for adults. Miller defines it without regard to children.
- E: Correct. Under Miller, a work is obscene only if all three prongs are met, and prong (c) asks whether the work, taken as a whole, lacks serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value. That prong protects valuable works even if isolated scenes might seem obscene.
Rule: Speech is obscene only if (a) the average person, applying contemporary community standards, would find the work as a whole appeals to the prurient interest; (b) it depicts specifically defined sexual conduct in a patently offensive way; and (c) the work as a whole lacks serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value (Miller).

## Practice Final 1 · Q13 · Protecting Kids: Child Pornography — Virtual images fall outside Ferber
A federal statute bans any computer-generated image that "appears to depict a minor engaging in sexually explicit conduct," whether or not any real child was used to make it and whether or not the work has serious value. An animation studio making an acclaimed film about the aftermath of child abuse, which includes a brief computer-generated scene, challenges the statute.

What is the most likely result?

A. Upheld, because child pornography is unprotected even when it isn't obscene.
B. Upheld, because the government's interest in protecting children is of surpassing importance.
C. Struck, because no real children are used to make virtual images.
D. Struck, because all sexually explicit material is protected unless it meets the Miller test.
E. Upheld, because offers to sell such images are speech integral to crime.

Answer: C
- A: Ferber's category covers material made with real children. Ashcroft v. Free Speech Coalition refused to extend it to images that only appear to depict minors.
- B: The interest is of surpassing importance, but Ferber tied it to the abuse of real children in production and the market for that abuse, which virtual images lack.
- C: Correct. Ashcroft v. Free Speech Coalition held that Ferber doesn't extend to sexually explicit images made without real children. The statute also ignored serious value, and Ferber itself had pointed to virtual images as a permissible alternative.
- D: Too broad. Child pornography made with real children is unprotected even if it isn't obscene under Miller (New York v. Ferber).
- E: Williams allows punishing offers and requests for material the speaker believes depicts real children. This statute bans the images themselves, not offers to sell them.
Rule: Child pornography made with real children is unprotected even if not obscene (New York v. Ferber), but the category doesn't reach virtual images or adult look-alikes (Ashcroft v. Free Speech Coalition). Offers of material believed to involve real children may still be punished (United States v. Williams).

## Practice Final 1 · Q14 · Protecting Kids: Violent Imagery — No new category for violence, even for minors
A state bans selling "ultra-violent" graphic novels to anyone under 18, citing studies finding a correlation between reading them and aggressive thoughts in teenagers. The state argues that it may adjust the obscenity standard for minors, as it may for sexual material, and that the law helps parents. Publishers sue.

What is the most likely result?

A. Struck, because violent material isn't unprotected, and the ban fails strict scrutiny.
B. Upheld under intermediate scrutiny, because the law's burden on adults is only incidental.
C. Struck, because any law that protects children is invalid if it burdens any speech.
D. Upheld, because a state may adjust obscenity for minors, and graphic violence is analogous to sex.
E. Upheld, because minors have no First Amendment right to receive material their parents haven't approved.

Answer: A
- A: Correct. Under Brown v. Entertainment Merchants, violent imagery is protected, so a content-based ban on sales to minors gets strict scrutiny. Correlation isn't causation, the law is underinclusive, and filling a modest gap in parental control isn't compelling.
- B: Intermediate scrutiny for incidental burdens comes from Paxton's age-verification law for material obscene as to minors. This ban targets protected content directly, so strict scrutiny applies.
- C: Too strong. Some child-protective laws survive, such as age verification (Paxton) and broadcast channeling (Pacifica). This one fails on its own record.
- D: Brown v. Entertainment Merchants distinguished Ginsberg, which adjusted an existing category, obscenity, that covers only sexual conduct. A state can't create a wholly new category of violence for children.
- E: Minors are entitled to a significant measure of First Amendment protection. There is no "free-floating power to restrict the ideas to which children may be exposed."
Rule: Violent imagery is protected even for minors; a content-based ban on selling violent material to minors gets strict scrutiny and fails without proof of causation and tight tailoring (Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association, following United States v. Stevens).

## Practice Final 1 · Q15 · Defamation — Actual malice is not ill will
A newspaper columnist who despises the state's attorney general writes that the attorney general "took a $50,000 bribe" to drop a case. The columnist honestly believed the claim, which came from a source who had been reliable for years, but it was false. At trial, the attorney general proves the columnist's intense personal hatred of him and that a more careful reporter would have called his office before publishing.

Can the attorney general recover?

A. Yes, because truth is a defense the columnist must prove, and he can't prove it.
B. Yes, because the columnist's hatred shows that he acted with malice.
C. Yes, because the columnist was negligent in failing to check with his office.
D. No, because he can't prove knowing or reckless falsity.
E. No, because criticism of public officials is absolutely protected.

Answer: D
- A: Sullivan rejected the common-law rule that put the burden of proving truth on the defendant, because forcing critics to guarantee truth leads to self-censorship.
- B: "Actual malice" is a term of art meaning knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard of the truth. It has nothing to do with ill will.
- C: Negligence suffices for a private plaintiff on a matter of public concern (Gertz), not for a public official suing over official conduct.
- D: Correct. Under New York Times v. Sullivan, a public official must prove actual malice: knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard of whether the statement was false. An honest belief based on a reliable source isn't reckless, and neither hatred nor carelessness substitutes.
- E: Only concurring Justices in Sullivan would have made criticism of officials absolutely immune. The Court adopted the actual-malice standard instead.
Rule: A public official can't recover for a defamatory falsehood about his official conduct without proving actual malice, meaning knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard of whether it was false; actual malice isn't ill will (New York Times v. Sullivan).

## Practice Final 1 · Q16 · Defamation — Private plaintiff, public concern: fault and damages
A regional magazine falsely reports that Lena Park, a private accountant with no public role, helped a city contractor hide kickbacks paid to council members. The reporter was careless but never doubted the story. Park sues and proves only negligence. She asks the jury for $2 million in presumed and punitive damages, with no proof of actual loss.

What may she recover?

A. Presumed and punitive damages, because she is a private person, and the state may set any standard it chooses.
B. Damages for actual injury on proof of negligence, but presumed or punitive damages only on proof of actual malice.
C. Presumed and punitive damages, because a private person's role in a business matter is purely private.
D. Nothing, because being named in a story about public corruption made her a public figure.
E. Nothing, because the story involved a matter of public concern, so she must prove actual malice to recover anything.

Answer: B
