TIP To analyze a Rule 12(b)(6) question: (1) state the Twombly/Iqbal standard; (2) list the elements of the claim; (3) sort the complaint's allegations into facts and conclusions, quoting them; (4) for each element, ask whether the facts make it plausible, considering any obvious alternative explanation; and (5) conclude, noting that dismissal is usually with leave to amend under Rule 15(a)(2).

### Heightened pleading: Rule 9

- Rule 9(b): fraud or mistake must be stated with particularity (who, what, when, where, how). Malice, intent, knowledge, and other conditions of mind may be alleged generally, but after Iqbal "generally" still means plausibly, not in a conclusory way.

- Rule 9(c): conditions precedent may be alleged generally, but a denial must be made with particularity. Rule 9(g): special damages must be specifically stated.

- ◆ Only the Rules or a statute (such as the securities-fraud pleading statute) may impose heightened pleading; courts may not create it on their own (Leatherman (1993)).

### Rule 11: certification and sanctions
RULE By presenting a paper to the court (signing, filing, submitting, or later advocating it), an attorney or unrepresented party certifies that, to the best of the person's knowledge, information, and belief, formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances: (1) it is not presented for an improper purpose (to harass, cause unnecessary delay, or needlessly increase cost); (2) its legal contentions are warranted by existing law or a nonfrivolous argument for changing the law; (3) its factual contentions have evidentiary support or, if specifically so identified, will likely have it after a reasonable opportunity for investigation or discovery; and (4) its denials are warranted on the evidence or reasonably based on belief or lack of information.

- Standard: objective reasonableness; subjective good faith is no defense.

- Safe harbor, Rule 11(c)(2): a sanctions motion must be made separately and served 21 days before it is filed; if the paper is withdrawn or corrected within that time, the motion may not be filed. The court may also act on its own by an order to show cause (no safe harbor).

- Sanctions, Rule 11(c)(4)–(5): limited to what suffices to deter repetition: nonmonetary directives, a penalty paid into court, or (on motion) the movant's reasonable attorney's fees. The law firm is ordinarily held jointly responsible. No monetary sanction against a represented party for frivolous legal contentions, and none on the court's own initiative unless the show-cause order issued before voluntary dismissal or settlement.

- Rule 11(d): Rule 11 doesn't apply to discovery (Rules 26 through 37 govern).

### Cases
Conley v. Gibson, 355 U.S. 41 (1957) MAIN CASE · WEEK 9
Facts: Black railroad clerks sued their union, alleging that the railroad abolished 45 jobs held by Black employees (filling them with white workers or rehiring the Black workers with lost seniority) and that the union, their exclusive bargaining agent, refused to protect them because of their race.
Held: The complaint stated a claim. The Rules require only a short and plain statement giving fair notice of the claim and its grounds, and a complaint shouldn't be dismissed unless it appears beyond doubt that the plaintiff can prove no set of facts entitling him to relief.
Why it matters: The notice-pleading era. Twombly retired the "no set of facts" language, but the "fair notice" language survives.
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007) MAIN CASE · WEEK 9
Facts: A class of telephone and internet subscribers sued the regional phone companies (the "Baby Bells") under § 1 of the Sherman Act, alleging they conspired to keep new competitors out of their markets and to stay out of each other's territories. The complaint relied on parallel conduct and a conclusory allegation that they had entered a "contract, combination or conspiracy."
Held: Dismissed (7–2). Parallel conduct is just as consistent with independent business decisions, and a bare allegation of conspiracy is a legal conclusion; without facts suggesting an actual agreement, the claim wasn't plausible.
Why it matters: The source of plausibility pleading. The Court was concerned about the enormous cost of antitrust discovery; the dissent warned it abandoned notice pleading.
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009) MAIN CASE · WEEK 9
Facts: Iqbal, a Pakistani Muslim detained after September 11, 2001 under harsh conditions, sued Attorney General Ashcroft and the Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Robert Mueller, among many officials. He alleged they knowingly and maliciously adopted a policy of subjecting him to harsh conditions solely because of his religion, race, or national origin, calling Ashcroft its "principal architect."
Held: Dismissed (5–4). The allegations of discriminatory intent were conclusory and not entitled to the assumption of truth. The remaining facts (thousands of Arab Muslim men were detained) were more likely explained by a legitimate policy of detaining people with possible links to the attacks, so purposeful discrimination wasn't plausible.
Why it matters: Extended plausibility to all civil actions and set out the two-step method. Rule 9(b)'s "generally" doesn't permit conclusory allegations of intent.

## 20. Responding to the Complaint

### Timing

- Serve an answer or Rule 12 motion 21 days after service of the summons and complaint; 60 days after the waiver request was sent if service was waived (90 if the defendant was outside the United States); the United States and its agencies and officers get 60 days (Rule 12(a)). After removal, see Rule 81(c) (Topic 12).

- A Rule 12 motion suspends the time to answer; the answer is then due 14 days after the court denies the motion or postpones ruling on it (Rule 12(a)(4)).

### Rule 12(b) defenses and waiver
Rule | Defense | When it is waived
12(b)(1) | Lack of subject-matter jurisdiction | Never. It may be raised at any time, even on appeal (Rule 12(h)(3)).
12(b)(2) | Lack of personal jurisdiction | Waived if (A) left out of a pre-answer Rule 12 motion that raised other Rule 12 defenses (Rule 12(g)(2)), or (B) neither raised by motion nor included in the answer or an amendment allowed as a matter of course (Rule 12(h)(1)).
12(b)(3) | Improper venue | Same as 12(b)(2).
12(b)(4) | Insufficient process (a defect in the summons) | Same as 12(b)(2).
12(b)(5) | Insufficient service of process | Same as 12(b)(2).
12(b)(6) | Failure to state a claim upon which relief can be granted | Preserved through trial: may be raised in any pleading, by a Rule 12(c) motion for judgment on the pleadings, or at trial (Rule 12(h)(2)), but not in a second pre-answer motion.
12(b)(7) | Failure to join a party under Rule 19 | Same as 12(b)(6).

- Rule 12(b) motions must be made before a responsive pleading. No defense is waived by joining it with others in one motion or pleading.

- Rule 12(c): judgment on the pleadings after the pleadings close. Rule 12(d): if matters outside the pleadings are presented on a 12(b)(6) or 12(c) motion and not excluded, the motion must be treated as one for summary judgment, with a reasonable opportunity for all parties to present material.

- Rule 12(e): a more definite statement where a pleading is "so vague or ambiguous that the party cannot reasonably prepare a response," moved for before responding. Rule 12(f): strike redundant, immaterial, impertinent, or scandalous matter or an insufficient defense.

TIP Classic question: the defendant files a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, loses, then answers and raises lack of PJ. PJ is waived because it was left out of the first Rule 12 motion. The defendant may still argue failure to state a claim at trial, and anyone may raise SMJ at any time.

### The answer: Rule 8(b)

- Rule 8(b)(1)–(2): state defenses in short and plain terms and admit or deny each allegation; a denial must fairly respond to the substance of the allegation.

- Rule 8(b)(3): a general denial is allowed only if the party in good faith intends to deny every allegation, including jurisdiction; otherwise deny specific paragraphs or deny all except those specifically admitted.

- Rule 8(b)(4): a party that intends in good faith to deny only part of an allegation must admit the part that is true and deny the rest.

- Rule 8(b)(5): stating a lack of knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief about an allegation's truth has the effect of a denial. ◆ Courts reject it where the information is within the party's own knowledge or control.

- Rule 8(b)(6): an allegation (other than one about the amount of damages) is admitted if a responsive pleading is required and it isn't denied.

- Rule 7(a) allows only these pleadings: (1) a complaint; (2) an answer to a complaint; (3) an answer to a counterclaim; (4) an answer to a crossclaim; (5) a third-party complaint; (6) an answer to a third-party complaint; and (7) a reply to an answer only if the court orders one.

### Affirmative defenses: Rule 8(c)
RULE A party must affirmatively state in its responsive pleading any avoidance or affirmative defense, including accord and satisfaction, arbitration and award, assumption of risk, contributory negligence, duress, estoppel, failure of consideration, fraud, illegality, injury by fellow servant, laches, license, payment, release, res judicata, statute of frauds, statute of limitations, and waiver.

- An affirmative defense is an independent reason the defendant should win even if the plaintiff's allegations are true; the defendant usually bears the burden of proving it. ◆ A defense not pleaded is generally waived, subject to amendment under Rule 15.

### Default and default judgment: Rule 55
1. Entry of default, Rule 55(a): the clerk must enter a party's default when it has failed to plead or otherwise defend and that failure is shown by affidavit or otherwise.
2. Default judgment by the clerk, Rule 55(b)(1): for a sum certain (or one that can be made certain by computation), on the plaintiff's request with an affidavit of the amount, against a defendant who has not appeared and is neither a minor nor an incompetent person.
3. Default judgment by the court, Rule 55(b)(2): in all other cases. A party that has appeared must receive written notice at least 7 days before the hearing. The court may hold hearings to determine damages or establish the truth of an allegation.
4. Setting aside, Rule 55(c): the court may set aside an entry of default for good cause and a default judgment under Rule 60(b).

- Default admits the well-pleaded factual allegations, but the court must still confirm the complaint states a claim (Virgin Records). Defaults are disfavored, and courts prefer decisions on the merits. ◆ A default judgment must not differ in kind from, or exceed in amount, what the pleadings demand (Rule 54(c)).

### Cases
Zielinski v. Philadelphia Piers, Inc., 139 F. Supp. 408 (E.D. Pa. 1956) MAIN CASE · WEEK 9
Facts: Zielinski was hurt on a pier when a forklift driven by Johnson struck him. His complaint alleged the forklift was "owned, operated and controlled" by Philadelphia Piers and its agents. Philadelphia Piers did own the forklift, but it had transferred its operations to Carload Contractors, which employed Johnson. Its answer generally denied the whole paragraph, its witnesses' pretrial testimony let Zielinski keep believing Johnson was its employee, and the same insurer covered both companies. By the time the truth emerged, the statute of limitations had run against Carload.
Held: The general denial of a partly true paragraph was ineffective. Philadelphia Piers was treated as having admitted that Johnson was its agent acting within the scope of his employment, and it was equitably estopped from denying agency at trial.
Why it matters: Deny with specificity: admit what is true and deny only the rest (Rule 8(b)(4)). A misleading denial can be treated as an admission.
Virgin Records America, Inc. v. Lacey, 510 F. Supp. 2d 588 (S.D. Ala. 2007) SUPPLEMENTAL READING · WEEK 9
Facts: Record companies sued Bertha Lacey for copyright infringement, alleging she downloaded and distributed eight identified songs online. She was served by leaving the papers with her son at her home (Rule 4(e)(2)(B)), never answered, and the clerk entered her default. The plaintiffs moved for a default judgment seeking only the statutory minimum damages.
Held: Default judgment granted under Rule 55(b)(2): $6,000 in statutory damages ($750 for each of the eight works), a permanent injunction, and costs. No evidentiary hearing was needed because the minimum statutory damages were fixed by law.
Why it matters: Default admits the well-pleaded facts, but the court must still find that the complaint states a claim, and it holds a damages hearing only when needed.

# Torts Outline

Subject: Torts | Type: Outline | URL: https://supertoadman.github.io/Wilmington-University-corner/subjects/torts/torts-outline/

Torts Condensed Exam Outline · Weeks 1–15 Torts (40018 / 40041) · Prof. Stephen Johnson · Wilmington University School of Law · Fall 2026

KEY Labels and cites MAIN CASE: a principal case in the assigned reading. NOTE CASE: a principal case from the same chapter, included for context. Cites: R2d § 13 means Restatement (Second) of Torts § 13; R3d is the Restatement (Third) of Torts (Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm unless noted). R3d Misc. Prov. is the Restatement (Third) of Torts: Miscellaneous Provisions (Tentative Draft No. 3, 2024); its boxes say "approved" for sections the ALI membership adopted (2022–2023) and "T.D. 3, draft" for sections still in draft. The Restatement supplement has the text of each, with the Comments for the T.D. 3 sections. Gray italic text comes from outside the class materials, such as Delaware law and later cases. Verify it before relying on it.

ROADMAP Every tort question runs the same five steps (all required) Professor Johnson frames tort law as a conflict-resolution device: when should the injured person be able to sue and win? Work every fact pattern the same way. 1. Who sues whom? List every plaintiff and every defendant, including employers, owners, hosts, and the government. Vicarious and direct claims are separate. 2. Which basis of liability? Intent (Parts II–III), negligence (Parts IV–IX), or strict liability (Parts XIII–XIV). Many facts support more than one. 3. Prima facie case. Run the elements one at a time, using the labels in the rule boxes. Name the element that is weakest on the facts. 4. Defenses and privileges. Consent, self-defense, necessity, comparative fault, assumption of risk, limitations, and immunity. 5. Remedy and allocation. Compensatory and punitive damages, joint and several liability, contribution, and indemnity.

# PART I — Foundations: Liability Based on Fault

## 1. From Strict Liability to Fault WEEK 1
What tort law is for

- A tort is a civil wrong, other than a breach of contract, for which the law gives the injured person a remedy, usually damages. Tort law is mostly state common law made by judges.

- Goals (weighed together): (1) compensating injured people; (2) deterring unsafe conduct and giving the actor the cost of the harm; (3) corrective justice, so the wrongdoer repairs the wrong; (4) spreading losses across insurers and enterprises; and (5) giving people a peaceful way to resolve conflict instead of self-help.

- Systemic bias (Goal B). Ask whose experience defines "reasonable," "outrageous," or "normal" use of land, and how damages rules value different people's lives and earnings. §§ 12, 27 and 33 flag where this matters.

The three bases of liability
Basis | What the plaintiff must show about the defendant's state of mind | Main examples
Intent | Purpose or knowledge with substantial certainty of the consequence (R2d § 8A) | Battery, assault, false imprisonment, IIED, trespass, conversion
Negligence | No intent. The conduct created an unreasonable risk of harm | Car crashes, slip-and-falls, malpractice
Strict liability | Neither intent nor fault. Liability follows from the activity itself | Abnormally dangerous activities, wild animals, trespassing livestock

History: the writs of trespass and case

- Trespass covered direct, forcible injuries and was effectively strict liability (Case of Thorns). Trespass on the case covered indirect injuries and came to require fault. The 19th century moved most accidental-injury law to a fault (negligence) basis (Brown v. Kendall).

- Burden of proof. Under fault-based liability, the plaintiff must prove the defendant was at fault. The defendant does not have to prove that it was blameless.

MAIN CASE Hulle v. Orynge (The Case of Thorns) (K.B. 1466) — strict liability in trespass Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 1 Facts: The defendant cut thorns from his hedge, and they fell onto the plaintiff's land. He went onto the land to retrieve them, and the plaintiff sued in trespass. The casebook excerpt prints only the arguments. Held: Brian, arguing as counsel in a view later adopted from the bench: every unwarranted invasion of another's land that causes damage is actionable, without regard to fault. A person who acts must act so as not to damage others. If A's timber falls on B's house, A is liable; if A, defending himself against C, strikes B with a stick, A is liable to B. Why it matters: This is the starting point: early trespass liability was strict. Compare Brown v. Kendall.

MAIN CASE Weaver v. Ward (K.B. 1616) — excuse of "utterly without fault" Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 1 Facts: Weaver and Ward were soldiers in a training skirmish. Ward's musket went off accidentally and wounded Weaver. Ward pleaded that the injury was accidental and against his will. Weaver demurred to the plea. Held: An actor is liable for a direct injury unless he shows it was "utterly without his fault," as where it was inevitable (for example, if someone had jerked his arm). A plea of accident alone is not enough. Judgment for Weaver on the demurrer. Why it matters: Fault enters as an excuse the defendant must prove. The burden is still on the defendant.

MAIN CASE Brown v. Kendall (Mass. 1850) — fault required; burden on plaintiff Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 1 Facts: Two dogs, one Brown's and one Kendall's, were fighting. Kendall beat at them with a four-foot stick to separate them. As he backed away and raised the stick over his shoulder, he struck Brown, who was standing behind him, in the eye. The trial judge told the jury that unless separating the dogs was a necessary act, Kendall was liable unless he used extraordinary care, and that he bore the burden on those points. Held: Shaw, C.J.: there is no liability for an unintended injury caused while doing a lawful act with ordinary care (the care prudent and cautious people use to guard against probable danger). The plaintiff bears the burden of proving the defendant's lack of ordinary care. Under the contributory negligence rule of the time, the plaintiff also lost if he failed to use ordinary care himself. The instructions placed the burden on the wrong party. A new trial was ordered. Why it matters: This is the American shift to negligence as the basis of accident liability, with the burden on the plaintiff.

MAIN CASE Cohen v. Petty (D.C. Cir. 1933) — sudden unforeseeable illness Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 1 Facts: Petty was driving with Cohen as a guest passenger. He suddenly fainted, lost control, and the car crashed, injuring Cohen. The evidence was that Petty had never fainted before and had no warning. The trial court directed a verdict for Petty. Held: There is no negligence when a driver loses control because of a sudden illness he could not foresee. A reasonable person could not have guarded against it, so there was no duty to do so. Affirmed. Why it matters: Foreseeability is the core of fault. Compare Breunig (§ 12), where the driver had warning.

MAIN CASE Spano v. Perini Corp. (N.Y. 1969) — blasting: strict liability Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 1 Facts: Perini's dynamite blasting for a tunnel nearby sent shock waves that wrecked Spano's garage and damaged Davis's car parked inside. There was no physical intrusion of debris and no proof of negligence. The trial court found for the plaintiffs; the Appellate Division reversed under an old rule requiring a physical trespass. Held: Fuld, C.J.: one who uses explosives is strictly liable for the resulting damage. It makes no difference whether debris entered the land (trespass) or concussion caused the damage (case), and no fault is needed. The blaster, who chose to engage in the activity, should bear its costs rather than the innocent neighbor. Reversed for the plaintiffs. Why it matters: Fault did not take over everything: abnormally dangerous activities remain strict liability (§ 32).

EXAM TIPS Name the basis of liability in your first sentence. If the defendant meant to cause the contact or invasion, start with intentional torts. If not, go to negligence, then consider strict liability. On the essay, plead the alternatives when the facts allow.

# PART II — Intentional Torts

## 2. Intent WEEK 1
RULE Intent: R2d § 8A; R3d § 1 An actor intends a consequence when (any one suffices): (1) the actor acts with the purpose (desire) of causing it; or (2) the actor knows that the consequence is substantially certain to result.

- Intent is about consequences, not acts. Raising an arm is voluntary. The question is whether the actor intended the contact, the apprehension, the confinement, or the entry.

- Substantial certainty is actual subjective knowledge, not what a reasonable person would have known. That would be negligence. A high probability or a known risk is not enough.

- Motive is irrelevant. A practical joke, a mistaken belief, or a good-faith purpose does not negate intent.

- Recklessness (conscious disregard of a known, high risk) is not intent for most intentional torts. IIED is the exception, and recklessness can also support punitive damages.

Single vs. dual intent

- Single intent (Wagner): the actor must intend the contact. Whether the contact is harmful or offensive is judged by the law.

- Dual intent: the actor must intend the contact and also intend that it harm or offend. White v. Muniz (Colo. 2000) took this view for an elderly woman with dementia.

- Most courts and R3d use single intent. The difference matters most for very young children and people with mental illness.

MAIN CASE Garratt v. Dailey (Wash. 1955) — substantial certainty Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.A Facts: Brian Dailey, five years nine months old, was in Ruth Garratt's backyard. Garratt said Brian pulled a lawn chair out from under her as she sat down. Brian said he had moved the chair, sat in it himself, and then saw her about to sit where it had been and could not move it back in time. She fell and broke her hip. The trial court first found for Brian. Held: Hill, J.: a battery is intended if the actor acts for the purpose of causing the contact or knows with substantial certainty that it will result. No desire to harm is needed. The case was remanded to decide whether Brian knew with substantial certainty that Garratt would try to sit where the chair had been. On remand the trial court found that he did, and the judgment for Garratt ($11,000) was affirmed on a second appeal. Why it matters: This is the leading substantial-certainty case. Children can form intent, and no hostility is needed.

MAIN CASE Wagner v. State (Utah 2005) — single intent Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.A Facts: Tracy Wagner was standing in line at a K-Mart when Sam Giese, a mentally disabled patient of the Utah State Developmental Center on a supervised outing, attacked her without provocation. Giese had a history of violence. The Wagners sued the state for negligent supervision. The state moved to dismiss, because the Governmental Immunity Act retained immunity for injuries "arising out of" a battery. The Wagners argued Giese could not commit a battery because he could not appreciate that his contact was harmful. Held: Battery requires only an intent to make the contact. The contact must be harmful or offensive as a matter of law, but the actor need not intend or understand that it is harmful or offensive. Giese committed a battery, so the claim arose out of a battery and the state was immune. Dismissal affirmed. Why it matters: This is the single-intent rule. Note the irony: the injured plaintiff argued against finding a battery, because battery triggered immunity.

MAIN CASE Ranson v. Kitner (Ill. App. 1889) — mistake no defense Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.A Facts: The defendants were hunting wolves and shot and killed the plaintiff's dog, which looked like a wolf. They acted in good faith. The trial court awarded the plaintiff $50. Held: A mistake about identity or ownership is no defense to an intentional tort. The hunters intended to kill the animal and are liable for its value. Affirmed. Why it matters: Intent is the intent to bring about the physical result. An honest mistake does not undo it, though a mistake can matter to privileges.

MAIN CASE McGuire v. Almy (Mass. 1937) — insane persons Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.A Facts: McGuire, a registered nurse, was hired to care for Almy, who was mentally ill, around the clock. During a violent episode Almy broke furniture, threatened to kill anyone who entered, and stood holding the leg of a piece of furniture over her head. When McGuire entered and reached for her hand, Almy struck her. The jury found for McGuire. Held: Qua, J.: an insane person who forms the intent to strike is liable for battery, even if the decision was irrational. The intent required is to do the act, not to harm. Policy supports the rule: of two innocent people, the one who caused the loss should bear it, and liability encourages guardians to restrain dangerous wards. Judgment for McGuire. Why it matters: Mental illness does not prevent intent. It can bear on punitive damages, and it is handled separately in negligence (Breunig, § 12).

MAIN CASE Talmage v. Smith (Mich. 1894) — transferred intent Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.A Facts: Several boys were on the roofs of sheds on Smith's property. Smith ordered them down and, before they had all left, threw a stick intending to hit one boy, Byron Smith. It hit another, Talmage, in the eye, and he lost the sight of that eye. Held: When an actor intends an unjustified injury to one person, it does not matter that another person was injured instead. Smith is liable to Talmage. Affirmed. Why it matters: Transferred intent works between people and, by the traditional rule, between the "trespass" torts.

RULE Transferred intent: R2d §§ 16, 20, 32 Intent transfers when the actor (any one suffices): (1) intends a tort against one person but commits it against another; (2) intends one of the five trespass-based torts but commits a different one; or (3) both. The five torts: battery, assault, false imprisonment, trespass to land, and trespass to chattels. Intent generally does not transfer into IIED (see § 5, R2d § 46(2)) or into conversion.

TRAP A child or a mentally ill person is liable for an intentional tort if he formed the intent. Parents are not vicariously liable at common law, though statutes may make them liable up to a cap. A parent can be liable for the parent's own negligence in supervising the child.

NOTE Restatement (Third): no immunity for minors or people with disabilities R3d Misc. Prov. Immunities §§ 6–7 (approved 2022): minors and adults with a mental or emotional disability are not immune from tort liability. Age and disability matter only to whether the person committed the tort, for example whether the person formed the intent for battery (as in McGuire and Wagner) or acted negligently (§ 12).

## 3. Battery and Assault WEEK 2
RULE Battery: R2d §§ 13 (harmful), 18 (offensive) The actor is liable when (all required): (1) the actor acts intending to cause a harmful or offensive contact with the person of another or a third person, or an imminent apprehension of one; and (2) a harmful or offensive contact with the plaintiff's person directly or indirectly results.

- Harmful means bodily harm: physical impairment, pain, or illness.

- Offensive means it offends a reasonable sense of personal dignity (R2d § 19), judged by social norms. A particular plaintiff's unusual sensitivity counts only if the defendant knew of it.

- Contact can be indirect: a thrown object, poison, a trap. It can also be with something closely identified with the body (Fisher).

- Awareness not required. A plaintiff who was asleep or anesthetized can recover for a battery discovered later.

- No damages needed. Nominal damages are available, and so are damages for the full harm, foreseeable or not. Punitive damages are available on proof of malice.

MAIN CASE Cole v. Turner (Nisi Prius 1704) — the least touching in anger Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.B Facts: The report records no facts. Chief Justice Holt stated the rules in the abstract. Held: (1) The least touching of another in anger is a battery. (2) Gently touching someone to get past them in a narrow way, without violence, is not a battery. (3) Violently and rudely forcing one's way past in a struggle is. Why it matters: The line between offensive contact and the ordinary contacts of social life has been drawn since the earliest cases.

MAIN CASE Wallace v. Rosen (Ind. App. 2002) — ordinary social contact Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.B Facts: Mable Wallace, recovering from foot surgery, came to her daughter's high school with homework and stopped at the top of a stairway to talk with her daughter and two friends. A fire drill began, and students poured down the stairs. Teacher Harriet Rosen told the group to "move it"; Wallace did not hear, so Rosen touched her on the back to get her attention. Wallace fell down the stairs. The trial court refused Wallace's instruction defining battery as "the knowing or intentional touching of one person by another in a rude, insolent, or angry manner," and the jury found for Rosen. Held: Kirsch, J.: the instruction was properly refused because the evidence did not support it, but the rule it stated is correct. Battery requires an intentional touching that is rude, insolent, or angry: one that would offend an ordinary person not unduly sensitive about her dignity. Tortious intent means an intent to violate another's legally protected interest, not hostility. A light touch to move someone along during a fire drill is not a battery. Affirmed. Why it matters: Contacts customary in social life (tapping a shoulder, jostling in a crowd) are not offensive. They are covered by implied consent.

MAIN CASE Fisher v. Carrousel Motor Hotel, Inc. (Tex. 1967) — contact with an object identified with the body Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.B Facts: Fisher, a Black NASA mathematician, was attending a business conference at the hotel. While he stood in the buffet line holding his plate, the manager of the hotel's club snatched the plate from his hand and shouted that a Negro could not be served there. Fisher was not touched and suffered no physical injury, but he was highly embarrassed. The jury found for Fisher, but the trial court entered judgment for the defendants notwithstanding the verdict, and the court of civil appeals affirmed. Held: Greenhill, J.: snatching an object from a person's hand in an offensive manner is a battery. Battery protects personal dignity, so contact with anything closely identified with the body counts. Damages for humiliation are recoverable without physical injury. The hotel was liable for punitive damages because the club manager acted in a managerial capacity within the scope of his employment. Reversed; judgment for Fisher on the verdict. Why it matters: This is the "extended personality" rule. It is also a bias case: battery redressed a racial insult when no IIED claim was available. For punitive damages against employers, see § 28.

RULE Assault: R2d § 21 The actor is liable when (all required): (1) the actor acts intending to cause a harmful or offensive contact, or an imminent apprehension of one; and (2) the plaintiff is thereby put in imminent apprehension of such a contact.

- Apprehension means expectation, not fear. A boxer can apprehend a punch without being afraid of it. The plaintiff must be aware of the threat at the time.

- Imminent: a threat of future harm ("I'll get you tomorrow") is not an assault (R2d § 29).

- Apparent present ability is enough, so an unloaded gun counts if the plaintiff does not know it is unloaded. A threat that is plainly impossible to carry out is not (Western Union).

- Words alone are not an assault unless acts or circumstances make the threat imminent (R2d § 31). Words can also negate an assault ("If you weren't my friend, I'd hit you").

- Conditional threats ("your money or your life") are an assault when the defendant has no right to impose the condition.

MAIN CASE I de S et ux. v. W de S (Assizes 1348) — assault without contact Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.C Facts: At night, W came to I's tavern, which was closed, and beat on the door with a hatchet, wanting wine. When I's wife put her head out of a window and told him to stop, he struck at her with the hatchet and missed. Held: Thorpe, C.J.: there was harm, and so a trespass, even though no blow landed. Putting a person in fear of a blow is actionable, and damages are recoverable. Why it matters: This is the origin of assault as a separate tort, which protects the mental interest in freedom from apprehension.

MAIN CASE Western Union Telegraph Co. v. Hill (Ala. App. 1933) — apparent present ability; employer's liability Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.C Facts: Mrs. Hill went to the Western Union office to have Sapp, the manager, fix her electric clock. Sapp, who had been drinking, said he would fix it if she would let him "love and pet" her, and reached across the counter toward her shoulder. She stepped back. The counter was 4 feet 2 inches high and so wide that Sapp, stretching, could barely reach its far edge. The jury found for Mrs. Hill against Western Union. Held: Samford, J.: an assault requires a well-founded apprehension of an imminent battery, which needs an apparent present ability to carry it out. The evidence on whether Sapp could reach her conflicted, so that issue was for the jury. But the judgment was reversed because Sapp's advance was a personal one, outside the scope of his employment, so Western Union was not liable for it. Why it matters: Reasonable apprehension and apparent ability are what count. It is also an early respondeat superior case (§ 31): the conduct must serve the employer's business.

| Battery | Assault
Interest protected | Bodily integrity and dignity | Freedom from apprehension of a contact
Contact | Required, direct or indirect | Not required
Plaintiff's awareness | Not required | Required at the time
Intent | To contact, or to cause apprehension; transfers | Same; transfers

EXAM TIPS A swing that misses is an assault (if the plaintiff saw it). A swing that connects is a battery, and also an assault if the plaintiff saw it coming. For an unseen blow from behind, there is a battery but no assault.

## 4. False Imprisonment WEEK 2
RULE False imprisonment: R2d § 35 The actor is liable when (all required): (1) the actor acts intending to confine the plaintiff (or a third person) within boundaries fixed by the actor; (2) the act directly or indirectly results in such a confinement; and (3) the plaintiff is conscious of the confinement or is harmed by it.

Means of confinement (any one suffices): (1) physical barriers; (2) physical force; (3) threats of immediate force against the plaintiff, the plaintiff's family, or the plaintiff's property; (4) asserted legal authority (false arrest); (5) duress, such as keeping the plaintiff's valuable property or purse; or (6) refusing to release the plaintiff when under a duty to provide a means of release (Whittaker).

- No reasonable means of escape. If an exit is reasonable, safe, and known, there is no confinement. A person need not take a dangerous or humiliating exit, such as leaving without clothes.

- Moral pressure or a wish to clear one's name is not confinement. Neither are future threats, or a demand to stay without any threat of force (Hardy).

- Duration is irrelevant to liability, though it matters to damages.

- Being shut out of a place is not confinement. The boundaries must be complete.

MAIN CASE Big Town Nursing Home, Inc. v. Newman (Tex. Civ. App. 1970) — punitive damages Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.D Facts: Newman, a retiree, was taken to the nursing home by his nephew on September 19, 1968. The admission papers said he would not be kept against his will. Three days later he tried to leave and to call a taxi. Staff stopped him, took away his phone privileges, locked up his clothes and bag, and caught and brought him back each time he tried to leave. He was put in a wing for senile patients, alcoholics, and the mentally ill, and repeatedly tied into a "restraint chair." He escaped on November 11, having lost 30 pounds. There was no court order of commitment. Held: False imprisonment is the direct restraint of a person's physical liberty without adequate legal justification. Big Town's whole course of conduct was meant to keep Newman in, in violation of his admission papers. Because it acted intentionally in disregard of his rights, exemplary damages were proper. Affirmed after Newman accepted a remittitur. Why it matters: Institutional confinement without consent or legal process is false imprisonment, and willful disregard of the plaintiff's rights supports punitive damages (§ 28).

MAIN CASE Parvi v. City of Kingston (N.Y. 1977) — consciousness of confinement Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.D Facts: Two Kingston police officers found Parvi, who was drunk, in a downtown alley. He told them he had nowhere to go, so they drove him to an abandoned golf course outside the city to "dry out" and left him. He wandered onto the New York State Thruway and was hit by a car. At trial he said he could not remember whether he had been aware of being confined. The trial court dismissed his false imprisonment claim. Held: Fuchsberg, J.: in New York, false imprisonment, a dignitary tort, requires that the plaintiff be conscious of the confinement. But a present memory of that awareness is not required. Alcohol or his injuries may have erased the memory, and other evidence could show he was aware at the time. Reversed. Why it matters: Under the dignitary-tort view, the plaintiff must know of the confinement or be harmed by it (R2d § 42). Dissent (Breitel, C.J.): Parvi remembered nothing and knew of the incident only from later conversations, so he did not make out a prima facie case.

MAIN CASE Hardy v. LaBelle's Distributing Co. (Mont. 1983) — voluntary submission Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.D Facts: Hardy, a temporary employee, was asked to "tour" the store and was taken into the manager's office, where other employees and a uniformed police officer were present. She was told she had been accused of stealing a watch. She denied it, agreed to take a lie detector test, passed, and received an apology. She testified that she felt she could not leave but that she stayed voluntarily to clear her name. The jury found for LaBelle's. Held: False imprisonment is the unlawful restraint of a person against her will. Hardy admitted she wanted to stay to exonerate herself, and no threats or force kept her there. Affirmed. Why it matters: Restraint against the plaintiff's will is required. Staying to protect one's reputation is not confinement.

MAIN CASE Enright v. Groves (Colo. App. 1977) — false arrest Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.D Facts: Officer Groves saw a dog running loose in violation of the Fort Collins leash ordinance. Mrs. Enright's 11-year-old son said it was his dog and that his mother was in a car at the curb. Groves demanded Mrs. Enright's driver's license. She gave her name and address but refused to produce the license. He told her to produce it or go to jail; she said "Isn't this ridiculous?" and he arrested her. She was later convicted of the leash violation, and a jury awarded her $1,500 for false imprisonment. Held: Probable cause, or a conviction for the offense for which the person was arrested, defeats a false arrest claim. But Groves arrested Enright for failing to produce her license, not for the leash violation, and no law required a person who was not driving to produce a license on demand. Groves had no authority to make the arrest. Affirmed. Why it matters: False arrest is false imprisonment under asserted legal authority. Justification depends on the offense for which the person was actually arrested.

MAIN CASE Whittaker v. Sandford (Me. 1912) — confinement by refusing release Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.D Facts: Whittaker had been a member of a religious sect abroad led by Sandford. She decided to leave and accepted his offer of passage home to America on his yacht, on his promise that she would not be detained on board, especially not to reconvert her. When the yacht reached port, Sandford refused to provide a boat to take her ashore, and she was kept on the yacht for about a month, though she was otherwise free to move about it. Held: Savage, J.: false imprisonment does not require laying hands on the plaintiff; it is enough that her freedom of movement is restrained. When the defendant has a duty to provide a means of release, as Sandford did here by his promise and control of the boats, refusing to do so is an imprisonment. The verdict was upheld on liability. Why it matters: An omission counts when there is a duty to release (R2d § 45). Compare the general no-duty-to-act rule in negligence (§ 21).

NOTE Shopkeeper's privilege and other justifications are in § 9 (Bonkowski) and § 10 (Sindle). Treat them as defenses after you have set out the prima facie case.

## 5. Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress WEEK 2
RULE IIED: R2d § 46(1); Harris v. Jones The defendant is liable when (all required): (1) the conduct is intentional or reckless; (2) the conduct is extreme and outrageous; (3) the conduct causes the emotional distress; and (4) the distress is severe.

- Outrageous means "so outrageous in character, and so extreme in degree, as to go beyond all possible bounds of decency," so that "atrocious" is the community's reaction (R2d § 46 cmt. d). Mere insults, indignities, threats, annoyances, and petty oppressions are not enough.

- Factors pointing to outrageousness (weighed together): (1) abuse of a position of power or authority, such as an employer, police officer, landlord, or collection agency; (2) knowledge of the plaintiff's special susceptibility; (3) repeated conduct or a campaign of harassment; (4) threats of violence; and (5) public humiliation or racial or other identity-based abuse.

- Recklessness: the defendant acts in deliberate disregard of a high probability that distress will follow.

- Severe: distress no reasonable person could be expected to endure. Physical symptoms are not required but help prove it. The intensity and duration of the distress count.

- Common carriers and innkeepers are traditionally liable for gross insults to passengers and guests even without outrageousness (Slocum discusses this exception).

MAIN CASE State Rubbish Collectors Ass'n v. Siliznoff (Cal. 1952) — recognizing the tort Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.E Facts: Siliznoff took over collecting rubbish from a brewery that an association member claimed. Association officers told him he had to join and pay, or they would beat him up, destroy his truck, and put him out of business. He signed notes to pay the association, then refused to pay. The association sued on the notes, and he cross-claimed for the distress the threats caused; he testified he was so frightened he became ill, vomited, and missed work. The jury found for Siliznoff. Held: Traynor, J.: one who, without privilege, intentionally causes severe emotional distress by outrageous conduct is liable, even without physical injury and even though the threats of future harm were not an assault. Mental suffering is already compensated as part of assault, battery, and false imprisonment, so it is anomalous to deny it standing alone. Affirmed. Why it matters: This case established IIED as a stand-alone tort. Physical injury is not required.

MAIN CASE Slocum v. Food Fair Stores of Florida (Fla. 1958) — mere insults Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.E Facts: Slocum asked a Food Fair employee the price of an item. He replied, "If you want to know the price, you'll have to find out the best way you can... you stink to me." She said the shock brought on a heart attack. The trial court dismissed her complaint. Held: There is no liability for mere insults, indignities, or threats, whatever their consequences. An ordinary person would suffer only slight distress from this remark, and the special liability of common carriers and innkeepers for insulting patrons does not extend to a grocery store. Making trivial insults actionable would also chill speech. Affirmed. Why it matters: This sets the floor: rudeness is not outrageous, and the plaintiff's unknown susceptibility does not make it so.

MAIN CASE Harris v. Jones (Md. 1977) — the four elements; severity Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.E Facts: Harris, a General Motors employee, had stuttered all his life and was nervous about it. His supervisor, Jones, knowing this, mimicked and ridiculed his stutter about 30 times over five months. Harris said this made him more nervous and worsened his stutter. The jury found for Harris against Jones and GM, but the trial court granted judgment notwithstanding the verdict. Held: Murphy, C.J.: Maryland recognizes IIED with four elements: (1) intentional or reckless conduct; (2) extreme and outrageous conduct; (3) causation; and (4) severe distress. Jones's conduct, knowing Harris's susceptibility, satisfied the first three, but Harris failed on severity. His stutter and nervousness predated the abuse, and he offered no evidence of how much worse they became. Affirmed. Why it matters: This is the elements case. Severity is a real hurdle, and a supervisor's power and knowledge of a susceptibility go to outrageousness, not severity.

RULE IIED aimed at a third person: R2d § 46(2) When outrageous conduct is directed at a third person, the actor is liable if he intentionally or recklessly causes severe emotional distress (any one suffices): (a) to a member of that person's immediate family who is present at the time, whether or not the distress results in bodily harm; or (b) to any other person who is present at the time, if the distress results in bodily harm. Most courts also require that the defendant know the plaintiff is present (Taylor).

MAIN CASE Taylor v. Vallelunga (Cal. App. 1959) — bystander IIED: presence known Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.E Facts: Vallelunga beat Taylor's father. Taylor watched the beating and suffered severe emotional distress. Her complaint did not allege that Vallelunga knew she was present or intended to distress her. The trial court sustained a demurrer. Held: A plaintiff who witnesses an attack on a family member recovers for her own distress only if the defendant knew she was present, so that he intended, or was substantially certain, to cause her distress. Affirmed. Why it matters: Intent does not transfer into IIED. Knowledge of the bystander's presence takes its place.

NOTE Bias lens and limits Racial slurs by an employer or supervisor can be outrageous because of the power imbalance and the history the words carry (Alcorn v. Anbro Engineering, Cal. 1970). Compare Fisher (§ 3), which used battery. The First Amendment limits IIED for speech on public matters: public figures must prove actual malice (Hustler Magazine v. Falwell, 1988), and speech on public issues in a public place is protected (Snyder v. Phelps, 2011).

EXAM TIPS IIED often comes up as a backup claim. Ask first whether a traditional tort (assault, battery, false imprisonment) fits. Then argue outrageousness with the factors and confront severity directly. Graders look for both elements.

## 6. Trespass to Land, Trespass to Chattels, and Conversion WEEK 3
RULE Trespass to land: R2d § 158 One who intentionally does any of the following is liable, whether or not harm results (any one suffices): (a) enters land in the possession of another, or causes a thing or a third person to do so; (b) remains on the land; or (c) fails to remove from the land a thing which he is under a duty to remove.

- Intent means intent to enter the land, not intent to trespass. Believing in good faith that the land is your own is no defense (compare Ranson). An involuntary entry, such as being thrown onto the land, is not a trespass.

- No damage needed (Dougherty). Nominal damages are available, and the actor is liable for any harm the intrusion causes, even if it was unforeseeable and caused without negligence.

- Airspace and subsurface. The possessor owns the space above the land within the zone of reasonable use, and the area beneath it (Herrin). Aircraft overflights in navigable airspace are privileged (United States v. Causby, 1946).

- Continuing trespass: staying, or leaving a thing on the land, after permission ends is a trespass (Rogers; R2d § 160).

- Unintended intrusions that are negligent or reckless are governed by negligence and require actual harm (R2d § 165).

- Plaintiff: the person in possession, such as a tenant, not necessarily the owner.

MAIN CASE Dougherty v. Stepp (N.C. 1835) — no damage required Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.F Facts: Stepp entered Dougherty's land without permission and surveyed part of it with a surveyor's chain, claiming it as his own. He marked no trees and cut no brush. The jury found for Stepp, apparently because there was no damage. Held: Ruffin, C.J.: every unauthorized entry on another's land is a trespass, whether or not it causes actual damage. The law infers damage, "if nothing more, the treading down the grass or herbage." Reversed; new trial ordered. Why it matters: Trespass protects the right to exclude. Nominal damages vindicate the right and can establish title.

MAIN CASE Herrin v. Sutherland (Mont. 1925) — shooting over land Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.F Facts: While hunting, Sutherland repeatedly fired his shotgun at ducks and other birds flying over Herrin's land, over his house and cattle. The shot did not land on the property, but the firing disturbed Herrin's quiet enjoyment. Held: Callaway, C.J.: firing through the airspace close to the surface is a trespass, though nothing touched the ground. A possessor's rights extend to the airspace he may reasonably use, and missiles crossing it endanger people and property. Affirmed. Why it matters: Intrusions into the airspace near the ground are trespasses.

MAIN CASE Rogers v. Board of Road Comm'rs for Kent County (Mich. 1947) — continuing trespass after a license Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.F Facts: The Board had a license to put up a snow fence on the Rogers farm each winter, on the condition that it remove the fence, posts included, at the end of each season. It left an anchor post in the ground. The next summer, Rogers's husband was mowing the field when his mower hit the post; he was thrown off and killed. The trial court dismissed the complaint. Held: Reid, J.: once the license expired, leaving the post on the land was a trespass, and the Board is liable for the resulting harm whether or not it was negligent. Reversed and remanded. Why it matters: R2d § 158(c): a lawful entry becomes a trespass when the duty to remove arises, and liability extends to the consequences.

RULE Trespass by airborne particles: Bradley; Borland v. Sanders Lead (Ala. 1979) An invasion by microscopic airborne particles is a trespass only if (all required): (1) it is an invasion affecting an interest in the exclusive possession of property; (2) the defendant intentionally did the act that resulted in the invasion; (3) it was reasonably foreseeable that the act could result in an invasion of the plaintiff's possessory interest; and (4) the property (the res) suffered substantial damage. If the particles cause no damage to the land itself, the claim is in nuisance (§ 33), which requires a substantial interference with use and enjoyment.

MAIN CASE Bradley v. American Smelting & Refining Co. (W.D. Wash. 1986) — particle trespass needs damage to the land Source: Canvas reading (9/8), from the opinion text in the course folder. Facts: The Bradleys owned land on the southern end of Vashon Island, about four miles north of ASARCO's copper smelter at Ruston, Washington. For years the smelter emitted particles of arsenic and cadmium that the wind carried onto their land; the particles were imperceptible to human senses. The Bradleys sued in trespass and nuisance. The federal court certified questions to the Washington Supreme Court, which held (104 Wash. 2d 677 (1985)) that intentionally emitting imperceptible pollutants that settle on another's land may be a trespass as well as a nuisance; that such a trespass requires proof of actual and substantial damages; and that the three-year trespass limitations period applies. Back in federal court, soil from the Bradleys' garden showed 53 ppm arsenic and 1.7 ppm cadmium, above normal background levels. ASARCO's experts said these levels posed no danger. The Bradleys offered no evidence of actual harm or of lost property value, only their worry about health risks. Held: Rothstein, J.: summary judgment for ASARCO. Trespass: under the test the Washington Supreme Court adopted from Borland, the plaintiff must show substantial damage to the land. Without that rule, "every landowner within a hundred miles of a manufacturing plant" could sue. The evidence showed the particles had not harmed the land, and claimed loss of value was unsupported. Nuisance: the plaintiff must show substantial interference with use and enjoyment. Worry about a health risk the evidence shows does not exist is not enough, because distress counts in nuisance only if it causes physical symptoms or accompanies an actual or threatened invasion of the plaintiff's person or security. Action dismissed. Why it matters: The modern rule for pollution trespass. Trespass protects exclusive possession and does not ask whether the defendant acted reasonably, so courts require real damage to the land before treating invisible particles as a trespass. Otherwise the claim belongs in nuisance, which balances reasonableness.

RULE Trespass to chattels: R2d §§ 217–218 Conduct (any one suffices): the actor intentionally (a) dispossesses another of the chattel; or (b) uses or intermeddles with a chattel in the possession of another. Liability, beyond nominal damages, only if (any one suffices): (a) the possessor is dispossessed; (b) the chattel is impaired as to its condition, quality, or value; (c) the possessor is deprived of the use of the chattel for a substantial time; or (d) bodily harm is caused to the possessor, or harm is caused to some person or thing in which the possessor has a legally protected interest.

MAIN CASE Glidden v. Szybiak (N.H. 1949) — harmless intermeddling Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.G Facts: Four-year-old Elaine Glidden climbed on the Szybiaks' dog, Toby, on the porch of a store and pulled its ears. The dog bit her. A New Hampshire statute made dog owners liable for bites unless the victim was committing "a trespass or other tort." The owner argued Elaine had committed a trespass to the dog. Held: Branch, C.J.: harmless intermeddling with a chattel is not actionable. A trespass to chattels requires actual damage to the chattel or deprivation of its use, and there was no evidence the dog was harmed. Because Elaine committed no tort, the statutory defense failed and she could recover. Why it matters: R2d § 218: harmless meddling with a chattel is not actionable, unlike trespass to land.

MAIN CASE CompuServe Inc. v. Cyber Promotions, Inc. (S.D. Ohio 1997) — spam as trespass to chattels Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 2.G Facts: Cyber Promotions sent unsolicited email advertisements to CompuServe's subscribers by the millions. CompuServe told it to stop and installed filters; Cyber increased its volume and falsified the return information to get past the filters. CompuServe sought a preliminary injunction on a trespass to chattels theory. Held: Graham, J.: electronic signals sent to a computer system can be a use of or intermeddling with a chattel (R2d § 217(b)). Harm was shown: (1) the volume burdened CompuServe's processing power and disk space, diminishing the equipment's value (§ 218(b)); and (2) subscribers complained and canceled, harming CompuServe's goodwill and business interests (§ 218(d)). Cyber's First Amendment defense failed because CompuServe is a private actor. Preliminary injunction granted. Why it matters: The old tort applied to new technology, though actual harm is still required. Intel Corp. v. Hamidi (Cal. 2003) found no harm from a few emails.

Conversion (the casebook's next section; not on the syllabus pages)
RULE Conversion: R2d § 222A Conversion is an intentional exercise of dominion or control over a chattel that so seriously interferes with another's right to control it that the actor may justly be required to pay its full value. Seriousness factors (weighed together): (a) the extent and duration of the actor's exercise of dominion or control; (b) the actor's intent to assert a right in fact inconsistent with the other's right of control; (c) the actor's good faith; (d) the extent and duration of the resulting interference with the other's right of control; (e) the harm done to the chattel; and (f) the inconvenience and expense caused to the other.

NOTE CASE Pearson v. Dodd (D.C. Cir. 1969) — copying information is not conversion Source: 13th ed. Ch. 2.H (pages the syllabus skips) Facts: Two former members of Senator Dodd's staff, aided by two current members, entered his office at night without authority, removed documents from his files, photocopied them, and put the originals back. They gave the copies to columnists Drew Pearson and Jack Anderson, who knew how they had been obtained and published articles based on them. The district court granted Dodd partial summary judgment on conversion. Held: J. Skelly Wright, J.: there was no conversion. The originals were returned before they were missed, so Dodd was not deprived of them. The information itself was not literary property, a scientific invention, or a secret business plan, the kinds of information the law protects as property. Reversed. Why it matters: Conversion protects tangible things and a few forms of intellectual property. The remedy for publishing information is privacy or defamation law.

| Trespass to chattels | Conversion
Interference | Minor: use, intermeddling, short dispossession | Serious: destroying, keeping, selling, major alteration
Damages | Actual harm or loss of use (no nominal damages without harm) | Full value at the time of conversion, a forced sale
Good faith | Irrelevant to liability | Irrelevant to liability, but a factor in seriousness
Example | Moving a car to another space | Stealing it, or wrecking it while joyriding

# PART III — Privileges and Defenses to Intentional Torts

## 7. Consent WEEK 3
RULE When consent is a defense Consent bars an intentional tort claim when (all required): (1) the plaintiff had the capacity to consent; (2) the plaintiff consented, actually or apparently, to the defendant's conduct or to substantially the same conduct; (3) the consent was not procured by fraud about an essential matter or by duress; and (4) the defendant stayed within the scope of the consent.

- Forms of consent (any one suffices):
- (1) Express, in words or writing;

- (2) Implied in fact, or apparent: the plaintiff's conduct reasonably appears to show consent, judged objectively (O'Brien). Silence counts where a reasonable person would object if unwilling.

- (3) Implied by custom: the ordinary contacts of social life and the rules of a game (Wallace, Hackbart).

- (4) Implied by law: in an emergency, when the person cannot consent, a reasonable person would consent, and the actor has no reason to think this person would refuse (R2d § 892D).

- Capacity. Children, intoxicated people, and people with significant cognitive impairments may lack capacity. A parent or guardian can consent for them.

- Fraud about the essential character of the act, not just a collateral matter, vitiates consent (De May; R2d § 892B(2)). A lie about collateral matters, such as payment, does not.

- Consent to a crime. The majority view is that consent to a criminal act, such as an illegal boxing match or a mutual fight, is ineffective, so each participant can sue. R2d § 892C makes consent effective unless the statute was meant to protect a class from its own poor judgment, as with statutory rape and child-labor laws.

- Burden: consent is usually an affirmative defense, but for offensive battery its absence is often treated as part of the plaintiff's case.

MAIN CASE O'Brien v. Cunard S.S. Co. (Mass. 1891) — consent shown by conduct Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 3.A Facts: To spare passengers quarantine on arrival in Boston, Cunard vaccinated immigrants on board against smallpox and posted notices in several languages. O'Brien stood in line with about 200 women. The surgeon examined her arm, said there was no vaccination mark, and she held up her arm and was vaccinated without objecting. She later claimed she had been vaccinated before, did not want it, and suffered ulceration from the vaccine. Held: Knowlton, J.: consent is judged by the plaintiff's outward conduct. A surgeon may act on what a person's behavior shows, and her standing in line and holding up her arm, without objecting, showed consent. Verdict for Cunard affirmed. Why it matters: Consent is judged objectively: the defendant may rely on outward manifestations. Note the power imbalance, though. Immigrants needed vaccination to land.

MAIN CASE Hackbart v. Cincinnati Bengals, Inc. (10th Cir. 1979) — consent in sports Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 3.A Facts: During a regular season game, Bengals fullback Charles "Booby" Clark, frustrated after a play had ended, struck Broncos safety Dale Hackbart on the back of the head with his forearm while Hackbart was kneeling. Hackbart suffered a serious neck fracture. The trial court ruled that professional football is so violent that tort law does not reach blows between players. Held: Doyle, J.: players consent to contact within the rules and customs of the game, not to an intentional blow the rules prohibit, struck in anger after the play. The NFL rules forbid striking an opponent on the head with a forearm. Liability can rest on intentional or reckless conduct. Reversed for a new trial. Why it matters: Consent is limited to the risks inherent in the activity, as defined by its rules and customs. Violations outside the game support liability for intentional or reckless conduct.

MAIN CASE Mohr v. Williams (Minn. 1905) — exceeding the scope of consent Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 3.A Facts: Mohr consented to an operation on her right ear. Once she was anesthetized, Dr. Williams found the right ear less serious than he had thought and, on examining the left ear, found it diseased and more in need of surgery. Without waking her, he operated on the left ear, successfully. She sued for battery. The jury awarded $14,322.50, but the trial judge granted a new trial as excessive. Both sides appealed. Held: Brown, J.: operating on a different part of the body than the one consented to is a battery, however skillful or beneficial. A surgeon may go beyond the consent only if he finds, during the authorized operation, a condition that endangers life or health and requires immediate action. The left ear was not discovered during the authorized operation, and its condition was not an emergency. The order for a new trial (on damages) was affirmed. Why it matters: Medical consent covers only the procedure authorized. Many courts now allow reasonable extensions of an operation when a condition is found under anesthesia and immediate action is in the patient's interest (Kennedy v. Parrott, N.C. 1956).

MAIN CASE De May v. Roberts (Mich. 1881) — consent procured by deceit Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 3.A Facts: Dr. De May attended Mrs. Roberts in childbirth at her home. He brought with him Scattergood, a young unmarried man with no medical training, whom the Robertses took to be the doctor's assistant. Scattergood stayed throughout the delivery and held Mrs. Roberts's hand during a contraction. Held: Marston, C.J.: consent obtained by deceit about a material fact is no consent. Mrs. Roberts allowed Scattergood's presence and touch only because she believed he was a medical assistant. Both De May and Scattergood are liable. Affirmed. Why it matters: Fraud about the essential nature of the act or the actor vitiates consent. The case is also an ancestor of the privacy tort.

Medical consent: battery or negligence?
Problem | Claim | Why
No consent at all, or a substantially different procedure (Mohr) | Battery | An unconsented touching; no expert testimony needed
Consent to the procedure, but material risks were not disclosed (Scott v. Bradford, § 13) | Negligence (informed consent) | A breach of the duty to disclose; causation must be shown
Consent obtained by lying about who will operate ("ghost surgery") | Battery | Fraud about an essential matter

## 8. Self-Defense and Defense of Others WEEK 3
RULE Self-defense: R2d §§ 63–65 The actor is privileged to use force when (all required): (1) the actor reasonably believes that another is about to inflict a harmful or offensive contact or confinement on him; (2) the threat is imminent, not past or future; and (3) the force used is reasonably necessary and proportionate to the threat. Deadly force (force likely to cause death or serious bodily harm) is privileged only if the actor reasonably believes he faces death or serious bodily harm.

- Reasonable mistake preserves the privilege. The test is whether a reasonable person would have believed force was needed. In Courvoisier v. Raymond (Colo. 1896), a store owner who shot a deputy sheriff, mistaking him for one of a rioting crowd, was entitled to an instruction on reasonable appearances.

- Retreat. Under R2d § 65, before using deadly force, the actor must retreat if he can do so in complete safety, except in his own dwelling. Many states impose no duty to retreat, and stand-your-ground statutes eliminate it outside the home. No one must retreat before using non-deadly force.

- Words alone never justify force. Neither does revenge for a completed attack.

- Excessive force: the defender is liable for the excess, and the original aggressor may then defend himself against it.

- Injury to a bystander: a defender who injures a third person while acting in privileged self-defense is liable only if he was negligent toward that person (R2d § 75). Transferred intent does not apply.

RULE Defense of others: R2d § 76 The actor may use the same force to defend a third person that he could use to defend himself when (all required): (1) the actor reasonably believes that the third person would be privileged to defend himself; and (2) the actor reasonably believes that his intervention is necessary to protect the third person. Mistake: the modern majority (and R2d) protects a reasonable mistake. The older rule put the intervenor "in the shoes" of the person defended, so he was liable if that person was actually the aggressor.

EXAM TIPS For any privilege, separate the elements: (1) the belief; (2) whether it was reasonable; (3) imminence; and (4) proportionality. Most exam answers turn on proportionality, such as deadly force against a non-deadly threat, or on the timing of force used after the threat ended.

## 9. Defense and Recovery of Property; the Shopkeeper's Privilege WEEK 4
RULE Defense of property: R2d §§ 77, 79, 85 A possessor may use force to prevent or end an intrusion onto land or chattels when (all required): (1) the intrusion is not privileged; (2) the possessor reasonably believes force is necessary to prevent or end it; (3) the possessor first asks the intruder to desist, unless asking would be futile or dangerous; and (4) the force is reasonable. Force intended or likely to cause death or serious bodily harm is never privileged to protect property alone.

- Mechanical devices (spring guns, traps) are privileged only to the extent the possessor could have used the same force in person, and only if a warning is given where needed (R2d § 85). A device cannot tell a burglar from a child or a firefighter.

- Mistake: unlike self-defense, a mistaken belief that the intruder is not privileged generally does not protect the defender, unless the intruder caused the mistake.

- Defense of the dwelling against someone threatening the occupants is governed by self-defense, so deadly force may be justified by a threat to people, not by the intrusion itself.

MAIN CASE Katko v. Briney (Iowa 1971) — spring guns Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 3.D Facts: The Brineys owned an unoccupied, boarded-up farmhouse that had been broken into repeatedly. They rigged a 20-gauge shotgun in a bedroom to fire at the legs of anyone who opened the door, and posted no warning. Katko broke in to steal old bottles and fruit jars. When he opened the bedroom door, the blast tore away much of his leg. He had pleaded guilty to larceny. The jury awarded $20,000 in actual and $10,000 in punitive damages. Held: Moore, C.J.: a possessor may not use, to protect property alone, force or a device intended to kill or seriously injure an intruder. Such force is justified only when the intruder is committing a violent felony or endangering human life. The law values human life and limb above property, even a trespasser's who is committing a crime. Affirmed. Why it matters: Human life and limb outweigh property interests. The force allowed through a device is no more than the possessor could use in person. Dissent (Larson, J.): the jury should have been told it could find the gun was set only to frighten, the rule had never been applied to a burglar, and punitive damages should not be awarded to a plaintiff engaged in crime.

RULE Recovery of chattels: Hodgeden; R2d §§ 100–106 An owner may use reasonable force to recover a chattel when (all required): (1) the owner was wrongfully dispossessed, by force, fraud, or theft (not merely a debtor's failure to return it); (2) the owner acts in fresh pursuit, promptly after discovering the taking; (3) the owner first demands its return, unless a demand would be futile or dangerous; and (4) the force used is reasonable and not likely to cause serious bodily harm.

MAIN CASE Hodgeden v. Hubbard (Vt. 1846) — fresh-pursuit recapture Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 3.E Facts: Hodgeden bought a stove from the Hubbards on credit, misrepresenting his finances. Discovering the fraud almost at once, they rode after him and overtook him a few miles away. When he refused to return the stove and drew a knife, one of them held him while the other took the stove. Hodgeden sued for assault and battery and won below. Held: Williams, C.J.: an owner who has been defrauded of goods may retake them by force if he acts without unreasonable delay and uses no unnecessary violence. The wrongdoer has no privilege to resist, and if he does, the owner may use the force needed to protect himself. Reversed. Why it matters: Self-help recapture is allowed only in fresh pursuit and with reasonable force. Later, the owner must go to court.

RULE Shopkeeper's privilege: R2d § 120A; Bonkowski A merchant may detain a person when (all required): (1) the merchant reasonably believes the person has taken, or is taking, goods without paying; (2) the detention is on the premises or in their immediate vicinity; (3) the detention is for a reasonable time and only to investigate; and (4) the detention is carried out in a reasonable manner, with no more force than is reasonably necessary. Most states codify the privilege. In Delaware, see 11 Del. C. § 840 (detention of suspected shoplifters).

MAIN CASE Bonkowski v. Arlan's Department Store (Mich. App. 1968) — merchant detention Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 3.E Facts: As Mrs. Bonkowski walked to her car after leaving the store, a store security guard stopped her outside, said someone had told him she had taken costume jewelry, and told her to empty her purse. She did so on a ledge outside the store and showed receipts for her items; he let her go. She claimed psychological harm. The jury awarded her $43,750. Held: Fitzgerald, J.: a merchant who reasonably believes a person has taken goods without paying may detain her for a reasonable investigation, in a reasonable manner, on or in the immediate vicinity of the premises. The jury should have been told about this privilege. Reversed and remanded for a new trial. Why it matters: The privilege resolves the merchant's dilemma of letting a suspected thief go or risking false imprisonment liability.

NOTE Bias lens The shopkeeper's privilege turns on "reasonable" suspicion. Studies and litigation show that store detentions fall disproportionately on Black shoppers ("shopping while Black"). Ask on the essay whether the grounds for suspicion were particular to the plaintiff, and whether the manner of detention was reasonable.

## 10. Necessity and Discipline WEEK 4
| Public necessity (Surocco; R2d § 196) | Private necessity (Vincent; R2d § 197)
When | The actor reasonably believes it necessary to avert an imminent public disaster, such as fire, flood, or epidemic | The actor reasonably believes it necessary to protect his own or a third person's person or property from serious harm
Privilege | Complete: no liability for the harm | Incomplete: privileged to enter and use, but liable for actual damage
Owner's resistance | The owner may not resist | The owner may not resist or expel. An owner who does is liable (Ploof v. Putnam, Vt. 1908: unmooring a boat in a storm)
Compensation | None from the actor. A taking claim against the government may lie. | The actor pays for the damage caused

MAIN CASE Surocco v. Geary (Cal. 1853) — public necessity Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 3.F Facts: During the great San Francisco fire of 1849, Geary, the alcalde, ordered Surocco's house blown up with gunpowder to stop the fire from spreading. Surocco was removing goods at the time and said he could have saved more of them if not for the blast. The trial court found for Surocco. Held: Murray, C.J.: destroying private property to stop a conflagration is privileged by public necessity, if done in good faith under apparent necessity. No action lies against the person who did it, even if the property would have been saved, because otherwise no one would act to save the community. Reversed. Why it matters: The community's safety outweighs one owner's property. The privilege is complete. Whether the destruction was actually necessary is judged by the circumstances at the time.

MAIN CASE Vincent v. Lake Erie Transp. Co. (Minn. 1910) — private necessity: pay for the damage Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 3.F Facts: The steamship Reynolds was unloading at Vincent's dock in Duluth when a violent storm arose. The crew kept the ship moored to the dock overnight, replacing lines as they broke. The waves threw the ship against the dock, causing $500 of damage. The jury found for Vincent. Held: O'Brien, J.: the ship was privileged by private necessity to stay at the dock, and keeping it there was prudent seamanship, not negligence. But a party who deliberately uses another's property to save his own must pay for the damage caused. Affirmed. Why it matters: This is the incomplete privilege: an act can be both justified and compensable. The dissent would have treated the damage as a risk of the dock owner's business. Dissent (Lewis, J.): the ship was lawfully at the dock and could not safely leave; the damage was an inevitable accident, and the dock owner, who invited the ship for profit, should bear the risk.

RULE Discipline and authority of law Discipline: a parent, a person in loco parentis, or a teacher may use reasonable force, or confinement, reasonably believed necessary to control, train, or educate a child (R2d §§ 147–155). Reasonableness considers (weighed together): (1) the child's age, sex, and condition; (2) the nature of the offense and the child's motive; (3) the influence of the child's example on others; (4) whether the force is necessary and appropriate to compel obedience; and (5) whether it is disproportionate or likely to cause serious harm. Restraint to protect people or property: reasonable detention, in time and manner, to prevent another from injuring people or damaging property in one's lawful custody is not unlawful (Sindle).

MAIN CASE Sindle v. New York City Transit Authority (N.Y. 1973) — justification for detention Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 3.G Facts: Students on a school bus run by the Transit Authority became unruly and vandalized it. The driver, Mooney, warned them, then locked the doors, skipped the remaining stops, and drove toward the police station. Sindle, 14, jumped out of a window to escape and was run over by the rear wheels. At trial he waived his negligence claim, and the judge refused to let the defendants plead justification and excluded evidence of it. The jury awarded damages for false imprisonment. Held: Jasen, J.: refusing leave to plead justification was an abuse of discretion; the defendants had the burden of proving it, and Sindle could not have been prejudiced. A restraint reasonable in time and manner, imposed to prevent injury to persons or damage to property in one's lawful custody, is not unlawful. The driver, entrusted with both the students and the bus, stood in a position like a teacher in loco parentis. Whether his detention was reasonable was for the jury. Reversed; new trial. Why it matters: Justification is a defense to false imprisonment, but its reasonableness is a fact question. Detaining every passenger, including the innocent, presses the limits.

NOTE Arrest without a warrant (background) A police officer may arrest without a warrant for a felony if he reasonably believes one was committed and that the arrestee committed it. A private citizen is privileged only if a felony was in fact committed and he reasonably believes the arrestee committed it. For a misdemeanor, an arrest without a warrant generally requires a breach of the peace committed in the arrester's presence. See Enright (§ 4): the justification must fit the offense for which the person was actually arrested.

ROADMAP Intentional torts and privileges: the week 5 MC checklist 1. Tort. Name each act and match it to a tort: contact (battery), apprehension (assault), confinement (false imprisonment), outrageous conduct (IIED), land (trespass), chattel (trespass to chattels or conversion). 2. Intent. Purpose or substantial certainty? Transferred between people or torts? Child, mental illness, or mistake does not defeat it. 3. Element traps.
