Awareness (needed for assault and, usually, false imprisonment; not for battery), imminence, reasonable means of escape, severity of distress, actual harm for chattels. 4. Privilege. Consent (scope, fraud, capacity), self-defense, defense of others, defense of property (never deadly force), recapture (fresh pursuit), shopkeeper, necessity (public is complete, private pays), discipline. 5. Damages. Nominal for battery, assault, and trespass to land; punitive damages for malice (Big Town, Katko, Fisher).

# PART IV — Negligence: The Standard of Care

## 11. The Negligence Case and Unreasonable Risk WEEKS 4–5
RULE The prima facie case for negligence The plaintiff must prove (all required): (1) duty, an obligation to conform to a standard of conduct for the protection of others against unreasonable risks; (2) breach, conduct that falls below that standard; (3) cause in fact, the conduct was a but-for or substantial-factor cause of the harm; (4) proximate cause, the harm is within the scope of the risk that made the conduct negligent; and (5) damages, actual harm to person or property (nominal damages are not available).

- Negligence is conduct, not a state of mind. It is the creation of an unreasonable risk of harm to others (R2d § 282). The plaintiff need not show the defendant knew of the risk, only that a reasonable person would have.

- Duty and breach. The general duty is reasonable care toward foreseeable plaintiffs (§ 21 covers limits). The standard is the reasonable person under the same or similar circumstances (§ 12).

- Unreasonable risk has two parts: (1) the risk must be foreseeable; and (2) a reasonable person would have taken a precaution against it, given its likelihood and severity and the burden of avoiding it.

MAIN CASE Lubitz v. Wells (Conn. Super. 1955) — foreseeability of harm Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.A Facts: Mr. Wells left a golf club in his backyard. His son, J. Wells Jr., picked it up and swung it at a stone without warning Judith Lubitz, who was playing nearby, and hit her in the jaw. She sued the son for negligent swinging and the father for leaving the club where it could cause harm. Held: Troland, J.: leaving a golf club in a yard is not negligent. It is not an inherently dangerous instrument, and the chance that a child would injure someone with it was not reasonably foreseeable. Demurrer as to the father sustained. Why it matters: Without a foreseeable risk there is no negligence. Contrast a loaded gun or a dangerous chemical left where children play.

MAIN CASE Blyth v. Birmingham Waterworks Co. (Ex. 1856) — the classic definition Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.A Facts: The waterworks company installed water mains and fire plugs that had worked properly for 25 years. During the severe frost of 1855, ice forced out a plug's stopper, and water flooded Blyth's house. The jury found for Blyth. Held: Alderson, B.: negligence is "the omission to do something which a reasonable man, guided upon those considerations which ordinarily regulate the conduct of human affairs, would do, or doing something which a prudent and reasonable man would not do." A reasonable company guards against ordinary frosts, not one of extraordinary severity. Reversed; judgment for the company. Why it matters: This is the standard definition of negligence. Foreseeability is measured by ordinary experience at the time.

MAIN CASE Pipher v. Parsell (Del. 2007) — foreseeable conduct of a passenger Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.A Facts: Parsell, 16, was driving two other 16-year-olds in a pickup truck at 55 mph, all three in the front seat. Passenger Biesel suddenly grabbed the wheel, and the truck veered toward the shoulder; Parsell regained control and did nothing. About 30 seconds later Biesel grabbed the wheel again; the truck left the road and hit a tree, injuring Pipher, the middle passenger. Parsell admitted at trial he could have told Biesel not to do it again, moved her, or made her get out. The trial judge ruled as a matter of law that Parsell had no duty to act after the first grab. Held: Holland, J.: a driver owes passengers and the public a duty of reasonable care. When it is foreseeable that a passenger's conduct may interfere with safe driving, failing to prevent it may breach that duty. After the first grab, a reasonable jury could find the second foreseeable and Parsell's inaction a breach. Breach and proximate cause were jury questions. Reversed. Why it matters: A Delaware Supreme Court case. Foreseeability can arise during the events, and whether the response was reasonable is usually for the jury.

RULE Weighing the risk: R2d §§ 291–293; R3d § 3 An act is negligent if its risk outweighs its utility. Factors (weighed together): (1) the foreseeable likelihood that the conduct will cause harm; (2) the foreseeable severity of any harm; and (3) the burden of precautions that would eliminate or reduce the risk, including the social value of the conduct.

MAIN CASE Chicago, B. & Q. R. Co. v. Krayenbuhl (Neb. 1902) — utility vs. danger Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.B Facts: Children often played on the railroad's turntable, which was near a public path. Company rules required it to be padlocked when not in use, but the rule was often ignored. Four-year-old Krayenbuhl went there with other children, who found the turntable unlocked (or unlocked it), and his foot was caught and severed above the ankle. The jury found for him. Held: A possessor who knows or has reason to know that young children will be attracted to a dangerous machine on its land must use reasonable care to protect them. Whether a precaution is required depends on balancing the machine's usefulness and the cost of the precaution against the danger. A lock costs little and would not impair the turntable's use. The judgment was reversed on other grounds (an error in the instructions). Why it matters: This is risk-utility balancing before the Hand formula. It is also an ancestor of the attractive nuisance doctrine (§ 26).

MAIN CASE Davison v. Snohomish County (Wash. 1928) — burden of precautions Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.B Facts: Coming off a county bridge onto a curved, elevated approach, Davison's car skidded, broke through the wooden guardrail, and fell. He claimed the rail was too weak to stop a car, the curve was improperly banked, and dirt on the road caused the skid. The jury found for Davison. Held: Beals, J.: a county is not required to build guardrails strong enough to stop cars on all elevated roads. The cost would be prohibitive and would discourage building roads. The banking deviation was small in relation to the whole slope, and the county is not liable for an ordinary accumulation of dirt. Reversed. Why it matters: The burden of the precaution, measured across all similar roads, can make a risk reasonable.

MAIN CASE United States v. Carroll Towing Co. (2d Cir. 1947) — the Hand formula Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.B Facts: In January 1944, in crowded New York Harbor, the barge Anna C was moored with others at a pier. A tug crew employed by Carroll Towing negligently readjusted the mooring lines, and the barges broke loose. The Anna C drifted against a tanker, whose propeller holed her, and she sank with her cargo of government flour. Its bargee had been ashore for 21 hours, though barges were constantly being moved in the harbor. The trial court divided damages. Held: Hand, J.: an owner's duty to guard against a barge breaking loose depends on three variables: (1) the probability that it will break away (P); (2) the gravity of the resulting injury (L); and (3) the burden of adequate precautions (B). Liability follows if B < P × L. Keeping a bargee aboard during the working hours of daylight, in a crowded wartime harbor, was a small burden compared with the risk. The owner's own negligence reduced its recovery. Affirmed. Why it matters: This is the canonical risk-utility test. On an essay, put rough values on B, P, and L and compare them.

NOTE Using and criticizing the Hand formula The formula compares the marginal (additional) precaution with the marginal reduction in risk. Values are often unquantifiable, and juries rarely do the arithmetic. Courts use it as a way to organize the argument. Critics say it values harm by market measures, such as lost earnings, which can undervalue harm to lower-income people, and that it treats safety as just another cost.

## 12. The Reasonable Person WEEK 5
RULE The standard: R2d § 283; R3d § 3 The standard of conduct is that of a reasonable person of ordinary prudence under the same or similar circumstances. It is objective: the actor's own good faith or best judgment does not count (Vaughan v. Menlove).

Characteristic | Rule | Case
Lack of judgment or intelligence | No allowance; the objective standard applies | Vaughan v. Menlove
Knowledge | Charged with what a reasonable person knows, including common facts and knowledge from reasonable inspection; superior knowledge counts | Delair v. McAdoo
Custom | Evidence of due care, not conclusive | Trimarco v. Klein
Emergency | A reasonable person in that emergency, if not of the actor's making | Cordas v. Peerless
Physical disability | A reasonable person with that disability | Roberts v. Louisiana
Children | A child of like age, intelligence, and experience, except in adult activities | Robinson v. Lindsay
Mental illness | No allowance, except sudden mental incapacity without warning | Breunig
Intoxication | Held to the standard of a sober person | (no case; R2d § 283C cmt. d)

MAIN CASE Vaughan v. Menlove (C.P. 1837) — objective standard Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.B Facts: Menlove built a hayrick near the edge of his land, beside Vaughan's cottages. He was warned several times that it was likely to catch fire. He said his stock was insured and he "would chance it," though he cut a chimney through it as a precaution. The hay ignited spontaneously, and the fire destroyed Vaughan's cottages. Menlove argued he should be liable only if he failed to act honestly and to the best of his own judgment. Held: Tindal, C.J.: the standard is objective: whether the defendant used the caution a man of ordinary prudence would use. A standard based on each individual's judgment would be "as variable as the length of the foot of each individual." The verdict for Vaughan stood. Why it matters: This is the origin of the objective standard. Low intelligence is no excuse.

MAIN CASE Delair v. McAdoo (Pa. 1936) — knowledge charged to everyone Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.C Facts: McAdoo tried to pass Delair's car when his left rear tire blew out, and his car crashed into Delair's. Witnesses said the tire was worn through to the fabric. McAdoo said he did not know the tires were worn. The jury found for Delair. Held: Kephart, C.J.: every adult is charged with knowledge of facts common to the community, such as gravity, fire, and the danger of worn tires. The owner or operator of a car is charged with knowledge of its condition that a reasonable inspection would reveal, and the wear here was visible. Affirmed. Why it matters: A defendant cannot plead ignorance of what everyone knows. Inspection duties arise from the activity.

MAIN CASE Trimarco v. Klein (N.Y. 1982) — custom as evidence Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.C Facts: Trimarco, a tenant in Klein's building, was badly cut when he fell through the glass door of his bathtub enclosure. The door was ordinary thin glass, though it looked like tempered glass. His expert testified that by the 1950s it had become the common practice of landlords to use shatterproof glass in such enclosures. The jury found for Trimarco, but the Appellate Division reversed, holding the landlord had no duty to replace the glass without notice of the danger. Held: Fuchsberg, J.: evidence of custom and usage by others in the same business is admissible to show what is reasonable, but it is not conclusive. Quoting Holmes: "What usually is done may be evidence of what ought to be done, but what ought to be done is fixed by a standard of reasonable prudence, whether it usually is complied with or not." The custom evidence was properly admitted. A new trial was ordered because of other erroneously admitted evidence. Why it matters: Custom is a sword (deviation is evidence of negligence) and a shield (compliance is evidence of care), but never conclusive. The T.J. Hooper (2d Cir. 1932, Hand, J.) holds that a whole industry can lag behind reasonable care.

MAIN CASE Cordas v. Peerless Transportation Co. (N.Y. City Ct. 1941) — sudden emergency Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.C Facts: A man who had just committed a robbery, chased by a crowd shouting "Stop thief," jumped into a Peerless cab, pointed a gun at the driver, and ordered him to drive. The driver started off, then threw the car out of gear, braked, and jumped out. The cab, still moving, mounted the sidewalk and hit Mrs. Cordas and her two children. Held: Carlin, J.: a person faced with a sudden emergency not of his own making is not held to the judgment he would use with time to reflect. He is judged by what a reasonable person would do in that emergency. The driver was not negligent; the law does not require heroism. Complaint dismissed. Why it matters: The emergency is a circumstance, not a separate standard. It does not help someone whose own negligence created the emergency.

MAIN CASE Roberts v. State of Louisiana (La. App. 1981) — physical disability Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.C Facts: Burson, a blind man, ran a snack bar in a state office building. He left the counter to go to the restroom without his cane, relying on his familiarity with the area and his "facial sense" of nearby obstacles, and bumped into Roberts, who fell and hurt his hip. Roberts sued the state as Burson's employer and for negligent supervision. His only evidence of Burson's negligence was an expert who had never examined Burson. The trial court dismissed. Held: Laborde, J.: a person with a physical disability must take the precautions that a reasonable person with the same disability would take. Burson's evidence showed his method of moving through familiar areas was reasonable, and Roberts did not prove otherwise. Affirmed. Why it matters: The disability is part of the circumstances, so the standard is a reasonable blind person, not a reasonable sighted one.

MAIN CASE Robinson v. Lindsay (Wash. 1979) — children in adult activities Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.C Facts: Billy Anderson, 13, was driving a snowmobile when an accident injured Kelly Robinson, 11, who lost full use of her thumb. The jury was instructed to judge Billy by the standard of a reasonable child of his age and found for him. The trial judge then granted a new trial, ruling that an adult standard should have applied. Held: Utter, C.J.: children are generally held to the standard of a reasonable child of like age, intelligence, and experience. But a child engaged in an inherently dangerous activity normally pursued only by adults, such as operating a powerful motorized vehicle, is held to the adult standard. Snowmobiles qualify. The new trial was properly ordered. Affirmed. Why it matters: This is the adult-activity exception. Some states hold that children under a set age, often 5 or 7, are incapable of negligence (tender-years rule).

MAIN CASE Breunig v. American Family Ins. Co. (Wis. 1970) — sudden mental illness Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.C Facts: Erma Veith, insured by American Family, was driving when she believed God was taking control of her car. Seeing a truck ahead, she stepped on the gas so the car would become airborne, believing she could fly like Batman. Her car crossed the center line and hit Breunig's truck. A psychiatrist testified she had a sudden delusion; there was also evidence she had had similar visions before. The jury found her negligent. Held: Hallows, C.J.: insanity is generally no defense to negligence, for policy reasons (weighed together): (1) between two innocent people, the one who caused the loss should bear it; (2) liability gives those interested in an insane person's estate a reason to restrain him; and (3) it prevents false claims of insanity. But a sudden mental incapacity that strikes without warning, like a heart attack or epileptic seizure, is an exception. Because the jury could find Veith had forewarning of her delusions, the verdict for Breunig was affirmed. Why it matters: The general rule rests on policies (weighed together): (1) between two innocent people, the one who caused the loss should bear it; (2) it encourages those responsible for the mentally ill to control them; and (3) it prevents false claims of insanity. Compare Cohen v. Petty (§ 1).

NOTE Bias lens: whose "reasonable"? The "reasonable man" became the "reasonable person." Critics argue the standard can still build in the perspective of the people who historically served as jurors and judges. Roberts takes disability into account, but mental illness gets no allowance (Breunig). Consider whether that distinction is principled. Some scholars argue for a "reasonable woman" standard in harassment contexts, or for considering the plaintiff's community when judging what is offensive or reasonable.

## 13. Professionals and Informed Consent WEEK 6
RULE The professional standard A professional must use (all required): (1) the knowledge and skill ordinarily possessed by members of the profession in good standing (in the same specialty and, under older rules, the same or a similar locality); (2) reasonable care and diligence in applying that knowledge and skill; and (3) his best judgment. Proof: the standard and its breach must be shown by expert testimony unless the negligence is obvious to a layperson, such as leaving a sponge in the patient or operating on the wrong limb (Boyce).

NOTE Restatement (Third): duties of medical providers R3d Medical Malpractice §§ 2–3 (approved 2022): a patient-care relationship arises when a provider manifests an intent to care for a patient and (any one suffices) (1) begins care without the patient's objection; (2) the patient reasonably believes the provider has undertaken care; or (3) the patient reasonably relies on the provider. Duties within the relationship (all owed): (1) to exercise reasonable care; (2) to comply with the requirements of informed consent; (3) to use reasonable care to protect confidential patient information; and (4) not to end the relationship without giving the patient a reasonable opportunity to find other care.

- Professional custom sets the standard. Unlike ordinary custom (Trimarco), what the profession does is the measure of care, not just evidence of it.

- Schools of thought: a doctor who follows a method accepted by a respectable minority of the profession is not negligent.

- Error in judgment: a professional is not liable for an honest error in an area where reasonable professionals disagree or the law is unsettled (Hodges).

- Specialists are held to the standard of a reasonable specialist in that field, usually national (Morrison).

MAIN CASE Heath v. Swift Wings, Inc. (N.C. App. 1979) — objective professional standard Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.C Facts: A small plane crashed shortly after takeoff, killing the pilot and his passengers. In the passengers' estates' suit against the pilot's estate, the jury was instructed that negligence meant failing to use the care that "an ordinarily prudent pilot having the same training and experience as" this pilot would use. The jury found the pilot not negligent. Held: Morris, C.J.: the instruction was wrong. A professional's standard is objective: the care of a reasonably prudent pilot with the knowledge and skill the profession requires. Tying the standard to the defendant's own training and experience would create a different standard for every defendant. New trial ordered. Why it matters: Even professionals are judged objectively. "Best judgment" is required, but it is not enough by itself.

MAIN CASE Hodges v. Carter (N.C. 1954) — lawyer's error in judgment Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.C Facts: Hodges's drugstore and its contents burned, and his four fire insurers refused to pay. His lawyers, Topping and Carter, sued and served process on the foreign insurers by mail through the state Commissioner of Insurance, the method in standard use for more than 20 years. The North Carolina Supreme Court then held that method invalid, and the limitations period had run. Hodges sued the lawyers for negligence, including their failure to obtain new summonses in time. The trial court entered a nonsuit. Held: Barnhill, C.J.: a lawyer is liable if the client's loss results from (1) a lack of the knowledge and skill ordinarily possessed by lawyers similarly situated, (2) a failure to use reasonable care and diligence, or (3) a failure to use his best judgment. A lawyer who acts in good faith and follows the settled practice of the bar is not liable for a mistake on a point of law later decided against him. Affirmed. Why it matters: Lawyers are not guarantors of results. They are liable for lacking ordinary skill, for failing to use reasonable care, or for not using their best judgment.

MAIN CASE Boyce v. Brown (Ariz. 1938) — expert testimony required Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.C Facts: In 1927, Dr. Brown set Mrs. Boyce's fractured ankle by surgically inserting a metal screw. In 1934 she returned with a swollen, painful ankle; he taped it and filed down her arch support but took no X-ray. In 1936, Dr. Kent X-rayed the ankle, found the bone around the screw had deteriorated, and removed the screw; she recovered. At trial, Dr. Kent testified about what he did in 1936 but not about the standard of care in 1934. The trial court directed a verdict for Dr. Brown. Held: Lockwood, J.: medical negligence must be proved by expert testimony that the doctor departed from the accepted standard of practice, unless the negligence is so grossly apparent that a layperson would have no difficulty recognizing it. A different method is not negligence, and failing to take an X-ray is not obvious negligence. Affirmed. Why it matters: The plaintiff's expert must address the standard and the breach, not just what he would have done.

MAIN CASE Morrison v. MacNamara (D.C. 1979) — national standard of care Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.C Facts: MacNamara, a nationally accredited medical laboratory in Washington, D.C., performed a urethral smear test for trichomonas on Morrison while he stood. He fainted and was seriously injured in the fall. The court excluded his expert's testimony that the national standard was to perform the test with the patient sitting or lying down, but admitted local doctors' testimony that in D.C. it was done standing. The jury found for the laboratory. Held: Newman, C.J.: the standard of care for board-certified physicians, hospitals, medical laboratories, and other health care providers is national. The locality rule was premised on disparities between urban and rural medicine that national certification has removed, and it can shield substandard local practice. The expert's testimony should have been admitted. Reversed and remanded. Why it matters: The locality rule is giving way to a national standard, at least for specialists and accredited facilities. Some states use a "same or similar locality" rule.

RULE Informed consent: Scott v. Bradford The plaintiff must prove (all required): (1) the physician failed to disclose a material risk of, or alternative to, the treatment; (2) had the risk been disclosed, the plaintiff would have declined the treatment (causation); and (3) the undisclosed risk materialized and injured the plaintiff. Exceptions (any one suffices): (1) emergency; (2) the risk was known to the patient or is common knowledge; (3) disclosure would seriously harm the patient (therapeutic privilege); or (4) the patient waived disclosure.

Question | Patient-oriented view (Scott; Canterbury v. Spence) | Physician-oriented view (traditional)
What must be disclosed? | What a reasonable patient would find material to the decision | What a reasonable physician would disclose (professional custom)
Expert testimony? | Not needed on what to disclose | Needed to prove the custom
Causation | Scott: subjective (would this patient have refused?). Canterbury and most courts: objective (would a reasonable patient have refused?) | Usually objective

MAIN CASE Scott v. Bradford (Okla. 1979) — informed consent Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.C Facts: Dr. Bradford performed a hysterectomy on Mrs. Scott to remove fibroid tumors. He did not tell her of the risks or of alternatives to surgery. After the operation she suffered incontinence and needed several corrective operations. She testified she would have refused the surgery had she been told. The jury found for the doctor. Held: Doolin, J.: a doctor must disclose the material risks of, and alternatives to, a proposed treatment. To recover, the patient must prove (1) the doctor failed to inform her of a material risk; (2) had she been informed, she would not have consented (judged subjectively, by her own testimony); and (3) the undisclosed risk occurred and injured her. The jury was properly instructed and simply did not believe she would have refused. Affirmed. Why it matters: Informed consent protects patient autonomy, and it is a negligence claim, not battery. Oklahoma's subjective causation test is the minority view.

MAIN CASE Moore v. Regents of the University of California (Cal. 1990) — disclosure of the physician's interests Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.C Facts: Moore was treated for hairy-cell leukemia at UCLA Medical Center by Dr. Golde. Golde learned that Moore's cells had unusual commercial value. Without telling him, Golde removed his spleen and, over seven years, took blood and other samples, developing a patented cell line with potential value in the billions. Moore sued for conversion, breach of fiduciary duty, and lack of informed consent. The trial court dismissed. Held: Panelli, J.: a physician must disclose personal interests unrelated to the patient's health, whether research or economic, that may affect his medical judgment. Failing to disclose states a claim for breach of fiduciary duty or lack of informed consent. But the court refused to recognize a conversion claim for the cells, because extending conversion would chill medical research. Remanded. Why it matters: The disclosure duty extends to conflicts of interest. Note the bias and consent issues: compare the Henrietta Lacks cell line.

## 14. Judge and Jury; Negligence Per Se WEEK 6
Judge and jury

- The judge decides duty and whether the evidence is sufficient. The jury applies the standard of care to the facts, unless reasonable people could not disagree, in which case the judge decides as a matter of law.

- Judges sometimes try to fix specific standards of conduct as rules of law, as in Holmes's "stop, look, and get out" rule for railroad crossings (Goodman, 1927). Cardozo limited that approach in Pokora.

MAIN CASE Pokora v. Wabash Ry. Co. (U.S. 1934) — standards for the jury Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.D Facts: Pokora drove his truck to a four-track railroad crossing. Boxcars on the first track blocked his view to the north. He stopped, looked, and listened, heard nothing, and drove slowly forward without getting out to look. On the main track he was hit by a train from the north. The trial court directed a verdict for the railroad on contributory negligence, citing Holmes's rule in Baltimore & Ohio R.R. v. Goodman (1927) that a driver who cannot see must get out and look. Held: Cardozo, J.: failing to get out of the vehicle to reconnoiter was not contributory negligence as a matter of law. Getting out may be futile, or more dangerous than not, since the train may arrive while the driver walks back. Standards of prudent conduct are ordinarily for the jury, and Goodman's rule must be confined. Reversed and remanded. Why it matters: Cardozo limited Goodman. Judges should rarely fix standards of conduct, which vary with the circumstances.

RULE Negligence per se: R2d §§ 286, 288A; R3d § 14 An unexcused violation of a statute is negligence when (all required): (1) the statute prescribes specific conduct for the safety of others; (2) the defendant violated it without excuse; (3) the plaintiff is within the class of persons the statute was designed to protect; (4) the harm is of the type the statute was designed to prevent; and (5) the violation caused the harm (cause in fact and proximate cause).

Effect of an unexcused violation | Approach | Case
Negligence as a matter of law (per se); the jury decides only causation and damages | Majority | Martin v. Herzog; Osborne
A rebuttable presumption of negligence; the defendant may prove an excuse | Many states, and R2d § 288A in practice | Zeni v. Anderson
Evidence of negligence that the jury may weigh | Minority (e.g., ordinances, traffic rules in some states) | Ney v. Yellow Cab (prima facie evidence)

Excuses, R2d § 288A(2) (any one suffices): (a) the violation is reasonable because of the actor's incapacity; (b) he neither knows nor should know of the occasion for compliance; (c) he is unable after reasonable diligence or care to comply; (d) he is confronted by an emergency not due to his own misconduct; or (e) compliance would involve a greater risk of harm to the actor or to others.
RULE The plaintiff's own violations: R3d Misc. Prov., Apportionment §§ 4 A–4 B (approved 2022) § 4 A (wrongful acts doctrine): a person injured by tortious conduct is not barred from recovery merely because she was engaged in an illegal, tortious, or otherwise wrongful act at the time. § 4 B(a): an injured victim is negligent if, without excuse, she violates a criminal statute or other safety regulation designed to protect against the type of accident her conduct caused, and she is within the class the statute protects. § 4 B(b): if that negligence is a factual cause of her harm, it reduces her recovery under comparative responsibility; otherwise it has no effect. This is negligence per se applied to the plaintiff, as in Martin v. Herzog and Zeni v. Anderson.

MAIN CASE Osborne v. McMasters (Minn. 1889) — statute fixes the duty Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.E Facts: A clerk in McMasters's drugstore, acting in the course of his employment, sold a deadly poison to Osborne's decedent without labeling it "poison," as a criminal statute required. The decedent took it by mistake and died. Held: Mitchell, J.: where a statute imposes a specific duty for the protection of others, one who neglects that duty is liable to those it was meant to protect, for the kind of injury it was meant to prevent and that the violation proximately caused. Negligence is the breach of a legal duty, whether the duty comes from common law or statute. The employer is liable for the clerk's breach. Affirmed. Why it matters: This is the classic statement of negligence per se and its class-of-persons and type-of-harm limits.

MAIN CASE Stachniewicz v. Mar-Cam Corp. (Or. 1971) — class of persons and type of harm Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.E Facts: A fight broke out in Mar-Cam's bar between a group in a booth, some visibly intoxicated, and Stachniewicz's party at a nearby table, after one of the group had been refused a dance. The bartender had received complaints about the group. Stachniewicz was later found unconscious outside the door with retrograde amnesia. He relied on Oregon Liquor Control Commission regulations barring service to visibly intoxicated persons and barring licensees from permitting loud, noisy, disorderly, or boisterous conduct on the premises. The trial court refused to treat the violations as negligence per se, and the jury found for the bar. Held: Holman, J.: violation of a statute or regulation is negligence as a matter of law when the injured person is in the class protected and the harm is the kind the rule was meant to prevent. The regulation against permitting disorderly conduct bears directly on the start of fights, so it was meant to protect patrons from this kind of injury, and the jury could infer his injuries came from the fight. Reversed and remanded. Why it matters: Courts often infer the legislature's purpose from the statute's text when legislative history is thin, which gives them latitude.

MAIN CASE Ney v. Yellow Cab Co. (Ill. 1954) — key-in-the-ignition statute Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.E Facts: A Yellow Cab driver left his cab unattended and unlocked with the key in the ignition, in violation of an Illinois Uniform Traffic Act section. A thief stole it and, while driving it, collided with Ney's car. The jury found for Ney, and the appellate court affirmed. Yellow Cab argued the statute was only a traffic regulation, not a safety measure. Held: Maxwell, J.: the statute was meant to protect public safety, including against the dangers of stolen cars driven carelessly, so its violation is prima facie evidence of negligence. Whether the thief's intervening crime cut off proximate cause was a fact question for the jury, which resolved it for Ney. Affirmed. Why it matters: Purpose decides class and harm. Courts split on key-in-ignition cases, and many find the thief's act superseding (§ 20). Dissent (Hershey, J.): leaving a key in the ignition is a minor cause of theft, the statute was not aimed at this harm, and the thief's act should be the proximate cause.

MAIN CASE Perry v. S.N. (Tex. 1998) — when courts decline negligence per se Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.E Facts: Two children attended a day-care center run by the Kellers, where Daniel Keller allegedly abused them physically and sexually. The parents sued the Kellers and three of their friends, Perry, White, and Quintero, who allegedly saw the abuse and did not report it, as the Texas Family Code required of anyone who believes a child is being abused. The trial court granted summary judgment for the friends; the court of appeals reversed on negligence per se. Held: Phillips, C.J.: the children were in the protected class and suffered the type of harm the statute addressed, but that is not enough. Weighing factors against adopting the statute as a tort standard (weighed together): (1) there is no common-law duty to report, so the statute would be the only source of the duty; (2) the statute does not clearly define when its duty arises; (3) liability would be imposed without regard to fault; (4) the injury results only indirectly from the violation, through the abuser's crime; and (5) the liability would be ruinous and out of proportion to the conduct, and would fall on a broad class of people. Violation of the reporting statute is not negligence per se. Reversed. Why it matters: Adopting a statute as the standard of care is a judicial choice. It is not automatic.

MAIN CASE Martin v. Herzog (N.Y. 1920) — unexcused violation is negligence itself Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.E Facts: Martin was driving a buggy at night without lights, in violation of a statute, when it collided with Herzog's car, which was coming around a curve without keeping to the right. Martin was killed. The trial judge instructed that driving without lights was not negligence in itself but only evidence of negligence. The jury found for Martin's estate; the Appellate Division reversed. Held: Cardozo, J.: the unexcused omission of a statutory safeguard is negligence in itself, not just evidence of it. Jurors have no power to relax a duty the statute imposes for the protection of other travelers. But the violation must also be a cause of the accident. Evidence that a car hit an unlighted buggy at night supports an inference that the lack of lights contributed. Affirmed (new trial). Why it matters: Negligence per se determines breach, but causation is still required. A violation that did not contribute to the harm does not matter.

MAIN CASE Zeni v. Anderson (Mich. 1976) — rebuttable presumption and excuse Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.E Facts: On a snowy winter morning, Zeni was walking to work. Rather than use the snow-covered sidewalk, she walked on a well-used path in the street, with her back to traffic, in violation of a statute requiring pedestrians to use sidewalks or face traffic. Anderson's car, possibly too close to the curb, hit her. The jury found for Zeni; the court of appeals reversed on the ground that her violation was negligence per se. Held: Williams, J.: violation of a statute creates a rebuttable presumption of negligence, which the violator may overcome by showing an adequate excuse. Rigid per se treatment would ignore reasonable justifications, like an impassable sidewalk. The issue was properly left to the jury. Reversed; verdict for Zeni reinstated. Why it matters: This is the modern middle position, and it reflects R2d § 288A excuses.

TRAP Traps to avoid Compliance with a statute is evidence of care, but not conclusive. The reasonable person may have to do more (R2d § 288C). Licensing statutes usually do not support negligence per se. Practicing without a license does not prove the treatment was negligent (Brown v. Shyne, N.Y. 1926). Check the purpose. A statute aimed at a different harm (e.g., a Sunday-closing law) does not make a violator liable for an unrelated accident.

# PART V — Proof of Negligence

## 15. Circumstantial Evidence and Notice WEEK 7

- Burden: the plaintiff must prove each element by a preponderance of the evidence. Circumstantial evidence is enough if it permits a reasonable inference that the defendant was negligent, and not just a guess.

- Premises conditions: the plaintiff must show (any one suffices) (1) the defendant created the dangerous condition; (2) the defendant had actual notice of it; or (3) the defendant had constructive notice, because the condition existed long enough that reasonable inspection would have discovered and remedied it.

MAIN CASE Goddard v. Boston & Maine R.R. Co. (Mass. 1901) — no evidence of notice Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.F Facts: Goddard got off a train and walked the length of a car along the platform, where many other passengers had just alighted. He slipped on a banana skin and fell. The trial court directed a verdict for the railroad. Held: Holmes, C.J.: the banana skin could have been dropped by one of the departing passengers within a minute before the fall. Without evidence it had been there long enough for the railroad to discover it, there was no negligence. Exceptions overruled. Why it matters: This is the first of the banana-peel cases: no evidence of time means no constructive notice.

MAIN CASE Anjou v. Boston Elevated Railway Co. (Mass. 1911) — circumstantial evidence of time Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.F Facts: Anjou got off a train at the Dudley Street terminal, waited for the crowd to clear, and followed a uniformed railway employee along a narrow platform toward a stairway he pointed out. She slipped on a banana peel and was hurt. Witnesses described the peel as dry, gritty, black, flattened, and trampled over. The trial court directed a verdict for the railway. Held: Rugg, J.: the railway had a duty to keep its platform reasonably safe, including by watching for and removing debris. From the peel's condition, the jury could infer it had been on the platform long enough to be discovered and removed. Exceptions sustained; judgment for Anjou under the terms of the report. Why it matters: The condition of the object can supply the evidence of time that Goddard lacked.

MAIN CASE Joye v. Great Atlantic and Pacific Tea Co. (4th Cir. 1968) — speculation is not enough Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.F Facts: Joye slipped on a banana in an A&P supermarket aisle. The banana was dark brown, sticky at the edges, and had dirt and sand on it, and the floor was dirty. The aisle may not have been swept for 35 minutes. No one knew how long the banana had been there or how it got there. The jury awarded Joye $10,000. Held: Craven, J.: without evidence of how long the hazard existed, there is no constructive notice. On this record a "jury could not tell whether the banana had been on A&P's floor for thirty seconds or three days." Reversed. Why it matters: A banana that browns on its own does not show how long it has been on the floor. Compare Anjou.

MAIN CASE Ortega v. Kmart Corp. (Cal. 2001) — inference from failure to inspect Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.F Facts: Ortega slipped on a puddle of milk in a Kmart and seriously injured his knee. He could not prove how long the milk had been there, but he showed Kmart had not inspected the area for 15 to 30 minutes, and perhaps as long as two hours. The jury awarded $47,000. Held: Chin, J.: a store owner must make reasonable inspections of areas customers use. The plaintiff may prove constructive notice by circumstantial evidence that the condition existed long enough for a reasonably prudent owner to discover and correct it, including evidence that the owner failed to inspect within a reasonable time. He need not prove exactly how long the hazard was there. Affirmed. Why it matters: The focus shifts from how long the hazard was there to how reasonable the inspection program was.

MAIN CASE Jasko v. F.W. Woolworth Co. (Colo. 1972) — mode of operation Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.F Facts: Jasko slipped on a slice of pizza on the terrazzo floor near Woolworth's "Pizza Hoagie Counter." Woolworth sold pizza by the slice on waxed paper to customers who often ate standing up, and it had employees clean the floor constantly. Jasko offered no evidence of how long the slice had been there. The trial court ruled for Woolworth. Held: Groves, J.: when a proprietor's method of operation makes dangerous conditions continuous or easily foreseeable, the plaintiff need not prove notice of the particular condition. The notice rule assumes dangers are unusual, and that assumption fails when the danger comes from the way the store chooses to operate. Reversed and remanded. Why it matters: The mode-of-operation rule reaches self-service and food-on-the-floor settings, where the danger comes from how the store chooses to operate.

MAIN CASE H.E. Butt Grocery Co. v. Resendez (Tex. 1999) — limits of mode of operation Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.F Facts: H-E-B displayed grapes in a bowl for customers to sample. The bowl sat on ice about five inches below the tabletop, and a three-inch rail ran around the table's edge. The floor was non-skid, mats surrounded the display, and warning cones stood nearby. Resendez slipped near the display. The jury found for her, and the court of appeals affirmed. Held: Per curiam: merely displaying produce for customer sampling, without more, does not create an unreasonable risk of harm. Resendez had to prove (all required) (1) actual or constructive knowledge of a condition; (2) that the condition posed an unreasonable risk; (3) the store's failure to use reasonable care to reduce it; and (4) causation. She failed on (2). Unlike the slanted display without mats in Corbin v. Safeway (Tex. 1983), H-E-B's display had safeguards. Reversed; judgment for H-E-B. Why it matters: Texas rejects mode-of-operation liability. Distinguish Jasko by the store's precautions and the jurisdiction's rule.

## 16. Res Ipsa Loquitur WEEK 7
RULE Res ipsa loquitur: R2d § 328D The jury may infer negligence when (all required): (a) the event is of a kind that ordinarily does not occur in the absence of negligence; (b) other responsible causes, including the conduct of the plaintiff and third persons, are sufficiently eliminated by the evidence; and (c) the indicated negligence is within the scope of the defendant's duty to the plaintiff. Traditional form (all required): (1) the accident is the kind that ordinarily does not happen without negligence; (2) the instrumentality was within the defendant's exclusive control; and (3) the plaintiff did not voluntarily act or contribute to it.

- Ordinarily does not occur without negligence is shown by common experience or, in technical cases such as medical malpractice, by expert testimony.

- Exclusive control is flexible today: the question is whether the defendant was probably responsible, as by control at the time of the negligent act, even if not at the time of injury.

- Specific evidence of negligence does not necessarily forfeit res ipsa, unless it fully explains how the accident happened.

MAIN CASE Byrne v. Boadle (Ex. 1863) — the thing speaks for itself Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.G Facts: Byrne was walking on a public street past Boadle's flour shop when a barrel of flour fell from an upper window and hit him. He had no evidence of why it fell. The trial judge nonsuited him for lack of evidence of negligence. Held: Pollock, C.B.: "A barrel could not roll out of a warehouse without some negligence." The fact of the accident is prima facie evidence of negligence, and the plaintiff is not bound to show it could not have happened without negligence. If there are facts consistent with due care, the defendant, who controls the barrel and knows what happened, must prove them. Rule absolute to enter the verdict for Byrne. Why it matters: This is the origin of res ipsa: an inference from the event itself, when the defendant has better access to the evidence.

MAIN CASE McDougald v. Perry (Fla. 1998) — res ipsa from common experience: the flying spare tire Source: Canvas reading (10/6), from the opinion text in the course folder. Facts: On July 26, 1990, McDougald was driving his Jeep Wagoneer behind a tractor-trailer that Perry was driving for his employer, C & S Chemicals, on U.S. Highway 60 in Bartow, Florida. As the truck crossed railroad tracks, its 130-pound spare tire came out of its cradle under the trailer and fell to the road. The trailer's rear wheels ran over it, and it bounced up and smashed McDougald's windshield. The spare sat in an angled cradle, held by its own weight and by a four-to-six-foot chain that Perry believed was the original chain from 1969. The chain had originally been fastened with a latch but was now held by a nut and bolt. Perry had done a pre-trip inspection but did not check every link. Afterward the chain was dragging, and he thought a link had stretched and slipped off the bolt. The chain was not preserved. The jury, instructed on res ipsa loquitur, found for McDougald. The district court of appeal reversed, holding that McDougald had not proved the accident would not ordinarily occur without negligence. Held: Wells, J.: res ipsa is a rule of evidence that permits, but does not compel, an inference of negligence. The plaintiff must show (1) the instrumentality was in the defendant's exclusive control and (2) the accident would not, in the ordinary course of events, have occurred without negligence by the one in control. Common experience shows that a spare tire carried on a truck, like a wheel on its axle, stays with the truck unless someone fails to use reasonable care: "no one expects the air to be filled with flying hubcaps." The plaintiff need not eliminate every other possible cause; it is enough that negligence is more likely than not. And direct proof was unavailable, because the chain and fastener were in the defendants' possession and were not preserved. The doctrine still applies only in "rare instances." Decision quashed; the jury's verdict on liability reinstated. Why it matters: Common knowledge can supply the first element without expert testimony (R2d § 328D cmts. c–d). Contrast events that often happen without negligence, like a tire blowout or a fall down stairs. The defendant's control of the evidence strengthens the inference. Concurrence (Anstead, J.): the result follows directly from Byrne v. Boadle (§ 16): "The common law tradition is alive and well."

MAIN CASE Larson v. St. Francis Hotel (Cal. App. 1948) — no exclusive control Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.G Facts: On August 14, 1945, V-J Day, crowds were celebrating in San Francisco. Just after Larson stepped out from under the St. Francis Hotel's marquee onto the sidewalk, a heavy overstuffed armchair fell from an upper window and knocked her unconscious. No one saw where it came from. The trial court granted a nonsuit. Held: Bray, J.: res ipsa loquitur applies only if the instrumentality was under the defendant's exclusive control and management. Hotel guests, who rent rooms and use the furniture, have partial control. The likeliest explanation was that a celebrating guest threw the chair, which the hotel could not prevent with reasonable care. Affirmed. Why it matters: If an equally likely cause lies outside the defendant's control, the inference fails.

MAIN CASE Cruz v. DaimlerChrysler Motors Corp. (R.I. 2013) — negligence must point to this defendant Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.G Facts: Cruz was cleaning out his minivan when its front airbags suddenly deployed and injured him. He sued the maker, DaimlerChrysler, and Ricky Smith Pontiac, the dealer that had sold him the van three years earlier. After DaimlerChrysler went bankrupt, he dropped it and pressed negligence claims against the dealer, relying on res ipsa loquitur. The trial court granted summary judgment for the dealer. Held: Indeglia, J.: under R2d § 328D, element (a) was met, since airbags do not ordinarily deploy during cleaning without negligence. But element (b) failed: after three years in Cruz's hands, the evidence did not eliminate other causes or point the negligence to the dealer. Affirmed. Why it matters: Element (b) of § 328D is the hurdle: other responsible causes must be sufficiently eliminated.

MAIN CASE James v. Wormuth (N.Y. 2013) — deliberate medical judgment Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.G Facts: During a procedure to biopsy a lung nodule, a guide wire Dr. Wormuth had placed became dislodged. He searched for it by hand for about 20 minutes, could not find it, and decided to end the operation rather than keep James under anesthesia longer and enlarge the incision. He told her afterward. Weeks later, when she complained of pain, he removed it in a second operation. She sued for malpractice but offered no expert testimony that leaving the wire departed from accepted practice, relying on res ipsa. The trial court granted judgment for the doctor. Held: Rivera, J.: res ipsa applies to foreign objects left in the body unintentionally. It does not apply when the doctor deliberately left the object based on his judgment that doing so was in the patient's best interest. That judgment must be challenged with expert testimony on the standard of care. Exclusive control was also lacking, since other staff had handled the wire. Affirmed. Why it matters: Res ipsa applies to forgotten sponges, not to deliberate choices. Those require expert proof.

MAIN CASE Sullivan v. Crabtree (Tenn. App. 1953) — procedural effect: permissible inference Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 4.G Facts: Sullivan, the plaintiffs' son, was a guest passenger in a truck Crabtree was driving down a mountain highway. The truck suddenly swerved from the right lane to the left, ran off the road, and overturned down a steep embankment, killing Sullivan. Crabtree testified that gravel or broken pavement might have made him lose control but could not say for sure. The jury found for Crabtree. Held: Felts, J.: the facts made a case for res ipsa, which is evidence from which the jury may infer negligence. But res ipsa does not compel the jury to find negligence, even when the defendant cannot fully explain the accident; the jury may draw the inference it finds more probable. The verdict for Crabtree was affirmed. Why it matters: Res ipsa usually creates a permissible inference, not a presumption, so the plaintiff can still lose.

Procedural effect of res ipsa | What it does | Where
Permissible inference | The case goes to the jury, which may or may not infer negligence | Majority (Sullivan)
Presumption | Shifts the burden of producing evidence; a directed verdict for the plaintiff if the defendant offers no rebuttal | Some states
Shift of the burden of proof | The defendant must prove it was not negligent | A few states, often for carriers

MAIN CASE Ybarra v. Spangard (Cal. 1944) — res ipsa against a surgical team Source: Canvas reading (Res Ipsa module, due 10/8), from the opinion text in the course folder. Facts: In October 1939, Dr. Tilley diagnosed Ybarra with appendicitis and arranged for Dr. Spangard to operate at a hospital owned and run by Dr. Swift. Dr. Reser, the anesthetist and Swift's employee, positioned Ybarra on the operating table, pulling him up so that the tops of his shoulders rested against two hard objects, and then anesthetized him. When Ybarra awoke the next morning, he had a sharp pain between his neck and right shoulder. It spread down his arm and led to paralysis and atrophy of the shoulder muscles. Two doctors testified the injury was traumatic, caused by pressure or strain, not by disease. Ybarra sued the doctors and nurses who had charge of him (Tilley, Spangard, Swift, Reser, and nurses Gisler and Thompson), but he could not say which one, or which instrumentality, injured him. The trial court granted nonsuits for all defendants. Held: Gibson, C.J.: res ipsa applies. (1) The injury was to a healthy part of the body away from the operation, which ordinarily does not happen without negligence, and (2) Ybarra contributed nothing to it. As for control, the test is right of control, not actual exclusive control. Every defendant in whose custody Ybarra was placed owed him ordinary care, employers answer for their employees, and the surgeon in charge answers for those who become his temporary servants during the operation. "Where a plaintiff receives unusual injuries while unconscious and in the course of medical treatment, all those defendants who had any control over his body or the instrumentalities which might have caused the injuries may properly be called upon to meet the inference of negligence by giving an explanation of their conduct." Reversed. Why it matters: Ybarra stretches exclusive control to a team of defendants because the unconscious patient cannot identify the wrongdoer and the evidence is in their hands. Otherwise, the court said, there would rarely be any compensation for patients injured while unconscious. Compare Larson (control shared with strangers defeats res ipsa) and Summers v. Tice (burden-shifting on causation, § 18). On retrial the defendants were found liable, and the judgment was affirmed (Ybarra v. Spangard, 93 Cal. App. 2d 43 (1949)).

EXAM TIPS On the exam, walk through each element of § 328D with the facts. The usual weak spot is (b): who else could have caused it? Then state the procedural effect: the jury may infer negligence but need not.

# PART VI — Causation

## 17. Cause in Fact WEEKS 7–8
RULE But-for causation: R2d § 432(1); R3d § 26 The defendant's negligence is a cause in fact of the harm if the harm would not have occurred without it. The plaintiff must show this by a preponderance of the evidence: more likely than not.

- The counterfactual: imagine the defendant acting with due care (the train at the speed limit, the stairs lit), and ask whether the harm would still have happened.

- Possibility is not enough (Kramer). Speculation, or an equally likely innocent explanation, fails.

- Expert proof is often needed for medical and toxic causation. The expert must reach "more likely than not." Under Daubert (9th Cir. 1995, on remand), in pages the syllabus skips, an epidemiological study must generally show that the agent more than doubles the risk (relative risk above 2.0).

MAIN CASE Perkins v. Texas and New Orleans R. Co. (La. 1962) — negligence that made no difference Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 5.A Facts: A train going 37 mph, over the 25 mph limit through the town of Vinton, hit a car at a blind crossing, killing Perkins's decedent, a passenger in the car. The car's speed could not be determined. The evidence showed that even at 25 mph the train could not have stopped in time once the car came into view. The jury found for Perkins, and the court of appeal affirmed. Held: Sanders, J.: negligence is not a cause in fact if the harm would have happened anyway. The engineer was negligent, but the plaintiff did not show that a slower train would have avoided the collision. Reversed; judgment for the railroad. Why it matters: Negligence must be causally linked to the harm. A defendant is not liable for harm that due care would not have prevented.

MAIN CASE Reynolds v. Texas & Pac. Ry. Co. (La. 1885) — negligence that increases the chance of harm Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 5.A Facts: Mrs. Reynolds, who weighed about 250 pounds, was hurried out of a brightly lit waiting room at night to catch her train and down unlit stairs to the platform. She fell and was badly hurt. The jury awarded $2,000. The railroad argued she might have fallen even if the stairs were lit. Held: Fenner, J.: when negligence greatly multiplies the chances of an accident and is of a kind that naturally leads to it, the mere possibility that it might have happened anyway does not break the causal connection. Courts look at "the natural and ordinary course of events," not remote speculations. Affirmed. Why it matters: The jury may infer causation from the fact that the harm is exactly what the negligence risked.

MAIN CASE Gentry v. Douglas Hereford Ranch, Inc. (Mont. 1998) — no evidence of but-for cause Source: Canvas reading (10/8), from the opinion text in the course folder. Facts: On November 5, 1994, Brent Bacon drove to the Douglas Hereford Ranch, owned by a company controlled by his wife's grandmother and leased to Pard Cattle Co. He planned to start the furnace in a house that his wife and her friend Barbara Gentry were going to paint, and then to go deer hunting. On the way he had fired his lever-action .30-30 at a fox, cocked another round into the chamber, and lowered the hammer onto the live round. After failing to start the furnace, he got the rifle from his car and walked back toward the house carrying it on his shoulder, with a finger on the trigger and his thumb on the hammer. As he reached the wooden steps to a deck, he stumbled and fell; the rifle went off, and the bullet struck Barbara Gentry in the head. She died 69 days later. Her husband sued the ranch and cattle companies, claiming that a loose bottom step and debris around it made Bacon fall, and that the ranch was vicariously liable as Bacon's employer. (Bacon was dismissed after filing for bankruptcy.) Bacon repeatedly testified that he did not know whether he tripped on something, missed the step, or was just clumsy. The trial court granted summary judgment for the defendants. Held: Trieweiler, J.: negligence requires (1) duty, (2) breach, (3) causation, and (4) damages. Cause in fact is the but-for test, and because an intervening act was alleged, proximate cause was also in issue. Gentry offered no evidence that any condition of the steps caused Bacon to stumble. One statement ("I think it was the step") was contradicted by his own testimony that he did not know why he fell, and "a suspicion, regardless of how particularized it may be," does not defeat summary judgment. Nor was the ranch vicariously liable: Bacon's free help with the furnace did not make him its employee, and when he fell he had abandoned that task and was going hunting for himself. Affirmed. Why it matters: But-for causation must be proved with evidence, not speculation about how an accident might have happened. Compare Reynolds (§ 17), where the jury could infer causation because the harm was exactly what the negligence risked. The case also previews respondeat superior (§ 31): no employment relationship, and no act within the scope of employment.

MAIN CASE Kramer Service, Inc. v. Wilkins (Miss. 1939) — possibility is not proof Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 5.A Facts: Wilkins, a guest at Kramer's hotel, was cut on the forehead when a piece of glass fell from a broken transom as he opened a door. The transom had been broken long enough that the hotel should have known. The wound never healed, and two years later a skin specialist found cancer at the spot. The undisputed expert testimony was that there was at most a remote possibility that the cut caused the cancer. The jury awarded damages including the cancer. Held: Griffith, J.: a mere possibility of causation does not support a verdict. Jurors have no experience with skin cancer, so they may not reject undisputed expert testimony on its cause. Wilkins may recover for the cut but not for the cancer. Affirmed on liability; reversed and remanded on damages. Why it matters: The more-likely-than-not threshold applies to each item of harm.

MAIN CASE Herskovits v. Group Health Cooperative of Puget Sound (Wash. 1983) — loss of a chance Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 5.A Facts: Group Health's doctors failed to diagnose Herskovits's lung cancer for about six months. Expert testimony showed that the delay reduced his chance of surviving five years from 39% to 25%. He died, and his estate sued under the survival statute. The trial court granted summary judgment because the estate could not show he probably would have survived (a better than 50% chance) with timely diagnosis. Held: Dore, J. (plurality): when a defendant's negligence substantially reduces a patient's chance of survival, the plaintiff need not show the patient probably would have survived; the reduction is enough to send causation to the jury, which decides what harm the increased risk caused. Damages are limited to those caused by the lost chance, not the death itself. Reversed. Why it matters: This is the leading lost-chance case. The concurrence treated the lost chance itself as the injury, valued proportionally (14% of the full damages). Concurrence (Pearson, J.): the lost chance itself is the compensable injury. Damages should be proportional: here, 14% of the full damages for death.

Approach to lost chance | Rule | Recovery
Traditional (all or nothing) | The plaintiff must show the patient more likely than not would have survived, so above 50% | Full damages, or nothing
Relaxed causation (Herskovits plurality) | A substantial reduction in chance lets the jury find causation | Damages caused by the lost chance
Lost chance as the injury (Herskovits concurrence; now the majority of courts that allow it) | The lost chance is itself the compensable harm | Proportional: the percentage of chance lost times full damages

## 18. Multiple and Indeterminate Causes WEEK 8
Situation | Test | Result | Case
Two negligent acts combine; neither alone would have caused the harm | But-for, as to each | Each is liable for the whole (joint and several) | Hill v. Edmonds
Two forces, each sufficient alone, combine (merged fires) | Substantial factor (R2d § 432(2); R3d § 27) | Each is a cause, even though neither is a but-for cause | Anderson v. Minneapolis
Two negligent defendants, only one caused the harm, and P can't tell which | Alternative liability: burden shifts to each D to prove it did not cause the harm | Joint and several, unless a D exculpates itself | Summers v. Tice
Many makers of a fungible product; P can't identify which one's product injured her | Market share liability | Each D liable for its share of the market (several) | Sindell

MAIN CASE Hill v. Edmonds (N.Y. App. Div. 1966) — concurrent causes Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 5.B Facts: Bragoli left his truck parked without lights in the middle of the road on a stormy night. Edmonds, driving with Hill as a passenger, saw the truck four car lengths ahead, swerved, and hit it; she remembered nothing more. The trial court found Edmonds solely responsible and dismissed the complaint against Bragoli. Held: When separate acts of negligence combine to produce a single injury, each tortfeasor is liable for the whole, even though his act alone might not have caused it. The accident could not have happened had Bragoli not left the unlighted truck in the road. Complaint against Bragoli reinstated; new trial ordered. Why it matters: An indivisible injury from concurrent negligence makes each defendant jointly and severally liable (§ 29).

MAIN CASE Anderson v. Minneapolis, St. P. & S. St. M. Ry. Co. (Minn. 1920) — the substantial factor test Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 5.B Facts: A fire the railroad negligently started merged with a fire of unknown origin, and the combined fire burned Anderson's property. There was evidence that either fire alone would have destroyed it. The jury was instructed to find for Anderson if the railroad's fire was a material or substantial element in causing the damage, and it did. Held: Lees, Commr.: if the railroad's fire was a material or substantial factor in causing the damage, the railroad is liable even if the other fire alone would have caused the same harm. Two known negligent fires would each be liable for the whole; the result should not change because the other fire's origin is unknown. Affirmed. Why it matters: The substantial factor test fills the gap where the but-for test would let both causes off. An older Wisconsin rule (Cook v. Minneapolis, St. P. & S. Ste. M. Ry., 1898) excused the defendant when the other fire was of natural origin. Anderson and R2d § 432(2) reject that limit.

MAIN CASE Summers v. Tice (Cal. 1948) — alternative liability Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 5.C Facts: Summers went quail hunting with Tice and Simonson, who were each given instructions on safe shooting. A quail flew up between them and Summers, and both fired toward him at the same time with birdshot of the same size. One pellet hit his eye and another his lip. No one could tell whose gun fired which pellet. The trial court found both defendants negligent and liable. Held: Carter, J.: when two defendants are both negligent and the plaintiff cannot prove which one caused his injury, the burden shifts to each defendant to prove he did not cause it. Otherwise both are jointly and severally liable. The defendants are wrongdoers, both put the plaintiff at risk, and they are better placed to explain what happened. Affirmed. Why it matters: R2d § 433B(3). The rule needs all the possible wrongdoers before the court and proof that all of them were negligent.

RULE Alternative liability (Summers; R2d § 433B(3)) The burden shifts when (all required): (1) every defendant acted tortiously; (2) the harm was caused by one of them; (3) the plaintiff, through no fault of her own, cannot prove which; and (4) all the possible wrongdoers are before the court.

MAIN CASE Sindell v. Abbott Laboratories (Cal. 1980) — market share liability Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 5.C Facts: Sindell's mother took DES, a drug to prevent miscarriage, while pregnant with her. DES caused cancer in some daughters years later, and Sindell developed cancer. About 200 companies had made DES from an identical formula, many pharmacies kept no record of which maker's pills filled a prescription, and Sindell could not identify the maker. She sued five makers. The trial court dismissed. Held: Mosk, J.: a plaintiff who cannot identify the maker of a fungible product through no fault of her own may recover if she joins makers of a substantial share of the market. Each defendant is liable for the share of the judgment matching its market share, unless it proves it could not have made the product that injured her. Summers v. Tice could not be applied directly, because the maker might not be before the court. Reversed. Why it matters: Market share liability is a narrow exception, mostly limited to DES. Hymowitz v. Eli Lilly (N.Y. 1989) used a national market and did not let a defendant exculpate itself.

RULE Market share liability (Sindell) A plaintiff may recover under market share liability when (all required): (1) the defendants made a product of identical formula (fungible); (2) the product injured the plaintiff; (3) the plaintiff cannot identify the maker through no fault of her own; and (4) the plaintiff joins makers of a substantial share of the relevant market. Liability is several, in proportion to market share.

EXAM TIPS State the but-for test first. Move to substantial factor only when there are two sufficient causes, and to burden-shifting (Summers, Sindell) only when the plaintiff cannot identify which negligent actor caused the harm. Don't use substantial factor to rescue a weak but-for case.

## 19. Proximate Cause: Unforeseeable Plaintiffs and Consequences WEEK 8
Proximate cause, which the R3d calls scope of liability, limits liability to harms that bear a sufficient connection to the defendant's negligence. Cause in fact is about physics; proximate cause is about policy and fairness.
RULE Scope of liability: R3d § 29 (the risk rule) An actor's liability is limited to those harms that result from the risks that made the actor's conduct tortious. Ask (all required): (1) what risks made the conduct negligent; (2) was the plaintiff within the class of persons put at risk; and (3) was the harm of the type that was risked? The extent of the harm and the precise manner in which it happened need not be foreseeable.

MAIN CASE Atlantic Coast Line R. Co. v. Daniels (Ga. App. 1911) — the need for a limit Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.A Facts: The opinion discusses the concept in general terms, without a fact pattern the casebook relies on. Held: Every act has endless consequences, so the law must draw a practical, somewhat arbitrary line. Words like "proximate" and "natural" describe where courts stop tracing the connection between a wrongful act and an injury. Why it matters: Proximate cause is a policy judgment about the limits of responsibility.

MAIN CASE Ryan v. New York Central R.R. Co. (N.Y. 1866) — the old first-house rule Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.A Facts: A spark from the railroad's engine in Syracuse set fire to its own woodshed, through careless management or the engine's poor condition. The fire spread to Ryan's house, 130 feet away, and destroyed it, along with several other houses. The trial court nonsuited Ryan. Held: Hunt, J.: the railroad was liable only to the owner of the first building burned. The spread of fire to other buildings is not a necessary or usual result of a spark, and liability for every building a fire reaches would be ruinous; everyone runs some risk from neighbors and can insure. Affirmed. Why it matters: This rule has been abandoned. Today the spread of fire is a foreseeable consequence. It shows how policy (a new industry, insurance, ruinous liability) drives proximate cause.

MAIN CASE Bartolone v. Jeckovich (N.Y. App. Div. 1984) — the eggshell plaintiff Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.A Facts: Bartolone, a bodybuilder, suffered minor neck and back injuries in a car accident caused by Jeckovich. He then had a complete psychotic breakdown. Experts testified that he had a traumatic childhood and had used bodybuilding and a strict regimen to cope, and that when the accident disrupted his routine, his latent condition broke down. The jury awarded $500,000, but the trial court set the verdict aside as unsupported. Held: Denman, J.: a defendant takes the plaintiff as he finds him and is liable for all damages proximately caused, even if they seem out of proportion to the incident because of a pre-existing condition. The jury was entitled to believe the testimony that the accident triggered his breakdown. Reversed; verdict reinstated. Why it matters: The eggshell plaintiff rule covers the extent of harm, including psychological harm. It is the clearest exception to foreseeability.

MAIN CASE Polemis v. Furness, Withy & Co. (C.A. 1921) — direct consequences Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.B Facts: Reported as In re Arbitration Between Polemis and Furness, Withy & Co. Furness chartered the ship Polemis, which carried petrol and benzine. While unloading at Casablanca, stevedores employed by the charterers carelessly let a plank fall into the hold. It struck something and caused a spark, which ignited petrol vapor, and the ship was destroyed. The arbitrators found that a spark could not reasonably have been anticipated, but that some damage to the ship from the falling plank could have been. Held: Once an act is negligent, the defendant is liable for all the direct consequences, even those that could not reasonably have been anticipated, so long as they are not due to an independent cause. Because some damage from dropping the plank was foreseeable, the fire was a direct result for which the charterers were liable. Why it matters: This is the direct-consequences test, which Wagon Mound No. 1 rejected.

MAIN CASE Overseas Tankship v. Morts Dock (P.C. 1961) — Wagon Mound No. 1: foreseeable kind of harm Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.B Facts: The Wagon Mound, moored about 600 feet from Morts Dock's wharf in Sydney Harbour, carelessly discharged a large quantity of furnace oil. The oil spread to the wharf, where Morts Dock's workers were welding. Two days later molten metal from the welding fell onto cotton waste floating on the oil, which ignited the oil, and the wharf burned. The trial court found that Overseas did not know, and could not reasonably have known, that furnace oil (flash point about 170°F) would burn when spread on water. It nonetheless found for Morts Dock under Polemis. Held: Viscount Simonds: Polemis is no longer good law. It is not consistent with justice that a negligent actor be liable for all consequences, however unforeseeable and grave, merely because they are "direct." Liability is limited to damage of the kind a reasonable person would have foreseen. Fouling of the wharf was foreseeable; fire was not. Reversed. Why it matters: The foreseeable-type-of-harm test. Liability matches the risk that made the conduct negligent.

MAIN CASE Overseas Tankship v. Miller Steamship Co. (P.C. 1967) — Wagon Mound No. 2: small but real risk Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.B Facts: The same fire damaged two ships owned by Miller Steamship that were being refitted at the wharf. On different evidence, the trial court found that the Wagon Mound's officers would have regarded fire as a possibility, though it would occur only in very exceptional circumstances, and it held for the defendant on the ground that the damage was not reasonably foreseeable. Held: Lord Reid: a reasonable person would not ignore a real risk, even a small one, if it could be eliminated easily and there was no valid reason for running it. Discharging oil into the harbor was unjustified, and the engineer should have known fire was possible, so the risk, though slight, made the defendant liable. Reversed; judgment for Miller. Why it matters: This is the same accident with a different result, because foreseeability is a finding of fact and it ties back to the Hand formula (§ 11).

MAIN CASE Palsgraf v. Long Island R.R. Co. (N.Y. 1928) — the unforeseeable plaintiff Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.B Facts: Mrs. Palsgraf bought a ticket to Rockaway Beach and was standing on the platform. Two men ran to catch a train that was pulling out. One guard on the train pulled and another on the platform pushed one of them aboard. He was carrying a small package wrapped in newspaper, which fell onto the rails. It contained fireworks and exploded. The shock knocked over scales at the far end of the platform, which struck Mrs. Palsgraf. The jury found for her, and the Appellate Division affirmed. Held: Cardozo, C.J.: "The risk reasonably to be perceived defines the duty to be obeyed." Negligence is not a tort in the abstract; it is a wrong only to someone within the range of apparent danger. Nothing about the package suggested danger to a person standing far away, so the guards' conduct, even if negligent toward the man or his package, was not a wrong toward Mrs. Palsgraf. Reversed; complaint dismissed. Why it matters: The leading case on unforeseeable plaintiffs. Cardozo frames it as duty (the zone of danger), Andrews as proximate cause. Dissent (Andrews, J.): everyone owes the world at large a duty to refrain from acts that unreasonably threaten others. When an act is negligent, the defendant is liable for the injuries it proximately causes, and proximate cause is a practical line drawn by "convenience, of public policy, of a rough sense of justice." Factors include a natural and continuous sequence, direct connection, foreseeability, and remoteness in time and space. Here the explosion's effect was close and direct, and he would have affirmed.

| Cardozo (majority) | Andrews (dissent)
Framing | Duty: is the plaintiff within the zone of foreseeable danger? | Proximate cause: is the harm too remote, as a matter of policy?
Duty owed to | Foreseeable plaintiffs only | Everyone who is harmed
Who decides | Usually the court (duty is a question of law) | Usually the jury
Factors | Foreseeability of harm to this plaintiff | (weighed together) (1) a natural and continuous sequence; (2) a direct connection without too many intervening causes; (3) whether the cause was a substantial factor; (4) foreseeability; and (5) remoteness in time and space

MAIN CASE Yun v. Ford Motor Co. (N.J. Super. App. Div. 1994) — plaintiff's own conduct as the sole proximate cause Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.B Facts: Chang was a passenger in a 1987 Ford van his daughter Yun was driving on the Garden State Parkway at night. The spare tire assembly fell off the back and rolled across both lanes to the guardrail. Yun pulled over on the right shoulder. Chang ran across the Parkway to retrieve the tire and was struck and killed by another car. Yun sued Ford and others, alleging a defective spare tire bracket. The trial court granted summary judgment. Held: Villanueva, J.: even assuming a defect, Chang's decision to cross a busy highway at night to retrieve a spare tire was so extraordinary and unforeseeable that it was the sole proximate cause of his death. Affirmed. The New Jersey Supreme Court reversed, substantially for the reasons of the Appellate Division dissent, which would let a jury decide whether his response was foreseeable (143 N.J. 162 (1996)). Why it matters: A plaintiff's extraordinary response can cut off proximate cause. Many courts leave the question to the jury and handle it as comparative fault.

EXAM TIPS Exam tips Type of harm: must be foreseeable (Wagon Mound No. 1). Extent of harm: need not be foreseeable (eggshell plaintiff, Bartolone). Manner of harm: need not be foreseeable if the type of harm was (Hughes v. Lord Advocate, H.L. 1963: a lamp exploded in an unforeseeable way, but the risk was burns). Plaintiff: must be foreseeable under Cardozo (Palsgraf). Rescuers are foreseeable (§ 20).

## 20. Intervening and Superseding Causes WEEK 9
RULE Superseding cause: R2d §§ 440–453; R3d § 34 An intervening act (of a third person, the plaintiff, or nature) breaks the chain of proximate cause only if it is a superseding cause. It is not superseding when it is foreseeable, or when it is within the very risk that made the defendant's conduct negligent (Derdiarian).
