Factors, R2d § 442 (weighed together): (a) the intervention brings about harm different in kind from that which would otherwise have resulted; (b) its operation or consequences appear extraordinary rather than normal; (c) it operates independently of any situation the actor created, or is not a normal result of that situation; (d) it is due to a third person's act or failure to act; (e) it is a third person's wrongful act toward the plaintiff; and (f) the degree of culpability of the third person's wrongful act.

- Usually not superseding (foreseeable): negligent medical treatment of the injury; rescue efforts; ordinary negligence of other drivers; the victim's reasonable reactions; and suicide by someone the defendant's negligence drove insane (Fuller).

- Usually superseding: an intentional crime or tort by a third person, unless the defendant's negligence created the very opportunity or the defendant had a duty to protect against it (R2d §§ 448–449); and an extraordinary act of nature.

- The trend: with comparative fault and apportionment, courts more often let the jury apportion than declare the later actor the only one responsible.

MAIN CASE Derdiarian v. Felix Contracting Corp. (N.Y. 1980) — intervening act within the risk Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.C Facts: Felix, a general contractor, was installing a gas main and had an excavation on one side of a road. It set up no adequate barrier. Derdiarian, a subcontractor's employee, was working beside a kettle of 400-degree liquid enamel. Dickens, who had not taken his epilepsy medication, had a seizure while driving, lost control, and crashed into the work site. Derdiarian was thrown into the air and splashed with the burning enamel. The jury found against Felix. Held: Cooke, C.J.: an intervening act does not break the causal chain if it is a normal or foreseeable consequence of the situation the defendant's negligence created. The very reason Felix's failure to barricade was negligent was the risk of a car entering the site. That the risk materialized in an unusual way, or that the driver was also negligent, does not relieve Felix. Proximate cause was properly left to the jury. Affirmed. Why it matters: If the intervening act is within the risk, it does not supersede. Proximate cause is usually a jury question.

MAIN CASE Watson v. Kentucky & Indiana Bridge & R.R. Co. (Ky. 1910) — negligent vs. malicious intervention Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.C Facts: Through the railroad's negligence, a tank car full of gasoline derailed, its valve broke, and gasoline poured into the street. Duerr struck a match, igniting the vapor, and the explosion injured Watson. There was conflicting evidence whether Duerr lit the match to light his cigar or did it deliberately to cause an explosion. The trial court directed a verdict for the railroad. Held: Settle, J.: the jury should have decided why Duerr lit the match. If he did it inadvertently, his act was a foreseeable consequence of the spill and the railroad remains liable. If he did it maliciously, the railroad could not reasonably have anticipated it, and his act is the sole proximate cause. Reversed; new trial. Why it matters: The traditional rule is that foreseeable negligence of a third person does not supersede, but a deliberate crime does. R2d § 448 moderates this when the defendant's negligence created the opportunity for the crime.

MAIN CASE Fuller v. Preis (N.Y. 1974) — suicide as an irresistible impulse Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.C Facts: Dr. Lewis, a surgeon, suffered head injuries in a car accident caused by Preis. He had been healthy before. Afterward he had 38 epileptic seizures, three on the day of his death, which drugs could not control. He became depressed, unsteady, and irritable, and seven months after the accident he shot himself, leaving notes saying he was sane. A neurologist testified he was in a post-seizure psychosis that put his conduct beyond his control. The jury awarded $200,000, but the Appellate Division reversed and dismissed. Held: Breitel, C.J.: suicide is not a superseding cause as a matter of law. A tortfeasor is liable for a suicide that results from an irresistible impulse caused by the injury, even if the decedent understood what he was doing. His notes declaring his sanity were not conclusive. The evidence supported the jury's finding. Reversed. Why it matters: The defendant's tort created the mental condition, so the plaintiff's act is not a free, informed choice that cuts off liability.

MAIN CASE McCoy v. American Suzuki Motor Corp. (Wash. 1998) — the rescue doctrine Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.C Facts: McCoy was driving on an interstate at night when the Suzuki Samurai ahead of him swerved off the road and rolled. He stopped to help and found the driver badly hurt. A state trooper asked him to set out flares. After the injured were cared for, McCoy was walking back to his car along the road when a hit-and-run driver struck him. He sued Suzuki, claiming the Samurai was defectively prone to roll over. The trial court granted summary judgment for Suzuki. The court of appeals reversed, holding that a rescuer need only show the defendant caused the danger. Held: Sanders, J.: the rescue doctrine applies in products cases. "Danger invites rescue," so a rescuer is a foreseeable plaintiff, and the rescuer is not presumed to have assumed the risk unless he acted rashly. But the doctrine does not relieve the rescuer of proving proximate cause of his own injuries. Whether Suzuki's defect proximately caused McCoy's injuries was a fact question, so summary judgment was improper. Court of appeals affirmed on different grounds. Why it matters: A rescuer is a foreseeable plaintiff. To invoke the doctrine, the rescuer shows (all required): (1) the defendant's negligence (or defect) caused the peril; (2) the peril was imminent; (3) a reasonably prudent person would have concluded that the peril existed; and (4) the rescuer acted with reasonable care in carrying out the rescue.

MAIN CASE Kelly v. Gwinnell (N.J. 1984) — social host liability Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.C Facts: Gwinnell drank at Zak's home and, according to the complaint, Zak served him until he was visibly intoxicated, then accompanied him to his car, chatted, and watched him drive off. Gwinnell's blood-alcohol level was later 0.286. He collided head-on with Kelly's car. Kelly sued Gwinnell and Zak. The trial court granted summary judgment for Zak, and the Appellate Division affirmed. Held: Wilentz, C.J.: a social host who directly serves liquor to an adult guest, knowing the guest is intoxicated and will soon drive, is liable to third parties injured by the guest's drunk driving. The law already made commercial servers and hosts serving minors liable, and the risk is foreseeable. The guest's drunk driving is not a superseding cause. Reversed. (The rule was applied prospectively.) Why it matters: This is the minority rule. Many legislatures, including California's, have rejected it, and the dissent said the legislature should decide. Delaware recognizes no dram shop or social host liability (McCall v. Villa Pizza, Del. 1994). Dissent (Garibaldi, J.): the competing social and economic interests (insurance, the burden on hosts) should be weighed by the legislature, not imposed by the court.

RULE Liability for providing alcohol: R3d Misc. Prov. (T.D. 3, draft) (a) If a statute (a dram shop act) governs, the statute controls. (b) Absent a statute, a commercial establishment is subject to liability for negligently providing alcohol (any one suffices): (1) to underage patrons, or (2) to visibly intoxicated patrons of any age, when the patron's intoxication factually causes later injury. (c) Absent a statute, a social host (1) is subject to liability for recklessly providing alcohol to underage guests, when their intoxication factually causes later injury; but (2) is not liable for providing alcohol to guests of legal drinking age, even past the point of intoxication. The draft rejects Kelly v. Gwinnell for adult guests, in line with most states.

MAIN CASE Enright v. Eli Lilly & Co. (N.Y. 1991) — policy limit: third-generation DES claims Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 6.C Facts: In 1960, Enright's grandmother took DES while pregnant with Enright's mother, Patricia. DES allegedly damaged Patricia's reproductive system in utero. Enright was born prematurely, with cerebral palsy and other disabilities, allegedly as a result. She sued Eli Lilly. The trial court dismissed her claim; the Appellate Division affirmed. Held: Wachtler, C.J.: a child injured because of a tort to her mother before the child was conceived has no claim against the original tortfeasor. Liability to those who took the drug or were exposed in utero serves deterrence; extending it to later generations would create staggering, open-ended liability and could deter drug development. Affirmed. Why it matters: Courts sometimes cut off liability for policy reasons, even where harm is foreseeable and causation is clear.

# PART VII — Duty

## 21. Duty and the Failure to Act WEEK 9

- Duty is a question of law for the court. The default is a duty of reasonable care to avoid creating risks of physical harm (R3d § 7). Courts limit or modify it for reasons of principle or policy.

- Factors used to decide duty (weighed together, as in Rowland and Tarasoff): (1) foreseeability of harm to the plaintiff; (2) the degree of certainty that the plaintiff suffered injury; (3) the closeness of the connection between the conduct and the injury; (4) the moral blame attached to the conduct; (5) the policy of preventing future harm; (6) the burden on the defendant and the consequences to the community of imposing the duty; and (7) the availability, cost, and prevalence of insurance.

- Misfeasance vs. nonfeasance. Acting carelessly (misfeasance) creates a duty. Merely failing to help (nonfeasance) generally does not.

Privity of contract
MAIN CASE MacPherson v. Buick Motor Co. (N.Y. 1916) — the end of the privity limit Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 8.A Facts: Buick sold a car to a retail dealer, who sold it to MacPherson. While he was driving, one of the wooden wheels collapsed because its spokes were made of defective wood, and he was thrown out and injured. Another company made the wheel, but a reasonable inspection by Buick would have revealed the defect. The jury found for MacPherson, and the Appellate Division affirmed. Held: Cardozo, J.: if a product is reasonably certain to place life and limb in peril when negligently made, and the maker knows it will be used by people other than the buyer without new tests, the maker owes those users a duty of care, regardless of privity. Buick was a manufacturer of finished cars and could not escape its duty to inspect components. Affirmed. Why it matters: MacPherson rejected Winterbottom v. Wright (1842), which required privity. A negligent manufacturer owes a duty to foreseeable users.

MAIN CASE H.R. Moch Co. v. Rensselaer Water Co. (N.Y. 1928) — nonfeasance in performing a contract Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 8.A Facts: The water company contracted with the City of Rensselaer to supply water for fire hydrants, public buildings, and private customers. A fire spread from a nearby building to Moch's warehouse. The company was promptly notified but failed to supply enough water pressure at the hydrants, and the warehouse burned. Moch sued for breach of contract, common-law tort, and breach of statutory duty. Held: Cardozo, C.J.: the company owed no tort duty to individual citizens. Its failure was the withholding of a benefit (nonfeasance), not the launching of "a force or an instrument of harm" (misfeasance). Citizens were only incidental beneficiaries of the contract, and recognizing the claim would make suppliers liable to an indefinite number of people. Dismissal affirmed. Why it matters: The test: has the defendant "launched a force or instrument of harm," or only failed to confer a benefit? Policy concerns about unlimited liability also played a role.

MAIN CASE Clagett v. Dacy (Md. Ct. Spec. App. 1980) — lawyer's duty to non-clients Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 8.A Facts: Dacy, an attorney, was hired by a mortgage lender to conduct a foreclosure sale. Because he did not follow proper procedures, the sale was set aside twice, and during the delay the borrower paid off the loan and redeemed the property. Clagett, the high bidder at both sales, sued Dacy for malpractice, claiming he lost a chance to buy the land and resell it at a profit. The trial court sustained Dacy's demurrer. Held: Wilner, J.: a lawyer owes no duty of care to a third party with whom he has no attorney-client relationship, unless the third party is an intended beneficiary of the representation, such as a will beneficiary. Bidders at a foreclosure sale are adverse to the lender's lawyer, who seeks the highest price while bidders seek the lowest. Affirmed. Why it matters: Privity still limits professional malpractice duties for economic loss, subject to the third-party-beneficiary exception.

No duty to rescue, and its exceptions
RULE The general rule: R2d § 314; R3d § 37 One who has not created the risk has no duty to act to protect or rescue another, even if the rescue would be easy and safe. The classic example is Yania v. Bigan (Pa. 1959): no duty to rescue a man who jumped into a water-filled pit at the defendant's urging. A duty to act arises (any one suffices): (1) a special relationship with the plaintiff, such as carrier-passenger, innkeeper-guest, possessor-invitee, custodian-ward, employer-employee, or school-student (R2d § 314A; L.S. Ayres); (2) the defendant created the peril, even innocently (R2d §§ 321–322); (3) the defendant undertook to help, then left the plaintiff worse off or induced reliance (R2d §§ 323–324); (4) a special relationship with the person who poses the danger, such as therapist-patient, parent-child, or custodian of a dangerous person (R2d §§ 315, 319; Tarasoff); (5) a statute imposes the duty; or (6) a contract imposes it.

MAIN CASE L.S. Ayres & Co. v. Hicks (Ind. 1942) — duty to aid a business invitee Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 8.B Facts: Hicks, a six-year-old boy shopping with his mother at the Ayres department store, fell on an escalator and caught his fingers in the moving parts. Store employees did not stop the escalator for an unreasonable time, and his injuries were made worse. The jury found the store liable for all his injuries. Held: Shake, C.J.: a store that invites customers onto its premises and controls the instrumentality that injured one of them must use reasonable care to aid the injured invitee, even if the store did not cause the original injury and the invitee was careless. But the store is liable only for the aggravation caused by its failure to act, not for the original injury. Reversed; new trial. Why it matters: This is the business-invitee exception. Liability is limited to harm caused by the failure to act.

MAIN CASE Hegel v. Langsam (Ohio C.P. 1971) — no duty to supervise adult students Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 8.B Facts: The Hegels' 17-year-old daughter enrolled as a freshman at the University of Cincinnati and was assigned to a dormitory. The university did not monitor her comings and goings. She stopped staying in the dormitory, became involved with criminals, was seduced, and began using drugs. Her parents demanded the university return her, but officials could not. The parents sued for failure to supervise. Held: Bettman, J.: a university has no duty to regulate the private lives of its students, control their comings and goings, or supervise their associations. It is an educational institution, not a nursery, boarding school, or prison, and students are presumed mature enough to care for themselves. Judgment on the pleadings for the university. Why it matters: There is no general custodial relationship between a college and adult students.

MAIN CASE Commonwealth v. Peterson (Va. 2013) — duty to warn of crime Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 8.B Facts: At about 7:15 a.m. on April 16, 2007, a gunman shot two students in West Ambler Johnston Hall at Virginia Tech, killing one. Police concluded it was a targeted domestic homicide, that the shooter had probably fled, and that a lockdown was unnecessary; they pursued a person of interest, a victim's boyfriend. University administrators sent a campus email about the shooting at 9:26 a.m. Around 9:40 a.m., the same gunman began shooting in Norris Hall, killing 30 more people, including Erin Peterson and Julia Pryde. Their estates sued the Commonwealth, and a jury found it negligent for failing to warn students sooner. Held: Powell, J.: assuming without deciding that a special relationship existed between the university and its students, there was no duty to warn of third-party criminal harm unless the harm was known or reasonably foreseeable. Based on what officials knew before the second shooting (a targeted killing, a shooter who had apparently fled), it was not reasonably foreseeable that students in classroom buildings would be harmed. Reversed; final judgment for the Commonwealth. Why it matters: Even where a special relationship exists, the duty extends only to foreseeable harm. Foreseeability usually requires knowledge of an imminent probability of injury.

MAIN CASE J.S. v. R.T.H. (N.J. 1998) — duty to protect from a spouse's abuse Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 8.B Facts: Two young sisters spent a great deal of time with their neighbor, R.T.H., at his horse barn. He sexually abused them over a period of time. Their parents sued him and his wife, claiming she knew or should have known of his conduct. The trial court granted summary judgment for the wife; the Appellate Division reversed. Held: Handler, J.: when a spouse has actual knowledge or special reason to know that her spouse is likely to abuse a particular person, she has a duty of reasonable care to prevent or warn of the abuse, and a breach can be a proximate cause of it. The court weighed foreseeability (the most important factor), the severity of the harm, the opportunity to prevent it, the parties' relationships, and public policy against child abuse. Affirmed; case remanded for trial. Why it matters: The duty is based on foreseeability, the relationship, and strong public policy against child abuse.

MAIN CASE Tarasoff v. Regents of University of California (Cal. 1976) — therapist's duty to protect third persons Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 8.B Facts: Prosenjit Poddar, a patient at the university's hospital, told his psychologist, Dr. Moore, that he intended to kill Tatiana Tarasoff, an identifiable young woman who had rejected him. Dr. Moore notified campus police and asked that Poddar be detained. Police held him briefly but released him when he seemed rational, and the psychiatry director ordered no further action. No one warned Tarasoff or her family. Two months later Poddar killed her. Her parents sued; the trial court sustained demurrers. Held: Tobriner, J.: when a therapist determines, or under the standards of the profession should determine, that a patient presents a serious danger of violence to another, the therapist must use reasonable care to protect the intended victim, by warning her, notifying the police, or taking other reasonable steps. The special relationship with the patient supports the duty. Confidentiality must yield: "The protective privilege ends where the public peril begins." The complaint stated a cause of action against the therapists (the police were immune). Why it matters: The special relationship with a dangerous person supports a duty to an identifiable victim. Most states now codify and limit the duty by statute, often to a serious threat against a reasonably identifiable victim.

NOTE Other duty limits in Ch. 8 (not on the syllabus pages) Negligent infliction of emotional distress: zone-of-danger and bystander rules (Daley v. LaCroix; Thing v. La Chusa). For the intentional tort, see § 5. Pure economic loss: generally not recoverable without physical harm (State of Louisiana ex rel. Guste v. M/V Testbank). Prenatal harm, wrongful birth, and wrongful life (Endresz; Procanik). Good Samaritan statutes shield people who give emergency aid in good faith from liability for ordinary negligence.

EXAM TIPS On a failure-to-act fact pattern, say the no-duty rule first, then go through each exception in the rule box and say which fits. If the defendant did something (drove, served drinks, let the patient go), consider whether it is really misfeasance.

# PART VIII — Defenses to Negligence

## 22. Contributory and Comparative Negligence WEEK 10
RULE Contributory negligence The defendant must prove that (all required): (1) the plaintiff failed to use reasonable care for her own safety; and (2) that failure was a cause in fact and a proximate cause of her harm. At common law, contributory negligence is a complete bar (Butterfield).

Exceptions to the bar (any one suffices): (1) last clear chance: the defendant had the last opportunity to avoid the harm (Davies v. Mann); (2) the defendant acted intentionally, willfully, wantonly, or recklessly; (3) the defendant violated a statute meant to protect the plaintiff from her own carelessness (e.g., child-labor laws); or (4) the plaintiff was a rescuer acting reasonably.
MAIN CASE Butterfield v. Forrester (K.B. 1809) — contributory negligence as a bar Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.A Facts: Forrester, repairing his house, put a pole across part of the road, though passage was still possible. At dusk, when candles were just being lit but a rider could see 100 yards ahead, Butterfield rode out "violently," did not see the pole, crashed into it, and was thrown and injured. There was no evidence he was drunk. The jury found for Forrester. Held: Lord Ellenborough, C.J.: a plaintiff cannot recover when his own lack of ordinary care contributed to the accident. "One person being in fault will not dispense with another's using ordinary care for himself." Had Butterfield ridden with ordinary care, he would have seen the pole. Judgment for Forrester. Why it matters: This is the origin of the all-or-nothing contributory negligence bar.

MAIN CASE Davies v. Mann (Ex. 1842) — last clear chance Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.A Facts: Davies fettered the forefeet of his donkey and turned it onto a narrow public road to graze. Mann's wagon, driven at a "smartish pace" by a servant who was not watching, knocked it down and killed it. Held: Lord Abinger, C.B., and Parke, B.: Davies's negligence in leaving the donkey on the road does not bar recovery, because Mann could have avoided the accident with ordinary care. Otherwise a driver could run over anything lawfully or unlawfully in the road. Verdict for Davies upheld. Why it matters: This is the origin of last clear chance, the main escape from the contributory negligence bar. R2d §§ 479–480 distinguish a helpless plaintiff (the defendant is liable if it knew or should have known) from an inattentive one (the defendant is liable only if it actually knew).

MAIN CASE McIntyre v. Balentine (Tenn. 1992) — adopting modified comparative fault Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.A Facts: McIntyre and Balentine collided at night on a highway. Both had been drinking, and there was evidence Balentine was speeding. The jury, instructed on contributory negligence, found them equally at fault, which barred McIntyre. Held: Drowota, J.: Tennessee abolishes contributory negligence and adopts modified comparative fault. A plaintiff may recover so long as her fault is less than the defendants' combined fault (the 49% bar), with damages reduced by her percentage. Last clear chance, remote contributory negligence, and joint and several liability are rendered obsolete. The jury might have apportioned fault differently under the new rule, so a new trial was ordered. Why it matters: This is the 49% bar version of modified comparative fault, adopted by a court rather than a legislature. Compare Li v. Yellow Cab (Cal. 1975), which adopted pure comparative fault.

System | Plaintiff recovers when her fault is | $100,000 damages, plaintiff 40% at fault | Plaintiff 50% at fault | Plaintiff 60% at fault
Contributory negligence (bar) | 0% | $0 | $0 | $0
Pure comparative fault (Li; about a dozen states) | Any amount below 100% | $60,000 | $50,000 | $40,000
Modified, 49% bar ("not as great as"; McIntyre) | Less than the defendants' fault | $60,000 | $0 | $0
Modified, 50% bar ("not greater than") | No greater than the defendants' fault | $60,000 | $50,000 | $0

- Contributory negligence remains the rule only in Alabama, Maryland, North Carolina, Virginia, and the District of Columbia.

- Delaware: modified comparative negligence, 50% bar. The plaintiff recovers if her negligence is not greater than the defendants' combined negligence (10 Del. C. § 8132).

- Effects of comparative fault: last clear chance is absorbed, implied assumption of risk is generally merged (§ 23), and the jury allocates percentages among all parties. Courts split on whether to compare the plaintiff's negligence with a defendant's intentional tort.

- Several defendants: most modified-comparative-fault states compare the plaintiff's fault with the defendants' combined fault, not with each defendant separately.

RULE Comparing fault: R3d Misc. Prov., Apportionment Topic 6, §§ 30–31 (approved 2022) These sections state the rules for tort claims for economic harm, applying the general Apportionment rules. § 30: a plaintiff's negligent or reckless conduct is not a basis for reducing her recovery against a defendant who intended the harm. § 31: against a defendant who did not intend the harm, the plaintiff's negligence that causes her harm, and is within her scope of responsibility, reduces her recovery in proportion to her share of comparative responsibility.

EXAM TIPS Do the arithmetic on the exam. First find the plaintiff's percentage and apply the jurisdiction's threshold. Then reduce the damages. Then allocate among defendants (§ 29). State the system you are using, especially on the open-book essay.

## 23. Assumption of Risk WEEK 10
Type | What it is | Effect today | Case
Express | The plaintiff agrees in advance, usually in writing, to release the defendant from liability for negligence | A complete bar if valid | Seigneur
Implied primary | The defendant owes no duty, or did not breach one, as to risks inherent in an activity (sports, spectators) | No liability: there is no negligence to compare | Blackburn (discussed)
Implied secondary, reasonable ("pure") | The plaintiff reasonably and knowingly encounters a risk the defendant negligently created | Not a defense; reasonable conduct is not fault | Blackburn
Implied secondary, unreasonable ("qualified") | The plaintiff unreasonably and knowingly encounters the risk | Merged into comparative fault; reduces damages | Blackburn

RULE Express assumption of risk (exculpatory agreements) An exculpatory clause is enforceable when (all required): (1) its language clearly and unambiguously releases the defendant from liability for its own negligence; (2) the injury falls within its scope; and (3) no exception applies. Exceptions (any one suffices): (1) the defendant's conduct was intentional, reckless, or grossly negligent; (2) the bargaining power was grossly unequal, as in an adhesion contract for an essential service; or (3) the transaction affects the public interest. Courts often use the Tunkl v. Regents factors (Cal. 1963): a business suitable for public regulation, offering an essential service, to any member of the public, with superior bargaining power and a standardized contract.

MAIN CASE Seigneur v. National Fitness Institute, Inc. (Md. Ct. Spec. App. 2000) — exculpatory clause in a gym contract Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.B Facts: Gerilynne Seigneur joined NFI's gym and signed a membership agreement in which she assumed "all risk of injury" from using the facilities and released NFI from all claims, expressly including its negligence. At her initial evaluation, she hurt her right shoulder on a weight machine. She and her husband sued for negligence, both vicarious (the employee's evaluation) and direct (negligent hiring and training). The trial court granted summary judgment for NFI. Held: Salmon, J.: an exculpatory clause is valid if it clearly and specifically releases the defendant from liability for its own negligence, unless (1) the conduct was intentional, reckless, wanton, or grossly negligent; (2) the bargaining power was grossly unequal; or (3) the transaction affects the public interest. The agreement was an adhesion contract, but that alone does not show grossly unequal bargaining power: Seigneur could have gone to another gym for a non-essential service. Health clubs are not in the public-interest category. Affirmed. Why it matters: Recreational releases are usually enforced. Releases in medical care, public utilities, and similar essential services usually are not.

RULE Implied assumption of risk The defendant must show that (all required): (1) the plaintiff actually knew of the specific risk (subjective knowledge); (2) the plaintiff appreciated its nature and magnitude; and (3) the plaintiff voluntarily chose to encounter it.

MAIN CASE Rush v. Commercial Realty Co. (N.J. 1929) — no voluntary choice Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.B Facts: Rush rented a house from Commercial Realty, which provided an outhouse as the only toilet for its tenants. Rush knew the floor was in bad condition. When she used it, she fell through a trap door in the floor into the pit below. The jury found for Rush, and the landlord appealed the denial of its motions for nonsuit and directed verdict. Held: Per curiam: assumption of risk requires a free and voluntary choice. Rush had no reasonable alternative to using the only toilet provided, and she was not required to leave her home and go elsewhere. Whether stepping on a floor she knew was in poor repair was contributory negligence was for the jury, but it was not assumption of risk. Affirmed. Why it matters: Voluntariness requires a genuine choice. A choice the defendant forces on the plaintiff does not count.

MAIN CASE Blackburn v. Dorta (Fla. 1977) — merging implied assumption of risk into comparative fault Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.B Facts: The court consolidated several cases, including car-accident cases, raising the same question: whether implied assumption of risk survived as a complete defense after Florida adopted comparative negligence in Hoffman v. Jones (1973). Held: Sundberg, J.: assumption of risk is a confused doctrine with many labels: express and implied, primary and secondary, strict ("pure") and qualified. Only implied, secondary, qualified assumption of risk has mattered as a defense, and it is indistinguishable from contributory negligence. It is therefore merged into comparative negligence and is no longer a complete bar. Express assumption of risk and the no-duty situations covered by primary assumption of risk are unaffected. Why it matters: This is the standard way courts sort the doctrine. The labels confuse; ask whether there was a duty and whether the plaintiff acted unreasonably.

TRAP Traps to avoid Primary assumption of risk is really a no-duty or no-breach argument. A baseball fan hit by a foul ball loses because the stadium owed no duty to screen every seat, not because of a defense (the "baseball rule"). Knowledge is subjective. A plaintiff who did not actually know of the specific risk did not assume it, though she may have been contributorily negligent for not knowing.

RULE Firefighter's rule: R3d Misc. Prov. (T.D. 3, draft) An actor who innocently or negligently creates a peril that brings a professional rescuer to the scene owes that rescuer no duty when the rescuer is injured by the very peril that brought the rescuer there, and the rescuer is injured while (all required): (1) on duty; (2) acting within the scope of employment; and (3) performing emergency activities. Compare the rescue doctrine (McCoy, § 20), which protects volunteer rescuers. The firefighter's rule rests on the idea that professional rescuers are paid and insured to face these risks.

## 24. Statutes of Limitation and Repose WEEK 11

- Statute of limitations: a claim must be filed within a set time after it accrues, typically 1–3 years for personal injury. It is an affirmative defense.

- Accrual: traditionally at the time of injury. Under the discovery rule, it accrues when the plaintiff discovers, or reasonably should have discovered, the injury and its cause (Teeters).

- Tolling (any one suffices): (1) minority; (2) mental incapacity; (3) the defendant's fraudulent concealment of the claim; or (4) a continuing tort or continuous course of treatment.

- Statute of repose: a fixed outer limit measured from the defendant's act (sale of a product, completion of construction, the medical procedure), regardless of when the injury is discovered. It can bar a claim before the injury occurs.

- Delaware: personal injury actions must be filed within 2 years (10 Del. C. § 8119). Medical negligence claims must be filed within 2 years of the injury, or within 3 years if the injury was unknown and could not reasonably have been discovered within the 2 years (18 Del. C. § 6856).

RULE Limitations and repose: R3d Misc. Prov. §§ 1–16 (T.D. 3, draft) When the limitations period starts (§§ 2–4): under the all-elements rule (§ 2), it starts when all elements of the claim have occurred. Under the discovery rule (§ 3), it does not start until the plaintiff discovers, or with reasonable diligence should have discovered, all the factual elements of the claim against the defendant (Teeters). For continuing torts (§ 4): (a) if the law requires all damages from repeated conduct to be sought in one action, it starts when it starts for any part; (b) if the injury is the cumulative, progressive result of repeated conduct, none of which alone causes an identifiable injury, it starts only after the conduct stops; and (c) for false imprisonment, it starts only after the confinement ends. Tolling and suspension (any one suffices): (1) continuous representation by a lawyer on the same or a related matter (§ 6); (2) continuous medical treatment for the same or a related condition (§ 7); (3) equitable tolling, when the plaintiff was diligently pursuing her rights but an extraordinary circumstance prevented a timely suit (§ 8); (4) equitable estoppel, when the defendant's words, conduct, or silence reasonably induced the plaintiff not to sue in time (§ 9); or (5) fraudulent concealment, which suspends the period until the plaintiff discovers, or should have discovered, the fraud (§ 10). Statutory tolling rules, such as minority, are left to the statutes (§ 5). Statutes of repose (§§ 12–15): a repose period runs from a specified event, such as the tortious act, the sale of a product, or the completion of a building, whether or not the plaintiff could yet sue (§§ 12–13). Common-law tolling does not suspend it (§ 14), but equitable estoppel and fraudulent concealment do (§ 15).

MAIN CASE Teeters v. Currey (Tenn. 1974) — the discovery rule in malpractice Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.C Facts: On June 5, 1970, after delivering Mrs. Teeters's child, Dr. Currey performed a bilateral tubal ligation to prevent future pregnancies. On December 6, 1972, she learned she was pregnant again, and on March 9, 1973, she delivered a premature child with severe complications. She sued on November 15, 1973. Currey pleaded the one-year statute of limitations, and the trial court agreed. Held: Henry, J.: in a malpractice action for negligent surgery, the limitations period begins when the patient discovers, or in the exercise of reasonable care should have discovered, the injury, not on the date of the operation. It would be unfair to bar a claim before the patient could know of it. Teeters sued within a year of discovery. Reversed and remanded. Why it matters: This is a judicial adoption of the discovery rule. Many legislatures responded with medical malpractice statutes of repose that cap the discovery period.

## 25. Immunities WEEK 11
RULE Immunities: R3d Misc. Prov. (approved 2022) Family and charitable immunity: there is no spousal, parental, child, or other family immunity (§§ 1–4), and, subject to contrary statutes, no charitable immunity (§ 5). Parental standard of care (§ 10A): (a) when a parent's conduct does not involve an unemancipated minor child's discipline, supervision, or care, the parent must use reasonable care; (b) when it does, the parent is liable to the child only for reckless conduct. Compare Zellmer, where Washington's parental immunity covered negligent supervision but not a stepparent. Government (§§ 9–10): a state is immune unless it consents to suit or abrogates its immunity. Even when it consents, and always for local governments, immunity remains for acts or omissions that (any one suffices) (1) are specifically immunized by statute; (2) are the exercise of a judicial or legislative function; or (3) are the exercise of an administrative function involving the discretionary determination of important governmental policy.

Family immunities

- Interspousal immunity rested on the fiction that husband and wife were one person, and on fears of collusion and disruption of family harmony. Nearly every state has abolished it (Freehe).

- Parental immunity bars a child's negligence claim against a parent in some states. Approaches (any one may apply): (1) abolished entirely, with a reasonable-parent standard (Gibson v. Gibson, Cal. 1971); (2) abolished except for the exercise of parental authority or discretion over the child's care (Goller v. White, Wis. 1963); or (3) retained for ordinary negligence but not for willful, wanton, or intentional harm (Washington, as in Zellmer).

MAIN CASE Freehe v. Freehe (Wash. 1972) — abolishing interspousal immunity Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.D Facts: Clifford Freehe was injured by a tractor that his wife, Hazel, owned as her separate property and kept on her separate farm. He sued her for negligently maintaining the tractor and failing to warn him of its condition. The trial court granted summary judgment for Hazel on interspousal immunity. Held: Neill, J.: interspousal immunity in personal injury cases is abolished. Its rationales fail: (1) husband and wife are no longer one legal person; (2) a suit will not disrupt a harmonious marriage, since spouses at peace will not sue or will drop the suit; and (3) criminal and divorce law do not compensate for injuries. Fraud and collusion are policed by the ordinary trial process. Reversed and remanded. Why it matters: This reflects the national trend. Fraud concerns are handled by the ordinary trial process and insurance law, not by a blanket bar.

MAIN CASE Zellmer v. Zellmer (Wash. 2008) — parental immunity and stepparents Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.D Facts: Three-year-old Ashley McLellan lived with her mother and her stepfather, Mr. Zellmer. While he was watching her, he started a video for her and went downstairs to build a fire. About an hour later he found the sliding door to the backyard open and Ashley floating in the pool. She was resuscitated but died two days later. Her mother and biological father sued him for wrongful death. He moved for summary judgment, claiming parental immunity because he stood in loco parentis. The trial court and court of appeals agreed with him. Held: Madsen, J.: Washington keeps parental immunity for negligent parental supervision, but it does not extend to a stepparent or anyone else who is not a biological or adoptive parent, even one acting in loco parentis. A stepparent does not acquire parental rights or obligations merely by the relationship. The stepfather is held to ordinary care. Reversed and remanded. Why it matters: Courts read the remaining family immunities narrowly.

Charitable immunity
MAIN CASE Abernathy v. Sisters of St. Mary's (Mo. 1969) — abolishing charitable immunity Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.D Facts: Abernathy, a patient at the Sisters of St. Mary's hospital, a charitable institution, was injured when a hospital employee negligently failed to help him as he moved from his bed to the bathroom. The trial court granted the hospital summary judgment on charitable immunity. Held: Henley, C.J.: charitable immunity is abolished. A charitable institution is liable for its own negligence and for its employees' negligence within the scope of their employment. Immunity "fosters neglect and breeds irresponsibility, while liability promotes care and caution," and modern charity is big business that can insure. Reversed and remanded. Why it matters: Almost every state has abolished or limited charitable immunity. Some states cap damages against charities or limit recovery to insurance.

Sovereign immunity
RULE Federal Tort Claims Act: 28 U.S.C. §§ 1346(b), 2671–2680 The United States is liable for the negligent or wrongful acts of federal employees acting within the scope of their employment, in the same manner as a private person under the law of the place where the act occurred. There is no jury trial and no punitive damages. Exceptions (any one bars the claim): (1) the discretionary function exception, § 2680(a); (2) most intentional torts, such as assault, battery, false imprisonment, and misrepresentation, § 2680(h), except for assault, battery, false imprisonment, and similar torts by law enforcement officers; and (3) injuries to service members incident to military service (Feres v. United States, 1950). Discretionary function test (all required for immunity): (1) the conduct involves an element of judgment or choice, because no statute, regulation, or policy prescribes a specific course; and (2) the judgment is of the kind the exception was designed to shield, one grounded in social, economic, or political policy.

MAIN CASE Deuser v. Vecera (8th Cir. 1998) — FTCA discretionary function Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.D Facts: Deuser attended the Veiled Prophet Fair on the grounds of the Jefferson National Expansion Memorial (the Gateway Arch) in St. Louis, a national park. Park rangers saw him grabbing women and urinating in public, arrested him, and turned him over to St. Louis police, who decided not to hold him. He was released in a parking lot, with no money or transportation, and later wandered onto an interstate and was struck and killed. His survivors sued the United States under the FTCA. The district court dismissed. Held: Bowman, J.: the discretionary function exception bars claims based on conduct that (1) involves an element of judgment or choice, and (2) is of the kind the exception was meant to shield, grounded in social, economic, or political policy. No mandatory policy dictated how the rangers had to handle a drunk, disorderly visitor; their choices to arrest him and turn him over to local police involved judgments about law enforcement priorities and resources. Affirmed. Why it matters: The exception sweeps in many operational law enforcement decisions, not just high-level policy.

State and municipal immunity

- Most states have waived immunity, in whole or in part, through tort claims acts. These often keep a discretionary function exception, cap damages, and require prompt notice of claims.

- The traditional line between governmental functions (immune: police, fire) and proprietary functions (liable: utilities, municipal businesses) survives in some states.

- Public duty doctrine: a duty owed to the public at large, such as police protection, is not a duty to any individual, unless there is a special relationship (Riss; DeLong).

- Delaware: the State Tort Claims Act (10 Del. C. § 4001) protects state officials and employees for discretionary acts done in good faith and without gross or wanton negligence. The County and Municipal Tort Claims Act (10 Del. C. § 4010 et seq.) grants immunity with listed exceptions.

MAIN CASE Clarke v. Oregon Health Sciences University (Or. 2007) — limits on legislated immunity Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.D Facts: Jordaan Clarke, an infant, had surgery at the state-run Oregon Health Sciences University to repair a congenital heart defect. Through employees' negligence, he suffered prolonged oxygen deprivation and permanent brain damage, leaving him totally disabled. He sought more than $17 million. The Oregon Tort Claims Act capped damages against the state at $200,000 and made the suit against the public body the exclusive remedy, barring claims against the individual employees. The trial court entered judgment for $200,000 against OHSU and dismissed the employees; the court of appeals reversed as to the employees. Held: De Muniz, C.J.: the remedy clause of the Oregon Constitution (Art. I, § 10) guarantees "remedy by due course of law for injury done" to person or property. Eliminating the claim against the negligent employees and substituting a $200,000 claim against the state, against damages exceeding $17 million, left an "emasculated" remedy that is no substitute. As applied, the exclusive-remedy provision is unconstitutional, and the claims against the employees may proceed. Court of appeals affirmed. Why it matters: State constitutions, not just legislatures, can limit how far immunity and damages caps reach.

MAIN CASE Riss v. City of New York (N.Y. 1968) — no duty to provide police protection Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.D Facts: For months, Linda Riss's rejected suitor, Burton Pugach, a lawyer, threatened to kill or maim her if she would not marry him. She repeatedly asked the police for protection and was refused. After she announced her engagement to another man, a thug hired by Pugach threw lye in her face, blinding her in one eye and permanently scarring her face. She sued the city for negligent failure to protect her. The complaint was dismissed. Held: Breitel, J.: absent a specific legislative mandate, a municipality is not liable for its failure to provide police protection to a member of the public, even one who was specifically threatened. Allocating limited police resources is a matter for the legislative and executive branches, and liability would expose the city to unlimited claims. Affirmed. Why it matters: The public duty doctrine. Compare Town of Castle Rock v. Gonzales (U.S. 2005), which found no constitutional right to enforcement of a restraining order. It is also a bias lens: the rule falls hardest on people, often women, who depend on the police for protection from violence. Dissent (Keating, J.): the city's immunity rests on a fiction and leaves the victim of official negligence without a remedy. The fear of crushing liability was exaggerated, and ordinary negligence principles should apply when the police ignore a known, specific threat.

MAIN CASE DeLong v. Erie County (N.Y. App. Div. 1982) — special duty through a 911 call Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 12.D Facts: Amalia DeLong called 911 to report that a burglar was breaking into her home and gave her address. The call-taker wrote down the wrong address, and the dispatcher sent officers of the Village of Kenmore to an address that did not exist. Concluding the call was a prank, they left. Standard procedure required checking the tape of the call to confirm the address; no one did. Relying on the promise of help, she stayed in the house, and minutes later the burglar killed her. A jury found the county and the village liable. Held: Hancock, J.: as a rule, a government is not liable for failing to provide police protection. But by setting up an emergency number, inviting the public to rely on it, and telling DeLong help was on the way, the government assumed a special duty to her. She relied on the promise, staying home instead of fleeing or seeking help. Failing to follow standard procedures breached that duty. Affirmed. Why it matters: A special relationship takes the case out of Riss. New York later framed the test (Cuffy v. City of New York, 1987) as (all required): (1) the municipality assumed, through promises or actions, an affirmative duty to act for the injured party; (2) its agents knew that inaction could lead to harm; (3) there was direct contact between its agents and the injured party; and (4) the injured party justifiably relied on the municipality's affirmative undertaking.

# PART IX — Premises Liability

## 26. Owners and Occupiers of Land WEEK 11
Harm to people outside the land

- Artificial conditions and activities: the possessor must use reasonable care to protect people on adjacent public ways from unreasonable risks (Salevan).

- Natural conditions: the traditional rule is no duty, though many courts require reasonable care as to trees near highways, especially in urban areas. Taylor applied reasonable care but rejected an urban-rural distinction.

MAIN CASE Taylor v. Olsen (Or. 1978) — trees beside a highway Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 9.A Facts: On a dark, windy January evening, Taylor's car struck a tree that had fallen across a rural highway from Olsen's adjoining timber land. After the accident, the tree was found to be decayed at its center, but nothing on its outside indicated decay. The trial court directed a verdict for Olsen. Held: Linde, J.: whether a landowner used reasonable care to protect travelers from conditions on the land is usually a jury question. But there must be evidence that a reasonable inspection would have revealed the danger, and there was none: no evidence that boring into an apparently healthy tree is a customary inspection. Affirmed. Why it matters: Liability for natural conditions depends on what a reasonable inspection would show.

MAIN CASE Salevan v. Wilmington Park, Inc. (Del. Super. 1950) — baseballs hit into the street Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 9.A Facts: Wilmington Park operated a baseball park next to East Thirtieth Street in Wilmington. Two or three foul balls a game went over the fence onto the street, and the park took only limited precautions. While walking on the street, Salevan was hit by a foul ball. He sued for his injuries. Held: Wolcott, J.: a landowner whose property adjoins a public street must take reasonable precautions to protect travelers from activities on the land. The park knew balls regularly left the grounds during its 68-game season, so its precautions were inadequate. Judgment for Salevan for $2,500. Why it matters: A Delaware case. The duty to people outside the land follows the ordinary negligence standard.

The common-law categories of entrants
Entrant | Who | Duty owed by the possessor | Case
Trespasser (undiscovered) | On the land without permission | Refrain from willful or wanton injury | Sheehan
Trespasser (discovered, or frequent on a limited area) | The possessor knows or should know the trespasser is there | Reasonable care in activities; warn of known, dangerous artificial conditions the trespasser is unlikely to discover (R2d §§ 334–337) | Sheehan
Child trespasser | See attractive nuisance (R2d § 339) | Reasonable care if the five elements are met | Krayenbuhl (§ 11)
Licensee | Enters with permission for her own purposes, including social guests | Warn of, or make safe, known dangerous conditions she is unlikely to discover. No duty to inspect | Barmore
Invitee | A public invitee, or a business visitor whose visit is connected to the possessor's business (R2d § 332) | Reasonable care, including reasonable inspection to discover dangers and making them safe or warning | Campbell; Whelan

MAIN CASE Sheehan v. St. Paul & Duluth Ry. Co. (7th Cir. 1896) — undiscovered trespassers Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 9.B Facts: Sheehan was walking along the railroad's track, at a place not open to public travel, when his foot slipped and caught in the rails. Before he could free it, a train ran over his foot. The crew did not see him until too late to stop. The trial court directed a verdict for the railroad. Held: Seaman, J.: a possessor owes no duty to anticipate trespassers, who take the land as they find it. The railroad's duty of reasonable care arose only when the crew discovered Sheehan in peril, and there was no evidence they could have stopped after seeing him. Public crossings differ, because their existence gives notice that people will be there. Affirmed. Why it matters: The duty to a trespasser starts when he is discovered.

RULE Attractive nuisance: R2d § 339 A possessor is liable for physical harm to trespassing children caused by an artificial condition on the land when (all required): (a) the possessor knows or has reason to know that children are likely to trespass where the condition exists; (b) the possessor knows or has reason to know of the condition and realizes or should realize that it involves an unreasonable risk of death or serious bodily harm to such children; (c) the children, because of their youth, do not discover the condition or realize the risk; (d) the utility to the possessor of maintaining the condition and the burden of eliminating the danger are slight compared with the risk to children; and (e) the possessor fails to exercise reasonable care to eliminate the danger or otherwise protect the children.

MAIN CASE Barmore v. Elmore (Ill. App. 1980) — social guests are licensees Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 9.B Facts: Barmore and Elmore were officers of the same Masonic lodge. In August 1977, Barmore went to Elmore's home to discuss lodge business. Elmore's adult son, who had a history of mental illness, attacked Barmore with a steak knife. Barmore sued Elmore for failing to protect him from a dangerous condition on the premises. The trial court ruled Barmore a licensee and directed a verdict for Elmore. Held: Lindberg, J.: Barmore was a licensee, not an invitee, because the visit primarily benefited the lodge, not Elmore. A possessor must warn a licensee only of hidden dangers he knows of. Although the son had a history of mental illness, there was no evidence that Elmore knew or should have known he was likely to attack that night. Affirmed. Why it matters: Classify the entrant first. A licensee gets a duty to warn only of known dangers.

MAIN CASE Campbell v. Weathers (Kan. 1941) — customers who do not buy Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 9.B Facts: Campbell was a regular customer of Weathers's cigar stand and lunch counter. One day he came in, stayed about 15 minutes without buying anything, and then went to use the toilet, which was open to the public. On the way he stepped into an open trap door and was injured. The trial court sustained Weathers's demurrer to the evidence. Held: Wedell, J.: a regular or prospective customer who enters a place of business open to the public is an invitee, even if he makes no purchase that day. A person who had no intention of becoming a customer, then or later, would not be. Whether Campbell was an invitee was for the jury. Reversed. Why it matters: The invitation test: a person who enters where the public is invited is an invitee.

MAIN CASE Whelan v. Van Natta (Ky. 1964) — the scope of the invitation Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 9.B Facts: Whelan bought some items at Van Natta's grocery and asked for a box. The grocer told him to look in the back room. While searching there, in the dark, he stepped into an unseen stairwell and fell. The trial court entered judgment for Van Natta. Held: Montgomery, J.: an invitee keeps that status only within the area of the invitation, the part of the premises where the possessor gives reason to believe his presence is desired for the purpose of the visit. Going into the back room for his own purpose (the box), with permission, made Whelan a licensee, owed only a warning of known hidden dangers. Affirmed. Why it matters: Status can change during a single visit.

MAIN CASE Rowland v. Christian (Cal. 1968) — abolishing the categories Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 9.C Facts: Rowland, a social guest in Christian's apartment, asked to use the bathroom. The porcelain handle of a faucet cracked and broke in his hand, severing tendons and nerves. Christian had known the handle was cracked and had told the building manager, but did not warn Rowland. The trial court granted summary judgment for Christian because a social guest is a licensee who takes the premises as he finds them. Held: Peters, J.: the status of the entrant as trespasser, licensee, or invitee does not determine the possessor's duty. The test is whether the possessor acted as a reasonable person in managing the property, in view of the probability of injury to others, weighing the Rowland factors. Status may bear on what is reasonable. Christian knew of a concealed danger Rowland was about to encounter and did not warn him, which a jury could find negligent. Reversed. Why it matters: The leading case rejecting the categories in favor of reasonable care, using the Rowland factors. Dissent (Burke, J.): the categories developed over many years and give needed certainty. Changing them is for the legislature.

RULE The Rowland factors Departures from the general duty of reasonable care are justified only after weighing (weighed together): (1) the foreseeability of harm to the plaintiff; (2) the degree of certainty that the plaintiff suffered injury; (3) the closeness of the connection between the defendant's conduct and the injury; (4) the moral blame attached to the defendant's conduct; (5) the policy of preventing future harm; (6) the extent of the burden to the defendant and the consequences to the community of imposing a duty of care with resulting liability for breach; and (7) the availability, cost, and prevalence of insurance for the risk involved.

- Where states stand: a minority follow Rowland and use reasonable care for everyone; a larger group merge licensees and invitees but keep the trespasser rule; and many, including Delaware, keep the traditional categories.

- Delaware's premises guest statute (25 Del. C. § 1501) bars a guest who enters without payment from suing the owner or occupier unless the injury was intentional or caused by willful or wanton disregard of the guest's rights.

- Open and obvious dangers: traditionally no duty to invitees, but R2d § 343A imposes liability if the possessor should anticipate the harm despite the obviousness, as when the invitee is distracted.

- Recreational use statutes limit duties to people using land for free recreation.

NOTE Landlords and tenants (the next sections of Ch. 9; not on the syllabus pages) At common law a lessor is not liable for conditions on leased land, with exceptions (any one suffices) (Borders v. Roseberry): (1) undisclosed dangerous conditions known to the lessor and unknown to the lessee; (2) conditions dangerous to people outside the premises; (3) premises leased for admission of the public; (4) parts of the land retained in the lessor's control that the lessee may use; (5) the lessor's contract to repair; and (6) negligent repairs by the lessor. Pagelsdorf (Wis. 1979) replaced this with ordinary care, and Kline (D.C. Cir. 1970) required landlords to take reasonable precautions against foreseeable crime in common areas.

# PART X — Damages

## 27. Compensatory Damages WEEK 12
Kind | Covers | Notes
Nominal | A small sum ($1) to vindicate a right | Intentional torts only; negligence requires actual harm
Compensatory: economic (special) | Past and future medical expenses, lost earnings, lost earning capacity, property damage | Future losses are reduced to present value
Compensatory: non-economic (general) | Pain and suffering, mental anguish, disfigurement, loss of enjoyment of life | No fixed measure; the jury's judgment, reviewed for excess. Many states cap these, especially in medical malpractice.
Punitive (exemplary) | Punishment and deterrence for malicious, willful, or reckless conduct | § 28

- Single recovery rule: all past and future damages are awarded in one lump sum. Some states allow periodic payments for large future losses.

- Present value: future economic losses are discounted to present value, and inflation may be considered.

- Remittitur and additur: a judge who finds a verdict excessive may order a new trial unless the plaintiff accepts a lower amount (remittitur). Additur, raising an inadequate verdict, is not allowed in federal court.

- Attorney's fees are not recoverable under the American rule. Contingent fees come out of the award.

- Property: the measure is diminution in market value, or the reasonable cost of repair, plus loss of use.

NOTE Loss of consortium: R3d Misc. Prov. §§ 48 A–48 C (approved 2022) A family member of a person physically or emotionally harmed by a tort may recover for the resulting loss of society, meaning affection, comfort, companionship, love, support, and services (any one relationship suffices): (1) a spouse (§ 48 A, including impairment of conjugal relations); (2) a parent of an unemancipated minor child (§ 48 B); or (3) a minor child of the injured parent (§ 48 C).

MAIN CASE Anderson v. Sears, Roebuck & Co. (E.D. La. 1974) — the elements of personal injury damages Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 10.A Facts: A defective heater made by Sears set fire to the Britain family's home. Their infant daughter, Helen, was burned over 40% of her body. She suffered extreme scarring, fingers fused together, and a permanently bent elbow, and faced many costly operations for the rest of her life. The jury awarded her $2,000,000, and Sears moved for a remittitur. Held: Cassibry, J.: to decide whether an award is excessive, the court examines each element of damages: (1) past physical and mental pain; (2) future physical and mental pain; (3) future medical expenses (here, some 27 projected operations and psychiatric care); (4) loss of earning capacity (she would likely never be self-supporting); and (5) permanent disability and disfigurement. Each element was supported, and the total was not excessive. Motion denied. Why it matters: This is the framework for valuing a serious personal injury case, element by element.

MAIN CASE Richardson v. Chapman (Ill. 1997) — excessive awards and remittitur Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 10.A Facts: Richardson was stopped at a red light when a semi-trailer driven by Chapman hit her car from behind. She became a quadriplegic. The trial court directed a verdict on liability against Chapman and his employer, and the jury awarded Richardson $22,358,814 (and her passenger, McGregor, $102,215). The defendants argued the award was excessive and that her expert's present-value calculations were wrong. Held: Miller, J.: an award is excessive if it falls outside the range of fair and reasonable compensation, results from passion or prejudice, or shocks the conscience. The jury's award for future medical costs was $1.5 million above the higher of the two figures offered at trial, which unitemized future costs could not explain, so $1 million was remitted. The rest, including large non-economic damages, was within the jury's discretion. Affirmed as modified. Why it matters: Future economic damages must rest on evidence. Non-economic damages get more deference.

RULE The collateral source rule Benefits the plaintiff receives from a source independent of the defendant do not reduce the damages the defendant must pay. Collateral sources include (any one suffices): (1) the plaintiff's own insurance, such as health, disability, or life insurance; (2) employment benefits, such as sick pay or pensions; (3) gratuitous services or payments from family, friends, or charity; and (4) government benefits. Reasons: the defendant should not benefit from the plaintiff's foresight or others' generosity, and many collateral sources are reimbursed through subrogation. Many states have modified the rule by statute, especially in medical malpractice.

MAIN CASE Montgomery Ward & Co. v. Anderson (Ark. 1998) — discounts as collateral sources Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 10.B Facts: Anderson fell in Montgomery Ward's Little Rock store and incurred about $25,000 in hospital bills. Her lawyer negotiated a 50% discount with the hospital. Ward moved to limit her proof to what she actually had to pay and to introduce the discount. The trial court held the discount was a collateral source and allowed evidence of the full bill. Held: Newbern, J.: gratuitous or discounted medical services are a collateral source and cannot be used to reduce the damages owed by a tortfeasor. The wrongdoer should not benefit from the plaintiff's good fortune, even if she recovers more than her out-of-pocket loss. The rule yields only when collateral-source evidence is relevant for another purpose (such as rebutting a claim of financial need or impeaching testimony). Affirmed. Why it matters: Courts split on whether the "billed" or the "paid" amount is recoverable when insurers negotiate discounts.

RULE Avoidable consequences (mitigation) The plaintiff cannot recover for harm she could have avoided with reasonable effort or expense after the injury, such as by getting reasonable medical treatment or following medical advice. The defendant must prove (all required): (1) a reasonable course of action was available to the plaintiff; (2) the plaintiff unreasonably failed to take it; and (3) it would have reduced the harm, and by how much.

MAIN CASE Zimmerman v. Ausland (Or. 1973) — refusing surgery and avoidable consequences Source: Canvas reading (11/10), from the opinion text in the course folder. Facts: Zimmerman, a substitute teacher, was injured in a car accident. Ausland admitted liability, so only damages were tried. She had a torn semilunar cartilage in her right knee, with swelling and pain after walking, and could no longer join in physical-education games or play volleyball and tennis. Her doctor testified the injury was permanent and would gradually get worse, and that she would "very probably" need surgery to remove the cartilage, after which recovery would be "fairly good." He had prescribed no treatment and said surgery is "not always" required. The defense doctor, who doubted the diagnosis, testified that if she had the tear, routine surgery would let her recover completely. Neither doctor said surgery was called for when he examined her, and no one testified about the operation's risks. The jury was instructed on permanent injury and life-expectancy tables and awarded $7,500. Ausland argued that because routine surgery could cure the injury, and she had a duty to mitigate, it could not be treated as permanent. Held: Tongue, J.: a plaintiff cannot recover for a permanent injury whose permanence she could have avoided by submitting to treatment, including surgery, that a reasonable person would accept in the same circumstances. The defendant bears the burden of proving an unreasonable failure to mitigate, and the question is ordinarily for the jury. The factors include (1) the risk involved in the operation; (2) its probability of success; and (3) the money or effort required; some courts add the pain involved. Here there was no evidence of the surgery's risk, no evidence that any doctor advised surgery, and no requested instruction on mitigation, so the court could not hold as a matter of law that she had to have surgery. The permanency issue was properly submitted. Affirmed. Why it matters: Avoidable consequences reduces damages, not liability, and courts are "cautious about insisting that due care requires submission to an operation." It concerns the plaintiff's conduct after the injury; comparative fault (§ 22) concerns her conduct before it.

NOTE Bias lens: valuing lives and earnings Lost earning capacity is often projected from statistical tables. Tables broken out by race and sex have predicted lower earnings and shorter work lives for women and people of color, which lowers their awards for the same injury (McMillan v. City of New York, E.D.N.Y. 2008, rejecting race-based life expectancy figures). Cal. Civ. Code § 3361 (2019) bars reducing these damages based on race, ethnicity, or gender. Non-economic damages make up a larger share of the recovery for children, retirees, and people outside the paid workforce, so caps on non-economic damages fall hardest on them.

## 28. Punitive Damages WEEK 12
RULE When punitive damages are available The plaintiff must show (all required): (1) a tort that supports compensatory damages (most states require actual damages); and (2) aggravated conduct: malice, fraud, oppression, or willful, wanton, or reckless disregard of others' rights. Many states require clear and convincing evidence. Evidence of the defendant's wealth is admissible. Vicarious punitive damages, R2d § 909 (any one suffices): the principal is liable for punitive damages because of an agent's act if (a) the principal authorized the doing and the manner of the act; (b) the agent was unfit and the principal was reckless in employing or retaining him; (c) the agent was employed in a managerial capacity and was acting in the scope of employment (Fisher, § 3); or (d) the principal or a managerial agent ratified or approved the act.

RULE Due process limits: BMW v. Gore (1996); State Farm v. Campbell (2003) A court reviewing an award considers three guideposts (weighed together): (1) the degree of reprehensibility of the defendant's misconduct; (2) the disparity between the actual or potential harm and the punitive award (the ratio); and (3) the difference between the punitive award and civil penalties authorized or imposed in comparable cases. Reprehensibility factors (weighed together): (1) whether the harm was physical rather than economic; (2) whether the conduct showed indifference to or reckless disregard of others' health or safety; (3) whether the target was financially vulnerable; (4) whether the conduct was repeated rather than isolated; and (5) whether the harm resulted from intentional malice, trickery, or deceit rather than accident.

MAIN CASE State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. v. Campbell (U.S. 2003) — ratio and out-of-state conduct Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 10.C Facts: Campbell, passing six vans on a two-lane highway, caused a crash that killed Ospital and permanently disabled Slusher. State Farm, his insurer, refused offers to settle for the $50,000 policy limits ($25,000 each), assured Campbell his assets were safe, and took the case to trial. The jury returned $185,849 against him, and State Farm at first refused to cover the excess, telling him to put a "For Sale" sign on his house. Campbell then sued State Farm for bad faith, fraud, and IIED. To show a nationwide scheme to cap payouts, he introduced evidence of State Farm's practices across the country over 20 years. The Utah jury awarded $1 million in compensatory damages (reduced from $2.6 million) and $145 million in punitive damages. Held: Kennedy, J.: the award violated due process under the Gore guideposts. (1) Reprehensibility: State Farm's conduct merited some punishment, but a state may not punish lawful out-of-state conduct or dissimilar conduct unrelated to the plaintiff's harm. (2) Ratio: few awards exceeding a single-digit ratio will satisfy due process, and where compensatory damages are substantial, a 1:1 ratio may be the limit; 145:1 is far beyond it. (3) Comparable penalties: the most relevant civil sanction was a $10,000 fine for fraud. Reversed and remanded. Why it matters: This sets the constitutional limit: the single-digit ratio, punishment only for conduct toward this plaintiff, and reprehensibility as the most important guidepost. Philip Morris USA v. Williams (2007) bars punishing for harm to nonparties.

MAIN CASE Exxon Shipping Co. v. Baker (U.S. 2008) — maritime cap of 1:1 Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 10.C Facts: In 1989 the Exxon Valdez ran aground on Bligh Reef in Prince William Sound, spilling millions of gallons of crude oil. Its captain, a relapsed alcoholic whom Exxon knew was drinking again, had left the bridge just before the grounding, though he was the only officer licensed to navigate that passage. Exxon paid over $1 billion to settle government environmental claims. Commercial fishermen and Native Alaskans sued for economic losses. The jury awarded $5 billion in punitive damages, which the Ninth Circuit reduced to $2.5 billion. Compensatory damages were about $507.5 million. Held: Souter, J.: as a matter of federal maritime common law, not constitutional due process, punitive damages for reckless conduct (without intentional or malicious wrongdoing or a profit motive) are limited to a 1:1 ratio with compensatory damages. The chief problem with punitive damages is unpredictability, and studies showed a median ratio below 1:1. Vacated and remanded, effectively reducing the award to about $507.5 million. Why it matters: The 1:1 ratio is a federal common-law rule for maritime cases. It is not a constitutional limit on the states.

MAIN CASE Cheatham v. Pohle (Ind. 2003) — split-recovery statutes Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 10.C Facts: Four years after their divorce, Michael Pohle distributed at least 60 copies of nude photos of his ex-wife, Doris Cheatham, and photos of the two of them having sex, around the small Indiana community where both lived and worked. She sued for invasion of privacy and IIED, and the jury awarded $100,000 in compensatory and $100,000 in punitive damages. Indiana's statute gave the plaintiff only 25% of a punitive award and sent 75% to the state's Violent Crime Victims Compensation Fund. Cheatham challenged the statute as a taking. Held: Boehm, J.: the statute does not violate the federal or Indiana Takings Clause. Punitive damages are quasi-criminal, serve public purposes, and compensate no one, so a plaintiff has no vested property right in them. The legislature could abolish punitive damages entirely, so it may limit the plaintiff's share. Judgment for the state on the challenge. Why it matters: Punitive damages are quasi-criminal. Several states use split-recovery statutes or cap punitive awards.

# PART XI — Multiple Defendants

## 29. Joint and Several Liability, Satisfaction, Release, and Settlement WEEKS 12–13
RULE When joint and several liability applies Each defendant is liable for the plaintiff's entire damages, and the plaintiff may collect from any one or more of them (but not more than once), when (any one suffices): (1) the defendants acted in concert, by agreement or by knowingly giving substantial assistance or encouragement (R2d § 876; Bierczynski); (2) independent tortfeasors caused a single, indivisible injury (Hill v. Edmonds, § 18); (3) one defendant is vicariously liable for another (§ 31); or (4) the defendants breached a common duty. Divisible injuries are apportioned: each defendant pays only for the harm it caused, and the plaintiff must prove the division (Bruckman, § 30). When the harm cannot reasonably be divided, many courts shift the burden of apportionment to the defendants.

MAIN CASE Bierczynski v. Rogers (Del. 1968) — concerted action: drag racing Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 7.A Facts: Race and Bierczynski were drag racing side by side on a public highway. Coming over a hill, they saw the Rogerses' car approaching. Race tried to swing back into his lane, lost control, and hit the Rogerses' car at about 70 mph. Bierczynski's car never touched it. The trial court held both racers jointly liable. Held: Herrmann, J.: participants in a motor vehicle race on a public highway are acting in concert, and each is liable for harm caused by any of them, because each participated in and encouraged the wrongful conduct. Otherwise the victim might be left with only an insolvent defendant, and the driver who happened to collide would bear the whole loss. Affirmed. Why it matters: A Delaware Supreme Court case. Concert of action makes every participant jointly and severally liable, even one who did not touch the plaintiff.

RULE Concerted negligence: R3d Misc. Prov. (T.D. 3, draft) Agreements to act negligently: actors are subject to liability for harm from concerted action when (all required): (1) they agree to engage in conduct that is negligent or reckless; (2) each engages in the agreed conduct; (3) at least one actor's agreed-to conduct factually causes physical, emotional, or dignitary harm to another; and (4) the harm is within the scope of liability of the agreed-to conduct. Their liability is joint and several unless a statute changes the rule. Aiding and abetting negligence: an actor is liable when (all required): (a) another commits a negligence tort causing physical, emotional, or dignitary harm to a third person; (b) the actor had actual knowledge that the other might engage in negligent or reckless conduct posing a risk to others; and (c) the actor substantially assisted or encouraged the other's conduct, and thereby increased the risk. A drag race (Bierczynski) fits both: an agreement to race recklessly, and mutual encouragement.

MAIN CASE Coney v. J.L.G. Industries, Inc. (Ill. 1983) — keeping joint and several liability Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 7.A Facts: Jasper was killed while operating a hydraulic aerial work platform made by J.L.G. Coney, as administrator of his estate, sued J.L.G. in products liability and negligence. J.L.G. argued that Jasper's employer was partly at fault and that, since Illinois had adopted pure comparative negligence, joint and several liability was abolished and its liability should be reduced by the employer's share. The question was certified to the Illinois Supreme Court. Held: Moran, J.: adopting comparative negligence does not require abolishing joint and several liability. Comparative negligence reduces the plaintiff's recovery by her own share of fault; it says nothing about relations among defendants. The injury remains indivisible, and the policy that the tortfeasor, not the injured plaintiff, should bear the risk of an insolvent co-defendant still applies. Affirmed and remanded. Why it matters: The traditional view: the risk of a defendant who cannot pay falls on the other defendants, not the plaintiff.

MAIN CASE Bartlett v. New Mexico Welding Supply, Inc. (N.M. App. 1982) — abolishing joint and several liability Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 7.A Facts: Bartlett was injured in an accident involving a New Mexico Welding vehicle and a third, unidentified car. The jury found Bartlett not negligent, New Mexico Welding 30% responsible, and the unknown driver 70%. Bartlett argued joint and several liability required New Mexico Welding to pay all his damages. The trial court ordered a new trial, and New Mexico Welding took an interlocutory appeal. Held: Wood, J.: in a pure comparative fault system, joint and several liability among concurrent tortfeasors is abolished. Fault-based apportionment should apply among defendants as it does between plaintiff and defendant, so each defendant pays only its own percentage. New Mexico Welding owed 30%. Reversed. Why it matters: The several-liability view: fault-based apportionment should run in all directions, and the plaintiff bears the risk of an unknown or insolvent defendant.

Approach | D1 60% (solvent), D2 40% (insolvent); P 0% at fault, $100,000 | Where
Joint and several | P collects $100,000 from D1. D1 seeks $40,000 contribution from D2 (worthless) | Coney; Delaware
Several only | P collects $60,000 from D1 and bears D2's $40,000 share | Bartlett
Hybrid: joint and several for economic damages only | D1 pays all economic damages and 60% of non-economic damages | California (Prop. 51)
