Hybrid: reallocation (R3d Apportionment) | The uncollectible share is reallocated among the solvent parties, including a plaintiff at fault, by their percentages | Minority

Satisfaction, release, and settlement

- One satisfaction: a plaintiff may obtain judgments against several tortfeasors but may collect full compensation only once. Full payment by one discharges the rest (Bundt).

- Release: at common law, releasing one joint tortfeasor released all. Today a release discharges only the person released unless it says otherwise (Cox; Uniform Contribution Among Tortfeasors Act). A covenant not to sue never discharged others.

- Credit for a settlement against the non-settling defendants' liability (any one approach): (1) pro tanto, a dollar-for-dollar reduction; (2) pro rata, a reduction by the settling defendant's per-capita share; or (3) proportionate share, a reduction by the settling defendant's percentage of fault (McDermott v. AmClyde, U.S. 1994, in admiralty).

MAIN CASE Bundt v. Embro (N.Y. Sup. Ct. 1965) — satisfaction by the state Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 7.B Facts: Two cars collided, and passengers sued the owners and drivers of both cars. The passengers had also sued the State of New York in the Court of Claims, for the same accident, and recovered judgments that the state paid. When the defendants learned of this, they moved to amend their answers to plead satisfaction and discharge. Held: Groat, J.: there is one wrong and one recovery. When a plaintiff receives full satisfaction from one joint tortfeasor, the others are discharged, and it does not matter that the payer was the state, which could only be sued in a different court. Motion granted. Why it matters: There is one injury and one recovery.

MAIN CASE Cox v. Pearl Investment Co. (Colo. 1969) — release with reservation Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 7.B Facts: Cox was injured on property owned by Pearl Investment and leased to Goodwill Industries. She settled with Goodwill for $2,500, signing an instrument that expressly reserved her right to sue anyone else who might be liable. When she sued Pearl, Pearl moved for summary judgment under the common-law rule that releasing one joint tortfeasor releases all. The trial court granted it. Held: Hodges, J.: an instrument that expressly reserves rights against other tortfeasors does not release them. (1) Contract law gives effect to the parties' intent, and Cox plainly did not intend to release Pearl; (2) there is no risk of double recovery, because Pearl gets credit for the $2,500; and (3) the nonsettling tortfeasor is helped, not hurt, by that credit. Reversed and remanded. Why it matters: The harsh common-law rule that releasing one released all gives way to the parties' intent.

MAIN CASE Elbaor v. Smith (Tex. 1992) — Mary Carter agreements Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 7.B Facts: Smith sued three doctors, Elbaor, Syrquin, and Stephens, for malpractice. Syrquin and Stephens entered a "Mary Carter" agreement: they guaranteed Smith $425,010 if she did not recover that much from Elbaor, and she would repay them from any recovery from Elbaor above that amount. They stayed in the case, and at trial their lawyers helped Smith against Elbaor. The jury found Elbaor 88% responsible and awarded $1,872,848 against him. Held: Gonzalez, J.: Mary Carter agreements are void as against public policy in Texas. They do not promote settlement, since they virtually guarantee a trial against the non-settling defendant, and they distort the trial by aligning supposed adversaries while the jury may not understand the true alignment. Reversed and remanded for a new trial. Why it matters: A Mary Carter agreement has (all required) (1) a settling defendant who stays in the case; (2) whose liability is reduced in proportion to the plaintiff's recovery from the non-settling defendants; and (3) whose agreement is often kept secret. Most states allow them with disclosure; Texas and a few others ban them. Dissent (Doggett, J.): the trial court disclosed the agreements to the jury and protected the adversarial process; so long as genuinely adverse parties remain, the search for truth is not impaired.

## 30. Contribution, Indemnity, and Apportionment WEEK 13
RULE Contribution A tortfeasor who pays more than its share of a common liability may recover the excess from other tortfeasors. It requires (all required): (1) common liability, so that the other tortfeasor was also liable to the plaintiff (Dreslin); (2) payment of more than the payer's fair share; and (3) no discharge of the other tortfeasor, as by a good-faith settlement (Slocum). Shares (one approach applies): (1) pro rata, equal shares per tortfeasor, under the older Uniform Contribution Among Tortfeasors Act (Delaware's version is 10 Del. C. § 6301 et seq.); or (2) comparative, in proportion to fault, in most comparative-fault states.

MAIN CASE Knell v. Feltman (D.C. Cir. 1949) — contribution without a joint judgment Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 7.C Facts: Langland, riding as a passenger in her friend Knell's car, was injured when it collided with Feltman's taxi. Because Knell was her friend, she sued only Feltman. Feltman filed a third-party complaint against Knell for contribution. The jury found both negligent. Held: Miller, J.: when an injury results from the concurrent negligence of two people who did not intend it, one who pays the judgment may obtain contribution from the other, even though the plaintiff did not obtain a joint judgment against both. Letting the plaintiff choose who pays the whole would be unjust and could invite collusion. Feltman could recover half. Affirmed. Why it matters: The common law barred contribution (Merryweather v. Nixan, 1799). Courts and statutes now allow it among negligent tortfeasors.

MAIN CASE Yellow Cab Co. of D.C., Inc. v. Dreslin (D.C. Cir. 1950) — contribution requires common liability Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 7.C Facts: Mrs. Dreslin was injured in a collision between a Yellow Cab and a car driven by her husband. Both drivers were negligent. She sued Yellow Cab, which cross-claimed against Mr. Dreslin for contribution toward whatever it paid her. Held: Proctor, J.: under interspousal immunity, the husband was not liable to his wife, so there was no common liability and no right of contribution. Allowing contribution would let the wife's recovery be shifted back to her husband indirectly, undercutting the immunity's purpose of preserving domestic peace. Affirmed. Why it matters: No liability to the plaintiff means no contribution. With immunities mostly abolished (§ 25), this matters less today.

MAIN CASE Slocum v. Donahue (Mass. App. 1998) — good-faith settlement bars contribution Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 7.C Facts: Donahue was backing his Ford out of his driveway when, he said, the engine raced and the car kept accelerating though he pressed the brake. It crossed the street, hit the curb, went airborne, and hit a fence, killing the Slocums' 18-month-old son. Donahue pleaded guilty to motor vehicle homicide; there was a vodka bottle under his seat. His expert blamed a defective floor mat. The Slocums sued Donahue, who brought in Ford for contribution and indemnity. Before trial, the Slocums settled with Ford for $150,000. The trial court dismissed Donahue's claims against Ford. Held: Under the Massachusetts contribution statute, a release given in good faith to one tortfeasor discharges it from liability for contribution to others. Donahue showed no collusion or bad faith: the amount was reasonable given the strong case against him, and the Slocums' use of experts Ford had retained was not collusive. Indemnity was unavailable because Donahue was not free of fault. Affirmed. Why it matters: Settlement bars encourage early settlement. Non-settling defendants get credit for the settlement, and they can challenge only its good faith.

RULE Indemnity Indemnity shifts the entire loss from one tortfeasor to another. It is available when (any one suffices): (1) a contract provides for it; (2) the payer was only vicariously liable for the other's tort, as an employer for an employee (§ 31); (3) the payer's fault was passive or secondary compared with the other's active or primary fault, under the traditional rule; or (4) a retailer who passed on a defective product seeks indemnity from the manufacturer. Many comparative-fault states replace the active-passive rule with comparative contribution.

RULE Settlement, indemnity, and contribution: R3d Misc. Prov., Apportionment Topic 6, §§ 34–36 (approved 2022) These sections state the rules for tort claims for economic harm, applying the general Apportionment rules. Settlement (§ 34): a nonsettling defendant gets a credit against the judgment equal to the settling person's percentage share of comparative responsibility (the proportionate-share approach), and neither the settling nor the nonsettling person may seek contribution from the other. Indemnity (§ 35): a person who discharges another's liability may recover the amount paid plus reasonable legal expenses if (any one suffices): (1) the indemnitor agreed by contract to indemnify; or (2) the indemnitee was liable only vicariously for the indemnitor's tort. Contribution (§ 36): a person who paid more than its share of comparative responsibility, and so discharged another's liability, may recover the excess from that person, except after a settlement, as above, or where indemnity is available instead.

MAIN CASE Bruckman v. Pena (Colo. App. 1971) — apportioning successive injuries Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 7.D Facts: On July 21, 1964, Pena was hurt in a collision caused by Bruckman, who was driving a truck owned by Armored. On June 11, 1965, Pena's injuries were aggravated in a second, unrelated accident. The jury was told to apportion his damages between the defendants and the later tortfeasor, but that "if you find the evidence does not permit such an apportionment, then the defendants are liable for the entire disability." It awarded $50,000. Held: Dwyer, J.: the plaintiff bears the burden of proving the damages the defendant's negligence caused. It was error to make the first tortfeasor liable for injuries from a later, independent accident just because apportionment is difficult. (A tortfeasor who aggravates a pre-existing condition is liable for the whole, but the reverse does not follow, since the first tortfeasor did not cause the later injury.) Reversed and remanded. Why it matters: Successive, independent injuries are apportioned. The first tortfeasor is liable for later aggravation only if it is a foreseeable result of the first injury, such as negligent medical treatment.

EXAM TIPS Exam tips 1. Plaintiff's fault. Apply the comparative fault threshold, then reduce the damages (§ 22). 2. Liability to the plaintiff. Joint and several, several, or hybrid? Divisible or indivisible harm? 3. Settlements. Is a settling defendant discharged? What credit do the others get? 4. Contribution and indemnity among defendants. Common liability? Pro rata or comparative shares? Grounds for full indemnity?

# PART XII — Vicarious Liability

## 31. Vicarious Liability WEEK 13
RULE Respondeat superior An employer is liable for an employee's tort when (all required): (1) the tortfeasor is an employee (a servant), meaning the employer controls or has the right to control the physical conduct of the work; and (2) the tort was committed within the scope of employment. Scope of employment, Restatement (Second) of Agency § 228 (all required): (a) the conduct is of the kind the employee is employed to perform; (b) it occurs substantially within the authorized time and space limits; (c) it is actuated, at least in part, by a purpose to serve the employer; and (d) if force is intentionally used, its use is not unexpectable by the employer.

- Rationales: the enterprise should bear the costs it creates as a cost of doing business; the employer can spread the loss and is best placed to prevent it; and the employer usually has the money.

- The employee remains liable. The employer who pays may seek indemnity from the employee (§ 30), though it rarely does.

- Going and coming rule: commuting is generally outside the scope of employment. Exceptions include special errands, travel required by the job, and risks created at work (Bussard).

- Frolic and detour: a minor deviation from the employer's business (detour) stays within the scope. A substantial departure for the employee's own purposes (frolic) does not, until the employee returns to the employer's business (O'Shea).

- Intentional torts are within the scope if done to further the employer's business or if they are a foreseeable, characteristic risk of the enterprise (Ira S. Bushey & Sons v. United States, 2d Cir. 1968: a drunken sailor opened a drydock's valves). Compare Western Union v. Hill (§ 3).

MAIN CASE Bussard v. Minimed, Inc. (Cal. App. 2003) — going and coming: a risk created at work Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 13.A Facts: Minimed had its offices sprayed with pesticide overnight. The next morning an employee, Hernandez, became ill from the fumes and left work early, declining to see the company doctor. Driving home, she rear-ended Bussard's car. Held: The going-and-coming rule does not apply when the employee's commute is affected by a risk arising from the job. The test is foreseeability in the respondeat superior sense: whether the conduct is so startling or unusual that it would be unfair to charge it to the business. Her impairment from workplace fumes was foreseeable. Summary judgment for Minimed was reversed. Why it matters: Foreseeability here asks whether the risk is typical of the enterprise, not the negligence version of foreseeability.

MAIN CASE O'Shea v. Welch (10th Cir. 2003) — frolic and detour Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 13.A Facts: Welch, an Osco Drug store manager, was driving his own car during work hours to Osco's district office to deliver Kansas City Chiefs tickets to other managers, a task done for the company. On a whim, he decided to pull into a service station to get an estimate on his car, turned left across traffic, and hit O'Shea's car. The district court granted summary judgment to Osco on vicarious liability. Held: McKay, J.: under Kansas law, as predicted, conduct reasonably incidental to the employment and foreseeable to the employer is within its scope. Under the "slight deviation" rule, a detour remains within the scope of employment; a frolic does not. A reasonable jury could find that a brief stop for a car estimate while on a work errand was a slight deviation. Reversed and remanded. Why it matters: The question is one of degree, so modern courts usually leave frolic and detour to the jury.

Independent contractors
RULE Employee or independent contractor: Restatement (Second) of Agency § 220(2) Whether a worker is a servant or an independent contractor is decided by the employer's right to control the details of the work. Factors (weighed together): (a) the extent of control which, by the agreement, the master may exercise over the details of the work; (b) whether or not the one employed is engaged in a distinct occupation or business; (c) the kind of occupation, and whether it is usually done under direction or by a specialist without supervision; (d) the skill required; (e) whether the employer or the worker supplies the instrumentalities, tools, and place of work; (f) the length of time for which the person is employed; (g) the method of payment, whether by the time or by the job; (h) whether or not the work is part of the regular business of the employer; (i) whether or not the parties believe they are creating a master-servant relationship; and (j) whether the principal is or is not in business.

MAIN CASE Murrell v. Goertz (Okla. App. 1979) — independent contractor Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 13.B Facts: Goertz delivered the Oklahoma Publishing Company's newspaper. He got into an argument with a customer, Murrell, and struck her. She sued Goertz and the publisher for assault and battery. Goertz had been hired by an independent distributor that contracted with the publisher; the publisher set general guidelines for delivery but did not supervise how carriers did their work. The trial court granted summary judgment for the publisher. Held: Reynolds, J.: an independent contractor is one who performs a service for another free from the other's control over the details of the work, except as to the result. The publisher had no direct relationship with Goertz and did not control his manner of delivery; general guidelines about results are not control. It is not vicariously liable. Affirmed. Why it matters: No vicarious liability for an independent contractor's torts, unless an exception applies.

Exceptions: the hiring party is liable for an independent contractor's negligence when (any one suffices): (1) the duty is nondelegable, as with duties imposed by statute or regulation for public safety (Maloney), duties of a possessor to invitees, and duties of a landlord to tenants; (2) the work is inherently dangerous (R2d §§ 416, 427); (3) the hirer was itself negligent in selecting, instructing, or supervising the contractor (direct liability, not vicarious); or (4) the contractor appeared to be the hirer's employee and the plaintiff relied on that appearance (apparent agency, as with hospital emergency rooms).
MAIN CASE Maloney v. Rath (Cal. 1968) — nondelegable statutory duty Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 13.B Facts: Rath's car hit Maloney's when its brakes failed. Three months earlier, Rath had had the brakes overhauled by a mechanic, Evanchick, whose negligent work caused the failure. Rath had no reason to know of the defect. The trial court entered judgment for Rath, because an owner is not liable for an independent contractor's negligence. Held: Traynor, J.: the statutory duty to maintain a car's brakes in good working order is nondelegable. An owner who hires an independent contractor to perform it is liable for the contractor's negligence, though the owner may seek indemnity from the contractor. This is not strict liability for brake failure; it refuses to let the owner shift responsibility to someone who may not be able to pay. Reversed. Why it matters: Traynor, J.: a nondelegable duty puts the loss on the person who benefits from the activity and can insure against it.

Joint enterprise, automobile owners, and imputed contributory negligence
RULE Joint enterprise (Popejoy) Each member of a joint enterprise is vicariously liable for the others' negligence in furthering it. A joint enterprise requires (all required): (1) an express or implied agreement among the members; (2) a common purpose to be carried out by the group; (3) a community of pecuniary interest in that purpose; and (4) an equal right to a voice in the direction of the enterprise, giving an equal right of control.

NOTE CASE Popejoy v. Steinle (Wyo. 1991) — no joint enterprise in family errands Source: 13th ed. Ch. 13.C (pages the syllabus skims) Facts: Mrs. Steinle was driving her daughter to buy a calf, which the daughter was to raise as a pet, when she collided with Popejoy's car. The Steinles owned a ranch, but the evidence was that the calf was not for the ranch business. Mrs. Steinle died in the accident. Popejoy, whose injuries first seemed minor, did not file a claim against her estate in time, and later sued Mr. Steinle's estate (he had since died) on the theory that he was vicariously liable as a member of a joint enterprise with his wife. The trial court granted summary judgment. Held: Golden, J.: a joint enterprise requires (1) an agreement; (2) a common purpose; (3) a community of pecuniary interest; and (4) an equal right of control. The pecuniary-interest element means the enterprise must be commercial and the act must further it. Buying a pet for their daughter was personal, so there was no joint enterprise, and a spouse is not vicariously liable for personal errands. Affirmed. Why it matters: Joint enterprise is mostly a business doctrine.

- Family purpose doctrine: the head of a household who provides a car for family members' use is liable for their negligent driving (Malchose, applying a totality-of-the-circumstances test). About a dozen states follow it.

- Owner-consent statutes make a car's owner liable for anyone driving with permission, often up to a cap.

- Negligent entrustment is the owner's own negligence in lending a car to an incompetent, inexperienced, or intoxicated driver. It is direct, not vicarious, liability.

- Imputed contributory negligence (the "both ways" rule): a driver's negligence is imputed to a plaintiff only if the plaintiff would be vicariously liable as a defendant for the driver's conduct (Smalich).

- Parents are not vicariously liable for their children's torts at common law. Statutes in most states impose limited liability for willful or malicious acts.

NOTE CASE Malchose v. Kalfell (N.D. 2003) — family purpose doctrine Source: 13th ed. Ch. 13.C (pages the syllabus skims) Facts: Eric Kalfell, an adult college student living away from home, struck a car driven by Kelly Malchose. She sued Eric for negligence and his parents, Lance and Lisa Kalfell, under the family purpose (family car) doctrine and for negligent entrustment. The parents were the titled owners, Eric listed their ranch as his address, they claimed him as a dependent, and they supported him at college; but Eric had used the car as loan collateral and had moved away. The trial court found Eric negligent and the parents liable under the family car doctrine. Held: Neumann, J.: the family car doctrine makes a head of household who furnishes a car for a family member's use, pleasure, or business liable for that member's negligent driving. Title is not required, and whether the doctrine applies depends on the totality of the circumstances. The parents' title, financial support, and dependency claim supported the finding, which was not clearly erroneous. Affirmed. Why it matters: Ownership of record is not required. What matters is who furnished and controlled the car for family use.

NOTE CASE Smalich v. Westfall (Pa. 1970) — imputed contributory negligence Source: 13th ed. Ch. 13.C (pages the syllabus skims) Facts: Smalich owned a car and was riding in it as a passenger while Westfall drove it with her permission. It collided with a car driven by Blank, and Smalich was killed. Her estate sued both drivers. The jury found for the estate against Blank and found that Westfall's negligence also caused the crash. The trial court entered judgment n.o.v. for Blank, imputing Westfall's negligence to Smalich as the owner. Held: Eagen, J.: a third person's negligence is imputed to a plaintiff only if their relationship would make the plaintiff vicariously liable as a defendant for that person's negligence. In car cases, only a master-servant relationship or joint enterprise justifies imputation. An owner-passenger ordinarily does not retain control over the details of driving, and the jury found no such control here. Reversed. Why it matters: The "both ways" test ties imputed contributory negligence to vicarious liability. Concurrence (Roberts, J.): imputed contributory negligence should be abolished entirely: a passenger cannot safely control a moving car even if he owns it.

# PART XIII — Strict Liability

## 32. Strict Liability: Animals and Abnormally Dangerous Activities WEEKS 13–14
Animals
Animal | Rule
Trespassing livestock | Strict liability for damage caused by livestock that trespass, except in "fencing-out" states, where the landowner must fence them out
Wild animals (wild by nature, such as bears or snakes) | Strict liability for harm resulting from the animal's dangerous propensities, even if the keeper used the utmost care (R2d § 507)
Domestic animals with known dangerous propensities | Strict liability once the keeper knows, or has reason to know, of the animal's abnormally dangerous tendency (scienter, the "one-bite rule"; R2d § 509). Many states impose strict liability for dog bites by statute.
Other domestic animals | Negligence only

MAIN CASE Sandy v. Bushey (Me. 1925) — contributory negligence no defense Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 14.A Facts: Sandy turned his horses out to pasture in a neighbor's field, where Bushey's horse was also pastured. Bushey knew his horse had vicious tendencies. While Sandy was in the pasture feeding his mare, Bushey's horse attacked and kicked him, seriously injuring him. Bushey pleaded Sandy's contributory negligence. Held: Sturgis, J.: the keeper of a domestic animal known to be vicious is strictly liable as an insurer; the plaintiff need prove only the keeping, the vicious propensity, and the keeper's knowledge (scienter). Because negligence is not the basis of liability, ordinary contributory negligence is no defense. Only a plaintiff who voluntarily and knowingly puts himself in harm's way, or provokes the animal, is barred. Defendant's motion overruled; judgment for Sandy. Why it matters: Contributory negligence does not bar strict liability, but knowingly encountering the danger does (R2d § 515).

Abnormally dangerous activities
MAIN CASE Rylands v. Fletcher (H.L. 1868) — the origin of strict liability for dangerous land uses Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 14.B Facts: Rylands, a mill owner, had a reservoir built on his land. The contractors did not seal abandoned mine shafts beneath it, and when the reservoir filled, the water broke through and flooded Fletcher's coal mine nearby. Rylands himself was not negligent. (The case was Fletcher v. Rylands below; the names reversed on appeal.) Held: Blackburn, J. (Exchequer Chamber): a person who brings onto his land and keeps there anything likely to do mischief if it escapes is strictly liable for the damage its escape naturally causes. Lord Cairns (House of Lords) limited this to a "non-natural use" of the land. Judgment for the mine owner. Why it matters: This is the source of strict liability for abnormally dangerous activities. Non-natural use came to mean an unusual use for the place, not merely something artificial.

RULE Abnormally dangerous activities: R2d §§ 519–520 One who carries on an abnormally dangerous activity is strictly liable for harm to the person, land, or chattels of another resulting from it, even if he exercised the utmost care (§ 519). The harm must be of the kind whose possibility makes the activity abnormally dangerous (Foster). Factors, § 520 (weighed together): (a) existence of a high degree of risk of some harm to the person, land, or chattels of others; (b) likelihood that the harm that results from it will be great; (c) inability to eliminate the risk by the exercise of reasonable care; (d) extent to which the activity is not a matter of common usage; (e) inappropriateness of the activity to the place where it is carried on; and (f) extent to which its value to the community is outweighed by its dangerous attributes. R3d § 20 (all required): (1) the activity creates a foreseeable and highly significant risk of physical harm even when reasonable care is exercised by all actors; and (2) the activity is not one of common usage.

- Typical examples: blasting (Spano, § 1), storing or using explosives, fumigation, crop dusting in some states, and certain toxic waste and hazardous chemical operations.

- Not usually: firearms use (Miller), driving, ordinary utilities, and transporting chemicals by rail (Indiana Harbor Belt).

- Policy: strict liability makes the actor consider the activity level and location, not just the care taken, because negligence law cannot reach the decision to do the activity at all (Posner in Indiana Harbor Belt).

MAIN CASE Miller v. Civil Constructors, Inc. (Ill. App. 1995) — firearms are not ultrahazardous Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 14.B Facts: Law enforcement officers were holding firearms practice at a gravel pit owned by Civil Constructors. Miller, on nearby property, was struck by a stray bullet that ricocheted out of the pit. He sued the pit's owners, including two counts of strict liability. The trial court dismissed the strict liability counts. Held: Bowman, J.: discharging firearms is not an ultrahazardous activity. Under the R2d § 520 factors, (1) reasonable care can make it safe, (2) guns are in common use, and (3) firearms practice at a gravel pit is appropriate to the place and has social value, especially for training police. Negligence, not strict liability, governs. Affirmed. Why it matters: Factor (c), whether reasonable care can eliminate the risk, often decides the case.

MAIN CASE Indiana Harbor Belt R.R. Co. v. American Cyanamid Co. (7th Cir. 1990) — shipping hazardous chemicals Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 14.B Facts: American Cyanamid, a chemical manufacturer, loaded 20,000 gallons of liquid acrylonitrile, a flammable and toxic chemical, into a leased rail tank car bound for New Jersey. At Indiana Harbor Belt's switching yard in suburban Chicago, about 5,000 gallons leaked from a faulty lid or valve. Nearby homes were evacuated, and the railroad spent about $981,000 on cleanup, which state authorities required. It sued the shipper. The district court held the shipper strictly liable. Held: Posner, J.: shipping acrylonitrile by rail is not abnormally dangerous. Strict liability is for activities whose risks cannot be eliminated by due care, so that the only way to reduce them is to change the activity's level or location. This spill resulted from carelessness, which negligence law can deter. Rerouting hazardous shipments around Chicago's rail hub is impractical, and the shipper did not control the car in transit. The relevant activity is transporting the chemical, not the chemical itself. Reversed and remanded for trial on negligence. Why it matters: Strict liability is for risks that care cannot prevent. Ask who controls the activity and whether a change in activity level or location is the real solution.

MAIN CASE Foster v. Preston Mill Co. (Wash. 1954) — harm outside the risk Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 14.C Facts: Foster raised mink on a ranch about two and a quarter miles from where Preston Mill was blasting to build a logging road. Mink are very nervous animals. The blasts frightened the mother mink during whelping season, and they killed their kittens. Foster told the company, which kept blasting. The trial court awarded Foster $1,953.68 on strict liability. Held: Hamley, J.: strict liability for an ultrahazardous activity covers only harm that results from the risk that makes the activity ultrahazardous, such as debris and concussion. The mink's reaction to noise and vibration came from their exceedingly nervous disposition, not from the normal risks of blasting. Reversed. Why it matters: The scope limit for strict liability works like proximate cause. Note also the abnormally sensitive activity of the plaintiff.

MAIN CASE Golden v. Amory (Mass. 1952) — act of God Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 14.C Facts: Amory and others owned a hydroelectric plant with a dike along a river. During a hurricane, the river flooded to unprecedented heights, and water overflowed and damaged the Goldens' land. The Goldens sued on strict liability (Rylands) and negligence. Held: Lummus, J.: the strict liability rule for the escape of stored water does not apply when the escape results from an act of God the owner had no reason to anticipate. The flood was beyond anyone's anticipation, and negligence was not shown. Exceptions overruled; judgment for the defendants. Why it matters: An unforeseeable force of nature is a defense to strict liability. A foreseeable storm is not.

EXAM TIPS Exam tips Defenses to strict liability: assumption of risk (knowing, voluntary exposure) and the plaintiff's abnormally sensitive activity are defenses. Ordinary contributory negligence is not (Sandy), but most comparative-fault states now compare it. Plead negligence too. If the activity fails the § 520 factors, the plaintiff still has a negligence claim. Products liability is the other major strict liability field (13th ed. Ch. 15), but it is not on the syllabus.

# PART XIV — Nuisance

## 33. Private Nuisance WEEK 15
RULE Private nuisance: R2d §§ 821D, 822 The defendant is liable when (all required): (1) its conduct is a legal cause of (2) a substantial invasion of the plaintiff's interest in the private use and enjoyment of land, and (3) the invasion is either (a) intentional and unreasonable, or (b) unintentional and otherwise actionable under the rules for negligent or reckless conduct or for abnormally dangerous conditions or activities.

- Plaintiff: a person with a possessory or property interest in the land, such as an owner or a tenant. A buyer of the land cannot sue the seller in nuisance (Philadelphia Electric).

- Substantial: a definite offensiveness, annoyance, or inconvenience to a normal person in the community, not a hypersensitive one.

- Intentional (R2d § 825): the defendant acts for the purpose of causing the invasion, or knows it is resulting or substantially certain to result. Continuing after notice of the harm makes an invasion intentional (Morgan).

- Nuisance and trespass: trespass protects exclusive possession against physical entry; nuisance protects use and enjoyment against noise, odors, smoke, vibration, light, and the like. The same conduct can be both.

RULE Unreasonableness: R2d §§ 826–828 An intentional invasion is unreasonable if (any one suffices): (a) the gravity of the harm outweighs the utility of the actor's conduct; or (b) the harm caused by the conduct is serious, and the financial burden of compensating for this and similar harm to others would not make the continuation of the conduct not feasible. Gravity of the harm, § 827 (weighed together): (a) the extent of the harm involved; (b) the character of the harm involved; (c) the social value that the law attaches to the type of use or enjoyment invaded; (d) the suitability of the particular use or enjoyment invaded to the character of the locality; and (e) the burden on the person harmed of avoiding the harm. Utility of the conduct, § 828 (weighed together): (a) the social value that the law attaches to the primary purpose of the conduct; (b) the suitability of the conduct to the character of the locality; and (c) the impracticability of preventing or avoiding the invasion.

MAIN CASE Morgan v. High Penn Oil Co. (N.C. 1953) — intentional nuisance despite due care Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 16.A Facts: Morgan owned a nine-acre tract with his home, a restaurant, and a trailer park. High Penn built an oil refinery on adjoining land about 1,000 feet from his house. Several days a week the refinery emitted nauseating gases and odors that made people on Morgan's land sick and interfered with their use of it. High Penn kept operating after notice and demand to abate. It argued that its plant was modern and carefully run, so without negligence it could not be liable. Held: Ervin, J.: a person who intentionally creates or maintains a private nuisance is liable for the resulting injury, regardless of the care or skill used to avoid it. The refinery was a nuisance in fact because of its location and operation, and continuing after notice made the invasion intentional. Negligence is not an element. The court found error on another point and ordered a new trial. Why it matters: Intentional nuisance does not depend on negligence. Due care is not a defense.

MAIN CASE Carpenter v. Double R Cattle Co. (Idaho 1985) — balancing harm and utility Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 16.A Facts: Homeowners sued Double R, whose feedlot had expanded to about 9,000 cattle, complaining of manure, odors, flies, and river pollution. The trial court refused instructions based on R2d § 826(b), which allows a nuisance finding when the harm is serious and the defendant could pay damages and still operate, even if the activity's utility outweighs the harm. The jury, told to weigh utility against harm, found for Double R. The court of appeals reversed. Held: Bakes, J.: Idaho declines to adopt § 826(b). A nuisance is not found where the utility of the activity outweighs the gravity of the harm. People in a developing state must accept some interference for the sake of important industries like cattle feeding. The trial court's instructions were correct. Court of appeals reversed; jury verdict reinstated. Why it matters: Courts are split on § 826(b), which separates whether the defendant must pay from whether the conduct must stop. Dissent (Bistline, J.): § 826(b) would require the feedlot to pay for the serious harm it causes without shutting it down; refusing even damages leaves the neighbors without any remedy for a real wrong.

NOTE CASE Philadelphia Electric Co. v. Hercules, Inc. (3d Cir. 1985) — no nuisance claim by a buyer against a seller Source: 13th ed. Ch. 16.A Facts: Pennsylvania Industrial Chemical operated a hydrocarbon resin plant on a site in Chester, Pennsylvania, on the Delaware River. It sold the site to Gould, which later sold it to Philadelphia Electric (PECO). Hercules acquired Pennsylvania Industrial and assumed its liabilities. Resins and chemicals from the old operations were found seeping into the river, and the state required PECO to clean up, at a cost of about $400,000. PECO sued Hercules in private and public nuisance. The jury found for PECO. Held: Higginbotham, J.: a buyer of land cannot sue the seller in private nuisance. The duty not to maintain a nuisance runs to neighboring owners and occupiers, not to a later buyer of the same land, whose remedies lie in the sale contract under caveat emptor. PECO also could not sue for public nuisance, because it suffered no injury different in kind from the public's (cleanup costs it was ordered to bear are not special injury). Reversed. Why it matters: Private nuisance protects neighbors. Public nuisance requires special injury (§ 34).

- Coming to the nuisance: a plaintiff who moves next to an existing nuisance is not barred, but the priority of the defendant's use is a factor in reasonableness and remedy (Spur, § 34).

- Right-to-farm statutes in most states protect established agricultural operations from nuisance suits by later neighbors.

- Bias lens: polluting land uses have long been sited near low-income communities and communities of color, the subject of the environmental justice movement. The § 827(d) factor, suitability to "the character of the locality," can entrench that pattern if the locality's character is the product of past siting decisions.

## 34. Public Nuisance and Nuisance Remedies WEEK 15
RULE Public nuisance: R2d § 821B A public nuisance is an unreasonable interference with a right common to the general public. Circumstances that may make it unreasonable (any one suffices): (a) the conduct involves a significant interference with the public health, the public safety, the public peace, the public comfort, or the public convenience; (b) the conduct is proscribed by a statute, ordinance, or administrative regulation; or (c) the conduct is of a continuing nature or has produced a permanent or long-lasting effect, and the actor knows or has reason to know that it has a significant effect upon the public right. Who may sue, § 821C: a public official, or a private person who suffered harm of a kind different from that suffered by the general public (special injury). A private plaintiff need not own land.

- Examples: blocking a public road or waterway, polluting a public water supply, operating an illegal business, and keeping a dangerous condition on a public way.

- Special injury: personal injury, property damage, or a distinct business loss usually qualifies. Greater inconvenience of the same kind usually does not.

- Modern mass litigation: states and cities have used public nuisance against makers of lead paint, opioids, and fossil fuels, with mixed results. Several state high courts (e.g., Oklahoma, 2021) have refused to extend it to the sale of lawful products.

Remedies
MAIN CASE Boomer v. Atlantic Cement Co. (N.Y. 1970) — permanent damages instead of an injunction Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 16.B Facts: Atlantic Cement built a $45 million cement plant near Albany that employed more than 300 people. Neighbors sued for injunctions and damages, alleging dirt, smoke, and vibration from the plant damaged their property. The trial court found a nuisance but refused an injunction, awarding temporary damages to the time of trial and leaving the neighbors to bring successive suits for later damages. Held: Bergan, J.: New York's rule was that a nuisance causing substantial damage must be enjoined, even if the defendant's cost of abating far exceeds the harm. But closing the plant would be drastic, and controlling air pollution is a matter for government, not private litigation. The court ordered an injunction that would be vacated once the plant paid permanent damages for the present and future harm to the plaintiffs' land, in effect granting the plant a servitude. Reversed and remanded to set permanent damages. Why it matters: The defendant can, in effect, buy a servitude to pollute. The dissent (Jasen, J.) said this licenses a continuing wrong and removes the incentive to reduce pollution. Dissent (Jasen, J.): the majority licenses a continuing wrong; once permanent damages are paid, the incentive to reduce pollution disappears, and the neighbors are forced to accept a servitude for a private party's benefit, a kind of inverse condemnation without public use.

MAIN CASE Spur Industries, Inc. v. Del E. Webb Development Co. (Ariz. 1972) — compensated injunction Source: principal case, 13th ed. Ch. 16.B Facts: Spur ran a large cattle feedlot west of Phoenix in an area long devoted to farming. Del Webb bought cheaper farmland nearby and developed Sun City, a retirement community. As it grew, it came within 500 feet of the feedlot, and flies and odor drifted over the homes, discouraging buyers. Webb sued to enjoin the feedlot as a public nuisance. An Arizona statute defined a public nuisance to include a place in a populous area that breeds disease-carrying flies. The trial court enjoined the feedlot but gave Spur no compensation. Held: Cameron, V.C.J.: (1) the feedlot, lawful when established, had become a public nuisance to the residents of Sun City, who were entitled to relief, so the injunction was proper even though Webb itself "came to the nuisance" and would have been barred if it alone were injured; (2) but because Webb, for profit, brought the people to the nuisance, it must indemnify Spur for a reasonable amount of the cost of moving or shutting down. Affirmed as to the injunction; remanded to fix the indemnity. Why it matters: The court protected the residents, who had a right to relief, while making the developer who created the conflict pay. This is the "fourth rule" in the table below.

Rule | Who wins | Remedy | Case
1 | The plaintiff | Injunction: the defendant must stop | Morgan; the traditional rule
2 | The plaintiff | Damages only: the defendant may continue and pay | Boomer
3 | The defendant | No nuisance: the plaintiff must tolerate the harm or buy the defendant out | Carpenter
4 | The plaintiff, at a price | Injunction conditioned on the plaintiff compensating the defendant | Spur

NOTE The four rules are from Calabresi & Melamed, Property Rules, Liability Rules, and Inalienability (Harv. L. Rev. 1972). On an essay, argue for the remedy that fits the facts: the relative harms, who came first, the number of people affected, and whether a court can supervise the remedy.

ROADMAP Negligence essay roadmap (all required) 1. Duty. Is there a general duty of reasonable care (affirmative conduct)? If the claim is failure to act, does an exception apply (§ 21)? Is the plaintiff foreseeable (Palsgraf)? Premises: what is the entrant's status (§ 26)? 2. Standard of care. Reasonable person, adjusted for children, disability, emergency, or a professional (§§ 12–13). Is there a statute supporting negligence per se (§ 14)? 3. Breach. Apply the Hand formula or the risk-utility factors to the specific precaution not taken (§ 11). Custom (Trimarco). Proof: notice, mode of operation, res ipsa (§§ 15–16). 4. Cause in fact. But-for; substantial factor for multiple sufficient causes; Summers or Sindell for unidentified defendants; lost chance (§§ 17–18). 5. Proximate cause. Foreseeable type of harm (Wagon Mound); eggshell plaintiff; intervening causes within the risk (Derdiarian), rescuers, medical treatment; superseding crimes (§§ 19–20). 6. Damages. Compensatory elements, collateral source, mitigation; punitive damages if reckless or malicious (§§ 27–28). 7. Defenses. Comparative fault (do the math), assumption of risk (which kind?), statute of limitations (discovery rule), immunities (§§ 22–25). 8. Allocation. Vicarious liability (scope, independent contractors, nondelegable duties); joint and several or several; contribution and indemnity (§§ 29–31).

Strict liability and nuisance at a glance
Claim | Fault needed? | Core test | Main defenses
Wild animals | No | Harm from the animal's dangerous propensity | Assumption of risk
Domestic animal with known vicious propensity | No (knowledge required) | Scienter | Assumption of risk; not contributory negligence (Sandy)
Abnormally dangerous activity | No | R2d § 520 factors; harm within the risk (Foster) | Act of God (Golden); assumption of risk; abnormally sensitive plaintiff
Private nuisance (intentional) | No negligence needed | Substantial and unreasonable invasion of use and enjoyment | Utility outweighs harm (Carpenter); coming to the nuisance as a factor
Public nuisance | Varies | Unreasonable interference with a public right; special injury for private plaintiffs | No special injury (Philadelphia Electric)

TRAP Common mistakes on Torts exams Treating intent as a desire to harm. Intent is purpose or knowledge of the consequence, and motive does not matter. Forgetting that assault needs awareness and battery does not. Applying transferred intent to IIED or conversion. Allowing deadly force to protect property. Calling a statute violation negligence per se without checking class of persons, type of harm, and excuse. Skipping cause in fact and jumping to proximate cause. Treating every intervening crime as superseding. Ask whether it was within the risk. Ignoring the jurisdiction's comparative fault threshold, or doing no arithmetic. Calling a failure to rescue negligence without first finding a duty to act. Assuming an employer is liable for an independent contractor without checking the exceptions.

EXAM TIPS Working the three parts of the final Closed-book short essay (30 minutes): state the rule with its labeled elements, apply each element to the facts, and conclude. Use case names only when they help. Closed-book multiple choice (30 questions, 60 minutes): about two minutes each. Identify the issue before reading the choices, and watch for the element the facts leave out. Open-book essay (90 minutes): spend the first 15 minutes on an issue list built from the roadmaps above. Use this outline's tables to check elements, not to look up rules for the first time. Argue both sides on reasonableness, proximate cause, and policy, then pick the better answer.

# Restatement (Third) of Torts: Miscellaneous Provisions

Subject: Torts | Type: Document | URL: https://supertoadman.github.io/Wilmington-University-corner/subjects/torts/torts-restatement/

The Sections of the Restatement (Third) of Torts: Miscellaneous Provisions (Tentative Draft No. 3, April 2024) that the Torts outline relies on. Statutes of limitations and repose (§§ 1–16), aiding and abetting, agreements to act negligently, the firefighter's rule, and liability for providing alcohol have their black letter, Comments, and Illustrations. The Sections the ALI membership approved in 2022 (Apportionment §§ 4 A–4 B and 27–37, Immunities §§ 1–10A, and Loss of Consortium §§ 48 A–48 C) appear as black letter only, as the draft prints them. Search by word, by "exact phrase" in quotes, or by section number (type 3 for the discovery rule), filter by outline topic, and open or close the Comments. The Projects number their Sections separately, so Immunities § 6 and Limitations § 6 are different Sections.

## § 1 Definition of Statute of Limitations
Topics: Statutes of Limitation and Repose (§ 24)

A statute of limitations is a statute that provides a plaintiff a legislatively defined period of time to sue on a cause of action against a defendant and that bars the cause of action after the legislatively defined period has expired without suit being brought.
Comment a: Scope and cross-references. This Section and the other Sections in Part 1 supersede Restatement Second, Torts § 899. For the definition of statutes of repose, see § 12. For the difference between statutes of limitations and statutes of repose, see § 12, Comment a. The terms “plaintiff” and “defendant” include potential plaintiffs and defendants for an action that has not yet been brought. For the doctrine of laches applicable to suits for injunctions and other specific relief, see Restatement Third, Torts: Remedies § 53 (Tentative Draft No. 3, 2024). The term “statute of limitations” is used to refer both to the statutes themselves and to the limitations periods established by those statutes, as in the title of Topic 2, “When the Statute of Limitations Begins to Run.”
Comment b: History of statutes of limitations. At common law, there was no counterpart of today’s statutes of limitations. The first general statute of limitations was the English Limitation Act of 1623, 21 Jac. 1, c. 16. That statute formed the model for the statutes of limitations that are found throughout the United States today.
Comment c: Statutes of limitations are statutes, and the language of each statute controls. The law restated by The American Law Institute’s Restatements “is generally common law, the law developed and articulated by judges in the course of deciding specific cases.” THE AMERICAN LAW INSTITUTE, CAPTURING THE VOICE OF THE AMERICAN LAW INSTITUTE: A HANDBOOK FOR ALI REPORTERS AND THOSE WHO REVIEW THEIR WORK 4 (rev. ed. 2015). Like the common law itself, every Restatement rule is subject to a statute that dictates a different result. Id. at 9. Here, as elsewhere, when a statute resolves the issue, that statute governs.

Certain subject matters dealing with statutes of limitations have been the subject of extensive common-law development. This Restatement focuses on the areas in which courts have developed common-law rules dealing with statutes of limitations, which are listed in Comment d. This Restatement does not include coverage of areas that are governed by constitutional provisions, statutes, or procedural rules, which are described in Comment e.
Comment d: Topics covered by this Part. As explained in Comment c, the topics relating to statutes of limitations that are covered by this Part are the topics that have been developed by the courts as a matter of common law. These topics are as follows:

Topic 2 addresses the question of when statutes of limitations begin to run. Topic 3 deals with the issue of when the running of statutes of limitations is suspended (or “tolled”). Most forms of tolling are creatures of statute; these statutory forms of tolling are briefly described, but not restated, in Topic 3. Some forms of tolling are matters of common law; these forms of tolling are restated in Topic 3.

Topic 4 concerns the effect of defendant misconduct on statutes of limitations, under the doctrines of equitable estoppel and fraudulent concealment.

Topic 5 deals with contracts shortening or lengthening the statute-of-limitations period.
Comment e: Topics not covered by this Part. Coverage of statutes of limitations in this Part does not include topics relating to statutes of limitations that are governed by constitutional provisions, statutes, or procedural rules. Among the topics not covered are the following:

Jurisdictions typically have multiple statutes of limitations. Which statutes of limitations apply to which causes of action is a fertile source of litigation. The outcome of such litigation is highly dependent on the language of the statutes, and this Part makes no attempt to restate such issues.

As mentioned in Comment d, most forms of tolling of statutes of limitations are creatures of statute. Common statutory forms of tolling are listed in § 5, Comment b, but no attempt is made to restate them in this Part.

As noted in Comment c, this Restatement does not address constitutional questions relating to the establishment or modification of statutes of limitations. Nor does it discuss procedural questions, including what a plaintiff needs to do in order to bring an action within the limitations period, and what a plaintiff can do to correct procedural missteps or avoid their consequences.

Lastly, because this Restatement addresses the application of statutes of limitations to common-law torts, this Restatement does not cover the application of statutes of limitations to statutory causes of action, although some such cases are considered when they illustrate rules that also apply to common-law torts.
Comment f: Purposes of statutes of limitations. Statutes of limitations reflect a legislative balancing of two conflicting purposes. On the one hand, statutes of limitations seek to afford plaintiffs a legislatively defined reasonable period of time in which to sue. On the other hand, statutes of limitations seek to protect defendants against having to confront stale causes of action when memories may have dimmed and evidence may have been lost. They aim to achieve this goal by barring causes of action after the legislatively defined reasonable period of time has expired without suit being brought.

Both of these purposes of statutes of limitations have a public as well as a private dimension. The purpose of providing plaintiffs a reasonable opportunity to bring their causes of action is supported by the public interest in resolving cases on the merits and affording redress for violations of legal rights. The purpose of protecting defendants against stale causes of action reflects the public interest in avoiding the diversion of judicial and societal resources to the litigation of untimely causes of action and the public interest in the greater accuracy of decisionmaking when memories and evidence are fresh.
Comment g: Statutes of limitations apply separately to each cause of action by each plaintiff against each defendant. As the black letter of this Section implies, each cause of action by each plaintiff against each defendant must be analyzed separately for statute-of-limitations purposes. A single transaction or occurrence may give rise to multiple causes of action. For example, a single transaction or occurrence may give rise to causes of action for fraud, negligent misrepresentation, professional malpractice, and breach of fiduciary duty. Each such cause of action must be analyzed separately for statute-of-limitations purposes. Different causes of action are often governed by statutes of limitations of different lengths, and the running of the statutes may start or be suspended at different times. As a result, depending on the facts and the applicable statutes, some causes of action arising from a transaction or occurrence may be time-barred, while others may not be.

The fact that each cause of action arising from a transaction or occurrence is considered separately for statute-of-limitations purposes contrasts with the broader definition of “claim” for purposes of claim preclusion under the Restatement of the Law Second, Judgments. Under that Restatement, the term “claim” includes “all rights of the plaintiff to remedies against the defendant with respect to all or any part of the transaction, or series of connected transactions, out of which the claim arose.” Id. § 24(1). The reason for this broader definition of “claim” in the Restatement of the Law Second, Judgments, is to avoid wasteful and unnecessary litigation by requiring that all claims arising from the same transaction or series of connected transactions be brought together, regardless of the legal theory on which such claims are based. Id. § 24, Comment a. In the case of statutes of limitations, this rationale necessarily yields to the fact that statutes of limitations often treat different causes of action differently.
Comment h: The role of federal law. When claims are brought under the Federal Tort Claims Act, 28 U.S.C. § 1346(b)(1), or under Section 1983, 42 U.S.C. § 1983, federal common law governs when the statute of limitations begins to run and the effect of defendant misconduct thereon. As a result, the federal courts in such cases act as another source of common law to be considered by the Institute in preparing this Restatement—a source entitled to respectful consideration, but not to determinative significance. This contrasts with situations in which the Institute is restating subjects governed exclusively by federal law, in which decisions of the Supreme Court of the United States are generally treated by the Institute as authoritative. For an example of a situation in which the rule adopted by this Restatement differs from the rule in the federal courts, see § 3, Comment d (addressing the facts that must be known by the plaintiff in order to start the running of the statute of limitations under the discovery rule restated in § 3).
Comment i: Statutes of limitations do not apply to defenses and recoupment. Although a cause of action that has not been brought within the statute-of-limitations period may not be asserted as an independent basis for relief, such a cause of action may be asserted by way of a defense or counterclaim for recoupment in response to an action brought by the opposing party arising out of the same transaction or occurrence. In that scenario, the otherwise barred cause of action may be asserted solely as a partial or complete defense or offset to the opposing party’s claim and not as a basis for affirmative relief against the opposing party.

Illustration:

1. Dogged Law Firm commits malpractice while representing Pinnacle LLC. Pinnacle is aware of the malpractice, and it therefore does not pay Dogged’s bill. Dogged waits until the statute of limitations has expired on Pinnacle’s malpractice cause of action and then sues Pinnacle for the unpaid bill. Pinnacle defends against Dogged’s action by contending that Dogged committed malpractice. Pinnacle may use the time-barred malpractice cause of action as a defense or offset against Dogged’s action, but Pinnacle may not obtain an affirmative recovery against Dogged on the time-barred malpractice cause of action.
Comment j: Presumptions in favor of or against statutes of limitations. Courts in nine jurisdictions maintain that, when there is doubt about whether the statute of limitations bars the action, the statute should be interpreted so as to enable the plaintiff to proceed on the merits. Courts in 11 states declare that statutes of limitations are favored and should be construed in favor of the defendant seeking to bar the claim. In at least one state, California, case law provides that statutes of limitations should be neither favored nor disfavored. The remaining states have not directly addressed the matter. Because neither of the two opposing presumptions enjoys more than limited support, and because the issue is one to be decided by each state based on its own standards of statutory construction, this Restatement takes no position on the matter.

## § 2 When the Statute of Limitations Begins to Run—All-Elements Rule
Topics: Statutes of Limitation and Repose (§ 24)

Except as otherwise provided in § 3 (discovery rule) or § 4 (continuing torts), the statute of limitations begins to run on a cause of action when all of the necessary elements of the cause of action have occurred.
Comment a: History, cross-references, and support. This Section and the other Sections in Part 1 supersede Restatement Second, Torts § 899. The terms “plaintiff” and “defendant” include potential plaintiffs and defendants for an action that has not yet been brought. For the doctrine of laches applicable to suits for injunctions and other specific relief, see Restatement Third, Torts: Remedies § 53 (Tentative Draft No. 3, 2024). This Section and the other Sections in Part 1 are subject to the contrary terms of any applicable statute. See § 1, Comment c. The rule of this Section is applied separately to each cause of action by each plaintiff against each defendant. See § 1, Comment g.

The rule that the statute of limitations starts to run when all elements of the cause of action have occurred enjoys overwhelming support. This Restatement uses the term “all-elements rule” as a shorthand for the rule.

As stated in the black letter, the all-elements rule is subject to the discovery rule (§ 3) and the special rules that address the narrow category of claims that are denominated “continuing torts” (§ 4).
Comment b: Rationale of the all-elements rule. The all-elements rule is a straightforward consequence of the basic purposes of statutes of limitations. One of those purposes is to provide plaintiffs with a legislatively defined reasonable period of time within which to sue on their causes of action. See § 1, Comment f. This purpose can be achieved only if plaintiffs are able to sue on their causes of action during the period when the statute of limitations is running. If the statute of limitations were to begin to run before a plaintiff is able to sue, the result would be that plaintiffs would have less time in which to file suit than the legislature intended to allow, and, in some cases, plaintiffs could lose the right to bring a cause of action without ever having been able to bring it. The latter result is possible under statutes of repose (see § 12, Comments b, d), but not under statutes of limitations.

Many statutes and courts state that the statute of limitations begins to run on a cause of action when the cause of action “accrues.” The primary meaning of the word “accrue” is “[t]o come into existence as an enforceable claim or right; to arise.” BLACK’S LAW DICTIONARY (11th ed. 2019). Therefore, the statement that the statute of limitations begins to run when a cause of action accrues means that the statute of limitations begins to run when the cause of action becomes an enforceable claim, i.e., when all the necessary elements of the cause of action have occurred.
Comment c: The injury rule: an imperfect substitute for the all-elements rule. With some frequency, courts say that the statute of limitations starts to run on a tort cause of action when the tort produces injury. Such courts often appear to believe that this injury rule is equivalent to the all-elements rule—which is frequently, but not inevitably, true.

The injury rule will produce the same results as the all-elements rule if and only if two conditions are satisfied: (1) injury is an essential element of the cause of action, and (2) injury is the last element to occur. If either of these conditions is not satisfied, the injury rule will not yield the same results as the all-elements rule.

An example of a tort for which condition (1) above is not satisfied is the tort of assault. Although anticipation of an imminent harmful or offensive contact is a necessary element of the tort of assault, physical or emotional injury is not. See Restatement Third, Torts: Intentional Torts to Persons § 105, Comment c and Illustration 1 (Tentative Draft No. 1, 2015). Therefore, the statute of limitations starts to run when the tort of assault is committed, regardless of whether the tort has caused any injury. See Comment f(2) below. Under the injury rule, the statute of limitations would never run on an assault that produced no injury. That is not the law.

An example of a tort for which condition (2) above is not satisfied is the tort of malicious prosecution. A necessary element of the tort of malicious prosecution is a favorable termination of the underlying criminal prosecution. Restatement Third, Torts: Liability for Economic Harm §§ 21(d), 23. This element normally occurs long after the underlying criminal prosecution has started to injure the plaintiff. Under the all-elements rule, the statute of limitations does not start to run until the favorable termination of the underlying criminal prosecution. See Comment f(4) below. Under the injury rule, the statute of limitations would start to run (and perhaps run its full course) before the malicious prosecution action could be initiated.

Because the injury rule cannot be relied on to produce the same results as the all-elements rule, use of the injury rule should be avoided.
Comment d: Latent or speculative injuries. In the case of so-called latent injuries, it may take years before a plaintiff who has been exposed to a harmful product or substance manifests a legally cognizable physical injury. In such a case, the statute of limitations does not start to run until the injury becomes sufficient to constitute a legally cognizable physical injury. This is not the result of a special rule for latent injuries. Instead, it represents a straightforward application of the all-elements rule.

Illustration:

1. Paolo is exposed to asbestos in 2005. Paolo first manifests sufficient injury from the asbestos exposure to allow him to sue for physical injury in 2020, when Paolo is diagnosed with asbestosis resulting from the exposure. The statute of limitations does not start to run on Paolo’s asbestosis claim until 2020.

Similarly, the statute of limitations does not start to run on a tort cause of action for which injury is a necessary element at a time when no injury has occurred. This rule follows from the fact that the plaintiff cannot sue on such a cause of action when there has been no injury.

This rule often finds application in legal malpractice cases. See Restatement of the Law Third, The Law Governing Lawyers § 54, Comment g. For example, if a lawyer commits legal malpractice by advising a client to enter into a transaction that exposes the client to unnecessary federal-income-tax liability, the statute of limitations does not start to run when the client enters into the underlying transaction, because, at that time, it remains speculative and unknowable whether the client will ever be subject to such additional tax liability. Instead, the statute of limitations begins to run at a time when it becomes foreseeable that the client will suffer an additional tax liability, such as when the client receives a notice of deficiency from the Internal Revenue Service. Similarly, in cases involving legal malpractice in an underlying litigation, the statute of limitations does not start to run until all appeals in the underlying litigation are exhausted or the matter is otherwise final. In addition, in cases involving legal malpractice, the continuous representation rule sometimes applies. For discussion, see § 6.

One specific application of the rule that speculative injury does not start the running of the statute of limitations is furnished by cases in which, at the time when the plaintiff first manifests sufficient symptoms of one disease to start the statute of limitations running with respect to causes of action concerning that disease, it is uncertain whether or not the plaintiff will later develop a separate and distinct disease resulting from the same exposure. If the plaintiff later develops that separate and distinct disease, the statute of limitations with respect to claims for that disease starts to run when that disease manifests itself sufficiently to allow an action to be brought on it, not from the earlier date when the first disease manifested itself.

Illustration:

2. Same facts as Illustration 1, except that, now, three years after he is diagnosed with asbestosis, in 2023, Paolo is diagnosed with mesothelioma, a separate and distinct disease. In 2020, when the statute of limitations began to run on Paolo’s asbestosis claim, it was speculative and uncertain that Paolo would later develop mesothelioma. The statute of limitations did not start to run on Paolo’s mesothelioma claim in 2020 when Paolo was diagnosed with asbestosis. Instead, the statute of limitations begins to run on Paolo’s mesothelioma claim in 2023, when that illness is diagnosed.
Comment e: Occurrence of additional injury does not restart statute of limitations. Once the statute of limitations has started to run on a tort cause of action because all the necessary elements of the cause of action have occurred, including some legally cognizable injury, the subsequent occurrence of additional injury resulting from the same tort does not restart the running of the statute of limitations. If the rule were otherwise, the statute of limitations would never expire so long as additional injuries continued to occur. (As explained in Comment d, the rule described in this Comment does not apply to a cause of action for future injury of a separate and distinct type whose occurrence is speculative and uncertain at the time the statute of limitations starts to run on the initial injury.)

Illustration:

3. Same facts as Illustration 2, except that, now, one year after Paolo is diagnosed with mesothelioma, Paolo’s mesothelioma dramatically worsens. Paolo’s physical deterioration does not restart the statute of limitations. The statute of limitations began to run on the causes of action based on mesothelioma in 2023, at the time of Paolo’s mesothelioma diagnosis.

The rule described in this Comment is closely related to the rule that damages in a tort case must include future damages as well as past damages. Restatement Third, Torts: Remedies § 5, Comment f (Tentative Draft No. 2, 2023). Given that well-established rule, future damages are recoverable, if at all, as soon as there is sufficient injury to support a tort cause of action, and the statute of limitations therefore starts to run at that time on future, as well as past, damages.
Comment f: Applications of the all-elements rule. Some common applications of the all-elements rule are described below. This list is not intended to be exhaustive, and results in any particular jurisdiction may vary depending, among other things, on particularized statutory language, as well as the elements of the cause of action in the relevant jurisdiction.

(1) Negligence, strict liability, and products liability. Injury is an essential element of causes of action for negligence, strict liability, and products liability. See, e.g., Restatement Third, Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm § 4, Comment b (listing elements of cause of action for negligently caused physical harm); id. §§ 20(a), 21, 22(a), 23 (listing elements of strict liability causes of action); Restatement Third, Torts: Products Liability §§ 1, 9, 10(a), 11 (listing elements of products liability causes of action). In such cases, injury will usually be the last essential element (or one of the last essential elements) to occur. When this is the case, the statute of limitations begins to run at the time of injury. See Comment c.

(2) Intentional torts to persons. Injury is not a necessary element of the tort of assault. See Restatement Third, Torts: Intentional Torts to Persons § 105, Comment c and Illustration 1 (Tentative Draft No. 1, 2015). The statute of limitations therefore starts to run when the defendant acts in a way that causes the plaintiff to apprehend imminent physical contact, regardless of whether the defendant’s action has caused any injury. See Comment c.

A necessary element of the tort of battery is bodily harm or offense. See Restatement Third, Torts: Intentional Torts to Persons §§ 1(c), 3 (Tentative Draft No. 4, 2019). Thus, the statute of limitations generally starts to run when such bodily harm or offense occurs.

For the special rule governing the commencement of the running of the statute of limitations on a false-imprisonment cause of action, see § 4, Comment g below.

(3) Fraud. For the special rule governing the commencement of the running of the statute of limitations on a cause of action for fraud, see § 10, Comment b below.

(4) Malicious prosecution. As noted in Comment c, a necessary element of the tort of malicious prosecution is a favorable termination of the underlying criminal prosecution. Restatement Third, Torts: Liability for Economic Harm §§ 21(d), 23. This element normally occurs long after the underlying criminal prosecution has started to produce injury to the plaintiff. Under the all-elements rule, the statute of limitations does not start to run on a cause of action for malicious prosecution until the favorable termination of the underlying criminal prosecution. In many states, the same rule applies to a cause of action for legal malpractice by criminal defense counsel.

(5) Conversion. The statute of limitations on a cause of action for conversion of personal property begins to run when the defendant’s possession of the property becomes wrongful, which happens immediately in the case of a defendant who initially takes possession wrongfully, and only when the plaintiff’s demand for return of the property is refused if the defendant’s initial possession was not wrongful. See Restatement Second, Torts § 899, Comment c. The operation of the all-elements rule in this instance has the paradoxical result that a defendant whose possession is wrongful from the outset enjoys the benefit of an earlier start date for the statute of limitations. This paradoxical result is often ameliorated by the discovery rule and the doctrines of equitable estoppel and fraudulent concealment. See § 3, Comments b, d, e and Illustration 1.

(6) Medical monitoring. Liability for medical monitoring requires the plaintiff to show that, owing to the defendant’s tortious conduct, the plaintiff needs diagnostic surveillance or testing the plaintiff would not otherwise need (i.e., an economic harm), but it does not require a showing of present physical injury. See Restatement Third, Torts: Miscellaneous Provisions, Medical Monitoring § __, Comment j (Tentative Draft No. 3, 2024) (explaining medical monitoring’s injury requirement). If the plaintiff subsequently suffers legally cognizable physical injury that was speculative and unknowable at the time of the cause of action for medical monitoring, the statute of limitations on a claim for such physical injury begins to run when the physical injury becomes legally cognizable. See Comment d above. See also Restatement Third, Torts: Miscellaneous Provisions, Medical Monitoring § __, Comment n (Tentative Draft No. 3, 2024).

(7) Wrongful death. States are divided on the question of when the statute of limitations begins to run on a cause of action for wrongful death, along lines that largely mirror the states’ differing views concerning the elements of the cause of action. Numerous states hold that, because the wrongful-death cause of action does not come into existence until the death of the victim, it is not barred even if the decedent’s own cause of action for the injuries that resulted in death would be barred. A primary rationale in those states is that the wrongful-death claim does not belong to the deceased but is created and vests in the survivors at the moment of death. Many states, to the contrary, conclude that the wrongful-death cause of action is barred when the statute of limitations on the decedent’s underlying personal-injury cause of action has expired. Viewing their wrongful-death cause of action as derivative, these states reason that the beneficiaries of the wrongful-death cause of action can sue only if the victim would still be in a position to sue if the victim were still alive. See generally Restatement Third, Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm § 70, Comment k (in Restatement Third, Torts: Miscellaneous Provisions (Tentative Draft No. 3, 2024)).

(8) Survival statutes. Survival statutes provide that preexisting tort causes of action may proceed despite the death of the victim or the tortfeasor. See Restatement Third, Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm §§ 71, 72 (in Restatement Third, Torts: Miscellaneous Provisions (Tentative Draft No. 3, 2024)). Because the elements of the preexisting causes of action remain unchanged, the time when the statute of limitations begins to run under the all-elements rule is not changed by the death of the victim or the tortfeasor. See id. § 71, Comment j.

(9) Consortium. Causes of action for spousal, child, and parental consortium have elements in addition to those required for the underlying victims’ causes of action. See Restatement Third, Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm §§ 48 A-48 C (added by Restatement Third, Torts: Concluding Provisions (now known as Restatement Third, Torts: Miscellaneous Provisions) (Tentative Draft No. 1, 2022)). As a result, statutes of limitations may start to run at different times for consortium causes of action than for the underlying victims’ causes of action. See id. § 48 A, Comment m (spousal consortium); § 48 B, Comment n (child consortium); § 48 C, Comment n (parental consortium).

(10) Vicarious liability. A cause of action for vicarious liability is based on the direct tortfeasor’s commission of a tort and the relationship between the direct tortfeasor and the vicariously liable defendant. See Restatement Third, Torts: Miscellaneous Provisions, Vicarious Liability § 1, Comment d (Tentative Draft No. 2, 2023). The statute of limitations on a vicarious-liability cause of action therefore starts to run at the same time that the statute of limitations begins to run on the cause of action against the direct tortfeasor.

(11) Contribution and indemnity. A necessary element of a cause of action for contribution or indemnity is that the party seeking contribution or indemnity has paid to the underlying plaintiff the amount which it now seeks to recover in part (contribution) or in its entirety (indemnity) from the defendant. See Restatement Third, Torts: Apportionment of Liability §§ 22(a), 23(a); id. §§ 35(a), 36(a) (added by Restatement Third, Torts: Concluding Provisions (now known as Restatement Third, Torts: Miscellaneous Provisions) (Tentative Draft No. 1, 2022)). Under the all-elements rule, the statute of limitations therefore does not start to run on a cause of action for contribution or indemnity until payment has been made to the underlying plaintiff. As a result, the statute of limitations may remain open on a cause of action for contribution or indemnity even when the statute of limitations has run on the underlying plaintiff’s causes of action. See Restatement of the Law Third, Restitution and Unjust Enrichment § 23, Comment g.
Comment g: Burden of proof. The burden of proof on the application of the all-elements rule is on the defendant relying on the statute of limitations.
Comment h: Judge and jury. Whether the factual requirements of the all-elements rule have been met is a question for the factfinder.

## § 3 When the Statute of Limitations Begins to Run—Discovery Rule
Topics: Statutes of Limitation and Repose (§ 24)
